column1: Ladies and gentlemen
column2: welcome to our press conference. Today is the first time that I have had the privilege and pleasure of chairing the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB. I am delighted to proceed now with reporting on the outcome of our meeting
column3: together with the Vice-President. The Governing Council meeting was also attended by the Commission Executive Vice-President
column4: Mr Dombrovskis.

column1: Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses
column2: we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged. We expect them to remain at their present or lower levels until we have seen the inflation outlook robustly converge to a level sufficiently close to
column3: but below
column4: 2% within our projection horizon
column5: and such convergence has been consistently reflected in underlying inflation dynamics.

column1: On 1 November we restarted net purchases under our asset purchase programme (APP) at a monthly pace of €20 billion. We expect them to run for as long as necessary to reinforce the accommodative impact of our policy rates
column2: and to end shortly before we start raising the key ECB interest rates.

column1: We also intend to continue reinvesting
column2: in full
column3: the principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the APP for an extended period of time past the date when we start raising the key ECB interest rates
column4: and in any case for as long as necessary to maintain favourable liquidity conditions and an ample degree of monetary accommodation.

column1: The incoming data since the last Governing Council meeting in late October point to continued muted inflation pressures and weak euro area growth dynamics
column2: although there are some initial signs of stabilisation in the growth slowdown and of a mild increase in underlying inflation in line with previous expectations. Ongoing employment growth and increasing wages continue to underpin the resilience of the euro area economy.

column1: The comprehensive package of policy measures that the Governing Council decided in September provides substantial monetary stimulus
column2: which ensures favourable financing conditions for all sectors of the economy. In particular
column3: easier borrowing conditions for firms and households are underpinning consumer spending and business investment. This will support the euro area expansion
column4: the ongoing build-up of domestic price pressures and
column5: thus
column6: the robust convergence of inflation to our medium-term aim.

column1: In the light of the subdued inflation outlook
column2: the Governing Council reiterated the need for monetary policy to remain highly accommodative for a prolonged period of time to support underlying inflation pressures and headline inflation developments over the medium term. We will
column3: therefore
column4: closely monitor inflation developments and the impact of the unfolding monetary policy measures on the economy. Our forward guidance will ensure that financial conditions adjust in accordance with changes to the inflation outlook. In any case
column5: the Governing Council continues to stand ready to adjust all of its instruments
column6: as appropriate
column7: to ensure that inflation moves towards its aim in a sustained manner
column8: in line with its commitment to symmetry.

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. Euro area real GDP growth was confirmed at 0.2%
column3: quarter on quarter
column4: in the third quarter of 2019
column5: unchanged from the previous quarter. The ongoing weakness of international trade in an environment of persistent global uncertainties continues to weigh on the euro area manufacturing sector and is dampening investment growth. At the same time
column6: incoming economic data and survey information
column7: while remaining weak overall
column8: point to some stabilisation in the slowdown of economic growth in the euro area. The services and construction sectors remain resilient
column9: despite some moderation in the latter half of 2019. Looking ahead
column10: the euro area expansion will continue to be supported by favourable financing conditions
column11: further employment gains in conjunction with rising wages
column12: the mildly expansionary euro area fiscal stance and the ongoing – albeit somewhat slower – growth in global activity.

column1: This assessment is broadly reflected in the December 2019 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area. These projections foresee annual real GDP increasing by 1.2% in 2019
column2: 1.1% in 2020 and 1.4% in both 2021 and 2022. Compared with the September 2019 ECB staff macroeconomic projections
column3: the outlook for real GDP growth has been revised down slightly for 2020.

column1: The risks surrounding the euro area growth outlook
column2: related to geopolitical factors
column3: rising protectionism and vulnerabilities in emerging markets
column4: remain tilted to the downside
column5: but have become somewhat less pronounced.

column1: According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column2: euro area annual HICP inflation increased from 0.7% in October 2019 to 1.0% in November
column3: reflecting mainly higher services and food price inflation. On the basis of current futures prices for oil
column4: headline inflation is likely to rise somewhat in the coming months. Indicators of inflation expectations stand at low levels. Measures of underlying inflation have remained generally muted
column5: although there are some indications of a mild increase in line with previous expectations. While labour cost pressures have strengthened amid tighter labour markets
column6: the weaker growth momentum is delaying their pass-through to inflation. Over the medium term
column7: inflation is expected to increase
column8: supported by our monetary policy measures
column9: the ongoing economic expansion and solid wage growth.

column1: This assessment is also broadly reflected in the December 2019 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column2: which foresee annual HICP inflation at 1.2% in 2019
column4: 1.4% in 2021 and 1.6% in 2022. Compared with the September 2019 ECB staff macroeconomic projections
column5: the outlook for HICP inflation has been revised up slightly for 2020 and down slightly for 2021
column6: mainly driven by the expected future path of energy prices.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: broad money (M3) growth stood at 5.6% in October 2019
column3: unchanged from the previous month. Sustained rates of broad money growth reflect ongoing bank credit creation for the private sector and low opportunity costs of holding M3 relative to other financial instruments. The narrow monetary aggregate M1 continues to be the main contributor to broad money growth on the components side.

column1: The growth of loans to firms and households remained solid
column2: benefiting from the continued pass-through of our accommodative monetary policy stance to bank lending rates. The annual growth rate of loans to non-financial corporations increased to 3.8% in October
column3: up from 3.6% in September
column4: while the annual growth rate of loans to households continued on its gradual upward path
column5: reaching 3.5% in October. Our accommodative monetary policy stance will help to safeguard very favourable bank lending conditions and will continue to support access to financing
column6: across all economic sectors and in particular for small and medium-sized enterprises.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with the signals coming from the monetary analysis confirmed that an ample degree of monetary accommodation is still necessary for the continued robust convergence of inflation to levels that are below
column3: but close to
column4: 2% over the medium term.

column1: In order to reap the full benefits from our monetary policy measures
column2: other policy areas must contribute more decisively to raising the longer-term growth potential
column3: supporting aggregate demand at the current juncture and reducing vulnerabilities. The implementation of structural policies in euro area countries needs to be substantially stepped up to boost euro area productivity and growth potential
column4: reduce structural unemployment and increase resilience. The 2019 country-specific recommendations should serve as the relevant signpost.

column1: Regarding fiscal policies
column2: the euro area fiscal stance is expected to remain mildly expansionary in 2020
column3: thus providing support to economic activity. In view of the weakened economic outlook
column4: the Governing Council welcomes the Eurogroup’s call for differentiated fiscal responses and its readiness to coordinate. Governments with fiscal space should be ready to act in an effective and timely manner. In countries where public debt is high
column5: governments need to pursue prudent policies and meet structural balance targets
column6: which will create the conditions for automatic stabilisers to operate freely. All countries should intensify their efforts to achieve a more growth-friendly composition of public finances.

column1: Likewise
column2: the transparent and consistent implementation of the European Union’s fiscal and economic governance framework over time and across countries remains essential to bolster the resilience of the euro area economy. Improving the functioning of Economic and Monetary Union remains a priority. The Governing Council welcomes the ongoing work and urges further specific and decisive steps to complete the banking union and the capital markets union.

column2: we have a policy by which we operate. We have a strategy that was defined and that has inspired the policy decisions that were made and that have been made up until this day. That will continue to inspire the policy decisions that are made until a strategy has been adopted – which is a while from now but I'm sure you'll have questions about the strategy. In that respect
column3: I would just adhere to what that strategy was
column4: what its developments were over the course of time. I think the point of symmetry is very clearly referred to in the introductory statement. One press conference after the other
column5: so I would refer you to that. You very gently nudged me into having a view as to whether there should be a band
column6: as to whether there should be this
column7: that or the other. I'm going to refrain from that. I know that some commentators would love me to disclose my principles
column8: my views and my philosophy. I think it would be largely unfair to the strategy review exercise that we are embarking upon as of today. I do have my views
column9: as have other members.

column1: My mission as President of the Governing Council is to harness all the views around and to make sure that we come to as close as possible a view that is shared by all
column2: in order to have as consistent and as effective a monetary policy in order to deliver on our mandate. As I said last time around
column3: we are going to look at many issues. Multiple views will be proposed. A lot of hard work is going to be put into the exercise
column4: but I would not exclude
column5: preclude or anticipate how we are going to deliver
column6: because that's the point of our strategy review exercise; it's how we deliver.

column1: Now
column2: you asked me about the risk tilted to the downside
column3: and how much tilted to the downside but less so than last time around. I think one of the key considerations we had on our mind was indeed the change in the level of uncertainties about trade and trade relationships
column4: and the expectations we have that those uncertainties will be dealt with
column5: hopefully in the future with the same type of approach… negotiations rather than adversarial positioning. Was there a discussion as to whether it was closer to balance than it was tilted to the downside
column6: but less skewed than it was? Yes
column7: we always have those discussions and that's
column8: I think
column9: completely justified because of the very mixed picture that we have of the economy. If you focus on certain signals
column10: or if you focus on certain indicators or certain surveys
column11: then you could have less downside. If you focus on others
column12: you could be a little bit more downside. So we tried to arrive at exactly what we thought collectively
column13: unanimously actually
column14: was the right level; which was still to the downside but less pronounced than it was at our last press conference. We still have uncertainties
column15: let's face it.

column1: What would be your advice for German savers? They lost billions of euros. Should they buy shares
column2: real estate
column3: or should they spend their money? They suffer from insecure pensions; what should they do?

column1: President Lagarde: You know
column2: I wish I was a financial adviser but in my position
column3: I am not. I know that Germany has plenty of terrific financial advisers
column4: excellent bankers and they will not be short of good advice to their customers. I would simply say that the role of the European Central Bank and the Eurosystem at large – which includes all national central banks – is to deliver on price stability. One of the avenues for delivery of that price stability is to make sure that there is growth of our economies and that that growth is sustainable and solid. The study and the work that has been done internally at the ECB demonstrates that because of the monetary policy
column5: including very low rates and possibly negative rates
column6: because of that monetary policy
column7: millions of jobs were created throughout the euro area. Growth was higher because of that so that's a very
column8: very strong argument to explain why monetary policy had to be what it is.

column1: As you have noted
column2: in my introductory statement – and I don't differ from my predecessor on that front – I think having amplifiers of our monetary policy by having the right fiscal policy
column3: be it by way of additional spending or reduced taxation
column4: for those countries that have the space to do that would certainly help in that regard.

column1: I have a question on the strategy because at the beginning of your tenure you said
column2: “I want to dust off the language of the Bank to help the citizens to understand what the Bank is for.” Now
column3: most citizens
column4: whether they are savers or borrowers
column5: they have just one thing in mind; when will the ECB raise the rates? The one announcement you are doing today is; yes
column6: we will launch a new strategy. Could you maybe explain right now in simple words to these people; why is it so important to review a strategy
column7: because maybe it's not very evident for them to understand this long-distance exercise?

column1: My second question
column2: a question on Davos. When you were Managing Director of IMF
column3: the world was waiting at your verdict on global growth at the opening of Davos. Now you are flying to Davos after this press conference
column4: but a bit at the end of the journey. A similar question: would it be not accurate to skip the January presser so you and the members of the Governing Council will have more time to spend in Davos and then meet the elite and the VIPs of the world? It will be the same each year; the calendar is like it is. Maybe more generally
column5: do we need eight pressers per year
column6: because a lot of analysts think
column7: when you see the previews of the analysts
column8: it is often no change
column9: no change
column10: no change for this year. Could be different in the future
column11: but would it be something maybe the strategy will discuss on the frequency of the monetary policy meetings with the presser?

column1: President Lagarde: Well
column2: first of all
column3: I regard our Governing Council
column4: our deliberations
column5: our scrutiny of the economy and our determination to deliver on price stability as our mission and my mission. Yes
column6: there are very interesting phenomena going on in the world. There are great conferences and great seminars to attend. But when something as important as our Governing Council meeting is scheduled
column7: I don't see any reason why we would change it. We will see whether next year or the year after and so on and so forth
column8: whether we need to reorganise a timetable
column9: but at this point in time
column10: frankly I think it would've been unwarranted
column11: to say the least
column12: to change anything. That's point number one.

column1: Point number two
column2: on the scope of the strategy: we are going to review a whole host of issues so yes
column3: it will have to do about how we deliver
column4: how we measure
column5: what tools we have
column6: and how we communicate. It will really encompass the entire communication approach when it comes to decision-making
column7: to publication
column8: to the use of language that we have
column9: to the outreach
column10: to the engagement with all stakeholders. All of that is going to be part and parcel of the strategy
column11: so it's a broad exercise. I think it touches on your first point: my commitment was really to be able to listen to the expectations of the people
column12: to better understand their economic concerns and their imperatives
column13: and how we can deliver on them. We will continue to benefit from the work of the researchers
column14: of the top-notch economists
column15: of the academics and
column16: yes
column17: their views will be harnessed at various events that will take place in the course of 2020. But it is also going to be our task and our goal to listen.

column1: That resonates with those of you who know how the Fed has organised its “Fed Listens”. We will be different because 19 member states do not all speak the same language. If we want to reach out to people
column2: we are going to have to use people's language
column3: literally. It will involve all the national central banks
column4: which will be also active participants in the process. That's what I mean by including
column5: reaching out and addressing the concerns. Now
column6: I take your point about the interest rates. I think that I have addressed that point earlier on by indicating that we have to use all the instruments that are available and that are proven to be effective – we will measure effectiveness
column7: by the way – in order to deliver.

column1: President Lagarde
column2: you've said before that the review will last until the end of the year. Assuming that that's still the valid assumption
column3: how do you plan to mitigate risk in the interim about creating uncertainty over the ECB's policy
column4: since the policy implications of the review are not yet clear? For instance
column5: is the view that the ECB can't or won't raise or cut interest rates as long as the review is being discussed
column6: justified?

column1: My second question is about tiering
column2: especially since the next reserve maintenance period is in six days. I'd like to know what the ECB has learned from its experiment with tiering so far since September
column3: whether you're satisfied with the impact on bank profitability and lending and money market rates
column4: and whether what you consider the costs and benefits to expanding the pool of exempted deposits or raising the rate on them.

column1: President Lagarde: You know
column2: I have a very simple-minded approach to your first question. It will be over when it is over. In other words
column3: we will have a new strategy when we have concluded the exercise. Our expectation at this point is that it will take a year. Our hope is that we can agree on that new strategy of the European Central Bank around November/December. December
column4: in my view
column5: would be the probable date for the conclusion and the communication of our strategy. When I say it will be over when it is over
column6: what it means is that in the meantime
column7: irrespective of our deliberations
column8: our consideration
column9: or engagement with academics
column10: with economists
column11: with civil society
column12: with European parliament and so on and so forth
column13: irrespective of all that – which will progress in parallel and will keep a lot of people busy both here in Frankfurt and in the 19 national central banks – we will conduct the same usual exercise of monitoring
column14: analysing
column15: drawing conclusion about the macroeconomic situation
column16: about the monetary situation
column17: about the markets
column18: because we look at that as well. Then we will draw our conclusions
column19: which will be independent from the strategy review that we're conducting separately.

column1: You had a second question
column2: yes
column3: the tiering. I don't think I'm disclosing any secret
column4: because at the time
column5: some of you commented about it. There were some Governing Council members that were a little bit sceptical about the effectiveness
column6: the benefit
column7: the justification of the tiering. I think the overall view – I think it was unanimous
column8: actually; I didn't hear anything to the contrary – the unanimous view is that the tiering system is operating extremely well. There is no discussion at this point in time to change the limit of six times
column9: as you know. But since September or since it was decided and as of the effective date
column10: as you know there was instant movement. It has proven to be effective
column11: no question about it.

column1: I have a question on climate change
column2: because you said early on that you want the ECB to play a pivotal role in fighting climate change
column3: also during the strategy review
column4: or including that in the strategy review. What does that mean concretely? What kind of things do you have in mind?

column1: Then one other aspect; you were saying as well that you want to bring the ECB closer to the people. If we bridge that to inflation
column2: there is a big gap between how people think inflation is actually developing and how inflation is measured in terms of
column3: people feel that inflation is a lot higher. Would you also include real estate price development in a new inflation measurement
column4: perhaps?

column1: President Lagarde: On climate change
column2: what I said
column3: I say and I will continue to say is that it is everybody's responsibility
column4: wherever he or she is
column5: to see what he or she can actually do to fight climate change and protect biodiversity. I insist on the two components. Let me tell you what we already do
column6: because it's not as if it's a newborn baby because I arrive; quite a lot had already been undertaken. I would refer you to an excellent speech that Benoît Cœuré had given back about six or eight months ago about these topics. I just want to summarise what we do
column7: because there are always questions and testing of her views versus the rest. Things are actually happening. First of all
column8: we have as you know an ECB staff pension fund and I'm looking at my paper because I don't want to give you anything that is wrong. We replaced the previous benchmarks for the equity funds by their low carbon equivalents. That came on the top of the selective exclusion and proxy voting guidelines that have already been in place for much longer than me. That's an add-on to what we had in place. It does not apply to a very
column9: very sizeable amount; it's roughly €1 billion
column10: but small rivers make very large oceans eventually when they are protected.

column1: The second deals with the ECB's own funds portfolio and that applies to the ECB paid-up capital and the general reserve funds. Altogether that's roughly – that's a little over €20 billion. On that
column2: we're investigating how climate change-related considerations can be better integrated than they are at the moment. As a first step
column3: we have decided to increase the share of green investment held in the portfolio
column4: subject to availability and liquidity of such funds
column5: of course. Now
column6: the third step has to do with our monetary policy portfolio
column7: which is much larger. As you know
column8: there is only a portion of that which is in corporate asset purchases. It's roughly
column9: take it or leave it
column10: €200 billion relative to over €2 trillion for the entire asset purchase programme. I think on that
column11: the strategy is going to have to review what it can – what the Bank can do
column12: should do
column13: how much it collides with the mandate. If so
column14: I think we should very expressly say so
column15: but if it doesn't
column16: I am giving you a for instance; it's not something that has been opined upon
column17: that has been considered at all
column18: but you can look at what ESG
column19: for instance
column20: criteria are respected by the issuers. You can assess the value of collateral in order to determine what is the risk associated with collaterals and so on and so forth.

column1: Those are just a few areas. In addition to that
column2: there is work also that is ongoing in various departments at the ECB to make sure that the climate risk is actually embedded in the work that they do in terms of risk assessment
column3: in terms of models
column4: in terms of their forecast. This is work in progress; it's not something that is completed and that is finished. I will
column5: myself
column6: finish with the area of financial stability because there is also work going on in order to define better stress testing. That framework normally should be completed at the end of 2020 at the latest. This is work that is internal to the ECB
column7: and that is separate from what the SSM is doing as well separately. We also have
column8: together with the European Systemic Risk Board
column9: a pilot framework that is under review as well and which should be completed as well in the fall of 2020. There is a lot going on and as you will see in the press release that you receive later on – in a very short while actually – you will see that environmental sustainability is captured very well in the description of our strategy review. It's right in there; second bullet point.

column1: You asked me another one? Yes
column2: real estate. As I said
column3: we will not leave any stone unturned
column4: and how we measure inflation is clearly something that we need to look at. Are we going to resolve the issues? I doubt it. Clearly
column5: the issue of housing and the distinction between the owner occupancy versus the non-owner occupancy
column6: the reality and the perception
column7: the difference between large urban centres and rural areas; all of that is infinitely difficult to apprehend and to calculate. But we need to look at it and we need to understand. If we believe that there is a clear miscalculation between what is there – which is roughly 6% of budget
column8: if I recall – and what is the perception
column9: we need to understand why. If there is a real difference
column10: which there might well be
column11: then we need to pass that on to Eurostat and have Eurostat do further and additional work. I'm not suggesting that it's going to be resolved in one year. When I was Finance Minister in France
column12: we had our issues with the value of real estate and it took a lot of time.

column1: I had a follow-up question on negative interest rates. It seems that there's growing scepticism within the Governing Council about the side effects of having interest rates below zero for a long period of time. We saw in the minutes from the last – from the December meeting
column2: there was some discussion about this. Was that discussed again today? Are they concerns that you share
column3: that negative rates have been in place for five years already and could be in place for years into the future? Are you concerned about the side – the impact of that on the economy?

column1: The second question was how you view negative rates compared with QE as a stimulus tool. If the Eurozone economy were to slow during the course of the year
column2: which tool do you think you might be – the ECB might be first – might turn to first to stimulate it?

column1: President Lagarde: Am I concerned? I'm concerned about low rate
column2: because low rate is predicated on low growth
column3: and I would much rather have much higher growth
column4: higher rates. This would be a really nice problem to have to deal with
column5: but this is not the situation we have at the moment. You will see that as part of our strategy review
column6: we are going to look at the potential side effects of the current circumstances
column7: which are low rate – let alone negative – but we have had low rates for a period of time. That hampers our ability to respond in case of exogenous shock
column8: as you know.

column1: Slow growth: I think we'll cross that bridge when we have to cross that bridge
column2: but as you also know
column3: different tools apply to different portions of the yield curve. Let's hope we don't have to do that
column4: because growth doesn't slow and growth continues to not only stabilise but accelerate in the going future. That would be a nice problem to have to deal with
column5: but if it did not
column6: then we really have to ask ourselves at which end of the yield curve we want to operate. That will determine which kind of instrument we want to use.

column1: I have another climate change question. There was the Bank for International Settlements published a report beginning of the week. I wondered if you had had a chance to look at it and if you had any reaction to it. The main takeaway I think was that climate change is a threat to financial stability. I wonder if you agree with that premise. I gather from your earlier answer you do
column2: but I would like perhaps your clear statement on that.

column1: Then secondly
column2: related question is: will the ECB wait for the strategic review before it incorporates any sustainability or climate change criteria into its monetary policy? In other words
column3: would it wait to adjust the corporate bond purchase programme until the strategy review has reached some kind of conclusion?

column1: President Lagarde: It's difficult to disagree with that finding of the BIS
column2: that climate change is actually a threat to financial stability. What's more
column3: it's that it's a threat and a risk that is hardly measured and taken into account by many actors. I believe that the action taken by the – suggested by the BIS
column4: the action recommended by other central banks; I can think of Mark Carney from the Bank of England
column5: for instance
column6: are completely justified. I was personally very pleased to see that the private sector is actually also taking action in that respect
column7: and certainly would welcome the involvement of other operators including their accounting firms and those that are setting the international accounting standards as well as the large asset managers
column8: as we've seen. I think we badly lack harmonised measurement systems that can be generally accepted and that are actually implemented.

column1: It is more of a personal view
column2: if I may say
column3: because it has not been debated in the Governing Council. I am not suggesting that I would sort of give you the ECB doxa on this matter. I would be surprised if they were very much against that position. What I tried to do when describing for you what we were already doing was to show that
column4: while we might not be ahead of the curve yet
column5: we are not sitting on our bottom doing nothing. We are taking climate change into account in order to improve the way in which we operate at the moment. Wherever we have the option to include climate change as one of our tools
column6: we are doing so. It is going to be an important matter that will be debated during the strategy review. What impact does it have? What consequences should we draw? Where does it impact the way in which we operate? All those questions will have to be debated.

column1: The last strategy review addressed an era where inflation was hard to tame
column2: not hard to stimulate. Since then
column3: technology
column4: globalisation
column5: even European integration have added an efficiency
column6: but have undermined the inflationary pressures. How can this strategic review address this fundamental shift? What yardsticks do you think personally should be assessed first for their relevance in today's era?

column1: The follow-up question: we can safely assume by now that ultra-low yields have not been enough of an incentive for governments
column2: for fiscal spending for growth. Is there something more efficient
column3: different that the ECB could do or influence in order to catalyse fiscal expansion? Or would it be considered too political? How central do you expect this issue to be in this strategic review?

column1: President Lagarde: You're completely right in that the situation has completely changed from 2003. We published a study just before December that takes stock of the last 20 years of euro use and implementation and monetary policy delivery. For ten years
column2: the goal was to fight inflation
column3: because inflation was way too high. Then the financial crisis was the pivotal point at which eventually inflation was too low. It's been a reversal of the situation and requires in my view that we actually look at the strategy very carefully to see how effective we can be in view of the change of circumstances
column4: some of which are structural factors that are here with us to stay. When you look at the ageing population
column5: when you look at the low productivity
column6: these are probably going to be with us for a long time. That justifies fully the need for a strategy review. We cannot operate as we did back in 2003 – which doesn't mean to say that we have to necessarily change this
column7: that or the other. But we have to look comprehensively at the effectiveness of our monetary policy. One thing that I know is central and anchored in our considerations will be the mandate that we are given under the Treaty
column8: which is that of price stability. That's the primary one.

column1: On fiscal expansion
column2: I would first of all observe that at the euro area level
column3: there is a very mild fiscal expansion as we speak. I would also observe that two of the countries that have fiscal space
column4: and I can think… You know who I am talking about. Two of those countries are now seriously looking...One has certainly gone pretty way out in order to explore how to expand more fiscally with their respective domestic budget. There's progress. We just need to all keep at it
column5: not because I want to influence fiscal policy. It's for the budget holders to decide. It's for the authorities that have competence in that respect to decide
column6: but simply because a good fiscal support would give much more effect to our monetary policy. That's why I think it's important that they do.

column1: I have one question on climate change: you have raised quite high expectations on the future role of the ECB on the fight against climate change. Do you not fear that it will be difficult to deliver on that?

My second question is on policy-making: brought consensus in the Governing Council has some obvious advantages. But it might also have some disadvantages like group think or the ECB might be vulnerable for mistakes. For example
column2: the Bank of England tried to have people in their monetary policy committee who challenged the existing views within the group. How important is it for you to reach unanimity or broad consensus in important monetary policy decisions?

column1: President Lagarde: You know
column2: on climate change: I know that we will have a debate and I know that there will be discussions and it's already out there
column3: that debate. Is there going to be mandate creep? Isn't that going to be a distraction? Why should it be the role of central banks? If they do so
column4: then yet again the legitimate authorities to implement climate change policies will feel that job is done
column5: they don't have to worry. I'm aware of all that
column6: but I'm also aware of the danger of doing nothing and I think that failing to try is already failing. We should at least try to explore every area where we can actually participate in a determination that is now the determination of the European Commission
column7: of many of the euro area leaders
column8: and which is now also creeping into the private sector. That's my personal take on that and I was very pleased to see that the environmental sustainability has found its right space in the monetary policy review that we are embarking upon.

column1: I draw a line between consensus building and repressing alternative views
column2: and I can assure you that we are not short of alternative views
column3: right? There are multiple views around the table on multiple aspects of monetary policies. I am not a despotic President of the Governing Council; all views are welcome. All governors have their space and time in order to share their perspective and submit their views. At the end of the day
column4: and at the end of the process
column5: we still have to complete the introductory statement and release the monetary policy decision if and when it is expected and required. I don't think it is repressing views. I don't think that it is sparing alternative views. I think it's intended to arrive at the best possible common understanding and a final decision. If we have a unanimous decision it's satisfactory. It means that we are converging altogether towards a decision. It may well be that we do not have unanimous decisions and that at some stage it will have to be a majority decision
column6: but we need a decision.

column1: Next week the United Kingdom will be formally out of the European Union and it starts a complex time to exit. Do you think the European financial system is ready for that? Are you worried in some way for that?
President Lagarde: You know
column2: it's one of the questions that I have asked the teams; what happens when Brexit happens? Are we all ready? Have we taken all the steps that we had to take? Have we alerted sufficiently the private sector operators to themselves take the right measures? My assessment today is that
column3: yes
column4: we have. Just to remind you
column5: back in March of 2019
column6: we activated swap lines with the Bank of England to make sure that on both sides of the Channel
column7: there would be enough euros and sterling so that operations could continue in a smooth manner despite the implementation of Brexit. We have alerted and reminded the banks of all the necessary measures that they have to take in order to be in a good position to continue to operate irrespective of Brexit. We have good reason to believe that this is so. Don't forget that there was this high-level working group between the Bank of England and the ECB at the level of both President and Governor in order to make sure that they had checked all the boxes and covered the potential risks. You never know. There can always be a risk somewhere
column8: but I think that in good conscience
column9: we have looked at everything that we thought was necessary.

column1: One more question for the climate change in Davos. At the World Economic Forum
column2: President of the Commission
column3: Ursula von der Leyen
column4: said how important the fight for Europe against climate change is. The Bank for Settlements has said it has the same view but we are against a green QE programme. What is your view on this issue?

column1: President Lagarde: I very strongly support the President of the Commission in that respect
column2: and in many respects
column3: for that matter. We are taking steps and we have taken steps already in order to play the role that we should play
column4: concerning the fight against climate change. We will look as part of the strategy review at what options we have to be even more intrusive
column5: more active in relation to the corporate purchase plan that we have in place
column6: and which continues to operate
column7: as you know
column8: because we are purchasers on a monthly basis of €20 billion. We reinvest as instruments come to maturity. We will look at that and see how we can play a role in accordance with our mandate
column9: indeed. On that word
column10: I think in accordance with our mandate indeed we have to stop the exercise
column11: it's perfect timing."|https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/press_conference/monetary-policy-statement/2020/html/ecb.is200123~0bc778277b.en.html

column1: 2020.02.20 13:30:00|Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday
column2: 22-23 January 2020|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel reviewed the latest financial market developments.
The period since the Governing Council’s monetary policy meeting on 11-12 December 2019 had been marked by three major events: the year-end
column2: the geopolitical tensions in the Middle East
column3: and the signing of the “phase-one” trade agreement between the United States and China. The trade agreement appeared to be the most significant
column4: as it had helped consolidate the general improvement in market sentiment that had gained momentum in early September 2019. Expectations that monetary policy would remain highly accommodative
column5: both in the United States and in the euro area
column6: further supported the improved market sentiment.

column1: The year-end
column2: as usual
column3: had been characterised by thin liquidity in money markets due to reporting and regulatory obligations. The turn of this year
column4: however
column5: had been the smoothest since 2016. Repo rates had remained mostly concentrated around levels prevailing before the turn of the year. Use of the Eurosystem’s securities lending facilities had also increased only slightly over the year-end. In the US money market
column6: the Federal Reserve’s injections of additional liquidity had mitigated any potential year-end tensions.

column1: The new year had started with geopolitical tensions escalating in the Middle East. However
column2: financial markets had proved rather resilient
column3: which could be explained by a number of factors. One had been the attempt by the authorities to quickly de-escalate the situation through their rhetoric. A second factor had been the prevailing high level of oil inventories in OECD countries. Combined with a global economy much less reliant on oil than in the past
column4: this cushioned the expected impact of supply-side disruptions on the oil price. A third factor might have been the general underlying improvement in market sentiment.

column1: This improved sentiment had been visible in global bond markets since early September 2019
column2: following indications that a phase-one trade deal between the United States and China was within reach. Since September 2019
column3: yields on 10-year German benchmark government bonds had increased by around 50 basis points. In addition
column4: the spread vis-à-vis the 10-year US Treasury benchmark had narrowed by some 30 basis points.

column1: Some insight into the reversal in the US-euro area interest rate differential could be derived from the breakdown of bond yields into the short-term rate expectations component and the term premia component. In both the United States and the euro area
column2: yields were currently well below their end-2018 levels
column3: but for different reasons. In the euro area
column4: the expected interest rate path during 2019 had been adjusted downwards much less than in the United States
column5: and had also partly reversed as sentiment had brightened in recent months. However
column6: the decline in term premia had proven much more persistent in the euro area. This might partly be linked to the resumption of net asset purchases by the ECB

column1: Since our last Governing Council meeting in late January

column1: In line with our mandate

column1: It was observed that the pandemic
column2: which had initially been viewed as primarily a global supply-side shock
column3: was being propagated to demand and was intensifying in Europe
column4: reducing activity across most sectors of the economy. Demand would be negatively affected as a result of job losses and any reduction in household income growth

column6: in the short term

column1: There was uncertainty about the need to revise the outlook for inflation in the medium term
column2: which was the policy-relevant horizon for the ECB’s price stability objective. On the one hand
column3: the temporary nature of the downturn suggested that there might be limited need for revisions to the medium-term outlook for inflation

The point was made that the ultimate medium-term implications were not independent of short-term events and that the magnitude and duration of the shock’s impact would in turn depend on the course of the pandemic and the policy reaction to it.

column1: On the monetary analysis
column2: members broadly concurred with the assessment provided by Mr Lane in his introduction that monetary dynamics had moderated

column1: Monetary policy stance and policy considerations

column2: members widely shared the assessment provided by Mr Lane in his introduction. Financial conditions and bank funding conditions in the euro area had tightened since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. Equity market valuations had dropped significantly in recent weeks
column3: as also shown in the presentation by Ms Schnabel

column5: the euro’s recent appreciation added to the tightening of financial conditions

column1: Members agreed that a decisive monetary policy response was required in the present circumstances

column1: As outlined by Mr Lane in his introduction
column2: members agreed that a first element of the policy response was to safeguard ample liquidity in the banking system by ensuring banks’ continued access to funding at attractive conditions as a necessary element to guard against a potential credit crunch. However
column3: it was also argued that this was not sufficient to ensure that the liquidity made available to banks would be passed on to the end-users. It was pointed out that
column4: whereas during the financial crisis of 2008 banks were at the heart of the problem

column1: Members also agreed that the second element of the proposed policy response

column3: was of paramount importance. Under the current conditions
column4: however

column1: Agreement also prevailed with regard to the third element of the required monetary policy response

column3: it was cautioned that instruments affecting the monetary policy stance would only become fully effective once the spread of the coronavirus had been contained by other policies. At the same time
column4: it was recalled that the ECB’s monetary policy had been highly accommodative since the financial crisis. It was emphasised that
column5: in order to maintain accommodative monetary conditions
column6: the Governing Council needed to consider using all the tools at its disposal in a flexible way.

column1: Against this background
column2: all members agreed with the package of monetary policy measures proposed by Mr Lane in his introduction
column3: namely: first
column4: offering additional LTROs to provide immediate liquidity support to the euro area banking system at an interest rate equal to the deposit facility rate; second
column5: applying more favourable terms to all TLTRO III operations during the period from June 2020 to June 2021; and
column6: third

column11: in particular in combination with the full allotment of the operations

column13: which required a longer lead time because of its operational complexity.

column1: Members widely shared the view that the proposed changes to the TLTRO III operations would support bank lending to the firms affected most by the spread of the coronavirus
column2: in particular SMEs. For the period from 24 June 2020 to 23 June 2021
column3: the interest rate on all TLTRO III operations outstanding during that time would be 25 basis points below the average rate applied in the Eurosystem’s MROs over the same period. For counterparties whose eligible net lending met the benchmark

column2: supporting credit flows to affected sectors and avoiding a tightening in credit supply. These amendments effectively lowered interest rates in a ring-fenced way for eligible counterparties and provided a strong incentive to banks not to cut lending. Linking the favourable terms to banks’ credit portfolios would incentivise banks not to cut credit at a time when the economy was in need. It was cautioned
column3: however
column4: that the reduction in the lending performance threshold to 0% might turn out to be insufficiently supportive if banks were forced to reduce their credit exposure because of supervisory concerns or market pressures
column5: possibly resulting in a contraction of credit. Members widely agreed that it was important to further investigate options for better incentivising banks to expand their lending to SMEs.

column1: In order to allow banks to make full use of the ECB’s lending facilities
column2: members widely welcomed Mr Lane’s proposal to task the Eurosystem committees with studying ways to further broaden the collateral framework. column1: Members generally agreed that the additional envelope for net asset purchases as part of the proposed policy package was essential to influence the level of the risk-free yield curve. In combination with the existing APP

column4: would support favourable financing conditions for the real economy in times of heightened uncertainty. Limiting the additional envelope to the current calendar year was deemed an appropriate response to a shock that was assessed as being temporary at this stage. The private sector purchases would provide a strong signal of support for favourable funding conditions in the corporate sector. A flexible expansion of APP net purchases was also seen as partially compensating for not cutting the deposit facility rate
column5: with the public sector purchases helping to preserve a risk-free rate that served as a benchmark for pricing many other financial products. A remark was made that although the envelope of €120 billion seemed large
column6: in the face of the disruptions that had been witnessed a larger volume would be justified. It was also remarked that an increase in the envelope of the APP could be seen as an appropriate way to support a coordinated policy response
column7: as the Governing Council was urging policymakers to take decisive fiscal measures.

column1: Overall
column2: it was felt that adding more volume to the APP was preferable to another reduction in the deposit facility rate. Additional net purchases would support policy transmission to the long end of the risk-free yield curve and provide some form of backstop for public and private bond markets. However
column3: some reservations were also expressed regarding the case for expanding the public sector purchase programme as a means of preserving or lowering the risk-free yield curve at a time when higher-rated government bond yields had fallen to record low levels in an environment of heightened risk aversion. It was also pointed out that
column4: in normal circumstances
column5: the relationship between the ECB’s capital key and the risk-free yield curve was stable
column6: whereas under the current conditions this relationship was distorted by a shift into safe assets
column7: calling for temporary and tactical flexibility in the APP purchases to address liquidity issues arising from this flight to safety. column6: however
column7: that it was difficult to distinguish whether observed spreads were driven by an increase in credit risk or a lack of liquidity.

column1: The view was widely shared that the present
column2: very challenging circumstances called for a maximum degree of cohesion
column3: consensus and unity in the Governing Council
column4: notwithstanding different preferences with regard to the various monetary policy instruments under consideration.

column1: In view of the expected temporary nature of the shock and the proposed measures
column2: members agreed that it did not seem appropriate to lower the deposit facility rate on this occasion. While a few members expressed their willingness to consider a cut in the deposit facility rate at the current meeting

column1: Monetary policy decisions and communication
On communication

column4: the Governing Council would continue to monitor closely the consequences of the spread of the coronavirus for the economy

column1: The President started the meeting by observing that
column2: while the policy measures taken by the Governing Council at its monetary policy meeting on 11-12 March 2020 had been well calibrated at the time
column3: the scale of the challenges faced had been highly uncertain. Meanwhile
column4: the situation had deteriorated significantly
column5: with nearly all euro area countries in full containment mode owing to the rapid spread of the coronavirus (COVID-19). The situation was unprecedented and the repercussions were also impossible to forecast accurately. Uncertainty on the economic front was creating severe strains in the financial markets

Ms Schnabel reviewed the latest financial market developments.
Since the Governing Council’s regular monetary policy meeting on 11-12 March 2020

Implied volatility had continuously trended upwards and
column7: over the two days prior to the current meeting

Mr Lane observed that the coronavirus pandemic represented a collective public health emergency with few precedents in recent history. It was also an extreme economic shock that required an ambitious

In their subsequent exchange of views

column3: financial markets had been exhibiting extreme volatility

column5: financial conditions had continued to tighten as risk-free interest rates further increased across all maturities and sovereign and corporate spreads widened significantly

column3: hence

column1: Incoming information confirms that the euro area economy is experiencing an unprecedented contraction. There has been an abrupt drop in economic activity as a result of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic and the measures to contain it. Severe job and income losses and exceptionally elevated uncertainty about the economic outlook have led to a significant fall in consumer spending and investment. While survey data and real-time indicators for economic activity have shown some signs of a bottoming-out alongside the gradual easing of the containment measures
column2: the improvement has so far been tepid compared with the speed at which the indicators plummeted in the preceding two months. The June Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections see growth declining at an unprecedented pace in the second quarter of this year
column3: before rebounding again in the second half
column4: crucially helped by the sizeable support from fiscal and monetary policy. Nonetheless
column5: the projections entail a substantial downward revision to both the level of economic activity and the inflation outlook over the whole projection horizon
column6: though the baseline is surrounded by an exceptional degree of uncertainty. While headline inflation is suppressed by lower energy prices
column7: price pressures are expected to remain subdued on account of the sharp decline in real GDP and the associated significant increase in economic slack.

column1: In line with its mandate
column2: the Governing Council is determined to ensure the necessary degree of monetary accommodation and a smooth transmission of monetary policy across sectors and countries. Accordingly
column3: we decided on a set of monetary policy measures to support the economy during its gradual reopening and to safeguard medium-term price stability.

column1: First
column2: the Governing Council decided to increase the envelope for the pandemic emergency purchase programme (PEPP) by €600 billion to a total of €1
column3: 350 billion. In response to the pandemic-related downward revision to inflation over the projection horizon
column4: the PEPP expansion will further ease the general monetary policy stance
column5: supporting funding conditions in the real economy
column6: especially for businesses and households. The purchases will continue to be conducted in a flexible manner over time
column7: across asset classes and among jurisdictions. This allows us to effectively stave off risks to the smooth transmission of monetary policy.

column2: we decided to extend the horizon for net purchases under the PEPP to at least the end of June 2021. In any case
column3: we will conduct net asset purchases under the PEPP until the Governing Council judges that the coronavirus crisis phase is over.

column1: Third
column2: the Governing Council decided to reinvest the maturing principal payments from securities purchased under the PEPP until at least the end of 2022. In any case
column3: the future roll-off of the PEPP portfolio will be managed to avoid interference with the appropriate monetary policy stance.

column4: and to end shortly before we start raising the key ECB interest rates.

column3: but below

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail
column2: starting with the economic analysis. The latest economic indicators and survey results confirm a sharp contraction of the euro area economy and rapidly deteriorating labour market conditions. The coronavirus pandemic and the necessary containment measures have severely affected both the manufacturing and services sectors
column3: taking a toll on the productive capacity of the euro area economy and on domestic demand. In the first quarter of 2020
column4: when containment measures were only in place from mid-March in most countries
column5: euro area real GDP decreased by 3.8%
column6: quarter on quarter. Information from surveys
column7: high-frequency indicators and incoming hard data all point to a further significant contraction of real GDP in the second quarter. Most recent indicators suggest some bottoming-out of the downturn in May as parts of the economy gradually reopen. Accordingly
column8: euro area activity is expected to rebound in the third quarter as the containment measures are eased further
column9: supported by favourable financing conditions
column10: an expansionary fiscal stance and a resumption in global activity
column11: although the overall speed and scale of the rebound remains highly uncertain.

column1: This assessment is also broadly reflected in the June 2020 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area. In the baseline scenario of the projections
column2: annual real GDP is expected to fall by 8.7% in 2020 and to rebound by 5.2% in 2021 and by 3.3% in 2022. Compared with the March 2020 ECB staff macroeconomic projections
column3: the outlook for real GDP growth has been revised substantially downwards by 9.5 percentage points in 2020 and revised upwards by 3.9 percentage points in 2021 and 1.9 percentage points in 2022.

column1: Given the exceptional uncertainty currently surrounding the outlook
column2: the projections also include two alternative scenarios
column3: which we will publish on our website following this press conference. In general
column4: the extent of the contraction and the recovery will depend crucially on the duration and the effectiveness of the containment measures
column5: the success of policies to mitigate the adverse impact on incomes and employment
column6: and the extent to which supply capacity and domestic demand are permanently affected. Overall
column7: the Governing Council sees the balance of risks around the baseline projection to the downside.

column1: According to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column2: euro area annual HICP inflation decreased to 0.1% in May
column3: down from 0.3% in April
column4: mainly on account of lower energy price inflation. On the basis of current and futures prices for oil
column5: headline inflation is likely to decline somewhat further over the coming months and to remain subdued until the end of the year. Over the medium term
column6: weaker demand will put downward pressure on inflation
column7: which will be only partially offset by upward pressures related to supply constraints. Market-based indicators of longer-term inflation expectations have remained at depressed levels. While survey-based indicators of inflation expectations have declined over the short and medium term
column8: longer-term expectations have been less affected.

column1: This assessment is also reflected in the June 2020 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column2: which foresee annual HICP inflation in the baseline scenario at 0.3% in 2020
column3: 0.8% in 2021 and 1.3% in 2022. Compared with the March 2020 ECB staff macroeconomic projections
column4: the outlook for HICP inflation has been revised downwards by 0.8 percentage points in 2020
column5: 0.6 percentage points in 2021 and 0.3 percentage points in 2022.

column1: Turning to the monetary analysis
column2: broad money (M3) growth increased to 8.3% in April 2020
column3: from 7.5% in March. Strong money growth reflects bank credit creation
column4: which is driven to a large extent by the acute liquidity needs in the economy. Moreover
column5: high economic uncertainty is triggering a shift towards money holdings for precautionary reasons. In this environment
column6: the narrow monetary aggregate M1
column7: encompassing the most liquid forms of money
column8: continues to be the main contributor to broad money growth.

column1: Developments in loans to the private sector continued to be shaped by the impact of the coronavirus on economic activity. The annual growth rate of loans to non-financial corporations rose further to 6.6% in April 2020
column2: up from 5.5% in March
column3: reflecting firms’ need to finance their ongoing expenditures and working capital in the context of rapidly declining revenues. At the same time
column4: the annual growth rate of loans to households decreased to 3.0% in April
column5: from 3.4% in March
column6: amid consumption constraints due to the containment measures
column7: declining confidence and a deteriorating labour market.

column1: Our policy measures
column2: in particular the very favourable terms for our targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTRO III)
column3: should encourage banks to extend loans to all private sector entities. Together with the measures adopted by national governments and European institutions
column4: they support ongoing access to financing
column5: including for those most affected by the ramifications of the coronavirus pandemic.

column1: To sum up
column2: a cross-check of the outcome of the economic analysis with the signals coming from the monetary analysis confirmed that an ample degree of monetary accommodation is necessary for the robust convergence of inflation to levels that are below
column3: but close to
column4: 2% over the medium term.

column1: Regarding fiscal policies
column2: an ambitious and coordinated fiscal stance remains critical
column3: in view of the sharp contraction in the euro area economy. Measures taken should as much as possible be targeted and temporary in nature in response to the pandemic emergency. The three safety nets endorsed by the European Council for workers
column4: businesses and sovereigns
column5: amounting to a package worth €540 billion
column6: provide important funding support in this context. At the same time
column7: the Governing Council urges further strong and timely efforts to prepare and support the recovery. We therefore strongly welcome the European Commission’s proposal for a recovery plan dedicated to supporting the regions and sectors most severely hit by the pandemic
column8: to strengthening the Single Market and to building a lasting and prosperous recovery.

column2: the unconditional refinancing operations together with the establishment of international swap lines were ensuring that liquidity in the banking system was protected. These measures had acted as a stabilising force during this exceptional period.

column2: financial conditions had tightened sharply since the escalation of the pandemic
column3: as the downward shift in risk-free rates had not been fully transmitted to the broader set of asset prices and yields that set the financial conditions for the real economy. In particular
column4: the upward pressure on average sovereign yields had contributed to higher corporate and bank bond yields and a decline in equity valuations
column5: especially for bank stocks.

column2: Mr Lane emphasised that two main factors called for further policy action at the current meeting. First
column3: the medium-term outlook for price stability was threatened by the fallout from the coronavirus crisis: in particular
column4: the baseline in the new projections saw 0.3 and 0.6 percentage point downward revisions in the 2022 headline and core inflation rates respectively

column2: the appropriate policy response was to increase the size of the PEPP envelope. In March
column3: the Governing Council had decided to launch the PEPP “to counter the serious risks to the transmission mechanism and the outlook for the euro area posed by the outbreak and escalating diffusion of the coronavirus”.
