column5: with a focus on boosting investment in priority areas such as the green and digital transitions.

column1: We are now ready to take your questions.
President Lagarde
column2: your words indicate to me that the exchange rate was a topic of discussion in the Governing Council today
column3: so could you give me a bit of detail about that discussion? How concerned are you about the current level of the euro? Do you think this strength is justified and how much does this affect the policy?

column1: A second question is about whether you discussed any change to any of your policies
column2: whether it's the PEPP or APP
column3: TLTRO
column4: tiering
column5: was there any change being discussed today?

column1: Lagarde: Yes
column2: indeed the Governing Council discussed the appreciation of the euro but as you know
column3: we do not target the exchange rate. Our mandate is price stability and clearly to the extent that the appreciation of the euro exercises a negative pressure on prices
column4: we have to monitor carefully such a matter. This was indeed extensively discussed during our Governing Council.

column1: On your second question concerning changes to our programmes
column2: we as always look at how effective and efficient our policies are and our purchase programmes have been. So when we look at the impact that a programme like the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme has been
column3: we can only acknowledge the fact that it has been efficient and it has been effective. Whether you look at the sovereign yields across the euro area
column4: whether you look at all indicators of fragmentation
column5: you can – and we can – and we certainly did take stock of the fact that it has worked in relation to both stabilisation of financing conditions and in respect of the risk of fragmentation. In addition to that
column6: clearly in terms of monetary stance we also acknowledge the fact that PEPP has also served its purpose
column7: although initially it was not intended for that particular aspect of our monetary policy
column8: but it did. So we decided to maintain our accommodative monetary policy
column9: and certainly under current circumstances it is very likely that the full envelope of PEPP will be used for the purpose of developing those policies.

column1: I have two questions. The first is on PEPP. The ECB does not fix the size of its net purchases programmes in relation to the size of government bond issuance. However what you called the ambitious fiscal measures in response to coronavirus pandemic by the euro area member states will result this year and next year in a massive increase in debt-to-GDP levels
column2: adding pressure on debt sustainability in some countries. Are you and the Governing Council worried that public debt increases might jeopardise financial stability and provoke unwanted tightening
column3: higher yields and spreads? So in that sense
column4: the market suspects the PEPP to be increased and what do you think about market expectations on that front?

column1: My second question is on banks. The take-up of the last TLTRO III tender was
column2: as you said
column3: very high but it also showed a fragmented banking system and some weaknesses. COVID-19 can create fragmentation and weaknesses in banking. So market expects more to be done for banks
column4: for example softening of the TLTRO III conditions. Is the Governing Council looking at that on European banks in the pandemic
column5: and the possible revision of existing rules or tools?

column1: Lagarde: Thank you very much for your many questions. Let me take the opportunity of your first question to first of all acknowledge and celebrate the fiscal measures that were taken. We had repeatedly over the course of time asked for fiscal measures to be taken
column2: and for fiscal policies to work hand in hand with monetary policy. This is clearly something that we have seen since mid-March both at the national and at the European level. If you combine all the fiscal measures that were taken at national levels
column3: you arrive at roughly a number of 4.5% of GDP consisting of measures that really have an impact on the outlook. That is not to mention the measures that were taken under the headline of guarantees
column4: which roughly account for about 20% of GDP. That's only at the national level. As I said in the introductory statement
column5: the Governing Council strongly welcomed not only the three safety net measures that were decided earlier in the summer to help both employees
column6: companies and sovereigns in total amount of €540 billion
column7: but it did really welcome strongly the breakthrough of the Next Generation EU fund of €750 billion which clearly will have an impact most of which
column8: by the way
column9: is not included in our projection as they are being published today. So these fiscal measures were necessary and I'm only pleased that they could be taken in due course and sometimes with the necessary waivers and exemptions that were required at the European level.

column1: Let me just add a few words about the programme that we put in place; the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme. Let me remind you that it had two functions and it was initially calibrated for €750 billion that was back on the 18th March. The dual function was the following: the first function was to stabilise market
column2: to ensure a smooth transmission of our policy measures. The second function was to ease our monetary policy stance
column3: to help counter the substantial downgrade of our inflation outlook caused by the pandemic. The PEPP announcement already in March
column4: and its recalibration later on in June have successfully stalled the tightening in financial conditions and contributed to easing the overall monetary policy stance. Clearly
column5: with markets stabilising and risks of fragmentation subsidising
column6: I'll remind you that we are pretty much back to the pre-COVID levels in terms of both spreads and dispersion of yields. The flexibility property of PEPP
column7: which is distinct from the attributes of the APP for instance
column8: has become less prominent. The role of the PEPP in easing our monetary policy stance has taken a central stage instead.

column1: In a nutshell
column2: fiscal measures were needed. They were taken rightly
column3: timely and efficiently. The PEPP as an emergency programme was clearly responding to the needs of the time. I would add that the TLTRO that you have referred to has also served the purpose that we intended
column4: which was to make sure that the economy was receiving abundant liquidity in order not to accumulate liquidity
column5: not to build buffers
column6: but in order to make sure that lending to the economy was taking place. TLTRO III was calibrated with that in mind
column7: so if banks can actually access a borrowing interest rate which can go down to -1%
column8: it is only under the condition that the lending to the economy
column9: corporate and households
column10: is actually tantamount to what it was or more than what it was
column11: prior to COVID-19. TLTRO III is very different from TLTRO I and TLTRO II in terms of take-up. We've observed at the time of this massive take-up for the first operation
column12: roughly €1.3 trillion
column13: that it was very well spread throughout the euro area. So it wasn't country specific
column14: it wasn't a category of banks in a country; it was across the board. The other thing that we have observed
column15: which tells us that it is effectively working
column16: is
column17: first
column18: the low interest rates which continue to apply both for corporates and for households and
column19: second
column20: the increased credit that is lent to the economy: 7% for the corporates
column21: 3% for the households.

column1: The banks themselves in the July bank lending survey that we have published actually say that TLTROs have helped them to lend to the economy. It shows in the numbers. Those banks that have taken up TLTROs have actually a larger proportion of loans to the economy than those that did not take up TLTROs. So in this stock-taking exercise
column2: both in relation to PEPP
column3: in relation to continued Asset Purchase Programmes otherwise and in relation to TLTROs
column4: we believe that our monetary policy tools as calibrated have worked well.

column1: My first question is about some recent comments by Philip Lane in which he talked about a two-stage policy approach to the PEPP. So he said its role is to counteract the negative shock to the expected inflation path caused by the pandemic. How widely is this view that ending PEPP will depend mostly on the outlook for inflation rather than just the immediate crisis effect shared among the Governing Council?
My second question is about the Fed's recent strategy shift
column2: where a lot of attention has been paid to the change in its inflation goal
column3: which is in itself something you might have some thoughts about. But it also introduced an important shift in how it assesses the health of the US labour market
column4: paying more attention to how marginalised groups fare in the economy. So I'd like to know what efforts the ECB is making to better understand the unique inequalities facing minority communities in the euro area as labour markets.

column1: Lagarde: I think I have just actually addressed the point that you are raising
column2: which is the dual function of the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme. It was a programme in and of its own and it had in its DNA
column3: as I think I have mentioned at one of our last press conferences
column4: flexibility which was clearly intended to address the issue of dispersion
column5: the risk of fragmentation and intended to make sure that our monetary policy was transmitted across all member states of the euro area. Clearly
column6: that function has worked
column7: is working and is critically important in order for our monetary policy to actually transmit throughout the whole region. It has a dual function in that the other function has to do with the monetary stance
column8: and clearly it will continue to address and deliver on that dual function. We very much hope that it continues to work on both accounts
column9: both the stabilisation of financing conditions
column10: the risk of fragmentation
column11: but also the monetary stance in order to make sure that inflation is going towards the medium-term objective that we are pursuing.

column1: As you know
column2: we increased the size of PEPP back in June and that was clearly intended to respond to the circumstances and to make sure that all the consequences resulting from the pandemic could be addressed through that Pandemic Emergency Programme
column3: whether it related to fragmentation
column4: to financial instability
column5: or to the monetary stance that was a direct consequence of the pandemic. So that continues and we've extended
column6: as you know
column7: the duration of our purchases as well as indicated the time frame during which we would continue to reinvest. We also indicated that all of that should not in any way predicate any obstacle to our delivery of monetary policy.

column1: Now
column2: your second question
column3: which is a broad one
column4: has to do with the strategy that has been developed with a bit of a lag time attributable to the pandemic by the Federal Reserve board. Clearly
column5: we have noted – as you have – that the dual mandate price stability and employment that the Fed pursues have been revisited. You have commented upon it and we have taken good note of those changes. As far as we
column6: at the ECB
column7: are concerned we had started our strategy review just like the Fed. We pressed the pause button during the time of the highest level of the pandemic crisis. We are about to resume. Actually our next seminar which will focus on inflation measurements is due to be held on September 23rd. This whole period of COVID-19 has not stopped the work streams
column8: the ten work streams that have been assigned with specific research and analytical themes. So we feel that we are up and about and ready to
column9: as I said earlier on
column10: turn every stone that will help us define our strategy in order to make sure that the ECB is fit for purpose and our monetary policy can deliver.

column1: Trust us
column2: we will be working on our strategy. I think it would be totally unwise and not loyal at all for me to already prejudge what the strategy review deliberations will be. There's an enormous amount of work that is being done
column3: but there will clearly be a focus on our definition of price stability. It's a cornerstone of any strategy of any central bank around the world. We will be extremely attentive and focussed on that.

column1: Do you think we will get deflation now in the Eurozone?
Lagarde: Well
column2: according to Eurostat's flash estimates
column3: inflation decreased to -0.2% in August from 0.4% in July. That decrease
column4: which hit the front page in some corners and was argued about
column5: reflected a drop in inflation excluding energy and food as well as lower food inflation
column6: which were partially offset by less negative energy inflation. Overall energy inflation remained a drag on headline inflation
column7: but with less negative rates since June
column8: still reflecting the old price drop in the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Food inflation in contrast increased sharply in April
column9: but this surge has since unwound and movements have normalised again to usual seasonal patterns. Inflation excluding food and energy declined as expected to 0.4% in August – and why is that? Well
column10: it is due to the temporary VAT German decrease and to the postponement… I'm sorry that I'm going into details but that's what it is. It's the postponement of garment sales in two of the major countries of the European Union
column11: from July to August
column12: and also to weak consumption demand.

column1: Clearly
column2: the September 2020 projection that will be published shortly does not foresee deflationary risk
column3: and it would not be a good economic analysis or inflation analysis to conclude that because of one measure or one month of negative results
column4: we are heading towards deflation. To the contrary actually; deflationary risks which were slightly higher back in June in our latest projections have receded in September. I know it's a bit of a convoluted way to address your question but I wanted to do that because the -0.2% in August was a bit of a wake-up call for some. We don't think that it is actually descriptive of a situation that we are interested in
column5: which is the medium-term evolution of inflation. Those deflationary risks identified previously have actually receded.

column1: I would like to revisit a theme that I read back in December but comes back strongly: as this is not your usual recovery
column2: it's not just about sectors restarting. The pandemic has hastened a structural shift in the economy
column3: wiping away whole sectors like retail and travel and leisure
column4: and bringing forward new ones; technology
column5: ecommerce
column6: healthcare. But this type of transition takes time
column7: until the sectors are mature enough to boost employment and output. Therefore the output gap will grow and will remain wider for longer. Is there an enhanced role that monetary policy can play to facilitate this transition? For instance
column8: can the ECB take a more active role to promote the needed types of investments through the bank lending channel? Or by targeting purchases of assets that would help drive more investment to certain sectors of the economy that have stronger growth potential? Do the banks in the Eurozone
column9: especially in the periphery
column10: need a special extra attention or support in order to cope with the capital challenges as well as with a lower demand for credit?

column1: Lagarde: I have to say that I agree with your analysis of the changes that we are seeing. It is a crisis like no other and it is a recovery that is very specific and very unusual as well. Let me also say that the mandate of the European Central Bank is price stability. To the extent that we can contribute to economic development by securing price stability
column2: this is our way to share the mission and the duties that we have in order to restructure and reorganise the economy in order for it to grow to the benefit of all.

column1: Second
column2: let me also mention that the way in which the Next Generation EU fund has been decided and the special focus that has been given to the green and digitalisation dimension of the investments seems to us to be exactly the right determination in order to respond to the challenge of restructuring the economy. If that in terms of investment is coupled with the right economic structural reforms in order to make sure that there is good leverage of those investments
column3: then certainly the response to the challenge will be strong. I would like to mention another way in which – well
column4: two other ways – in which we contribute our share under our mandate to the restructuring and the recovery of our economies. The first one is using an instrument like TLTRO in the volume that it has
column5: this is clearly intended to fuel credit to the economy
column6: to make sure that operators
column7: whether they are families or enterprises
column8: can actually have access to credit and can participate in the recovery of the economy.

column1: Second
column2: under our various purchase programmes as you know
column3: we have an allocation that is dedicated to public institutions. So to the extent that the European Commission
column4: either directly or through other entities of its choice
column5: issues bonds and raises financing
column6: then certainly it would qualify as a public institution
column7: the bonds of which we could buy. So it's not that I'm looking forward to it
column8: but it is also our way to participate in the effort that will be a much more collective effort and that is these new instruments that were decided over the course of the summer.

column1: I have a question about your comments on the strength of the euro. You were saying that you have discussed it extensively but at the same time
column2: you and the ECB don't seem to be overly concerned about the strength of the euro. Was that view shared by all policy makers?

column1: Then another question on Brexit. The ECB has called on banks to make serious provisions now for Brexit so what do you think will be the dominant scenario for now and what are you calling on banks to do?
Lagarde: I think I've been quite clear and quite explicit in the introductory statement concerning the role that the appreciation of the euro plays. I will refer you back to page 3
column2: at the top of the page
column3: where we say: at the same time
column4: in the current environment of elevated uncertainty
column5: the Governing Council will carefully assess incoming information
column6: including developments in the exchange rate
column7: with regard to its implications for the medium-term inflation outlook. As a good observer of our introductory statements
column8: exchange rate and the appreciation of our currency was not mentioned in previous documents. So that is clearly an indication of the fact that we do not target
column9: but we monitor and we monitor carefully because obviously the appreciation of our currency has an impact on our inflation. As I said
column10: it's not a policy target for us. I am not going to comment on the level of our currency
column11: but it is clear that the external value of the euro is an important determinant of price setting in the euro area. So we will continue to monitor the development and be very attentive to that.

column1: I think you had a second question which had to do with Brexit. Brexit
column2: I think
column3: for quite a while has been included as one of the downside risks attributable to geopolitical development. And that is included in our projection. Clearly we are not in the negotiating seat. The negotiations are handled very ably by Michel Barnier under the mandate that was assigned to him by the European Council. We are carefully monitoring as well the developments. We very much hope that after the Brexit that was decided and became effective as of January 2020
column4: the outcome of the negotiations
column5: notwithstanding the negotiation posturing
column6: and what has been observed in the last few days
column7: will lead to a positive outcome so that the projected downside risk that we have included in our projection will not be made worse.

column1: I guess I had a follow up on the exchange rate question. You were quite clear that the ECB is looking at it closely
column2: but I wondered if you could say anything about whether the development so far has been basically benign or if it's something that is worrying most members.

column1: The second question was on the possibility of cutting interest rates. It seems as though most of the focus has been on the PEPP and how that would be the main tool if you needed to provide more stimulus. But could an interest rate cut be helpful? I think investors are pricing a small interest rate cut. Do you think that could be helpful to support the economy in the shorter term?
Lagarde: As I said
column2: the European Central Bank does not target the exchange rate. Our mandate is price stability and to that end
column3: we have a medium-term inflation aim which we try to pursue using all the monetary policy tools that are available. It is clear that we are currently observing through the analysis that we do
column4: we are observing negative pressure on the price level. That is partly attributable – largely attributable actually – to the appreciation of the euro. While we don't target at any level
column5: and I have not
column6: do not and will not comment on any level
column7: we are also monitoring carefully the appreciation of our currency in relation to its impact on our inflation medium-term level. On your other question
column8: let me take this opportunity to remind you that if and when necessary
column9: and warranted by circumstances
column10: and in accordance with our mandate
column11: the Governing Council is determined to use all the policy tools that it has available
column12: and to deploy them and calibrate them as necessary and as appropriate in order to deliver on our mandate.

column1: That applies to all our policy tools
column2: so I did mention the particular impact of PEPP because that is the most recent development that we've had and recalibrated back in June. I did refer to the APP and to the targeted long-term refinancing operations because they were also the latest one. But it doesn't mean to say that I am excluding all the other tools that we have available. Indeed if and when it was needed
column3: we will not hesitate to use the tools as appropriately and as adequately as is needed. There are circumstances under which Asset Purchase Programmes are more efficient in order to reach our goals. There are circumstances where interest rates are more efficient. We have considered for the last few months that the Asset Purchase Programmes were the right tool in order to reach our goal.

column1: Two questions
column2: if I may. You have mentioned that it's very likely that the full envelope of PEPP will be used even with the rebound on the economic activity. Do you think that we will probably see another increase on its volume before the end of the year?

column1: My second question is about the Spanish banking merger that involves CaixaBank and Bankia. I would like to know your opinion about it and whether this was the kind of concentration that the ECB was looking for
column2: or it is another lost opportunity for just national operations.

column1: Lagarde: Let me tell you that we have not discussed any expansion of the envelope of PEPP. You're giving me a very nice opportunity to hand the floor over to my colleague
column2: Vice President de Guindos
column3: because your question clearly relates to a topic that he is even more familiar than I am about.

column1: De Guindos: As you are fully aware
column2: we do not enter into any kind of assessment of evaluation of concrete operations. But we have made this generic recommendation based on financial stability considerations. One of the main vulnerabilities that we have indicated in the past and most prominently after the pandemic
column3: is the low profitability of the European banks and the low valuations that this low profitability is giving rise to. Consolidation is one of the instruments. This is a generic call
column4: a generic recommendation as I have said before in order to improve the profitability of the European banks to get rid of excess capacity and to reduce the cost structure of the European banks. But we do not have any sort of concrete comment with respect to very specific or particular operations as the one that you have mentioned.

column1: I would like to know; what do you believe is today missing in the architecture of the currency union? The second question; what do you believe would it take in the next five years to have a fully prospering euro area?
Lagarde: I think we have said for a long time that for the currency union to be more complete and its architecture designed to the full possible extent
column2: we would like to see a fully-developed banking union with all its attributes so that there is a euro area banking system with easy cross-border mechanisms
column3: with resolution mechanisms
column4: with backstop facility in place and with much more solid principles of a union than we have.

column1: Second
column2: I think we've also consistently indicated that we would like to see a capital markets union which would apply throughout the euro area at least
column3: and that would facilitate access to capital by enterprises and large corporates
column4: without the discrepancies and the different regulatory regimes and filing requirements that currently apply in order to make sure that money actually flows to where it is needed in order to finance investment. I think we clearly also are pleased to see that there is at least embryonic joint fiscal capacity that was decided pre-COVID-19 in order to facilitate convergence and competitiveness and hopefully investment on a cross-member state basis throughout the euro area. I would mention those three key components in order to strengthen the currency union that we have. I'm delighted to see that under the presidency of Paschal Donohoe we have a convergence of view on some of those items in order to support the euro area and make it a stronger player on the European scene.

column1: Could I ask a bit more about the strategic review? There have been some suggestions that you maybe should look to speed up the strategic review
column2: especially after the Federal Reserve announced the results of its own review and adopted a more dovish stance. Could you perhaps split the strategic review and decide on the inflation target first and then come to the rest of it later?

column1: Second question: do you detect
column2: and are you worried about
column3: signs of divergence in the economic recovery of the Eurozone?

column1: Lagarde: On our strategy review
column2: as you know we had to pause for a little while because of COVID and because of the necessity to actually concentrate all the brain power and all the forces of the ECB on devising those new tools and making sure that we could actually respond to the objectives that we had. We are now resuming our strategy review with the appropriate sequence of seminars with reactivated work in the various work streams that have been identified. Let me just give you – I know that you're probably familiar with it already – but mention for all the audience the various work streams that we have. I think it really demonstrates the scope of our review and the depth that we want to develop in so doing. We will cover topics like inflation measurements; that's an important one that is often debated. That's coming up on September 23rd. We will also work on the ECB's price stability objective
column3: as I said earlier. It's one of our key focuses. Euro system modelling
column4: very important in order to identify whether we are capturing all the right ingredients and whether we are working them out in the adequate way.

column1: We will also discuss digitalisation and the impact that it has from a monetary policy point of view. I have in mind
column2: obviously
column3: such matters as the payment system
column4: the euro digital currency
column5: possibly. Our topics will include climate change as those who listen carefully to me
column6: it's a topic that I am very keen about
column7: which I believe has a systemic dimension that applies actually to price stability. We will include also financial stability and macroprudential policies
column8: non-bank financial intermediation
column9: communication and the interaction between monetary policy and fiscal policies. Now
column10: I have limited illusion about the absence of leaks in all the work that will be done
column11: but my hope is that we can have sufficiently cohesive a process so that we can actually as we move along possibly signal directions without actually settling on any particular final considerations
column12: because all these topics actually interact and will matter when it comes to defining our overall strategy.

column1: That's really what I wanted to say about our strategy review
column2: added to which there will be a public dimension to it because we will have
column3: inspired by the Fed process actually
column4: which itself was inspired by the Canadian central bank
column5: we will have an outreach that will really include as many stakeholders as possible ranging from NGOs and civil society to obviously members of parliament
column6: and particularly the European Parliament
column7: with which we will have a constant dialogue.

column1: On the issue of divergence
column2: I think that's what I tried to say when I used the words uneven
column3: incomplete and uncertain. As a result of these three components
column4: we are likely to see divergence. We are seeing divergence actually
column5: depending on how bad countries were hit by coronavirus
column6: depending on what fiscal position they started from
column7: depending on how much fiscal space they had available
column8: depending on the strength of their banking sector and so on and so forth.

column1: What we are hoping is that the European Union instrument that has been decided
column2: the Next Generation EU fund
column3: will actually address some of those divergences and dispersions within the euro area and within the European Union as well in order to direct as much as possible of the funding
column4: particularly in terms of grants
column5: to those countries that have been most hit and that are likely to come out of the process with less recovery than the others. I think that the flexibility that we have embedded in PEPP is also a tool that we have used in order to help in that process.

column1: 2020.10.08 13:30:00|Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday
column2: 9-10 September 2020|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel reviewed the financial market developments since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 15-16 July 2020.
The functioning of euro area financial markets had
column2: by and large
column3: been restored. Stress symptoms had largely dissipated and liquidity had returned to the market. The Composite Indicator of Systemic Stress (CISS) remained only marginally higher than before the coronavirus (COVID-19) period
column4: with the difference primarily being driven by still elevated volatility
column5: particularly in stock markets.

column1: Financial conditions had also improved broadly in the euro area. The GDP-weighted government bond curve had shifted further down and had returned to its pre-crisis level. Large parts of the curve were again in negative territory and very close to the lowest level ever recorded. Government bond spreads too had reached
column2: or were close to
column3: their pre-crisis levels and investment-grade corporate bond spreads had fallen by nearly 20 basis points since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. High-yield bond spreads had even fallen by nearly 50 basis points.

column1: One factor that might explain the general resilience of financial markets was the growing divergence between the number of COVID-19 fatalities
column2: which remained stable at low levels
column3: and the number of new infections
column4: which had more than tripled since the beginning of August 2020. Many market participants believed that this divergence – if it were to persist – would lower the risk of widespread lockdowns
column5: resulting in less of a downside risk to economic activity.

column1: It was notable that there was a growing dispersion in the extent of easing of financial conditions across advanced economies
column2: with the euro area lagging behind. The dispersion could largely be explained by two factors
column3: namely developments in global stock markets and shifts in exchange rates.

column1: Even after the developments of the past few days
column2: the Standard & Poor’s 500 stock market index was still up by around 50% from its mid-March 2020 trough and remained above pre-crisis levels. Chinese stocks were also trading well above pre-pandemic levels. In the euro area
column3: by contrast
column4: stock prices had increased by only around 32% since mid-March 2020 and remained well below pre-crisis levels.

column1: Idiosyncratic factors could partially explain these divergences. One factor was the sectoral composition of stock markets as
column2: despite the recent correction
column3: the technology sector continued to benefit most from the pandemic. Technology stocks had a larger weight in the United States than in the euro area. A second factor was the fall in equity risk premia that had contributed substantially to the rise in valuations in the United States. In the euro area
column4: the reversal in risk premia had been slower.

column1: Differences in portfolio rebalancing might have contributed to the divergence in risk premia. Over the summer real interest rates had declined notably faster in the United States than in the euro area. Real ten-year US Treasury yields were currently close to historical lows and
column2: for the first time since 2013
column3: were lower than equivalent yields in the euro area. Empirical evidence suggested that a marginal increase in inflation expectations tended to raise stock valuations
column4: and this effect was considerably greater when real rates were in negative territory. Negative real yields also reduced the opportunity cost of holding a zero-coupon asset such as gold
column5: which helped explain in part why gold prices had increased so strongly over the course of this year.

column1: Furthermore
column2: declining real rates were also likely to have accelerated the depreciation of the US dollar. The euro nominal effective exchange rate had been on an upward trend since the crisis had struck
column3: driven to a large extent by the euro’s appreciation against the US dollar. Thus far the euro had appreciated by some 7% against the US dollar from its pre-pandemic level. Investors tended to reduce their holdings of US dollar-denominated debt securities when break-even inflation rates increased

column1: Let me now explain our assessment in greater detail

column1: Lagarde: Let me just sum up what we have decided and then I’ll go into the actual description of the package and the reasons behind it. What we have decided

column4: a temporary targeted and flexible asset purchase programme that is specifically designed for the pandemic; on TLTRO III which is intended to provide as much refinancing as possible to those banks that are lending to the economy; and to offer a very attractive rate for those that actually comply with the objective. column5: if not increase
column6: lending to the economy. And then of course we also decided on all the measures that come with it

column1: So let us take the duration first: there was a discussion as to how long the extension should be and why should there be an extension in the first place? Well
column2: because clearly we are facing circumstances that are more difficult in the short-term and that difficulty has been caused by the second wave and the containment measures that have been taken as a result of that second wave. I think it’s fair to say that we all had anticipated that there would be a possible second wave. It was actually embedded in previous projections. However
column3: the depth of it
column4: the duration of it and the containment measures associated with it were not anticipated to the extent that they actually occurred and are still taking place. So
column5: it was sensible to extend [the PEPP programme] because of the impact that it has on the economy in the short order. And I remind you that the fourth quarter is going to be negative
column6: -2.2% we believe

column8: it’s fairly simple: we are
column9: fortunately
column10: economists. In addition to having all the economic knowledge and being able to anticipate
column11: we also have to be very aware and attentive to health literature and the forecast that scientists have regarding immunity in respect to the roll-out of vaccinations. That’s how we came up with this nine months’ extension because we have good reasons to believe so - you read the same material. We try to make sense of all of that. We have good reasons to believe that by the end of 2021
column12: with all the uncertainty associated with it
column13: let’s face it
column14: that we will have reached sufficient herd immunity. Also to hope that by the end of 2021 the economy will begin to function under more normal circumstances and that in particular the service sector will no longer be impaired by a lot of this social distancing and these restrictions that apply at the moment and do not facilitate the growth of the sector.

column1: So
column2: that takes you into the beginning of 2022 where the economy really begins to recover seriously
column3: where recovery takes root and where we are essentially two years after the beginning of COVID. So

column5: the volume of additional purchases that we have considered is clearly intended to deal with our focus

column8: it’s all nicely embedded in that long and fairly complicated sentence but that is what has driven our calibration of the additional PEPP that we have decided.

column6: ourselves

column1: The Governing Council recognises the key role of the Next Generation EU package and stresses the importance of it becoming operational without delay. It calls on Member States to accelerate the ratification process

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel reviewed the financial market developments since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 20-21 January 2021.
Sovereign yield curves across advanced economies had steepened
column2: while new coronavirus (COVID-19) cases had fallen
column3: the pace of vaccination had accelerated and a large fiscal stimulus programme in the United States was expected to be soon put into law. The measurable rise in commodity prices had added to upward pressure on long-term nominal bond yields. The increase in long-term bond yields had been more muted in the euro area than in other advanced economies. The euro area GDP-weighted yield curve remained considerably flatter than throughout most of the years preceding the COVID-19 pandemic and it had largely the same shape and location as observed just before the outbreak of the pandemic. Moreover
column4: sovereign spreads had remained resilient
column5: even narrowing in some jurisdictions. Accordingly
column6: the increase in yields reflected primarily a rise in the euro area risk-free rate.

column1: A decomposition of the ten-year overnight index swap rate indicated that investors had hardly changed their views on the expected future path of short-term rates. Recent yield increases had instead reflected
column2: by and large
column3: rising term premia. As the increase in term premia coincided with a notable rise in inflation swap rates
column4: it was likely that the inflation risk premium had become larger as investors had started reappraising the balance of risk around the inflation outlook. An increase in the inflation risk premium at the current juncture suggested that investors no longer only saw downside risks around the future inflation outlook as they had done for most of 2020.

column1: Real ten-year risk-free interest rates had fluctuated over time but had fallen back close to the levels prevailing around the 9-10 December 2020 Governing Council meeting. They were currently some 120 basis points below their average since 2008. Real short and medium-term rates had been insulated from the recent bond market sell-off and had continued to hit new historical lows in recent weeks.
Credit markets had remained resilient to the increase in bond market volatility and in risk-free rates
column2: which suggested that investors remained fundamentally positioned for higher growth. Credit spreads across all rating classes
column3: and in particular for high-yield bonds
column4: had continued to narrow over the past few weeks supported by a visible recovery in realised earnings. Changes in the corporate default outlook mirrored expectations of a significantly improved growth outlook
column5: contributing to favourable valuations in credit markets.

column1: In stock markets
column2: the EURO STOXX 50 index had further extended its gains
column3: gradually approaching pre-pandemic levels. ECB staff analysis suggested that the rise in risk-free rates and the deterioration in the short-term earnings outlook due to the prolongation of containment measures had pulled stock prices lower in recent weeks. However
column4: the combination of better long-term earnings expectations on the back of vaccination roll-outs and the associated improvement in risk sentiment had more than offset this drag on stock prices. Yet
column5: in some economies
column6: the rise in risk-free rates had increased risks to asset valuations
column7: which remained predicated on expectations of an extended period of low interest rates.

column1: Developments in emerging markets provided further evidence of investors so far having been able and willing to absorb the rise in risk-free rates. In February
column2: portfolio inflows into emerging markets had continued at a robust pace
column3: although they had started to reverse during the week ahead of the current meeting.

column1: Finally
column2: in foreign exchange markets
column3: expectations of higher US growth and a less accommodative US monetary policy had put upward pressure on the nominal effective exchange rate of the US dollar and also on the US dollar exchange rate against the euro. At the same time
column4: risk sentiment continued to put some downward pressure on the US dollar on the back of hopes that a resolution of the pandemic and spillover effects from US fiscal policy would kick start and nurture a strong global cyclical upswing.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Mr Lane reviewed the global environment and the recent economic and monetary developments in the euro area.
As regards the external environment
column2: there was an upgrade of the outlook as a result of a combination of ongoing vaccinations
column3: learning effects on how to live with the pandemic and the additional fiscal stimulus in the United States. In the March 2021 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column4: global activity and trade had been revised up over the projection horizon after the global economy bounced back during the second half of 2020 at a faster pace than envisaged. Based on the latest Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI)
column5: output in services had particularly improved of late. Global trade was not yet back to pre-crisis levels and the pace of trade expansion had stalled at the turn of the year
column6: with trade in services continuing to be a drag on overall trade owing to limitations on travel and tourism. Since the Governing Council’s January monetary policy meeting
column7: oil prices had risen by 23% and had climbed to USD 67.8 per barrel
column8: close to pre-pandemic levels. In terms of the exchange rate
column9: the euro had depreciated against the US dollar (-2.0%) but remained broadly stable in nominal effective terms (-0.3%).

column1: Turning to the euro area economy
column2: growth in the last quarter of 2020 had been stronger than expected
column3: but the ongoing restrictions would have a negative impact on growth in the first quarter – and perhaps also the second quarter – of 2021. Based on the March 2021 staff projections
column4: real GDP would recover to exceed its pre-crisis level (of the fourth quarter of 2019) in the second quarter of 2022 and continue to increase at a robust rate thereafter. However
column5: the recovery was expected to vary across the different GDP components and to rely quite heavily on fiscal support over the next two years.

column1: Zooming in on the latest economic developments
column2: containment measures had had to remain stricter in the first quarter of 2021 than previously expected
column3: holding back the near-term recovery but not really changing the overall path. Based on the latest PMIs for February
column4: the divergence in manufacturing and services growth dynamics was expected to continue.

column1: Household savings continued to mirror pandemic-driven consumption dynamics. Savings seemed to have been accumulated mostly by older households
column2: who typically had a lower propensity to consume out of income and wealth. They were therefore less likely to spend their savings as soon as lockdown measures were relaxed. By contrast
column3: the younger population had seen a bigger deterioration in their financial situation
column4: with low-skilled services and jobs particularly hit by the pandemic. Linked to recent delays in vaccination campaigns
column5: households expected normal activities to resume with some delay.

column1: Investment remained quite resilient overall. Data for the production of capital goods gave encouraging signals about ongoing business investment. The resilience in capital goods production was also supported by foreign demand. Housing investment was expected to remain subdued in the near term.
Trade had weakened at the turn of the year
column2: driven mainly by weak intra-euro area exports
column3: notwithstanding continued growth in extra-euro area exports. Leading indicators for manufacturing exports had continued to rise based on improvements in both shipping and survey indicators available for February.

column1: Labour markets remained resilient on the back of strong fiscal support but some indicators pointed to vulnerabilities further ahead. Overall
column2: survey indicators of employment perceptions had risen somewhat
column3: indicating an expansion for the first time since the onset of the pandemic
column4: but developments remained uneven across countries and sectors. The low-tech services sectors were those most adversely affected by the second and third waves of the pandemic. With the tightened restrictions
column5: the importance of job retention schemes had increased again in recent months.

column1: Turning to nominal developments
column2: the short-term inflation outlook for 2021 had been revised up in the March 2021 ECB staff projections
column3: while the inflation path embedded in the December 2020 Eurosystem staff projections was broadly confirmed for the outer years of the projection horizon. The projected profile of inflation in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) was quite volatile
column4: mainly as a result of energy prices. HICP inflation was expected to jump from 0.3% in 2020 to 1.5% in 2021
column5: before falling back to 1.2% in 2022
column6: and to increase again to 1.4% in 2023. The profile for HICP inflation excluding energy and food (HICPX) had shifted up somewhat
column7: showing a gradual increase from 0.7% in 2020 to 1.3% in 2023.

column1: Zooming in on recent developments
column2: headline inflation had increased sharply to stand at 0.9% in January and February
column3: after four consecutive months at -0.3%. The unchanged rate in February 2021 was the result of less negative energy inflation being offset by a decline in HICPX inflation to 1.1% in February (from 1.4% in January)
column4: which was substantially higher than the 0.2% recorded in the last four months of 2020.

column1: The recent upswing in headline inflation reflected a number of factors
column2: including less negative energy inflation
column3: the end of the temporary VAT rate reduction in Germany
column4: changes in sales patterns (timing and volumes) in some countries and the stronger than usual changes in HICP weights for 2021. Linked to the tightening of containment measures
column5: the share of price imputations in the HICP increased further in January. The overall impact of price imputations on the change in HICP inflation remained unclear
column6: adding to the high uncertainty as to whether the recent pick-up in inflation signalled genuinely increasing price pressures.

column1: Key wage measures

column1: 2021.05.14 13:30:00|Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday
column2: 21-22 April 2021|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel reviewed the financial market developments since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 10-11 March 2021.

Euro area government bond yields had decoupled from US Treasury yields – which had continued to increase in the course of March 2021 before retreating somewhat in April – and had remained broadly unchanged since late February 2021. In part
column2: this reflected the renewed rise in coronavirus (COVID-19) infections and the tightening of lockdowns in the euro area
column3: which had affected near-term growth expectations. However
column4: it also reflected the impact of the Governing Council’s monetary policy decisions in March and the preceding communication
column5: convincing markets of the ECB’s determination to maintain favourable financing conditions. The ECB’s recent measures had been effective in shielding euro area long-term rates from spillovers
column6: with regard to both the risk-free yield curve and sovereign spreads.

column1: A decomposition of the euro area ten-year overnight index swap rate into inflation and real components showed that nominal rates and their underlying components had remained broadly unchanged since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. Since the start of 2021
column2: the observed synchronised pick-up in market-based measures of longer-term inflation compensation across advanced economies likely reflected optimism regarding global growth.

column1: Model estimates suggested that the bulk of the increase in the inflation component was driven by inflation risk premia
column2: and hence did not yet reflect a significant increase in investors’ genuine inflation expectations. In contrast to the inflation component
column3: long-term real rates in the euro area had remained broadly unchanged since the start of 2021. This was also the case for medium-term real rates
column4: which were particularly relevant for borrowing conditions for firms and which had remained at or close to historical lows throughout the recent global bond market sell-off. This suggested that the ECB’s measures had been effective in insulating not only longer-term sovereign bond yields but equally – or even more so – the short to medium end of the yield curve.

column1: In a similar vein
column2: interest rate expectations over the next two years had remained unchanged since the Governing Council’s monetary policy meeting in January 2021. Markets were not pricing in any changes in the deposit facility rate until the first quarter of 2024. Rate expectations remained well anchored by the ECB’s forward guidance.

column1: Other asset prices served as a cross-check of the recent drivers of financing and financial conditions. Credit spreads across rating classes had remained stable
column2: and had even decreased for high-yield bonds. The growth-driven nature of the bond market sell-off and the ECB’s accommodative monetary policy had thus kept a lid on corporate spreads.

column1: The optimism regarding global growth had also been the key driver of stock markets. Supported by the accelerating roll-out of vaccines
column2: strong global economic data and the further improvement in longer-term earnings growth expectations
column3: stock prices had rallied beyond pre-pandemic levels in the euro area. However
column4: this development masked significant cross-country heterogeneity. An important driver of this was the sectoral composition of countries’ stock markets. Those with a large share of sectors that had benefited from the crisis had tended to outperform their peers during most of 2020
column5: a trend that had reversed after the positive news on vaccines in November 2020.

column1: However
column2: the surge in the prices of risky assets also created risks
column3: with high equity price valuations being seen as dependent on continuing highly accommodative interest rates. One indicator was the equity duration
column4: the inverse of the dividend yield
column5: which stood at the highest level since the dot-com bubble in both the United States and the euro area.

column1: Overall
column2: recent financial market developments had had a positive effect on financing and financial conditions in the euro area. Sovereign yields and spreads had remained compressed and stock prices had risen
column3: while the euro exchange rate had appreciated only slightly.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Mr Lane reviewed the global environment and the recent economic and monetary developments in the euro area.
A new wave of infections had hit economies around the globe. At the same time
column2: the world had been learning to live with the pandemic
column3: so the impact on output was more limited than in the first wave in spring last year. Overall
column4: there were positive signals for the global recovery
column5: which remained investment-led
column6: while consumption was lagging. The incoming data also pointed to a continued recovery in global trade
column7: with goods trade surprising on the upside in January. Oil prices had remained essentially flat since the March monetary policy meeting. At the same time
column8: the euro exchange rate
column9: too
column10: was basically flat
column11: with the euro appreciating slightly both against the US dollar (1.2%) and in nominal effective terms (0.6%).

column1: In the euro area economy
column2: headwinds resulted from lockdowns
column3: especially for services
column4: while investment dynamics were supportive. Short-term indicators pointed to a recovery starting in the second quarter of 2021. Focusing on the latest developments
column5: large asymmetries between industry and services prevailed. Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Indices (PMIs) had been increasing for some time and showed very strong readings. There was also a strong recovery in services PMIs even though not quite into expansionary territory yet. Retail sales remained weak owing to new restrictions introduced to limit the spread of COVID-19.

column1: The high level of containment measures had continued to delay the recovery in consumption
column2: as consumers
column3: surveyed for example by the European Commission
column4: remained cautious. Indicators for major purchases expected in the coming 12 months
column5: business retail sales expectations and orders for consumer goods had all improved but remained below pre-pandemic levels. Meanwhile
column6: private investment continued to recover. While growth in construction investment had remained muted in the final quarter of 2020
column7: the forward-looking indicators were positive
column8: with business expectations and construction confidence all ticking upwards. Growth in both extra- and intra-euro area goods exports had steadily recovered from the lows recorded in the second quarter of 2020. Tourism
column9: which owing to the pandemic was the sector most affected in services trade
column10: showed early signs of picking up.

column1: Labour market indicators continued to be heavily affected by government support programmes
column2: which complicated the assessment of underlying developments. Unlike previous crises
column3: the pandemic had disproportionately affected employment and average hours worked in “high-contact” market services sectors. Overall
column4: the main labour market indicators were relatively stable
column5: with the unemployment rate standing at 8.3% in February – broadly unchanged since November – despite the new wave of the pandemic and the associated lockdowns. However
column6: high numbers of discouraged workers and people in job retention schemes pointed to continued vulnerabilities.

column1: Turning to nominal developments
column2: headline inflation had increased to 1.3% in March
column3: driven primarily by a strong further increase in energy price inflation
column4: reflecting predominantly base effects but also recent oil price dynamics. Temporary and technical factors had continued to play an important role for inflation
column5: although the impact from changes in expenditure weights had diminished.

column1: Focusing on the more persistent components of inflation
column2: measures of underlying inflation continued to hover around levels seen in spring 2020 and did not provide a broad-based signal of a sustained pick-up. Furthermore
column3: statistical issues linked to the effects of weights
column4: tax changes and imputations continued to imply some uncertainty about the direction of underlying inflation.

column1: According to the latest ECB Survey of Professsional Forecasters for the second quarter of 2021
column2: headline inflation expectations had been revised up for 2021
column3: while medium and longer-term expectations were by and large stable. Meanwhile
column4: market-based measures of long-term inflation expectations continued to increase
column5: with the five-year forward inflation-linked swap rate five years ahead standing at 1.53% on 19 April 2021
column6: which was 8 basis points higher than at the time of the March monetary policy meeting.

column1: Turning to financial conditions
column2: long-term risk-free rates were broadly unchanged from the level prevailing at the time of the March meeting. Yield increases observed since the end of 2020 had been driven mainly by term premia and not by the expectations component. Equity and corporate bond markets were driven by expectations of an improving growth outlook. Overall
column3: financial conditions remained broadly unchanged. Looking at policy rate expectations
column4: the EONIA forward curve remained stable at the short end.

column1: With respect to monetary developments
column2: annual M3 growth had declined marginally in February but remained at a high level (12.3%). Firms and households had continued to accumulate deposits at a pace similar to previous quarters. Looking at the sources of money creation
column3: Eurosystem asset purchases and bank loans to the non-financial private sector in February had remained at levels comparable to those seen in the second half of 2020. While volumes of lending to firms had increased marginally in February
column4: the annual growth rate of bank loans to firms remained high (at 7.1% in February) only because it was still affected by the very large flows observed between March and May 2020. Bank lending rates for firms remained close to their historical lows..

column1: According to the latest euro area bank lending survey
column2: banks saw a further decline in demand for loans to firms
column3: which was mainly explained by weakness in demand for the financing of investment and the fading of financing needs for working capital
column4: reflecting the availability of liquidity buffers and direct government support. A moderate net percentage of banks had indicated a further tightening of credit standards in the first quarter of 2021
column5: following two quarters of significantly more pronounced tightening. However
column6: the tightening by banks was less than had been expected in the previous quarter. Credit standards for loans to households for house purchase had eased slightly in the first quarter of 2021 after four quarters of continued tightening
column7: supported by competition among lenders.

column1: With respect to fiscal policy
column2: some countries had recently scaled up fiscal support in response to lockdown extensions. Across euro area countries
column3: fiscal support was
column4: on average
column5: stronger in the more severely hit countries but with quite some heterogeneity across countries. Following a strong fiscal impulse in 2020
column6: fiscal support was expected to remain sizeable in the euro area in 2021.

column1: Monetary policy considerations and policy options
Summing up
column2: Mr Lane remarked that the recovery in global demand and additional fiscal measures were supporting global and euro area activity. At the same time
column3: setbacks in vaccination campaigns
column4: together with persistently high rates of new coronavirus infections in several countries and the associated tightening of containment measures
column5: were restricting economic activity in the short term. Overall
column6: incoming information
column7: including high-frequency indicators
column8: indicated that economic activity was likely to have contracted again in the first quarter
column9: but pointed to a resumption of growth in the second quarter. Progress with vaccination campaigns and the envisaged gradual relaxation of containment measures underpinned the expectation of a firm rebound in economic activity
column10: especially in the second half of 2021.

column1: Risks to the euro area growth outlook continued to be on the downside in the near term
column2: but remained more balanced over the medium term. Upside risks stemmed from: better prospects for global demand
column3: supported by sizeable fiscal stimulus; more rapid progress in vaccination campaigns; and a faster than expected reduction in household savings once social and travel restrictions were lifted. However
column4: the new wave of the pandemic
column5: including the spread of virus mutations
column6: and a slower vaccine roll-out represented downside risks for the growth outlook over the coming quarters.

column1: Headline inflation had risen to 1.3% in March from the 0.9% recorded in January and February
column2: owing mainly to strong increases in energy price inflation. At the same time
column3: underlying price pressures were subdued in the context of weak demand and significant slack in labour and product markets
column4: but were expected to increase somewhat in 2021 owing to short-term supply constraints and the recovery in domestic demand. Inflation would exhibit some volatility for the remainder of the year. Survey-based measures and market-based indicators of longer-term inflation expectations remained at low levels compared with the ECB’s inflation aim
column5: although market-based indicators had continued to increase
column6: mainly driven by higher inflation risk premia.

column1: Amid continued robust risk sentiment in global financial markets
column2: euro area financing conditions had remained broadly stable of late. In particular
column3: risk-free rates and sovereign bond yields had moved sideways and appeared to have decoupled from the repricing in US interest rates. At the same time
column4: the rise recorded earlier in the year in these key indicators in the upstream segment of the transmission chain still posed a risk to the wider set of financing conditions
column5: which in turn warranted close monitoring.

column1: Against this background
column2: Mr Lane proposed that the Governing Council leave its prevailing monetary policy configuration unchanged and confirm its very accommodative monetary policy stance. Since the incoming information confirmed the joint assessment of financing conditions and the inflation outlook carried out at the March monetary policy meeting
column3: the Governing Council should continue to conduct net asset purchases under the pandemic emergency purchase programme (PEPP) in the current quarter at a significantly higher pace than during the first few months of the year.

column1: As regards external communication
column2: two aspects were important. First
column3: the Governing Council needed to reaffirm its current practice of conducting a comprehensive joint evaluation of the prevailing state of financing conditions against the inflation outlook at monetary policy meetings in which policy deliberations were informed by a new round of staff projections. In line with this practice
column4: a new comprehensive joint assessment should be conducted at the next monetary policy meeting in June. Second
column5: it was important to highlight that calibrating purchases under the PEPP so as to counter the adverse effects of the pandemic on the medium-term inflation outlook was only one element in achieving the aim of stabilising medium-term inflation around levels below
column6: but close to
column7: 2%. Ample monetary policy support remained crucial beyond the pandemic period in order to support inflation and return it to the inflation aim. The Governing Council therefore needed to continue to stand ready to adjust all of its instruments
column8: as necessary
column9: to fulfil its mandate.

column1: 2. Governing Council’s discussion and monetary policy decisions
Economic and monetary analyses
With regard to the economic analysis
column2: members generally agreed with the assessment of the current economic situation in the euro area and the risks for activity provided by Mr Lane in his introduction. While the recovery in global demand and the sizeable fiscal stimulus were supporting global and euro area activity
column3: the near-term economic outlook remained clouded by uncertainty about the resurgence of the pandemic and the roll-out of vaccination campaigns. Looking ahead
column4: progress with vaccination campaigns and the envisaged gradual relaxation of containment measures underpinned the expectation of a firm rebound in economic activity in the course of 2021. Inflation had picked up over recent months on account of some idiosyncratic and temporary factors and an increase in energy price inflation. At the same time
column5: underlying price pressures remained subdued in the context of significant economic slack and still weak demand.

column1: As regards the external environment
column2: members broadly shared the assessment by Mr Lane that the global economic outlook continued to improve despite the new wave of infections occurring worldwide. Reference was made to recent forecasts from international institutions. Notably
column3: in its April 2021 World Economic Outlook
column4: for 2021 the IMF had revised its expectations for global growth up to 6% and had projected world trade to rise by over 8%. Attention was drawn
column5: in particular
column6: to positive news regarding economic developments in the United States and to the further growth recorded in China at the beginning of the year
column7: reflecting an exceptional recovery since the start of the pandemic a year earlier. With respect to the latest exchange rate developments
column8: it was noted that the euro had appreciated slightly since the Governing Council’s last monetary policy meeting. It was underlined that a further appreciation of the exchange rate could have adverse implications for the inflation outlook.

column1: Turning to euro area developments
column2: real GDP had declined by 0.7% in the fourth quarter of 2020
column3: remaining well below its pre-pandemic level. Incoming economic data
column4: surveys and high-frequency indicators suggested that the resurgence of the pandemic and the associated intensification of containment measures might have led to a decline in activity in the first quarter of 2021
column5: but they also pointed to a resumption of growth in the second quarter.

column1: In discussing the economic outlook for the euro area
column2: members judged that
column3: although the current situation remained fragile and subject to a high degree of uncertainty
column4: recent data could overall be seen as confirming that GDP growth was broadly in line with the March 2021 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area. This assessment was also supported by the latest IMF and OECD forecasts. There had been a rise in infection rates
column5: particularly among young people
column6: a delay in the roll-out of vaccination campaigns and some concerns about the safety of vaccines. A prolongation of containment measures had acted as a drag on growth in the first quarter of the year
column7: but there was also good news in that vaccination campaigns were now gaining momentum in the euro area
column8: which could be expected to lead to a gradual easing of lockdown measures. This would
column9: in particular
column10: support the recovery in the services sector
column11: which had been the sector most affected by the crisis. It was also encouraging that evidence of the efficiency of the vaccination campaigns was becoming stronger and that the share of the population that had received a first or even second dose was increasing more rapidly. The learning behaviour of households and firms in response to restrictions during the pandemic was considered to be another positive factor supporting growth.

column1: However
column2: it was also underlined that the outlook continued to depend on how quickly the vaccination campaigns proceeded
column3: as well as on the spread and transmission of different variants of the COVID-19 virus. Uncertainty about both the timing and the strength of the recovery in the euro area remained
column4: with some grounds for caution as evidenced by the sequence of downward revisions to the growth rate expected for the first quarter of the year. It was also stressed that the outlook for both growth and inflation remained dependent on the support of fiscal policy measures and the very accommodative monetary policy stance. Moreover
column5: it was pointed out that the impact of the pandemic differed across countries in the euro area. While in some countries activity was expected to return to pre-pandemic levels by the end of 2021
column6: in others – especially those in which the services sector had been most affected – it was expected still to be below the pre-pandemic level at the end of 2022.

column1: Members generally expected a stronger recovery to take place in the second half of 2021 but emphasised that uncertainty surrounding the near-term growth outlook remained high. A key question was how consumers would respond to an easing of lockdown measures. It was recalled that the March 2021 ECB staff projections exercise had been based on the assumption that the household saving ratio would gradually return to its pre-crisis level and that there would not be any substantial unwinding of the excess savings that had been accumulated during the pandemic.
In assessing the risks to growth
column2: a range of views was advanced concerning the likely behaviour of consumers. It was suggested that forced savings might unwind more dynamically than expected. A one-off boost to consumption later in the year was considered a possibility
column3: based on previous observations
column4: when higher consumption had followed lower infection rates and an easing of restrictions last summer. Still
column5: it was also possible that the boost to consumption from pent-up demand might unfold more gradually. At the same time
column6: it was argued that consumers might prove to be more cautious in their spending this year.

column1: Against this background
column2: it was generally felt that risks to activity had become more balanced over the medium-term horizon

column6: as I said

column1: By the same token
