We have an interest in the governance of the euro area and we are very keen to see as much of a fiscal union as is possible given that we have a monetary union and that the current crisis has demonstrated amply that when monetary and fiscal policy work in intelligent synchronization
column3: it can be very efficient. But I am not going to pass judgement on one proposal or the other
column4: however respectable the authors are. We
column5: the Governing Council of the ECB
column6: have said that we would like to see rules that are simpler
column7: that are more user-friendly
column8: that provide for a counter-cyclical response. We have also said that we believe that a fiscal capacity would be appropriate in order to respond collectively to shocks.

column1: There are other proposals that are being floated but the decision will ultimately depend on what the leaders are prepared to compromise and are prepared to accept. From our perspective
column2: the more fiscal union there is
column3: obviously the better for our monetary policy.

column1: I asked this question in December; I'm going to ask it again
column2: and forgive me
column3: but do you think the market
column4: in pricing several rate increases this year by the ECB
column5: has got ahead of itself?

column1: Secondly
column2: can you tell us what your view is on the impact of tensions between Russia and Ukraine on the economic outlook and particularly the outlook for inflation?

column1: I don't know what answer I gave you to the December question
column2: and I might be giving you a similar answer – although it will be in the light of a different indication from the economic situation and certainly different inflation numbers and different labour market numbers. When it comes to interest rate hikes
column3: we have a forward guidance which has been approved by the Governing Council which identifies three pillars or three criteria
column4: if you will
column5: that need to be satisfied in order for rates to be hiked. I don't want to insult you by repeating those three criteria
column6: but I will actually! We have the inflation at target
column7: which is 2%
column8: well ahead of the projection horizon; we have
column9: second
column10: the durability so that we see it staying at target until the end of the horizon; and third
column11: we need to see underlying inflation that is sufficiently strong to determine progress towards target.

column1: We will apply these three criteria at each and every step of the way
column2: and we will determine if and when they are satisfied in order to possibly hike rates. But don't forget that we also have a sequence
column3: and the sequence is that we will not hike rates until we have completed net asset purchases. So I think what comes first comes first; we have to look at net asset purchases. We are conducting a step-by-step guide of those net asset purchases. We will determine in March what is the assessment
column4: on the basis of the data that is then available and we will see what pace
column5: what speed
column6: what amounts we will apply to this net asset purchase programme for the rest of '22.

column1: You asked me a more political question on which I am not going to take a political stance
column2: but I will simply say that the geopolitical clouds that we have over Europe
column3: if they were to materialise
column4: would certainly have an impact on energy prices and
column5: through energy prices
column6: an increased cost throughout the whole structure of prices. It would also impact growth as a result of reduced income and possibly as a result of reduced consumption and deferred investment. The pure economic impact would certainly be more significant than what we are seeing at the moment in terms of prices. We are very attentive to that and by the way
column7: we include that in our scenario when we prepare the projection and the work that is submitted to Governing Council members at the time of the next Governing Council meeting. I will say separately that peace is a lot better than any kind of war from an economic point of view
column8: and I have seen that in other parts of the world in previous lives.

column1: The first one is on inflation. You mentioned several times now the upside surprises of inflation in December and January. Does that mean that the December projections from the ECB staff
column2: that they are already outdated
column3: especially the projections that inflation will fall below 2% in 2023

column1: My second question is on the degree of monetary policy accommodation: if inflation is significantly higher than expected
column2: this means that real interest rates are lower than thought. So monetary policy is more expansionary than thought. Isn't that in itself a reason to recalibrate monetary policy and to tighten monetary policy?

column1: On the latter one: it's obvious that monetary policy has to continue to support the economy and you mentioned it yourself: the whole panoply of instruments that we use
column2: that are currently working
column3: is also explaining some of the good results that the economies are showing at the moment.

column1: On the upside surprise: we did not only use the word upside in relation to surprises; we used it in relation to risk. Risk is to the upside in our projection. We hardly ever – I'd have to double-check in the last 20 years
column2: we may have in the past – but in the recent past we have not actually mentioned
column3: we have not included in our monetary policy statement the characterisation of risks in relation to inflation. I think that is a very explicit indication that it might very well be significantly higher than what we had expected over the course of the year
column4: and possibly higher than we had anticipated at the end of the year. Risk is to the upside
column5: in particular in the near term.

column1: I have got a quick question on your March projections that you've highlighted now repeatedly: if those updated forecasts show inflation exceeding your 2% target in 2023 and 2024
column2: would that
column3: in your present view
column4: be a reason to start slowing bond purchases earlier than currently suggested?

column1: Thank you for your pointed question
column2: but I am not going to speculate on what the Governing Council will decide. I think you have the answer
column3: but I am not going to speculate here on what the decision will be.

column1: I was wondering in light of these events if you had measured any kind of what degree of monetary contraction could cause the decision of ending the special rate period of the TLTROs.
Actually we have not discussed TLTROs at all in this particular Governing Council meeting
column2: and it's one of the items that I'm sure we will debate at our March meeting
column3: or later actually. I think they end in June '23[

column1: ] if I recall
column2: yes.

column1: In the beginning of the press conference you said that there was a unanimous concern within the Governing Council about inflation. Just to be sure: does it mean that the monetary policy decision taken today was also taken unanimously?
My second question
column2: if I may: to what degree does the scenario or the risk of rising bond spreads determine the pace of normalisation of monetary policy of the ECB
column3: especially given the fact that sovereign debt has exploded so much during the pandemic?

column1: I think I said that there was general concern around the table about inflation and the impact it has on our fellow Europeans. Equally
column2: there was general consensus about the outcome of our decision. I wouldn't call it a monetary policy decision
column3: so to speak
column4: because what we are doing is we are continuing the normalisation of monetary policy and we are considering what will possibly happen and what options we offer ourselves
column5: what optionalities will be around in response to the uncertainty at future monetary policy meetings. That's what we did in depth and very thoroughly today. There was general consensus on these issues around the table
column6: I can assure you.

column1: Now
column2: you asked me a question about the spreads: I would like to just observe that we are not seeing any such development. While yields have moved up
column3: spreads have not widened in any significant manner. So we very much look into these matters very carefully and we have no reason to believe that it is going to be different. If it was
column4: we are obviously going to respond and we have all the tools
column5: all the instruments and the adequate flexibility if it is justified.

column1: I would like to focus on the energy prices: if I listen to you and your colleagues one always has the impression that energy prices are something a central bank can't do much about. It has to be taken and this is partly taken as justification for the current monetary policy. On the other hand
column2: one could argue that the current policy is leading to the fact that the dollar is rising quite significantly against the euro. Since most energy – or maybe all energy – is being calculated in US dollars
column3: it basically is another factor why energy prices are rising. So there is a criticism that one could argue that the current monetary policy stance of the ECB actually is fuelling inflation rather than combatting it. I hope you won't just say we don't focus on the exchange rate
column4: but what would you say to this criticism?

column1: It is the case that the very high inflation numbers that we observe are at least 50% caused by energy prices. Oil
column2: gas
column3: electricity and they all interrelate
column4: gas having a stronger bearing than in previous years because of the price mechanisms depending on the length of contract and all the rest of it. I will spare you the details
column5: but 50% of the current inflation is caused by energy prices. If the ECB was to first of all reduce and finish its asset purchases
column6: and then raise interest rates in short order
column7: do you think it would have any impact on energy prices? No
column8: it is not in the ambit of monetary policy to decide the price of the barrel that is organised predominantly outside of Europe.

column1: Now
column2: true that most of those contracts are in the US dollar currency but if I look at the significant appreciation/depreciation
column3: it varies a little bit. The euro has depreciated a little bit. I don't want to be in the wrong numbers
column4: but it's no more than 3% over the course of the last 12 months[

column1: ]. I don't think that we can attribute to the European Central Bank the high cost of energy which impacts 50% of the inflation and the price paid by the consumers. Having said that
column2: the European Central Bank and its Governing Council at large are focussed on its mandate
column3: which is price stability. We are going to stick to the objectives that are set by the Treaty; that is price stability at 2% in the medium term. Believe me
column4: as soon as it is required and the conditions are satisfied
column5: we will act because it is our duty and we shall do so.

column1: I have two questions. The first question is on the lower bound: if inflation were to be too high relative to the 2% target
column2: the ECB would respond. Your response will come from the lower bound and from negative interest rates
column3: which is really exceptional. Can you tell us how the Central Bank
column4: the ECB
column5: can respond to higher inflation coming from the lower bound?

column1: My second question is on your step-by-step approach: the Governing Council expects net purchases to end shortly before it starts raising the key ECB interest rates and end its APP net purchases. What does this “shortly before” mean if inflation was going too high for too long?
Well
column2: how do you hike interest rates? By hiking interest rates. And clearly
column3: we will have a very sophisticated determined approach and analysis to doing that. We will only do that in the sequence that we have fixed for ourselves
column4: and which has been agreed
column5: which is that we will look at net asset purchases first
column6: gradually
column7: on a data-dependent basis. Then we will look at interest rates.

column1: Now
column2: you asked the question about net asset purchases
column3: and I'm not sure exactly what your concern was about the net asset purchases and what is the… What was the question?

column1: It was “shortly before”…
Of course
column2: “shortly before.” Shortly before is probably a little shorter than just before
column3: and that again is going to be in the estimation of the Governing Council
column4: data dependent
column5: and based on the assessment that is conducted. I would say this: we are not there yet for the reasons that I have just mentioned
column6: which are that we will be very faithful to our sequence. We are still conducting net asset purchases. We will stop the Pandemic Emergency Programme net asset purchases in March and then we will look at the net asset purchases under the APP. Don't assume too much in terms of the immediacy of hikes; we will not be complacent
column7: but we are not going to be rushed into a process. We will follow the sequence that we have set for ourselves. We will verify the forward guidance criteria and we will be gradual in whatever we do.

column1: It's very crucial to avoid the so-called second-round effects in the setting of wages and prices. In times where we see people are going on the street to defend their purchase power
column2: especially in France
column3: would you go as far as to call the unions to wage moderations in the coming period to avoid these second-round effects – which are not yet there
column4: of course?

column1: The second question is: we had an interview with World Bank Vice President
column2: Carmen Reinhart
column3: today in Spiegel
column4: using harsh words towards central banks; telling that they are only independent on paper. For that
column5: she said that the level of public debt is so far so high that the central banks are so hesitant to act. What is your take about this?

column1: Well
column2: on the latter question: I have not seen what Carmen has written so I'm not going to comment on that. She is an expert on sovereign debt and she has held that view for a long
column3: long time that excessive sovereign debt is a great burden and should be addressed by sovereigns. I am not going to challenge or second-guess her analysis. I know this is her field and I am not surprised that she's addressing that in her capacity as chief economist of the World Bank and clearly
column4: I am sure
column5: focussed on emerging markets and low-income countries.

column1: On the second-round effect
column2: don't get me wrong: what we are saying is that we are not seeing wage increases that would be likely in the conditions of the markets as they are
column3: where we are seeing unemployment as low as it has ever been
column4: where we are seeing participation back to the level where it was pre-COVID
column5: and where gradually the output gap is closing and there is less and less slack in the economy. We are waiting for that movement on wages and our duty of course is to make sure that through a second-round effect
column6: that would not be addressed by monetary policy
column7: inflation would run out of control and would spiral. This is not what we are seeing
column8: and we certainly don't want to see it
column9: but I am not here saying that there should be wage moderation. There is clearly an adjustment to be had which I am hoping we will see in the course of '22. That would be the economic logic of what we are seeing at the moment.

column1: By the way
column2: as I am finishing on that question
column3: I think we should be a little bit cautious about what I am hearing a lot
column4: which is constant comparisons between the US and the euro area
column5: the Fed and the ECB. We are really operating in different environments
column6: with different economic data. Just to give you an example: our demand here in the euro area is pretty much back to where it was pre-COVID. In the US it is 30% up. Ask yourself why; this is because of this massive fiscal stimulus that the US economy has had
column7: unlike the euro area
column8: where it has been more moderate
column9: not excessive and which is producing the sort of measured pace at which some factors are significantly improving."|https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/press_conference/monetary-policy-statement/2022/html/ecb.is220203~ca7001dec0.en.html

column1: 2022.03.03 13:30:00|Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday
column2: 2-3 February 2022|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments

Ms Schnabel reviewed financial market developments since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 15-16 December 2021. Markets had digested well the Governing Council’s decisions in December 2021 to discontinue net asset purchases under the pandemic emergency purchase programme (PEPP) in March 2022 and to adjust the future path of purchases under the asset purchase programme (APP). The day after that meeting
column2: ten-year overnight index swap (OIS) rates and euro area GDP-weighted sovereign yields had been lower than before the meeting. Nevertheless
column3: long-term real and nominal interest rates had increased globally from the exceptionally low levels that had prevailed after the discovery of the Omicron variant of the coronavirus (COVID-19) in late November last year.

column1: A model-based breakdown of the recent increase in ten-year euro area risk-free rates suggested that it had been mainly driven by two factors. The first was a change in investors’ assessment of the economic impact of the Omicron variant. Developments over the past few weeks had reinforced the impression that the Omicron wave might be sharp but short-lived
column2: and the drag it exerted on economic growth weaker than initially feared. The second factor pushing interest rates higher in recent weeks had been a reappraisal of the global monetary policy outlook. In the United States
column3: investors had brought forward the expected time of “lift-off”
column4: with the first hike currently expected in March. They had also priced in more tightening over the next two years
column5: and were now expecting balance sheet runoff to start sooner.

column1: In the euro area
column2: rising inflation compensation had added to the upward pressure from higher real rates
column3: as markets had revised up their expectations of the future path of inflation in response to the renewed upside surprises to inflation in December and January. Recent energy price developments had added to perceptions in the market that inflation risks were rising. Brent crude oil prices had increased to about USD 90 per barrel
column4: the highest level since 2014 and about 25% higher compared with mid-December. According to futures curves
column5: oil prices were expected to remain high over the medium term. Gas spot and futures prices
column6: too
column7: were higher than before the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting
column8: reflecting the growing tensions between Russia and Ukraine as well as low inventories.

column1: These developments had contributed to a continued reappraisal of the medium-term inflation outlook for the euro area. First
column2: respondents to the Survey of Monetary Analysts (SMA) saw upside risks to inflation over the entire horizon covered by the SMA. Second
column3: survey-based indicators of long-run inflation expectations had been revised up. In the SMA
column4: in particular
column5: they had risen to 2% from 1.8% in December. This was the highest they had ever been since the start of the SMA. Likewise
column6: in January long-term inflation expectations from Consensus Economics had reached 2% for the first time since 2015. Market-based measures of longer-term inflation compensation had remained at around 2%. Furthermore
column7: in the inflation options market
column8: investors were pricing in a probability of around 30% that inflation over the next five years would
column9: on average
column10: be above 2.5% and a probability of around 50% that it would be above 2%.

column1: In this environment
column2: markets had significantly revised their expectations about the monetary policy outlook in the euro area. Compared with December
column3: the OIS forward curve had steepened visibly for short-term maturities. Markets were pricing in a cumulative 50 basis point hike in the deposit facility rate (DFR) by mid-2023
column4: which would raise the DFR to 0%. As usual
column5: these dates had to be treated with caution because the market rates included term premia. Allowing for such premia
column6: market pricing implied that the DFR would actually rise above zero somewhat later. SMA participants
column7: too
column8: were now expecting the first DFR increase to be one quarter earlier
column9: in the third quarter of 2023
column10: with a much steeper path after lift-off than they had anticipated in December.

column1: Developments in options markets suggested that investors had revised not only their expectations about the central future path of short-term interest rates
column2: but also their expectations about the distribution of risks around this path. This distribution had become more skewed to the upside. Nevertheless
column3: monetary policy in the euro area was still expected to normalise at a measurably slower pace than in many other economies
column4: as could be seen from the developments in foreign exchange markets. The euro had temporarily fallen against the US dollar to the lowest level since June 2020. At the time of the meeting
column5: the euro was still down against the US dollar by more than 6% compared with a year ago and was trading close to its 2019 average. In nominal effective terms
column6: the euro was down by around 3% compared with a year ago.

column1: With investors preparing for faster policy normalisation globally
column2: risk assets that had benefited from the long period of very low interest rates might have been expected to come under pressure. However
column3: risk assets had in fact remained resilient overall
column4: in particular in the euro area. According to market intelligence
column5: real interest rates currently remained at levels that were supportive for growth and risk assets.

column1: In euro area sovereign bond markets
column2: yield spreads over German ten-year Bunds had remained around their December levels with few exceptions. The resilience of these spreads was noteworthy in the current environment. The change in the expected future policy path – by the logic of the ECB’s sequencing – implied a significant reduction in the amount of assets expected to be bought under the APP. The picture was very similar in the euro area corporate bond markets
column3: where spreads had only increased marginally. Thus
column4: financing conditions for euro area firms had remained highly favourable.

column1: As regards developments in global equity markets
column2: stocks had first declined visibly in the United States
column3: but had then recovered a good part of their losses. In the euro area
column4: stock markets had suffered only very moderate losses compared with December 2021. Here the impact of higher discount rates had been offset by continued upward revisions to longer-term earnings expectations and improved risk sentiment. All in all
column5: therefore
column6: the rise in real and nominal interest rates had so far been absorbed well by financial markets
column7: as real financing conditions remained favourable amid high inflation and expectations of continued buoyant global growth in the coming years.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
In his review of global developments Mr Lane noted that the Omicron variant had led to a sharp rise in global coronavirus cases in January. Although these cases appeared milder than in previous waves
column2: many parts of the world had strengthened their containment measures. Whereas previous waves had seen a rotation between advanced economies and emerging markets
column3: in the recent wave a lot of countries across the globe had found themselves in a similar situation. This could imply a stronger
column4: more synchronised rebound compared with earlier waves. The most recent loosening of containment measures in some countries was confirming the expectation that Omicron case numbers could fall quickly once a sufficient level of immunity had been reached.

column1: The Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) for both manufacturing and services at the global level continued to point to an ongoing recovery at the turn of the year. But there were signals of a slowdown in the near term
column2: especially in manufacturing. Supply bottlenecks continued to restrain global activity. While these bottlenecks seemed to be levelling off according to various indicators
column3: they remained substantial.

column1: The euro exchange rate had depreciated since the December meeting of the Governing Council
column2: both against the US dollar (-0.9%) and in nominal effective terms (-1.2%). Taking a longer-term perspective
column3: the exchange rate appreciation observed in 2020 had largely been reversed
column4: bringing the exchange rate closer to its pre-pandemic level. Oil prices had increased sharply (+28%) since the December meeting
column5: with the oil futures curve shifting upward until the end of 2024. Most of the oil price increase since the December meeting could be attributed to supply factors and the recent failure of some OPEC+ members to step up production.

column1: In contrast to oil prices
column2: gas prices had declined by 33% since the December 2021 Governing Council meeting. This was due to the relatively mild winter in Europe and the redirection of imports of liquified natural gas from Asia to Europe
column3: which had more than offset the large drop in gas imports from Russia. Concerning the outlook for gas prices
column4: it was important to recognise that supply shocks tended to have a more persistent effect on gas prices when inventories were low
column5: which was currently the case. Global food prices had increased by 6% since the December meeting following poor harvests
column6: rises in shipping costs and higher fertiliser prices as a result of rising energy costs.

column1: Turning to developments in activity in the euro area
column2: Mr Lane noted that after a strong performance in the middle of last year there had been a significant slowdown at the end of the year. Real GDP had grown by 0.3%
column3: quarter on quarter
column4: in the fourth quarter of 2021 (according to Eurostat’s flash estimate) following a growth rate of 2.3%
column5: quarter on quarter
column6: in the third quarter. In the fourth quarter of 2021 euro area GDP had reached its pre-pandemic level. The slowdown in GDP growth reflected the intensification of the pandemic
column7: persisting bottlenecks and still high energy prices.

column1: In Europe
column2: COVID-19 cases had risen more than tenfold since mid-November
column3: but with the emergence of the Omicron variant the number of intensive care admissions was no longer rising in line with the number of infections. Nevertheless
column4: health concerns among consumers had increased. The European Commission survey of December 2021 showed that households had become less optimistic about their near-term spending
column5: especially in sectors providing contact-intensive consumer services.

column1: Turning to production
column2: pressures exerted by supply bottlenecks had levelled off
column3: but there was no evidence so far of a significant decline in those bottlenecks. Production of transport equipment continued to be dampened by shortages of semiconductors and by logistical problems. As a result
column4: capacity utilisation had fallen and stocks of almost finished and finished goods had risen in the sector. Production of other capital goods remained robust.

column1: Turning to trade in goods and services
column2: the accumulated level of export orders remained higher than before the pandemic
column3: but the flow of new orders was diminishing
column4: most likely owing to the still acute bottlenecks.

column1: The recovery in the labour market continued to be strong. Unemployment had declined to 7.0% in December
column2: which was the lowest unemployment rate since the creation of the euro area. The December 2021 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections foresaw a significant improvement in labour market conditions and the latest data were in line with that prediction.

column1: The number of people employed
column2: which included workers in job retention schemes
column3: was basically back to its pre-pandemic level in the third quarter of 2021. However
column4: total hours worked were still below the pre-pandemic level
column5: with the gap between the two measures mainly being explained by job retention schemes. Across sectors
column6: the recovery in hours worked in services had accelerated more in the second and third quarters of 2021 than in the manufacturing sector.

column1: To assess how tight the labour market was
column2: it was useful to look at the ratio between the vacancy rate and the unemployment rate and to compare this ratio across the euro area and the United States. In the United States
column3: even before the pandemic there had been more jobs available than people unemployed
column4: i.e. the ratio had been above one. While the ratio had fallen to below 0.5 in mid-2020
column5: it had climbed back up to 1.5 at the end of 2021. By contrast
column6: in the euro area although a pick-up could be observed in this ratio at the end of 2021
column7: the number of vacancies posted was only around 30% of the number of people unemployed. Thus
column8: the situation in the euro area was very different from that in the United States. Still
column9: the outlook for employment in the euro area continued to be positive and to improve
column10: with all euro area PMI employment indicators standing above the expansion threshold of 50.

column1: Turning to inflation
column2: Eurostat’s HICP flash estimate for January had been released on the first day of the Governing Council meeting and had only been reflected in the analysis to a limited extent. The latest inflation data would be integrated more fully in the analysis for the March meeting. In recent months around half of the headline inflation rate had resulted directly from energy inflation
column3: but the contribution of food prices had increased.

column1: According to Eurostat’s flash release
column2: headline inflation had increased slightly further to 5.1% in January 2021 – from 5.0% in December and 4.9% in November. This was substantially higher than foreseen in the December projections. Energy inflation had been very high in January
column4: with fuel prices accounting for the largest share of this figure. The rise in energy inflation could increasingly be explained both by higher electricity prices
column5: which had been affected by various policies
column6: and by higher gas prices.

column1: Prices for unprocessed food had exceeded their projected price increase by more than than prices for processed food. The latter mainly reflected increases in prices within the EU’s internal market amid global rises in both energy costs and prices for international commodities.
With respect to non-energy industrial goods (NEIG) inflation
column2: the contribution of durable goods had continued to increase
column3: which could be attributed to supply bottlenecks as well as to the energy price rise. However
column4: price dynamics for the other components of NEIG indicated that the increase in NEIG inflation was broad-based across items. The indirect contribution of energy to non-energy inflation items was relevant in this context
column5: since all non-energy sectors used energy as an input. Typically
column6: the energy input was less than 10% of overall costs
column7: but energy price increases as high as 28.6% were going to affect many individual categories of goods.

column1: Further up the pricing chain
column2: pipeline pressures for NEIG inflation continued to build up
column3: partly reflecting the rise in energy production costs. Import prices for intermediate goods remained at unusually high levels and domestic producer price inflation for non-food consumer goods had increased further to stand at a new historical high. The annual rate of change in import prices for final non-food consumer goods
column4: which had been negative for most of 2020 and had a dampening effect on NEIG inflation
column5: had increased further and added to pipeline pressures for NEIG. This reflected both the higher goods prices that euro area importers had to pay but also the effect of the depreciation of the euro.

column1: A range of indicators of underlying inflation had moved up to levels above 2%. However
column2: there were important temporary factors behind this
column3: in particular the effects of bottlenecks and high energy prices. A rise in the price of energy increased the price level for other goods in the input-output matrix across the board. However
column4: this did not necessarily imply that high inflation was going to persist. Historically
column5: measures of underlying inflation were good predictors of future inflation
column6: as they were to some extent designed to reflect persisting developments. But temporary factors were clearly also playing a role in the present situation.

column1: Comparing recent headline inflation developments in the euro area and the United States
column2: many issues were similar in qualitative terms. However
column3: in quantitative terms HICP inflation excluding food and energy (HICPX) stood at 2.6% in December in the euro area
column4: while in the United States the CPI less food and energy was 5.5%. While part of the higher inflation in the United States could be explained by the higher increases in rents and their larger weight in the CPI
column5: the biggest difference related to the effects on core inflation of supply disruptions
column6: bottlenecks and the reopening of the economy. These effects had so far been much more evident in the US data.

column1: Turning to indicators of wage developments in the euro area
column2: growth in negotiated wages had remained low in recent months
column3: although the labour market was “hotter” in some countries than in others. Overall
column4: however
column5: there was no evidence of any big structural change in the behaviour of negotiated wages. Nor did expectations of labour costs point to any evidence so far of significant second-round effects from the current high level of inflation.

column1: Regarding sources of domestic inflation
column2: it was noteworthy that in the euro area most energy was imported and import prices for energy had increased by almost 50% in the second half of 2021. This had led to a big drop in the terms of trade. This drop was essentially a tax on Europe paid to the rest of the world. The income effect of the deterioration in the terms of trade was estimated at around 2.5% of GDP. According to another calculation
column3: the most recent balance of payments data showed that payments by EU countries for energy imports had risen from €200 billion in the first 11 months of 2020 to €335 billion in the first 11 months of 2021. This was a 66% increase.

column2: 9-10 March 2022|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel reviewed the latest financial market developments since the Governing Council’s monetary policy meeting on 2-3 February 2022. Before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine
column2: the shift in the ECB’s communication agreed at the February meeting had contributed to the orderly adjustment in financial markets towards less accommodative financial conditions that were more consistent with a changing medium-term inflation outlook. The uncertainty triggered by the war had temporarily halted and partly reversed the repricing of monetary policy expectations globally
column3: leading to heightened volatility across market segments. However
column4: so far
column5: market stress and dislocations appeared less severe than at the peak of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic shock.

column1: The largest market impact of the Russian invasion of Ukraine to date had been on commodity prices
column2: with oil and gas registering new multi-year highs and futures curves shifting up significantly from already elevated levels. The resulting energy price rise had contributed to a substantial reappraisal by markets of the euro area inflation outlook. First
column3: the entire inflation-linked swap-based forward curve had shifted significantly upwards and was now above 2% up to the ten-year horizon. As these measures contained inflation risk premia
column4: genuine inflation expectations were likely to be somewhat lower. Moreover
column5: longer-term indicators of market-based inflation expectations had also moved materially higher
column6: going above 2%. Most of this uptick had come at the beginning of the previous week when markets had started to price in a shallower path for the anticipated tightening of euro area monetary policy.

column1: With inflation continuing to surprise on the upside
column2: a discernible repricing of euro area monetary policy expectations had been observed at the start of the year. Most of the upward shift in the forward curve for the overnight index swap (OIS) rate observed prior to the war had happened before the Governing Council’s 2-3 February meeting. The Russian invasion of Ukraine had halted and partly reversed the repricing of ECB policy rate expectations
column3: as markets had priced in around a two-month postponement of a first interest rate hike relative to pre-war expectations. Investors expected one 25-basis point increase around the turn of the year
column4: while the expected speed of the tightening cycle after “lift-off” remained broadly unchanged. Uncertainty around policy rate expectations based on information from option prices had also increased. Since February
column5: the distribution of risks around the expected path of the three-month EURIBOR had widened substantially
column6: reflecting the heightened uncertainty surrounding both the economic and the inflation outlook. The more pronounced skewness of the distribution suggested that markets had become even more concerned about upside risks to inflation.

column1: Risk-free long-term yields on both sides of the Atlantic had continued to move in close step
column2: even though the drop in German Bund yields had been somewhat more pronounced than for US Treasury yields. This signalled that investors seemed to see the war driving only a small wedge between the growth outlook in the United States and in the euro area. The sharp and unprecedented widening of the Bund-OIS spread following the Russian attack suggested that flight to safety had been a more relevant factor than the repricing in monetary policy expectations
column3: which affected Bund and OIS yields to the same extent.

column1: Developments in real interest rates could similarly be characterised as having gone through two phases since the Governing Council’s February monetary policy meeting. In the first phase
column2: before the Russian invasion
column3: real yields had increased strongly at the short and the long end of the curve in line with a gradual normalisation of financial conditions following the reappraisal of monetary policy expectations globally. After the Russian attack
column4: real yields had fallen sharply across global risk-free sovereign yield curves driven by safe haven flows
column5: with the decline being more pronounced at the short end
column6: also reflecting a sharp increase in expected inflation.

column1: Spreads of euro area sovereign bond yields over German Bund yields had initially widened after the Governing Council’s February monetary policy meeting
column2: but the speed and magnitude of the adjustment had remained contained. The relative resilience reflected three factors: first
column3: the continued strong ECB monetary stimulus
column4: including from the substantial stock of acquired assets and the ECB’s announced re-investment policies; second
column5: the combination of a long period of low interest rates and the increase in the weighted average maturity of public debt
column6: which reduced the sensitivity of the cost of debt servicing to rising risk-free rates; and third
column7: the easing of pandemic restrictions as well as sound growth expectations
column8: also in view of structural reforms and investments related to the Next Generation EU programme. The same factors had played a role in the resilience of spreads in response to the latest geopolitical risk shock.

column1: Developments in equity markets signalled that the uncertainty about the direct implications of the invasion was expected to be greater for the euro area than for other major currency areas. Most of the recent decline in equity prices likely reflected a rise in the equity risk premium
column2: consistent with the flight to safety in bond markets.

column1: Looking at exchange rates
column2: until the start of the war the EUR/USD exchange rate had co-moved very closely with changes in policy rate expectations. With the onset of the war
column3: the US dollar had appreciated as investors moved into classic safe-haven currencies
column4: despite broadly unchanged relative monetary policy expectations.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Mr Lane went through the latest economic
column2: monetary and financial developments in the global economy and the euro area. He started by noting that the economic shock from the Russian invasion of Ukraine came in the context of otherwise solid foundations for a strong recovery in the euro area this year. It was therefore useful to recall the point at which the economy had been before the start of the war.

column1: The global economy was recovering from the pandemic. The Omicron wave had had a short-lived negative impact
column2: mainly on services. This was shown by the change in output Purchasing Managers’ Indices (PMIs) by industry – particularly for tourism and recreation – from November 2021 to February 2022. However
column3: with the Omicron wave fading and economies reopening
column4: it was natural to expect a catch-up. The latest data also suggested that there had been a slight improvement in supply bottlenecks
column5: especially in the United States and the United Kingdom. Once supply bottlenecks eased
column6: more production could be expected to take place to satisfy demand. Trade in goods was already above pre-pandemic levels
column7: but there was still ample scope for catching up in tourism during 2022 and this could be a strong engine of growth for European countries.

column1: Looking at developments in commodities and exchange rates
column2: the picture for oil prices was changing by the day
column3: with the oil price on 7 March clearly above the level assumed in the March 2022 ECB staff projection exercise. Regarding the exchange rate
column4: a distinction needed to be drawn between what was happening in bilateral movements of the euro exchange rate and the evolution of the euro’s effective (trade-weighted) exchange rate. The heightened uncertainty from the Russian invasion had led investors to move into safe-haven currencies. The euro had appreciated strongly against the currencies of central and eastern European countries and had depreciated notably against the US dollar. When weighting the different developments
column5: in nominal effective terms
column6: the fall in the euro had not been very pronounced.

column1: Turning to the euro area
column2: some improvements had been observed in supply bottlenecks
column3: although they remained acute. However
column4: there was a risk that the Russia-Ukraine war could lead to further bottlenecks. Reviewing the demand components of GDP
column5: the recovery in private consumption had been very strong until the third quarter of 2021
column6: i.e. before the Omicron wave. The strength of the recovery had reflected higher incomes and a running down of savings. This had led to more robust consumption even though fiscal support had been reduced from the levels at the height of the pandemic. This positive trend had been reversed in the fourth quarter of 2021
column7: when private consumption fell
column8: largely on account of higher energy and consumer prices
column9: which translated into a decline in real disposable income. This mechanism was expected to operate also in the first quarter
column10: despite the expectation that a reduction in savings could partly buffer a decline in consumption. The energy price shock had been negatively affecting private consumption
column11: as people had experienced an increase in their cost of living and a reduction in purchasing power.

column1: Investment had recovered in the fourth quarter of 2021. This was largely due to a sharp rebound in the automotive industry
column2: which had been a drag on investment in the previous quarters. Housing investment continued to be affected by large demand but also supply bottlenecks in production. Demand for houses or house renovation remained elevated
column3: even though the most recent data showed a slight dip in expectations. On the production side
column4: although recent surveys indicated some easing in the shortages of materials
column5: equipment and labour
column6: these were still close to their historical peaks.

column1: To appreciate the impact of the energy price shock on real income
column2: it was useful to look at the deterioration in the trade balance and in the terms of trade. The euro area goods trade balance had progressively worsened
column3: resulting in a deficit at the end of 2021. The deterioration had been largely driven by an increasing deficit in the energy balance. A similar deterioration was visible in the terms of trade. In the final quarter of 2021
column4: the contribution of energy to the deterioration in the terms of trade had been 4 percentage points of GDP. When accounting for gains from companies charging higher export prices to their global customers
column5: the net loss of income vis-à-vis the previous year due to the energy price shock had amounted to 2 percentage points at the end of 2021.

column1: With regard to labour market developments
column2: the evidence continued to point to a recovery story
column3: with the PMI employment index remaining in expansionary territory (above 50) in all sectors in February. The unemployment rate had continued to fall and was 6.8% in January. The job vacancy rate showed that more and more sectors were recording a greater number of vacancies. The euro area vacancy rate had not reached the level seen in the United States
column4: but it was consistent with strengthening labour demand.

column1: Turning to the March 2022 ECB staff projection exercise
column2: Mr Lane noted that the variables used in the technical assumptions had already changed significantly since the 28 February projection cut-off date
column3: which had already been moved back from 24 February on account of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. The projection exercise foresaw real GDP growing by 3.7% in 2022. This represented a downward revision of 0.5 percentage points for 2022
column4: which was mainly due to the impact of the Ukraine crisis on energy prices
column5: confidence and trade. GDP growth in 2023 and 2024 was broadly unrevised from the December 2021 Eurosystem staff projections. On the nominal side
column6: following a series of unprecedented energy price shocks
column7: headline inflation was now expected to average 5.1% and core inflation 2.6% in 2022. Headline inflation in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) was expected to remain slightly above 2.0% in 2023 and to fall to 1.9% in 2024. Since the December 2021 projections
column8: headline inflation had been revised up by 1.9 percentage points and core inflation by 0.7 percentage points for 2022.

column1: As regards the saving ratio
column2: some decline was foreseen over the projection horizon
column3: with households expected to reduce savings to cushion the energy price shock in the short term and to boost their consumption spending later in the horizon as the economy reopened.

column1: Owing to the high uncertainty surrounding the consequences of the military conflict for the euro area
column2: the ECB staff had prepared two scenarios: an “adverse” scenario and a “severe” scenario. Both scenarios entailed a permanent loss of income
column3: with the level of GDP projected to be significantly lower than in the baseline. The adverse scenario assumed additional sanctions against Russia
column4: with euro area energy market disruptions as well as rising uncertainty and financial repercussions. On top of these features
column5: the severe scenario included a higher price sensitivity of energy markets to supply cuts
column6: additional financial tightening and stronger second-round effects from higher wages on inflation. In both scenarios inflation would be significantly higher in the short term
column7: but it would fall back to slightly below target in 2024.

column1: Moving to a model-based analysis of risks to the inflation outlook
column2: two alternative approaches were used in the assessment. The first approach relied on model simulations
column3: which estimated the probability that annual HICP inflation would be higher than 2% in 2024. This indicated that risks were broadly balanced
column4: with most model simulations showing that the probability of inflation being above target in 2024 was less than 50%. The second approach was that of calculating the forecast probability for HICP inflation one year and three years ahead
column5: based on financial and monetary indicators. With this approach
column6: too
column7: the forecast probability of inflation being above 2% in 2024 was less than 50%. Overall
column8: the two approaches suggested that there were risks in both directions
column9: but the risks looked broadly balanced. These analyses therefore confirmed the view that end-point inflation in 2024 would be around the 2% target.

column1: Similarly
column2: according to the March Survey of Monetary Analysts (SMA)
column3: the median of the distribution of longer-term inflation expectations remained around 2%
column4: meaning there was no significant difference from the February round. Given the relative stability of the inflation expectations component
column5: it could also be argued that movements in the real rate were being driven by developments in the risk premium. As regards the balance of risks
column6: SMA respondents saw risks to inflation in 2024 to be balanced around the inflation target. This fairly even distribution between levels above and below 2% implied that there were both upside and downside risks to inflation.

column1: Turning to the latest inflation developments
column2: HICP headline inflation had been increasing strongly since summer 2021
column3: reaching 5.8% in February 2022. The most important contribution to the rise in inflation was from energy
column4: which in February accounted for 3.1 percentage points of the 5.8% inflation rate increase
column5: as energy prices rose by 31.7%. Among the energy components
column6: not only fuel but also gas and electricity had contributed significantly to the increase in energy inflation. The prices of other HICP components
column7: such as food
column8: goods and services
column9: had also been rising. Since energy was an input in every sector
column10: whenever there was a very large and persistent energy price shock the pass-through to other components would become stronger. Indicators of underlying inflation
column11: which traditionally sought to identify the persistent elements of inflation
column12: had been increasing. Taken at face value
column13: they signalled that headline and core inflation would be higher in the future.

column1: However
column2: while these indicators captured medium-term inflation developments well in normal times
column3: they were currently affected by two shocks: the pandemic shock and the massive energy price shock. This called for careful analysis of what was behind inflation dynamics in the present environment and behind the developments in the different components of core inflation
column4: i.e. inflation excluding food and energy.

column1: Starting with goods inflation (non-energy industrial goods)
column2: in recent times about 1 percentage point of goods inflation could be attributed to a combination of supply bottlenecks – as captured by PMI supply delivery times – and oil prices. Historically
column3: goods inflation had been hovering around 0.5%. Then
column4: more recently
column5: it had risen to around 1.5%
column6: before increasing further to above 2% in the latest data. However
column7: 1 percentage point of the increase was estimated to be due to factors that were not persistent
column8: namely supply bottlenecks and the energy price shock.

column1: Mr Lane went on to explain that the March HICP staff projection was built around the assumption that the energy price shock was a level effect and would not last. The same assumption applied to the bottlenecks
column2: which also generated a level effect that would nonetheless not be a permanent source of inflation. Therefore
column3: for goods inflation
column4: there were temporary reasons why inflation was high. Once these shocks vanished
column5: inflation was expected to fall.

column1: The second component of core inflation
column2: services inflation
column3: included similar temporary elements. One key temporary element was the reopening of the economy
column4: which also needed to be interpreted as a level rather than permanent effect on inflation.

column1: When looking at the whole projection horizon and cumulating the impact of the energy price shock on core inflation from the last quarter of 2021
column2: ECB staff analysis showed that around 3 percentage points of the cumulative increase in core inflation had been driven by the indirect effects of energy. In the short term (until early 2023)
column3: the indirect impact was estimated to account for the bulk of the increase in core inflation. But over time
column4: with the disappearance of slack and the levelling-off of the energy effect
column5: core inflation would return to being mostly determined by the traditional factors and a Phillips curve-type effect would start kicking in. In short
column6: these analyses showed the very large effect that energy prices
column7: supply bottlenecks and the reopening were having on core inflation.

column1: Turning to wages
column2: the March staff projection was built on the observation that
column3: so far
column4: there had been no signs of strong wage pressures
column5: which was in line with the assessment that the labour market was not very tight. The projection suggested a gradual pick-up in wages in 2022
column6: on the basis of the evidence collected on new wage settlements. Since collective bargaining agreements frequently covered one to two years
column7: examining agreements that had already been concluded was informative about increases in negotiated wages in the coming months. For the euro area as a whole
column8: growth in compensation per employee in 2023 was projected to be 3.4%
column9: with the impact of the minimum wage increase in Germany estimated to be around 0.5 percentage points.

column1: With regard to fiscal policies
column2: the March ECB staff projections showed continued improvement in the euro area fiscal outlook. The expected path of fiscal correction was gradual and largely due to the improved cyclical component. Overall
column3: the euro area fiscal deficit was projected to still remain higher than in the pre-pandemic period. The debt-to-GDP ratio was also expected to improve – by about 10 percentage points between 2020 and 2024 – largely thanks to the strong projected path of growth
column4: which was foreseen to return to its pre-pandemic trajectory.

column1: While fiscal balances were expected to improve
column2: interest payments had been revised upwards since the December projections. However
column3: it was important to remember with regard to interest payments that a lot of expiring ten-year bonds were still paying rates of interest that were higher than current rates. Looking at the measures that governments had implemented or announced to cushion the impact of the energy price shock
column4: for the euro area aggregate the baseline incorporated an associated impact of about 0.2% of GDP in 2022. Additional measures – not yet included in the baseline – had recently been approved in several countries.

column1: Monetary policy considerations and policy options
Summing up
column2: Mr Lane stressed that the Russian invasion of Ukraine would have a material impact on economic activity and inflation through higher energy and commodity prices
column3: the disruption of international commerce and weaker confidence. The prospects for the economy would depend on how the conflict evolved
column4: on the impact of economic and financial sanctions and on possible further measures. In any event
column5: the degree of uncertainty would remain extraordinarily high.

column1: At the same time

column2: 13-14 April 2022|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel reviewed the latest financial market developments
column2: noting that since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 9-10 March 2022 investor risk sentiment had improved considerably. Euro area equity prices had moved close to the levels recorded prior to the war in Ukraine
column3: sovereign spreads had narrowed
column4: and risk-free yields had increased markedly. At the same time
column5: market-based measures of inflation compensation had continued to creep higher and stood well above the Governing Council’s 2% target over the entire horizon.

column1: Developments in sovereign yields in the euro area since the previous monetary policy meeting highlighted three facts. First
column2: the GDP-weighted sovereign yield curve in the euro area had shifted upwards since the March meeting and currently stood considerably above the levels recorded prior to the war across the entire maturity spectrum. Second
column3: the euro area yield curve had become steeper. Third
column4: despite the recent rise
column5: both short and long-term euro area nominal bond yields remained low from a historical perspective.

column1: A model-based breakdown of the recent increase in ten-year euro area risk-free rates pointed to two main factors driving the upward shift in sovereign yields since the previous meeting. First
column2: the improvement in the global and euro area macroeconomic outlook and risk sentiment suggested that investors did not see the war’s effect on growth as being sufficiently strong and long-lasting to derail the recovery. The second
column3: and related
column4: factor reflected the anticipated monetary policy response. Consistent with expectations of continued growth and the sharp repricing of the inflation outlook
column5: markets expected a faster pace of monetary policy normalisation in the euro area to bring real yields out of negative territory.

column1: Breaking down long-term yields into real rates and the inflation component showed that the rise in nominal long-term interest rates in the euro area since the Russian invasion of Ukraine mainly reflected a marked reappraisal of the inflation outlook by investors
column2: while real interest rates had fallen slightly since March
column3: despite the recent increase in nominal yields.

column1: The rising inflationary pressures were also evident from the inflation-linked swap forward curve
column2: which had shifted markedly higher from the already elevated levels prevailing at the time of the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. This increase in inflation compensation had stemmed from higher inflation risk premia. Genuine inflation expectations had increased only moderately. The sharp rise in inflation risk premia signalled that investors demanded higher compensation for holding inflation risks in their portfolio. The five-year forward inflation-linked swap rate five years ahead
column3: which was a market-based measure of longer-term inflation expectations
column4: stood at around 2.4%. This suggested that even over the longer term investors attached a higher probability to inflation turning out to be higher than expected
column5: rather than lower than expected.

column1: Compared with March
column2: the shift in market-based indicators of monetary policy expectations had been substantial. The overnight index swap (OIS) forward curve had become markedly steeper
column3: with market participants pricing in just under a full 25 basis point rate hike in July this year and almost three 25 basis point rate hikes by the end of the year. Thereafter
column4: markets expected the hiking cycle to continue
column5: with six 25 basis point interest rate hikes expected in 2023. This suggested that markets saw the need for substantial policy action to secure medium-term price stability
column6: reflecting the current
column7: very negative
column8: real short and long-term yields.

column1: The median participant response to the Survey of Monetary Analysts (SMA) showed that the first interest rate hike was still expected to take place in the fourth quarter of 2022
column2: but the share of SMA participants expecting an earlier lift-off had now increased to around 40%. The expected path after lift-off
column3: however
column4: was substantially shallower compared with the path suggested by market pricing. This possibly indicated that rising term premia
column5: on the back of high remaining uncertainty about the pace of policy normalisation
column6: had contributed to the steeper forward curve
column7: with markets’ genuine expectations probably being somewhat lower than indicated by the forward curve. Higher uncertainty about expected euro short-term money market rates
column8: as priced in by the market
column9: was in line with the premise of the ECB’s “reaction function” becoming more data-dependent.

column1: Markets were preparing for a substantially more pronounced US hiking cycle
column2: compared with expectations in March
column3: and now expected the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) to hike rates by about 250 basis points over the next 12 months
column4: with the federal funds rate expected to level off at a level above 3%. Moreover
column5: the FOMC had hinted at a rapid reduction in its USD 9 trillion balance sheet
column6: beginning as soon as at its next policy meeting in May.

column1: Limited movements in the exchange rate of the euro against the US dollar since the March monetary policy meeting suggested that the recent reappraisal by markets of the euro area monetary policy outlook was offsetting
column2: at least in part
column3: the downward pressure on the euro from the pronounced reappraisal of US monetary policy expectations. At the same time
column4: the depreciation of the euro since the beginning of the year in response to the change in relative monetary policy expectations vis-à-vis the United States had been larger than was suggested by cross-country regularities.

column1: Developments in euro area sovereign bond markets were consistent with limited risks of stagnation or recession. Sovereign spreads had been on a sustained downward trend since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting.
Furthermore
column2: the recent strong recovery in equity prices reflected
column3: first and foremost
column4: a reversal of the earlier increase in the equity risk premium
column5: mirroring the improving risk sentiment. A more fundamental factor explaining the resilience of equity prices
column6: and of risk assets more generally
column7: was that the earnings outlook for euro area firms had remained relatively robust
column8: despite the war. Earnings expectations over the next 12 months had
column9: so far
column10: not been lowered. Longer-term earnings expectations had decreased substantially
column11: but had stabilised at very elevated levels. Analysts continued to expect annual earnings growth of about 20% over the next three to five years
column12: compared with a long-run average of around 8%.

column1: The cautious optimism displayed by market participants did not mean that investors were dismissing downside risks. As geopolitical risks remained elevated
column2: markets continued to price in heightened tail risks. For instance
column3: downside risks to equity markets remained elevated in the euro area. Another risk emanated from high margin calls in commodity futures markets
column4: which had caused a large increase in the liquidity demand of non-financial corporations that were hedging their energy price exposures.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Mr Lane went through the latest economic
column2: monetary and financial developments in the global economy and the euro area. For global developments
column3: the Spring 2022 World Economic Outlook (WEO) projections from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) had significantly downgraded the forecast of world GDP growth for 2022 and also for 2023. The downward revision was very large for Russia but also significant for countries close to the war zone and reliant on Russia for their imports of energy and metals.

column1: Global supply chain bottlenecks had started to ease after the turn of the year. However
column2: as a consequence of the war and the new lockdowns in China
column3: that easing was stalling
column4: or even reversing
column5: and forward-looking indicators had started to point to a deterioration in global trade dynamics.

column1: The oil price had declined notably from the peaks observed after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Compared with the day of the March Governing Council meeting
column2: the shorter-run futures path of oil prices was lower
column3: but it was still higher compared with the cut-off date (28 February) for the March ECB staff projections.

column1: There had been relatively minor movements in the euro effective exchange rate since the March Governing Council meeting. Taking a longer-term perspective
column2: the euro exchange rate had largely returned to pre-pandemic levels both in effective terms and against the US dollar.

column1: Turning to euro area activity
column2: the Russian invasion of Ukraine had led to a spike in uncertainty
column3: as indicated for example by the European Commission’s uncertainty measure. The recent evolution of confidence indicators suggested a deterioration in the short-term outlook
column4: owing to the rise in energy prices
column5: the increased uncertainty and the new wave of supply disruptions generated by the war and the lockdowns in China. However
column6: the outlook for the third quarter was still relatively positive
column7: as a boost from tourism could be expected in the summer. Similarly
column8: the assessment for the fourth quarter remained positive. So far
column9: the assessment was that the war would lead to a temporary slowdown in growth
column10: but not a persistent downgrade.

column1: Looking at the components of domestic demand
column2: private consumption was likely to have contracted in the first quarter
column3: with a negative carry-over from the drop in retail sales in December 2021 and the further rise in energy prices hitting incomes. Pandemic restrictions had been lifted
column4: but households had shown a strong negative reaction to the outbreak of the war
column5: with consumer expectations plunging in March. In particular
column6: household expectations regarding their own future financial situation – which generally were a good predictor of consumer spending – had deteriorated sharply.

column1: With regard to business investment
column2: the uncertainty shock was expected to be more harmful to investment than consumption. While investment spending plans would certainly be affected by heightened uncertainty
column3: these plans could also be affected by the rise in energy costs. Historically
column4: the data showed a negative relationship between production costs and the profit rate
column5: so it should not be expected that higher costs would be fully passed through to consumer prices.

column1: While trade data capturing the outbreak of the war were not yet available
column2: the deficit on the energy and food trade balance had continued to deteriorate since the beginning of the year
column3: as import prices for energy and goods continued to increase. This deterioration was partly compensated for by an improvement in the non-energy and non-food trade balance. The Purchasing Managers’ Index for manufacturing export orders had fallen into contractionary territory in March owing to the war in Ukraine and lockdowns in China.

column1: Looking at labour market developments
column2: the unemployment rate continued to decline and the labour market participation rate continued to improve. Across sectors
column3: employment in market services
column4: including tourism
column5: had not yet returned to its pre-pandemic level
column6: while the public sector had been a key driver of job creation
column7: with public sector employment standing about 3% above the pre-pandemic level at the end of 2021. However
column8: in March 2022 household expectations regarding unemployment had increased visibly
column9: albeit much less than at the start of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

column1: One important factor cushioning the impact of the shock was fiscal policies. The bulk of the euro area measures addressed the hike in energy prices
column2: but part of the new package of measures also increased spending on defence and refugees.

column1: Turning to the latest inflation developments
column2: headline inflation in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) had hit a new high of 7.5% in March
column3: up from 5.9% in February. By far the biggest contribution came from the energy component
column4: with over 4 percentage points. The recent increase in energy inflation was very large and the reaction of the economy could be subject to non-linearities
column5: as the response of the economy – in terms of both inflation and output dynamics – might not be proportional to its response to the usually much smaller fluctuations in energy prices.

column1: Breaking down energy inflation

column1: Your point number two is: why not 50 [basis points] in July? Well
column2: we are coming out of 11 years of no interest rate move. We are on our path to exit negative interest rates soon. It is good practice

column4: and say the following: “throughout this process the Governing Council will maintain optionality
column5: data-dependence
column6: gradualism and flexibility in the conduct of monetary policy”. So all four will matter and there will be circumstances when one might be more important than another.
