column1: 2022.07.07 13:30:00|Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Amsterdam on Wednesday and Thursday
column2: 8-9 June 2022|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel reviewed the latest financial market developments. Since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 13-14 April 2022
column2: there had been a major shift in monetary policy expectations and actions around the world as inflation had continued to surprise to the upside.

column1: The main developments in financial markets revolved around four main themes. First
column2: volatility in financial markets was high by historical standards
column3: reflecting the longer than expected persistence of high inflation and the associated uncertainty about the extent and pace of monetary policy adjustment required to restore price stability over the medium term. Second
column4: monetary policy normalisation in the euro area was expected to proceed at a significantly faster pace than at the time of the Governing Council’s 13-14 April meeting
column5: with a rate lift-off expected in July. Third
column6: expectations of a steeper policy path contributed to halting and partly reversing both the rise in inflation risk premia and the marked depreciation of the euro
column7: thereby offsetting part of the renewed rise in oil prices. Fourth
column8: changes in monetary policy expectations had brought the valuations of riskier assets closer to their long-term averages
column9: in both fixed income and stock markets.

column1: The increase in volatility witnessed globally over the previous few months had been reflected in higher implied volatility across virtually all main asset classes: bonds
column2: equities and foreign exchange. The higher volatility went hand in hand with a deterioration in market liquidity. While such volatility was not surprising at turning points in monetary policy
column3: its magnitude had been amplified by the combination of shocks hitting the world economy: the war in Ukraine
column4: the energy transition
column5: global excess demand and China’s zero-COVID policy.

column1: Three sources of policy uncertainty were behind the current volatility: (i) the extent of the required policy adjustment
column2: (ii) the pace of the policy adjustment
column3: and (iii) the transmission of changes in policy rates to market interest rates and bank lending rates.

column1: Regarding the first source of uncertainty
column2: related to the extent of the required policy adjustment in the euro area and other major currency areas
column3: investors had significantly repriced expected terminal rates – the peak interest rates expected by markets at the end of the normalisation or tightening cycle not corrected for term premia. This strong repricing of terminal rates had been a major factor in the recent increase in nominal long-term bond yields. While
column5: the rise in nominal ten-year overnight index swap (OIS) rates had been driven by rising inflation compensation
column6: the real ten-year rate had increased markedly in 2022.

column1: Market feedback suggested that the uncertainty about the extent of policy normalisation was driven by two main factors: uncertainty about the level of the neutral rate
column2: and hence the level of the equilibrium real rate of interest
column3: and uncertainty about the need to take policy rates above the neutral rate.

column1: The second source of uncertainty
column2: which related to the pace of policy adjustment
column3: meant markets had not only repriced the terminal rate but were also expecting a significantly swifter policy normalisation than at the time of the Governing Council’s 13-14 April meeting. Surveys continued to lag market prices.

column1: The pace of policy adjustment expected by investors was dependent on the perceived degree of anchoring of longer-term inflation expectations. Survey-based measures of inflation expectations gave different indications regarding the risks of unanchoring
column2: depending on the underlying sample.

column1: Market-based measures of long-term inflation compensation had declined from their decade-high level recorded in April but had started to rise again lately and remained above 2%. These developments reflected markets’ changing views on the likelihood of a recession
column2: in particular market expectations of a resilient growth outlook
column3: as well as the ECB’s communication pointing towards a rate lift-off in July. The ECB’s communication had been an important factor behind the decline in inflation risk premia at longer horizons
column4: as it emphasised the commitment to protect price stability.

column1: The third source of uncertainty in financial markets related to the expected strength of the transmission of changes in the key ECB interest rates to money market and bank lending rates. The weaker the expected transmission
column2: the stronger and swifter the required policy adjustment in the eyes of investors. The strength of policy transmission also depended on the extent and expected pace of a decline in excess liquidity.

column1: Excess liquidity was now expected to decline more slowly than previously assumed. This was because higher expectations of a prospective rise in the key ECB interest rates would lead banks to postpone repayment of the funds from targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTROs).
Changes in policy rate expectations had been transmitted to broader financial markets. Equities had sold off as expected
column2: coming down from the elevated levels that had been underpinned by historically low real interest rates. At the same time
column3: since the 13-14 April monetary policy meeting
column4: euro area stock markets had outperformed other indices despite expectations of a steeper policy path.

column1: In euro area fixed income markets
column2: spreads had continued to widen as markets repriced the future path of policy. Despite challenging liquidity conditions and elevated volatility
column3: neither sovereign bond markets nor corporate bond markets had seen excessive moves. However
column4: there had been a marked differentiation across issuers. Spreads had increased the most in Italy and Greece
column5: where debt-to-GDP ratios were highest
column6: and for corporate high-yield issuers
column7: for whom credit risk was the largest. Spreads had increased less in Spain and Portugal and for corporate investment grade issuers.

column1: Although expectations of monetary policy tightening had firmed almost everywhere
column2: the euro had appreciated visibly against the currencies of many advanced economies since the Governing Council’s meeting on 13-14 April. The US dollar was the most notable exception.

column1: The marked and persistent depreciation of the euro against the US dollar
column2: the currency in which oil imports were predominately invoiced
column3: had tangible and immediate effects on inflation
column4: and therefore on inflation expectations. Since May 2021
column5: oil prices had increased by 88% in US dollar terms but by 111% in euro terms. At the same time
column6: the ECB’s communication since the start of the year had provided a counterweight to the downward pressure on the euro that had resulted primarily from the forceful action of the Federal Reserve System.

column1: All in all
column2: the outlook for inflation and hence for monetary policy would remain a key driver of asset prices for the foreseeable future. In this context
column3: higher volatility was a natural reflection of price discovery in an environment in which central banks found it harder to provide clear forward guidance given the uncertainty around the policy outlook.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Mr Lane went through the latest economic
column2: monetary and financial developments in the global economy and the euro area. Starting with the international environment
column3: there had been a noticeable slowdown in the global trade of goods in the first quarter of 2022. The most recent data for March pointed to the contraction being largely driven by developments in China. As lockdown measures there had continued into the second quarter
column4: it was likely that the loss of global trade momentum would persist. The war in Ukraine and the lockdown in China had interrupted the easing in global supply pressures in March. In the euro area
column5: Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) delivery times had deteriorated in March
column6: but in May there was some improvement.

column1: Looking at exchange rates
column2: the euro was marginally weaker against the US dollar
column3: while it had appreciated slightly in nominal effective terms since the Governing Council’s 13-14 April meeting. Oil prices had increased notably since the April meeting. The June Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area were therefore based on higher oil prices
column4: but the slope of the futures curve remained negative. Other commodity prices had moderated since the meeting
column5: with gas
column6: metals and food prices declining. The June staff projections had seen a significant downward revision of world growth
column7: with the projection for 2022 down from 4.1% to 3.0%. The lower projected growth implied a downward revision of euro area foreign demand
column8: especially in 2023.

column1: Turning to the euro area
column2: real GDP had grown by 0.6% in the first quarter of 2022 according to Eurostat’s latest estimate. However
column3: excluding Ireland
column4: euro area GDP was up by only 0.3%. The contribution of domestic demand to euro area growth had been negative
column5: amid the lockdowns at the start of the quarter and the outbreak of the war in Ukraine.

column1: The June staff projections had revised the quarterly GDP profile down but still embodied a significant recovery over the summer and into the fourth quarter. Short-term estimates were subject to high uncertainty for the rest of the year. The projections had generally been within the range of the available short-term forecasting tools
column2: but the range of these estimates was wide on account of the high uncertainty. Indicators of uncertainty had risen sharply following the outbreak of the war
column3: especially for manufacturing and
column4: to a lesser extent
column5: services. The PMI composite indicator was still above 50
column6: but the PMI for manufacturing output had fallen as the indicator of services business activity had risen.

column1: With regard to private consumption
column2: households were increasingly feeling the squeeze on their real incomes from rising energy and food prices. The Consumer Expectations Survey showed that households did not expect to be able to maintain consumption in real terms. The survey also pointed to a reduction in saving flows.

column1: Housing investment was affected by a jump in input costs. Construction used materials that relied on imported commodities. As a result
column2: shortages of materials and equipment continued to accumulate in the construction sector. Rising construction costs were expected to put a break on growth in housing investment. The Consumer Expectations Survey indicated that the perceived attractiveness of housing as an investment was decreasing. The elevated uncertainty was expected to weigh on housing investment over the course of the year.

column1: Data on capital goods production had shown a significant recovery at the end of 2021 with the rebound in car production. Following the outbreak of the war
column2: however
column3: production in the sector had seen little progress.

column1: The euro area goods trade balance had deteriorated owing to the rising cost of imported energy and food. The overall trade balance had deteriorated by about 4 percentage points since the start of 2021
column2: of which about 2.5 percentage points was due to the energy and food balance. This captured the real income cost of having to pay more money to the rest of the world.

column1: A key reason for the good third-quarter prospects was tourism
column2: by far the sector hit hardest by the pandemic. All available indicators were pointing to a very strong recovery
column3: with expectations for demand in the summer months well above their pre-pandemic levels.

column1: For the labour market
column2: the evidence suggested that the very good recovery had continued in the first quarter of 2022. Growth in employment was overall consistent with a return to the pre-pandemic relationship between GDP and employment
column3: after the break caused by the pandemic and the support measures put in place. This also meant that the recovery in economic activity currently explained most of the recovery in employment. The unemployment rate had declined again in April
column4: in particular in countries such as Spain
column5: where the recovery in tourism had helped to create jobs. Survey data continued to signal favourable labour market developments.

column1: Turning to fiscal policies
column2: the June staff projections had incorporated a significant amount of new support measures related to the war and compensation for energy price increases. These new measures amounted to roughly 1% of GDP for the euro area as a whole
column3: with the figure varying across countries. GDP growth was expected to be supported mainly in 2022
column4: as some of the measures were likely to be withdrawn later in the forecast horizon. Their impact on inflation was expected to be on the downside in 2022 and to largely reverse in 2023

column4: the full reopening of the economy is supporting spending in the services sector. As people start to travel again
column5: tourism is expected to help the economy in the third quarter of this year. Consumption is being supported by the savings that households built up during the pandemic and by a strong labour market.

column1: Fiscal policy is helping to cushion the impact of the war in Ukraine for those bearing the brunt of higher energy prices. Temporary and targeted measures should be tailored so as to limit the risk of fuelling inflationary pressures. Fiscal policies in all countries should aim at preserving debt sustainability
column2: as well as raising the growth potential in a sustainable manner to enhance the recovery.

column1: Inflation

Inflation increased further to 8.6 per cent in June. Surging energy prices were again the most important component of overall inflation. Market-based indicators suggest that global energy prices will stay high in the near term. Food inflation also rose further
column2: standing at 8.9 per cent in June
column3: in part reflecting the importance of Ukraine and Russia as producers of agricultural goods.

column1: Persistent supply bottlenecks for industrial goods and recovering demand
column2: especially in the services sector
column3: are also contributing to the current high rates of inflation. Price pressures are spreading across more and more sectors
column4: in part owing to the indirect impact of high energy costs across the whole economy. Accordingly
column5: most measures of underlying inflation have risen further.

column1: We expect inflation to remain undesirably high for some time
column2: owing to continued pressures from energy and food prices and pipeline pressures in the pricing chain. Higher inflationary pressures are also stemming from the depreciation of the euro exchange rate. But looking further ahead
column3: in the absence of new disruptions
column4: energy costs should stabilise and supply bottlenecks should ease
column5: which
column6: together with the ongoing policy normalisation
column7: should support the return of inflation to our target.

column1: The labour market remains strong. Unemployment fell to a historical low of 6.6 per cent in May. Job vacancies across many sectors show that there is robust demand for labour. Wage growth
column2: also according to forward-looking indicators
column3: has continued to increase gradually over the last few months
column4: but still remains contained overall. Over time
column5: the strengthening of the economy and some catch-up effects should support faster growth in wages. Most measures of longer-term inflation expectations currently stand at around two per cent
column6: although recent above-target revisions to some indicators warrant continued monitoring.

column1: Risk assessment
A prolongation of the war in Ukraine remains a source of significant downside risk to growth
column2: especially if energy supplies from Russia were to be disrupted to such an extent that it led to rationing for firms and households. The war may also further dampen confidence and aggravate supply-side constraints
column3: while energy and food costs could remain persistently higher than expected. A faster deceleration in global growth would also pose a risk to the euro area outlook.

column1: The risks to the inflation outlook continue to be on the upside and have intensified
column2: particularly in the short term. The risks to the medium-term inflation outlook include a durable worsening of the production capacity of our economy
column3: persistently high energy and food prices
column4: inflation expectations rising above our target and higher than anticipated wage rises. However
column5: if demand were to weaken over the medium term
column6: it would lower pressures on prices.

column1: Financial and monetary conditions
Market interest rates have been volatile as a result of the pronounced economic and geopolitical uncertainty. Bank funding costs have risen in recent months
column2: which has increasingly fed into higher bank lending rates
column3: in particular for households. While the volume of bank lending to households remains strong
column4: it is expected to decline in view of lower demand. Lending to firms has also been robust as high production costs
column5: inventory building and lower reliance on market funding have created a continued need for credit from banks. At the same time
column6: demand for loans to finance investment has declined. Money growth has continued to moderate owing to lower liquid savings and lower Eurosystem asset purchases.

column1: Our most recent bank lending survey reports that credit standards tightened for all loan categories in the second quarter of the year
column2: as banks are becoming more concerned about the risks faced by their customers in the current uncertain environment. Banks expect to continue tightening their credit standards in the third quarter.

column1: Conclusion
Summing up
column2: inflation continues to be undesirably high and is expected to remain above our target for some time. The latest data indicate a slowdown in growth
column3: clouding the outlook for the second half of 2022 and beyond. At the same time
column4: this slowdown is being cushioned by a number of supportive factors.

column2: 7-8 September 2022|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel started by noting that the narrative in financial markets had shifted since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting in July. Initially
column2: fears of a recession had dominated global asset prices and financial conditions had eased on the expectation that the pace of interest rate increases by central banks around the world would slow down
column3: as a recession was perceived to do part of the job of bringing inflation back to the target level. However
column4: more recently the focus of investors had gradually shifted back towards a tighter monetary policy stance as inflation outcomes had continued to be higher than expected.

column1: In this environment
column2: there had been four key observations. First
column3: volatility in interest rate markets remained at historically high levels
column4: reflecting very high uncertainty regarding inflation
column5: as well as heightened data dependence of monetary policy. Second
column6: monetary policy normalisation in the euro area was now expected to proceed at a significantly faster pace than had been expected at the time of the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. Third
column7: the summer rally in risk assets had been halted and partly reversed by investors’ reappraisal of the future path of monetary policy. Finally
column8: the sensitivity of euro area sovereign bond yield spreads to policy rate expectations remained notably weaker than before the Governing Council’s ad hoc meeting on 15 June 2022.

column1: Volatility in global interest rate markets and currency markets remained elevated. The heightened volatility in interest rate markets had primarily been driven by the uncertainty around the future course of inflation and the shift of monetary policy to a meeting-by-meeting approach
column2: which had increased data dependency.

column1: Regarding the change in policy rate expectations
column2: markets had reassessed both the extent and the pace of policy normalisation. After reaching a trough in late July
column3: the “terminal rate” (the level at which market participants expected the policy interest rate to peak) had rebounded markedly and currently stood close to the peak seen in mid-June. The expected speed of progress towards this terminal rate had also increased
column4: as investors expected a less gradual tightening cycle.

column1: The steeper expected policy path partly reflected the fact that investors attached an increasing probability to a scenario of inflation being higher for longer. Investors now expected inflation to peak in December
column2: instead of September
column3: as had been expected at the time of the July meeting. Options markets also pointed to rising upside risks to inflation
column4: with investors currently pricing in a probability of around 15% that inflation would
column5: on average
column6: be above 4% over the next five years. Moreover
column7: some measures of longer-term inflation compensation had started to creep higher again.

column1: In the euro area
column2: with the latest increase in front-end inflation swap rates
column3: real short-term rates were expected to remain highly accommodative for some time to come. This contrasted markedly with developments in the United States
column4: where
column5: according to market-based estimates
column6: comparable rates were expected to be in restrictive territory in 2023.

column1: Ms Schnabel then explained how the reappraisal of monetary policy expectations had been transmitted to broader financial markets. Equity prices had increased notably during the summer
column2: in spite of the weaker growth outlook
column3: but had started to decline in the second half of August owing to increased concern about inflation – and the associated increase in discount rates – and weaker corporate earnings growth expectations. Yet
column4: the decline in risk asset prices had been partly offset by an improvement in investor sentiment
column5: as investors now required less compensation for holding risky assets instead of risk-free bonds. Overall
column6: US stock markets were slightly down
column7: while euro area markets were notably below the levels prevailing at the time of the Governing Council’s July meeting. A key factor in this divergence had been the sharp rise in European energy prices
column8: which weighed on households’ real disposable income and firms’ earnings expectations.

column1: High energy prices in Europe and rising downside risks to growth in the euro area relative to the United States were also weighing on the euro exchange rate
column2: as was the divergence of the expected path of the policy rate differential between the two economies.

column1: In euro area fixed income markets
column2: in tandem with the repricing of other risk assets
column3: corporate bond spreads had temporarily narrowed during the early summer
column4: in line with a recovery in investors’ risk appetite
column5: before reversing some of the narrowing in August.

column1: Euro area sovereign spreads had gradually widened
column2: reflecting the shift in policy rate expectations. Yet
column3: the link between spreads and interest rate expectations seemed to have become weaker since the Governing Council’s ad hoc meeting on 15 June 2022.

column1: In money markets
column2: the pass-through of the 50 basis point rate hike in July had been smooth
column3: with some exceptions in the repo and Treasury bill markets. Specifically
column4: there had been only a partial pass-through to German non-general collateral rates following the July hike
column5: mainly reflecting the scarcity of German Bund collateral.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Mr Lane then went through the latest economic
column2: monetary and financial developments in the global economy and the euro area. After the unusually high economic growth rates recorded at the start of the year as sectors reopened
column3: global activity had slowed to the average growth rates observed before the pandemic. The deceleration in trade
column4: coupled with a fall in new export orders
column5: pointed to a continued loss of momentum. Despite a reduction in the Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) for suppliers’ delivery times
column6: resulting from weakening demand and the partial resolution of supply bottlenecks
column7: the overall level of supply bottlenecks remained elevated. The euro had been depreciating since the start of 2021
column8: driven in part by monetary policy expectations and the worsening terms of trade.

column1: Turning to euro area activity
column2: there had been a significant moderation in the manufacturing sector since the start of 2022
column3: with the PMI for manufacturing output falling below the threshold of 50 – indicating a contraction – in the second quarter. The level of the PMI for services activity had been higher but was also weakening – even in the accommodation and food sectors
column4: which had benefited most from the reopening of the economy. After the euro area economy had grown by 0.8% in the second quarter of 2022
column5: mechanical short-term forecasting tools pointed to a substantial slowdown in activity in the third and fourth quarters.

column1: Focusing on demand components
column2: private consumption had recovered significantly in the second quarter thanks to a strong contribution from the consumption of services
column3: while the consumption of durable goods had continued to be weak over the period. The European Commission survey pointed to a significant weakening of demand for contact-intensive services in the future
column4: together with a weakening of demand for goods from already low levels. The European Commission’s uncertainty indicator pointed to a big increase in household uncertainty and in the perceived need for precautionary savings.

column1: Moving on to investment
column2: after a first quarter that had still been affected by supply bottlenecks and lockdowns
column3: non-construction investment had recorded a strong growth rate in the second quarter of 2022. By contrast
column4: the contribution of construction investment had been limited
column5: with housing investment declining. Survey indicators suggested a moderation in non-construction investment in the second half of the year.

column1: The euro area goods trade balance had stabilised at around 3% of GDP in June
column2: with the energy balance resulting in a deficit of around 5% of GDP in the second quarter. The effect on income of the terms-of-trade loss amounted to about 5 percentage points
column3: which constituted the income transfer to energy-exporting countries outside the euro area and implied 5 percentage points less available income for domestic spending.

column1: The labour market had remained robust in the second quarter
column2: but the PMI for employment signalled a moderation in the third quarter across all sectors. An analysis of the relationship between unemployment and the job vacancy rate – the Beveridge curve – helped to better understand the dynamics in the labour market. In the euro area there was currently a historically low unemployment rate and a historically high vacancy rate. By comparison
column3: in the United States the ratio of vacancies to unemployment was a lot higher.

column3: but all other components also played significant roles.

column4: was related to the assumption of a speedier pass-through of energy and food inflation to core inflation. From the last quarter of 2023 onwards

column3: as reflected in monthly changes
column4: some indicators had started to flatten or had even turned slightly negative. This was likely due to the fact that these indicators were more sensitive to changes in oil prices

column2: some measures remained robust. However

column4: i.e. goods in the early stages of the production chain

column2: it was not only supply shocks that were important

column4: it was important to distinguish between a recovery in demand and a situation of excess demand.

column1: This distinction also mattered for the comparison of inflation in the euro area and in the United States. In the United States
column2: the pick-up in core inflation was closely matched by a pick-up in wage growth. This was not the case in the euro area
column3: where there was a clear disconnect between the evolution of core inflation and that of negotiated wages. In the euro area
column4: inflation in items in the HICP basket with a relatively high share of wages in direct input costs had broadly followed the dynamics of negotiated wages and had thus remained quite contained overall. The large movements in euro area core inflation were instead due to other components
column5: such as manufacturing goods and other items with a relatively low share of wages in direct input costs. It followed that the factors behind the increase in core inflation in the two economies were different

column2: in the second quarter euro area negotiated wages had grown by 2.4%. The experimental ECB wage tracker pointed to a gradual acceleration in wage growth over the coming quarters. Recently concluded wage agreements included increases of around 3%
column3: on average
column4: in the euro area for both 2022 and 2023. However
column5: in the agreements concluded in the third quarter
column6: wage increases for 2023 were slightly lower than in the agreements concluded in the second quarter. So far there had not been an accelerating trend in the data.

column2: the Survey of Monetary Analysts (SMA) showed that analysts had been continuously re-estimating the inflation rate for this year and next year. However
column3: for 2023
column4: the projected inflation rate was 4%
column5: which was significantly below the 5.5% inflation rate included in the September staff projections. The SMA also pointed to a stable 2% inflation rate for 2024. Three-year ahead inflation expectations
column6: as measured by responses to the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey
column7: had jumped in March this year and since then had continued to fluctuate around the March level.

column4: inflation compensation measures embedded a very steep decline
column5: to around 2%
column6: by mid-2024.

column1: Financial market developments

Ms Schnabel noted that uncertainty had increased in financial markets since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 7-8 September 2022. This had occurred amid persistently high inflation and elevated fears of a recession
column2: with increased attention on potential financial instability. Inflation concerns had remained the dominant driver of financial market developments
column3: as inflation outcomes had continued to surprise to the upside
column4: leading to a renewed adjustment of market expectations for monetary policy globally. Against the background of persistent inflation surprises
column5: investors had sharply revised up their expectations regarding central banks’ “terminal policy rate” (the level at which market participants expected the current interest rate cycle to peak) as embedded in risk-free rates
column6: for all major advanced economies
column7: albeit to different degrees.

column1: In the euro area
column2: compared with expectations at the time of the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting
column3: market pricing and survey evidence now pointed to expectations of a faster pace of policy rate hikes and a markedly higher terminal rate. Forceful policy action was bringing about a tightening of financial conditions
column4: with medium to longer-term real interest rates moving notably higher and risk assets continuing to be sold off. However
column5: there was still a high degree of uncertainty about the extent of the policy adjustment needed to rein in inflation. At the same time
column6: investors had gradually shifted their attention towards the side effects of the sharp global rate hiking cycle
column7: amid tighter funding conditions for lower-rated entities
column8: low market liquidity and heightened volatility in repo markets.

column1: The heightened concerns about inflation had resulted in euro area risk-free yields being much more sensitive to news about inflation in 2022 than had been the case in 2021. In contrast
column2: the relationship between risk-free yields and news about growth had remained rather weak
column3: suggesting that market participants expected central banks to focus primarily on inflation.

column1: In the United States
column2: the adjustment of near-term rate expectations in financial market prices had been even more pronounced. Unlike in the euro area
column3: the forward rate curve in the United States showed a marked inversion
column4: signalling expectations of a reversal of rate hikes in the course of 2023.

column1: In the euro area
column2: real interest rates had increased across the entire maturity spectrum since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. However
column3: they were still deeply negative at short maturities and remained below the levels prevailing in previous tightening cycles
column4: such as in December 2006
column5: when inflationary pressures had been far less intense.

column1: On the back of repeated upward inflation surprises and heightened uncertainty about the path of monetary policy required to tame inflation
column2: market-based measures of longer-term inflation compensation in the euro area had trended upwards in recent weeks. They now stood above the levels observed at the time of the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting
column3: despite the sharp reappraisal of monetary policy expectations. Additional inflationary pressure could emanate from the ongoing depreciation of the euro. So far this year the euro had weakened by 13% vis-à-vis the US dollar. Considering that the bulk of commodities were denominated in US dollars
column4: such currency developments had exacerbated the energy price shock.

column1: The reappraisal of monetary policy expectations had led to a broad-based tightening of financial conditions beyond risk-free rates. The global sell-off in equity markets had continued also in the euro area
column2: even though analysts had lately made only limited downward revisions to euro area firms’ longer-term earnings prospects and earnings expectations remained at a high level overall. Cyclically adjusted price-earnings ratios had come down markedly from the elevated levels prevailing during the extended period of accommodative monetary policy. They were now much closer to
column3: albeit still above

column1: Monetary policy considerations and policy options
In view of the protracted period of excessively high inflation and the risk that this may add to medium-term price pressures
column2: Mr Lane proposed that the three key ECB interest rates be raised again by 75 basis points at the present meeting. With this third major policy rate increase in a row
column3: substantial progress would be made in withdrawing monetary policy accommodation. Since the ECB’s policy rates were still accommodative
column4: a large increase would underscore the Governing Council’s commitment to taming inflation by reducing support for demand and ensuring inflation expectations remained anchored at the medium-term target. As a further tangible sign of this commitment
column5: it should be communicated that the Governing Council expected to raise rates further. The future rate path should be based on the evolving outlook for inflation and the economy
column6: following a meeting-by-meeting approach.

column1: In addition to further rate normalisation
column2: Mr Lane proposed changing the terms and conditions of the third series of targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTRO III). During the acute phase of the pandemic
column3: the TLTROs had played a key role in countering downside risks to price stability. In that period the ECB had granted exceptionally favourable conditions to credit institutions that borrowed via these operations
column4: with the aim of sustaining the supply of bank loans to the real economy at a time when banks were likely to pull back and disengage from credit intermediation. At present
column5: in view of the unexpected and extraordinary rise in inflation
column6: the instrument needed to be recalibrated to ensure that it was consistent with the broader monetary policy normalisation process and to reinforce the transmission of policy rate increases to bank lending conditions. It was therefore necessary to adjust the interest rates applicable to TLTRO III from 23 November 2022 and to offer banks additional voluntary early repayment dates.

column2: it would contribute to the normalisation of bank funding costs. The ensuing normalisation of financing conditions would
column3: in turn
column4: exert downward pressure on inflation over the medium term. Moreover

column4: comply with its governance

column7: many of them have accumulated sufficient buffers
column8: or sufficient provisions
column9: in order to go through the current crisis

column1: Do you think that the inflation rate will already fall in December? And do you think it will be more difficult to go on hiking rates if inflation is falling in the future?
It may well be that the December number of HICP
column2: and possibly core inflation
column3: be a little bit lower. But we have good reasons to believe that January and February
column4: for instance
column5: are likely to be higher. So we cannot be fixated on one single number. We have to look at a trend
column6: we have to look at the inflation outlook
column7: we have to consider what has been achieved

column9: because for the moment

column1: I have two questions. The first one is about the impact of balance sheet reduction. Recently
column2: Mr de Guindos admitted that the ECB was unaware of the consequences of starting the review to reduce the balance sheet
column3: as he lacks prior experience. Have you discussed about that possible impact? Could you help us to shed some more light on this?

column1: In second place
column2: we’ve seen how recently the ECB has increased its warnings about banks
column3: saying that they are being very bullish on the outlook
column4: but my question is
column5: isn’t the ECB also being overly optimistic in saying that the recession would be relatively short-lived and shallow?

column1: Thank you for your question
column2: but the Vice President is much more equipped than me to address your question.

column1: De Guindos: Well
column2: the question on the banks: we have always indicated that the interest rates is improving the short-term profitability of the European banks
column3: but that we should not be blinded because of this improvement
column4: this short-term improvement in profitability. And that we should take into consideration perhaps a broader picture of the situation. In that sense
column5: first of all
column6: we are projecting that financing conditions are tightening
column7: and this will have an impact on the funding of the European banks. And simultaneously the slowdown of the economy will have also an impact on the solvency of the clients of the banks. So that’s the approach. It’s a cautious approach. The recent improvement in the return on equity of the European banks
column8: but simultaneously we have to look a little bit further away
column9: and in that respect we have to take into consideration the solvency of the clients and the impact that the increase in the interest rates is going to have on the funding of the European banks.

column1: With respect to the question of the balance sheet
column2: well
column3: I think that the point that I wanted to make is quite clear. The reduction of the balance sheet – QT – is a new experience for us. It’s a new tool for the ECB. In that respect
column4: that’s why as the President has indicated
column5: we have to be predictable
column6: and we have to be measured and prudent in the implementation of QT
column7: and that’s what we have discussed in the Governing Council
column8: and that’s why we have decided that we will start with that reduction of our balance sheet of €15 billion

column10: and we will continuously assess the impact that this measure is having on financing conditions
column11: on the monetary situation

column1: Yesterday
column2: the FRB [Federal Reserve Board] decided to slowdown the pace of hiking interest rates. What is the implication for the ECB’s monetary policies? Of course
column3: I know monetary policy decisions are made by each central bank
column4: but is it possible the ECB will continue to raise interest rates after the FRB has finished raising rates?

column1: Thank you for your question
column2: because it helps me to clarify one thing. Anybody who thinks that this is a pivot for the ECB is wrong. We’re not pivoting
column3: we’re not wavering. We are showing determination and resilience in continuing a journey where we have
column4: if you compare – comparisons are odious
column5: but if you were to compare with the Fed – we have more ground to cover. We have longer to go
column6: and that is the reason why we have very specifically added messages in our monetary policy statement to reflect that fact. This is not a pivot. We’re not slowing down. We’re in for the long game. Which is why we said we have to rise significantly
column7: we have to move at a steady pace
column8: we have to reach levels that are sufficiently restrictive
column9: so that the interest rate takes us to the inflation of 2% timely
column10: and we have to remain at those levels to make sure that we actually have sufficient certainty that we are there
column11: and that we have
column12: indeed
column13: tamed inflation. So I know that it is tempting to assume that
column14: oh
column15: well
column16: all central banks are doing the same thing at the same time. Not quite. The ECB is not pivoting.

column1: My first question is about cryptocurrencies
column2: because now that Mr Bankman-Fried is behind bars
column3: and we have the thousands bankruptcy of cryptocurrency
column4: are you still worried – I mean
column5: Mr Panetta was very severe in the last days – but what is your opinion about cryptocurrencies? How should they be regulated
column6: and are you still worried that a big tech like Facebook might one day announce its cryptocurrency?

column1: My second question is about Italy
column2: because the markets have become quite calm around Italy
column3: and it didn’t seem so in the summer
column4: because it was a new government
column5: do you think that the TPI [Transmission Protection Mechanism] is already having an effect on the markets

column1: On your first question
column2: I entirely support the views expressed by Mr Panetta
column3: who has been actively engaged in framing the digital euro that we have worked on
column4: and of which we will know the future in October 2023. That’s the time when we will actually decide whether we go for real. But I have long
column5: long ago indicated that cryptoassets – I wouldn’t call them cryptocurrencies – but cryptoassets need to be regulated on a global basis. I remember when I said that some three years ago. It made some people laugh. I still think to this day – and I’m not the only one – that there has to be a framework
column6: a regulation
column7: supervision
column8: transparency of information
column9: so that there are no misled consumers with tempting offers as a result of those cryptoassets being around. I feel quite strongly about that
column10: and I’m pleased that there are colleagues around the world that are now of the same view
column11: and whether it’s Terra
column12: LUNA
column13: FTX or others
column14: we are clearly seeing that the lack of regulation
column15: the lack of supervision
column16: is exposing consumers around the world. I’m really pleased to see
column17: as well
column18: that MiCA
column19: at the European level
column20: is a breakthrough. I’m not sure that it’s enough. I hope it’s MiCA 1 and there will be a MiCA 2
column21: to go further
column22: but at least we are setting some standards which
column23: hopefully
column24: will inspire others around the world to also develop such a framework.

column1: In relation to TPI
column2: as you know
column3: this is a tool that is in the toolbox
column4: that
column5: together with the flexibility of reinvestments
column6: is intended to make sure that our monetary policy is transmitted smoothly across the entire euro area. And as far as we can tell
column7: our monetary policy is currently well transmitted around the euro area. But it’s
column8: obviously
column9: a tool that we have available
column10: that we shall use if necessary. It’s not intended to deal with country fundamentals
column11: but it’s intended to address the issue of transmission of monetary policy.

column1: I have one question similar to the question Jerome Powell got yesterday. Compared to the October meeting
column2: some of the financial conditions have become looser
column3: actually. Bond yields have gone down
column4: for example. So does that not undermine your fight against inflation? What’s your view on that?

column1: Second question
column2: you want to raise rates at a steady pace
column3: 50 basis points. That somehow reminds me of forward guidance. Why are you giving up this flexibility to decide from meeting to meeting?

column1: Let me make that point clear. Forward guidance
column2: we certainly take it as a principle in relation to QT. We’re very explicit. We refer to €15 billion on average per month over a period of four months
column3: and then we will reassess at the end of the second quarter. On the issue of interest rates
column4: we will be looking at data. We will be data-dependent
column5: and we will review data
column6: particularly when we have projection meetings that are every three months or so. We will reassess very carefully. But what we know today is
column7: given the financing conditions
column8: as you mentioned
column9: given the expected terminal rate embedded in our projections
column10: this is not enough
column11: and we need to take this fight and continue the battle against inflation. So we will continue that at a steady pace. Based on the information that we have available today
column12: that predicates another 50-basis-point rate hike at our next meeting
column13: and possibly at the one after that
column14: and possibly thereafter
column15: but everything will also be determined by the review of data. So don’t assume that it’s a one-shot 50; it’s more than that. I don’t know how many more times. So it shouldn’t be regarded as the new normal
column16: but in the current circumstances
column17: we believe that this the right approach on a steady-pace basis.

column1: The forecast for growth in 2023 was down to 0.5%
column2: which leaves very little room for avoiding a recession. Now that you say that you will raise the rates again many times. Don’t you fear that it would lead to the eurozone to fall into a recession?

column1: As I mentioned earlier on
column2: in our staff projections we anticipate at the turn of the year
column3: meaning fourth quarter
column4: possibly
column5: first quarter of 2023
column6: a shallow and short-lived recession. We also anticipate that after that shallow and short-lived recession
column7: for various reasons that we can go into
column8: including this issue of the supply bottleneck
column9: the base effects on the energy front
column10: the active and robust labour markets
column11: we anticipate that the recovery will pick up
column12: which is the reason why we have this 0.5% projection for growth in 2023. But we also believe
column13: because it is our job
column14: that we have to deliver on our mandate of price stability. And under the current circumstances with the data we have
column15: with the inflation projections that have been updated on the occasion of this meeting we have to stay the course and raise significantly interest rates
column16: which is what we are doing today
column17: and do so at a steady pace
column18: because we have more ground to cover. We will need to do that up until such time when our interest rates will deliver the 2% inflation target that we have.

column1: 2023.01.19 13:30:00|Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday
column2: 14-15 December 2022|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments

Ms Schnabel noted that since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 26-27 October 2022 the narrative in financial markets had shifted from inflation concerns to expectations that central banks worldwide would slow down
column2: halt and ultimately reverse interest rate hikes. The data on the US consumer price index (CPI) for October
column3: interpreted as an early sign of an easing of inflation pressures
column4: had prompted a market repricing of policy rate expectations for the United States. This had been further reinforced by the US CPI inflation figures for November
column5: which had again surprised on the downside. The resulting rebound in investor risk appetite had led to a broad-based easing of global financial conditions
column6: showing up in lower nominal and real yields
column7: tighter credit spreads and buoyant equity markets in the euro area – all of which worked against the ECB’s intention to withdraw monetary policy accommodation.

column1: These developments had occurred in an environment in which news about the euro area economy had turned more positive. At the same time
column2: there had been a notable upward repricing by markets of the near-term inflation outlook
column3: and the risk of longer-term inflation expectations becoming unanchored remained elevated. Market conditions remained challenging as uncertainty about monetary policy and volatility in market interest rates continued to be high
column4: amid low liquidity and collateral scarcity.

column1: Market hopes of a turning point in inflation developments and a change in direction
column2: or “pivot”
column3: of global monetary policy appeared to have spilled over into euro area interest rate expectations. The euro area overnight index swap (OIS) forward curve had become inverted
column4: signalling expectations of moderate cuts in the ECB’s key policy rates over the next two to three years. By contrast
column5: near-term market pricing remained broadly unchanged. The expected “terminal rate” at the peak of the present hiking cycle continued to stand at around 2.8% and market participants expected the key ECB interest rates to increase by 50 basis points both at the present meeting and at the meeting in February 2023
column6: with a final 25 basis point increment expected in March 2023.

column1: Spillovers from the United States had been the predominant driver of recent movements in euro area risk-free yields
column2: as reflected in their sensitivity to macroeconomic news from the United States. The reappraisal of rate expectations in the euro area beyond the near term seemed to be at odds with domestic developments
column3: such as incoming data on the macroeconomy
column4: energy prices and the market-based inflation outlook.

column1: In particular
column2: economic data releases in the euro area had recently turned positive after a period of weaker than expected outcomes
column3: pointing to waning risks of a deep and protracted recession
column4: which market participants had previously considered a key factor putting downward pressure on euro area inflation. At the same time
column5: natural gas prices had rebounded sharply from the lows recorded in late October owing to mild weather conditions and full storage facilities
column6: and they were now at levels comparable to those seen in early summer
column7: pointing to renewed tightness in the European gas market.

column1: On the back of receding downside tail risks to economic growth and higher energy prices
column2: there had been a notable upward repricing of market-based expectations for inflation in the near term. Looking at the evolution of longer-term inflation expectations in the euro area
column3: signals of upside risks were observed both in market-based indicators and in surveys. In the ECB Survey of Professional Forecasters and the ECB Survey of Monetary Analysts (SMA) the distribution of responses had shifted markedly over the course of the past few months
column4: with a significant and rising share of respondents expecting a sustained period of inflation above the ECB’s 2% target.

column1: Despite higher near-term inflation expectations and upside risks to the longer-term inflation outlook
column2: the global repricing of monetary policy rate expectations had led to an easing of broader financial conditions in the euro area. Market participants’ expectations that central banks would cut policy rates soon after reaching the terminal rate had led to a decline in longer-term yields relative to short-term yields.

column1: The recent repricing of policy rate expectations had led to a decrease in euro area real GDP-weighted sovereign bond yields across the maturity spectrum since the peak reached in mid-October. Real rates were again in negative territory across all maturities up to ten years. Moreover
column2: yield spreads had continued to narrow in euro area sovereign and corporate bond markets. Market expectations of a global monetary policy pivot had had the most pronounced effect on equity markets
column3: which had seen a renewed “relief” rally. The downward trend in cyclically adjusted price-earnings ratios had been reversed just when they had been approaching their long-run averages.

column1: Developments in exchange rates had closely reflected the drivers of recent broader market developments. The sustained rally of the US dollar appeared to have come to an end
column2: in line with an unwinding of long positions in US dollars. The change in the monetary policy outlook for the United States
column3: the return to a “risk-on” environment and a comparatively better economic outlook for the euro area had been the main drivers of the appreciation of the euro since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting.

column1: Conditions remained challenging in euro area money and repo markets
column2: although there had been significant improvements lately. Year-end tensions arising from collateral scarcity in jurisdictions with high credit ratings had decreased
column3: as illustrated by the significant increase in the respective repo rates for the turn of the year. These positive dynamics had to be seen in the light of the decisions taken by authorities
column4: including the Eurosystem and national debt management offices
column5: over the last few weeks to alleviate collateral scarcity. Overall
column6: however
column7: pricing in the repo market remained expensive
column8: as various factors such as market positioning
column9: interest rate volatility and valuation effects continued to exacerbate the structural factors behind collateral scarcity in the secured money market.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: the repayment of funds under the ECB’s targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTROs) and the prospective future reduction of the Eurosystem’s portfolios of securities held for monetary policy purposes
column3: together with the expected significant new issuance activity
column4: were expected to support the availability of collateral in 2023.

column1: In the unsecured money market segment
column2: the observed downward pressure on bank borrowing rates reflected the availability of excess cash to be invested at a time when policy rates were rising quickly. This had led to EURIBOR rates being persistently lower than the equivalent OIS rates for maturities of up to three months since the start of the policy rate hiking cycle last summer.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Starting with the international environment
column2: Mr Lane highlighted that global trade momentum had softened significantly towards the end of 2022. Looking ahead
column3: the global Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) indicator for new export orders was well below the threshold of 50
column4: pointing to continued weakness in global trade. The weakening in trade had reduced the pressures on supply chains. Indeed
column5: the PMI indicator for suppliers’ delivery times had continued to improve up to November. This suggested that this factor that had been holding back production and pushing up prices for a long time was diminishing and could be expected to disappear next year.

column1: The euro had appreciated in nominal effective terms since the Governing Council’s monetary policy meeting in October
column2: after depreciating for almost two years. Regarding commodity prices
column3: the oil futures curve had declined since the October meeting. By contrast
column4: gas spot prices had rebounded strongly
column5: while futures prices had remained broadly unchanged at elevated levels since October.

column1: Turning to the euro area
column2: real GDP growth had slowed to 0.3% in the third quarter of 2022. This reflected a record increase in investment in Ireland
column3: which
column4: on an annualised basis
column5: had grown by 850% compared with the previous quarter. Excluding Ireland
column6: real GDP in the euro area had grown by 0.2%. With regard to the demand components of GDP
column7: private consumption had grown strongly in the second and third quarters of 2022
column8: particularly in Germany
column9: Spain and Italy
column10: as the growth of nominal consumer income and the use of accumulated savings had compensated for the high rate of inflation. In the final quarter of 2022
column11: however
column12: private consumption was projected to have stagnated on account of declining real incomes
column13: while households were expected to have become more reluctant to dip into savings. After continuously declining since the start of Russia’s war in Ukraine
column14: consumer confidence had improved somewhat in October and November
column15: but remained low from a historical perspective. Moving to investment
column16: residential investment growth had been in negative territory since the spring
column17: while the growth of non-construction investment (excluding the contribution from intellectual property products in Ireland) had decelerated in the third quarter of 2022 and was expected to contract in the final quarter.

column1: Turning to trade
column2: the significant decline in the goods trade balance that had started in mid-2021 had been interrupted in September owing to a small improvement in energy import prices and European firms being able to charge higher prices and sell more non-energy goods to the rest of the world. These developments had helped to partially offset the higher energy bill.

column1: Short-term economic activity indicators and mechanical short-term GDP forecasting continued to suggest a contraction in economic activity in the fourth quarter of 2022. At the sectoral level
column2: PMI indicators for the manufacturing sector continued to point to weak output but had improved somewhat owing to the continued easing of supply bottlenecks
column3: which had allowed firms to work through their order backlogs. In the services sector
column4: forward-looking indicators of economic activity were declining
column5: in line with a normalisation following the boost from the reopening of the economy in the first part of the year.

column1: Labour markets had seen a significant recovery in employment in the wake of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. However
column2: total hours worked per person employed had recovered to a much more limited extent. Looking ahead
column3: PMI indicators were pointing to a deceleration in employment growth across sectors. Regarding measures of labour market tightness
column4: countries with low unemployment also had a high vacancy rate
column5: while countries with high unemployment had a low vacancy rate.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: according to the December 2022 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area
column3: annual average real GDP growth was projected to slow down markedly from 3.4% in 2022 to 0.5% in 2023
column4: and then to rebound to 1.9% in 2024 and 1.8% in 2025. Compared with the September 2022 ECB staff projections
column5: the outlook for growth had been revised up by 0.3 percentage points for 2022
column6: owing to positive surprises over the summer
column7: and down by 0.4 percentage points for 2023. The GDP growth outlook had remained unchanged for 2024.

column1: Risks to the growth outlook were on the downside
column2: especially in the near term. Russia’s war in Ukraine remained a significant downside risk to the economy. Energy and food costs could also remain persistently higher than expected. There could be an additional drag on growth in the euro area if the world economy were to weaken more sharply than expected. In the downside scenario in the December projections – which assumed a complete cut-off of Russian gas – real GDP would contract by 0.6% in 2023 before recovering to grow by 0.2% in 2024 and 2.0% in 2025.

column1: Turning to fiscal policies
column2: in 2022 the size of fiscal measures to compensate for the energy crisis had increased from 1.2% of GDP
column3: as embedded in the September ECB staff projections
column4: to 1.9% of GDP according to the December Eurosystem staff projections. The December projections also implied a strong upward revision to the fiscal support measures for 2023
column5: which were now estimated at 1.9% of GDP
column6: with some of these measures expected to remain in place in 2024 (0.5% of GDP) and in 2025 (0.2% of GDP). The cyclically adjusted primary balance
column7: which had deteriorated to -3.4% of GDP in 2020
column8: was seen reaching -1.3% in 2022
column9: as pandemic-related measures were progressively withdrawn. It was projected to deteriorate again in 2023
column10: to -1.6% of GDP
column11: before improving by almost 1 percentage point in 2024 to -0.7% of GDP.

column1: Moving to the latest inflation developments
column2: according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: headline inflation had declined to 10.0% in November
column4: from 10.6% in October
column5: owing to lower energy inflation
column6: which was partly offset by an increase in food inflation. The decline in energy inflation in November mainly reflected lower crude oil and gas price inflation. Energy inflation was expected to drop further in December as a result of the fiscal measures taken in some euro area countries. However
column7: in January and February 2023 it was expected to increase again
column8: as many utility companies adjusted their prices in January or February. Subsequently the December staff projections foresaw a decline in energy inflation. However
column9: this was much more gradual than had been projected earlier
column10: reflecting a delayed pass-through of wholesale gas and electricity prices to customers with long-term contracts.

column1: Food inflation had increased to 13.6% in November and was projected to continue its upward trend into early 2023 before declining from mid-year. The expected increase until early 2023 was due to the fact that the large increases seen in international food commodity prices had not yet fully passed through to retail prices. For goods inflation
column2: there had been a slowdown in price rises at the early stages of the production chain
column3: which had not yet passed through to retail prices. The observed significant slowdown in intermediate goods inflation should start to be visible in retail goods inflation in the course of 2023.

column1: Indicators of underlying inflation had remained at high levels in October
column2: with most measures still increasing but some stabilising – notably those affected by the lower month-on-month energy inflation. The momentum in domestic inflation had been slowing down since mid-2022
column3: which could be related to the easing of the indirect effects of energy prices and supply bottlenecks. At the same time
column4: inflation in wage-intensive components of the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) had been picking up over the past few months.

column1: Negotiated wage growth had continued to increase in the third quarter and the experimental ECB wage tracker pointed to a substantial further rise in the growth of negotiated wages in the next few quarters. In the seven countries covered by the wage tracker
column2: agreements signed so far in the fourth quarter of 2022 implied wage increases of around 5%
column3: both in 2022 and in 2023
column4: which was broadly in line with the December staff projections.

column1: The November round of the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey reported that perceptions of current inflation had stabilised at 10%
column2: clearly showing that consumers were paying attention to the level of inflation. One-year ahead inflation expectations showed the first signs of a reversal
column3: declining from 5.4% in October to 5.0% in November
column4: while three-year ahead inflation expectations remained stable at around 3%.

column1: Turning to the key features of the December 2022 projections
column2: inflation had been revised up significantly to an average of 8.4% for 2022
column3: 6.3% for 2023 and 3.4% for 2024. Inflation was projected to average 2.3% in 2025. The upward revisions had been driven by a combination of repeated inflation surprises in recent months (with the exception of November)
column4: more persistent pipeline price pressures and faster wage growth. The annual averages masked the strong downward base effects in energy inflation
column5: which were projected to bring headline inflation down from 10.0% in the fourth quarter of 2022 to 3.6% in the last quarter of 2023. Inflation was then projected to ease further to 3.3% in the last quarter 2024 and 2.0% from the third quarter of 2025 onwards. The somewhat unusual time profile of inflation over 2023 and 2024 was due to the fact that the fiscal measures designed to tackle the energy price crisis were expected to dampen inflation in 2023
column6: but push it up in 2024
column7: when many of these measures were scheduled to be unwound.

column1: Core inflation (i.e. HICP inflation excluding energy and food) was projected to average 3.9% in 2022 and 4.2% in 2023
column2: before falling to 2.8% in 2024 and 2.4% in 2025. Strong wage growth amid robust labour market dynamics was a primary contributor to the persistence of core inflation
column3: but the indirect effects of higher energy and food costs on core inflation remained substantial in 2023 and in 2024
column4: and also played a role in explaining core inflation in 2025. The past depreciation of the euro would also push up core inflation in 2023 and 2024. The projected core inflation rates in 2024 and 2025 would have been significantly lower without the estimated indirect effects of energy inflation and the effect of the exchange rate.

column1: Risks to the inflation outlook were primarily on the upside. In the near term existing pipeline pressures could lead to stronger than expected rises in retail prices for energy and food. Over the medium term risks stemmed primarily from domestic factors
column2: such as a persistent rise in inflation expectations above the ECB’s target or higher than anticipated wage rises. By contrast
column3: a decline in energy costs or a further weakening of demand would lower price pressures. The updated downside scenario in the December projections that reflected these risks pointed to higher inflation than in the baseline in 2023 and 2024 (at 7.4% and 3.6% respectively) as energy prices spiked
column4: whereas in 2025 inflation was seen dropping below the baseline
column6: as the downward impact from the demand channel started to dominate. Uncertainty about the impact of monetary policy tightening also constituted a risk to the inflation projections
column7: with a wide range of estimates across different modelling approaches.

column1: To reflect the high uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook
column2: the December baseline projection had been accompanied by sensitivity analysis as well as a downside scenario. The mechanical impact of the technical assumptions used in the baseline would have implied slightly lower GDP growth for 2023 and significantly lower GDP growth for 2024 than in the September projections. The technical assumptions would also have implied significantly lower inflation for 2023 and a higher inflation rate for 2024 than projected in September. At the same time
column3: an extension of the current fiscal measures into 2024
column4: which was not an unrealistic assumption in view of governments’ attempts to buffer the energy price shock
column5: could lift inflation measurably in 2025. The downside scenario
column6: which assumed a complete halt of Russian gas and oil supplies leading to disruptions in production and trade
column7: resulted in higher inflation than in the baseline for 2023 and 2024 – indicating the prevalence of upside risks to inflation – while pointing to lower inflation for 2025.

column1: Turning to monetary and financial developments

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel noted that the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 14-15 December 2022 had left a visible footprint in euro area financial markets
column2: with a welcome increase in real interest rates to levels that were more consistent with a timely return of inflation to the 2% target.

column1: However
column2: while the “terminal rate” priced in the euro area real overnight index swap (OIS) forward curve had edged up initially
column3: a sharp decline in expected inflation
column4: on the back of lower gas prices and inflation surprises to the downside
column5: had later contributed to market participants revising down their rate expectations. Expectations of rapid disinflation had also induced markets to price in material rate cuts as of 2024
column6: suggesting that they judged the period of restrictive monetary policy needed to rein in high inflation to be relatively short.

column1: These developments
column2: alongside further signs of a more resilient euro area economy and the reopening of China’s economy
column3: had boosted risk sentiment. Risk premia had declined measurably across market segments
column4: compressing bond spreads and boosting equity prices
column5: while the euro had appreciated further across the board as sentiment towards the euro area improved. However
column6: the compression in risk premia was predicated on the markets’ firm conviction that inflation dynamics were on a steep and sustained downward trajectory towards 2%. A stronger persistence of underlying price pressures could lead to a reappraisal of the monetary policy outlook and a correction in asset prices
column7: as suggested by the strong market reaction
column8: during the week
column9: to some higher than expected inflation prints.

column1: Documenting the substantial changes in real interest rates that had occurred since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting
column2: it was noted that the euro area real OIS forward curve had shifted upwards
column3: with the real two-year OIS rate having turned positive for the first time since the 2008-09 global financial crisis. The upward shift reflected the impact of the ECB’s December communication
column4: as well as a decline in expected inflation that had been most pronounced over the near term. While the rise in real rates did not necessarily imply that rates were now restrictive
column5: especially considering the uncertainty about the level of the neutral rate
column6: it could
column7: if persistent
column8: mark the end of a long era of negative real interest rates.

column1: Model-based analysis suggested that the decline in the market-based inflation outlook had two broad origins. First
column2: after a long phase of upside surprises to inflation
column3: some misses to the downside relative to expectations for euro area headline inflation had been observed since November. Second
column4: there had been a substantial decline in gas prices
column5: which had
column6: at present
column7: a much larger impact on inflation swap rates than in the past
column8: at both the short and the long end of the inflation swap curve. This increased sensitivity to changes in gas prices may have contributed to an increasing disconnect between the market-implied inflation path and that of professional forecasters. Two factors raised doubt about the markets’ benign view of inflation. First
column9: the growing signs that a technical recession in the euro area had become less likely. And second
column10: the reopening of China’s economy.

column1: As markets were seemingly discounting these risks to the inflation outlook
column2: they also questioned whether the ECB would keep rates in restrictive territory for a sustained period. While the market-implied path for future short-term interest rates foresaw a further tightening over the short run
column3: in line with the ECB’s December communication
column4: it also envisaged a reversal as of 2024. The expected terminal rate in the euro area had initially shifted notably upwards in response to the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. However
column5: it had gradually fallen back as investors reappraised the inflation outlook. Furthermore
column6: markets currently expected a significant number of rate cuts over the course of 2024. In other words
column7: given that investors expected a fast and sustained return of inflation to 2%
column8: they expected policy rates to remain at a restrictive level for only a short period of time.

column1: Investors had also become more certain about the revised expected interest rate path. Implied volatility over a horizon of up to one year was now at its lowest since spring 2022
column2: although it remained high from a historical perspective. The decline in interest rate volatility
column3: however
column4: masked important differences in the drivers of uncertainty
column5: with model-based analysis suggesting that uncertainty about the ECB’s “reaction function” had increased
column6: while inflation uncertainty had declined.

column1: These developments were not confined to the euro area. Investors
column2: globally
column3: expected major central banks to cut their key policy rates this year or next
column4: as headline inflation was expected to ease rapidly from high spot levels. In response to some first signs of a turning point in headline inflation
column5: investors were signalling that they believed rate cuts would soon be needed. This was despite warnings from central bank officials around the world that interest rates would probably stay higher for longer than markets expected
column6: since core inflation – as measured by excluding energy and food from the overall index – remained elevated. Overall
column7: therefore
column8: markets had taken a view that the global economy
column9: including the euro area
column10: was at an inflection point
column11: with stronger growth and lower inflation than previously expected. Such positioning was putting market pricing at a considerable risk of correction should inflation prove more persistent.

column2: there had been a broad-based compression of risk premia. In euro area sovereign bond markets
column3: spreads had fallen across jurisdictions
column4: despite the ECB’s December announcement that the asset purchase programme (APP) portfolio would start to decline as of March 2023 and expectations of a faster run-off as of the third quarter. In euro area corporate bond markets
column5: spreads for non-financial corporate bonds were around 25% lower than late-October levels. The rally in financial markets
column6: spurred by the prevailing disinflation narrative
column7: had been especially pronounced in stock markets

column9: in particular
column10: having made significant gains.

column2: amid lower gas prices
column3: had also been a key driver behind the euro’s continued appreciation since the 14-15 December meeting. This appreciation had been broad-based against most major currencies
column4: with the Japanese yen being a notable exception.

column1: In this environment of a more positive risk sentiment
column2: market functioning had also improved notably
column3: as reflected in lower volatility and improved liquidity in euro area sovereign bond markets. This made a further positive contribution to investors’ risk absorption capacity. At the same time
