column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Mr Lane observed that the world economy had further decelerated in the fourth quarter of 2022
column2: with the global Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) for both manufacturing and services output falling below the threshold of 50 at the end of 2022. Consistent with low activity
column3: international trade had also slowed in the final quarter of 2022. Despite the deceleration
column4: global growth projections had improved for 2023
column5: owing partly to the relaxation of pandemic restrictions in China. The euro had continued to appreciate since the 14-15 December Governing Council meeting. In trade-weighted terms
column6: the exchange rate had returned to the level observed at the beginning of 2022.

column1: The slowdown in global demand
column2: together with the unusually warm winter and effective gas saving measures
column3: had led to a sharp decline in energy prices. European gas prices had fallen by around 50% since the December monetary policy meeting. According to the futures curve
column4: they were expected to remain around present levels
column5: easing concerns about storage levels for next winter. Oil prices had ticked up since the December meeting but remained significantly below mid-2022 levels. The sharply lower energy prices and easing of supply bottlenecks could be interpreted as a partial reversal of the large negative supply shock that had been observed since 2021.

column1: The euro area economy had slowed further in the fourth quarter of 2022 but had proved more resilient than expected in December. The PMI composite output indicator had risen above the threshold of 50 in January 2023
column2: after falling well into contractionary territory last autumn. However
column3: unlike services
column4: manufacturing output was still below the threshold. Manufacturing was once again the principal drag on overall output
column5: despite the continued easing in supply bottlenecks that had particularly benefited car production and sales. Strong demand for leisure activities
column6: tourism and hospitality were cushioning the slowdown in services activity.

column1: The latest round of the Commission’s household survey suggested that euro area households had revised their expectations on consumer prices 12-months ahead sharply downwards and their expectations on the economic situation upwards. The less pessimistic view on the economic situation also supported the improvement in their expectations on the financial situation and would help private consumption in the period ahead. These survey results supported the interpretation of a reversal of the negative supply shock.
Housing and business investment were clearly weakening
column2: owing partly to tighter financing conditions. The Commission’s business survey had shown that supply constraints
column3: rather than demand constraints
column4: had so far been the strongest factor limiting production. In particular
column5: shortages of material and equipment were constraining production in the capital goods sector. While output in this sector had been supported by the easing of supply bottlenecks and firms working through backlogs of orders
column6: especially in the car industry
column7: new orders remained weak. For the construction sector
column8: the PMI for both output and new orders had been on a downward trend since early 2022.

column1: Nonetheless
column2: Mr Lane continued to expect that the economy would recover over the course of the year
column3: on the back of a robust labour market
column4: rising wages and fiscal support measures
column5: as well as current headwinds fading away. If the favourable supply-side developments persisted
column6: these would provide further support to the recovery in activity.

column1: The decline in energy inflation had meant an improvement in the terms of trade. A significant drop in import price inflation had been followed by a less pronounced decline in export price inflation. This asymmetry in the price adjustment had led to a significant improvement in the euro area current account at the end of 2022.
The labour market continued to be resilient. The unemployment rate had stabilised at 6.6% in December
column2: far below the pre-COVID level. The PMI for employment
column3: which had declined from its very high mid-2021 level
column4: was still firmly positive. This suggested that firms were continuing to increase their labour force. In terms of vacancies

column6: but the level remained very high.

column1: Compared with December expectations
column2: risks to the growth outlook had become more balanced. Russia’s war against Ukraine continued to be a significant downside risk to the economy and could again push up energy and food costs. There could also be an additional drag on euro area growth if the world economy were to weaken more sharply than expected at present. Moreover
column3: the recovery would face obstacles if the pandemic were to re-intensify and cause renewed supply disruptions. However
column4: the adverse energy shock could fade away faster than anticipated and
column5: while the security of European gas supplies remained vulnerable to global supply risks

column7: euro area companies could adapt more quickly to the challenging international environment. This would support higher growth than currently expected.

column2: and further to 8.5% in January

column6: there was some variation across the sub-categories

column8: defined as the annualised three-month-on-three-month percentage change in prices
column9: the deceleration of inflation dynamics between December and January was notably stronger than suggested by the annual rates in these components.

column1: The uncertainty surrounding Eurostat’s January flash HICP estimate was greater than usual
column2: as it contained an estimate of the figure for Germany. In January there had also been the usual change in the HICP weights
column3: reflecting changes in expenditures over the previous year. Across items
column4: one of the most important changes was the increased weight of services
column5: as households had returned to a more normal consumption profile.

column1: Measures of underlying inflation continued to stand at high levels. However
column2: those indicators that included an energy component saw a turnaround. In addition
column3: the recent dynamics of core inflation showed that there had been a levelling-off of momentum.

column1: Looking at the determinants of goods inflation
column2: energy-sensitive items had continued to provide a strong contribution until December 2022. Looking ahead
column3: the contribution of energy-sensitive items could be expected to decline. However
column4: it was uncertain whether the pace of the reduction was likely to be symmetric to that of the increase. But the contribution of non-energy-sensitive items was increasing.

column1: To reconcile the still increasing contribution of energy-sensitive items with the fall in energy costs
column2: it was useful to look at pipeline pressures. Those pressures had declined for food inflation
column3: in particular for international food commodity prices and for European farm gate prices. But the producer price index for processed food was still increasing
column4: owing to long transmission lags. Similarly
column5: for goods inflation
column6: there had already been a significant decline in pipeline pressures for intermediate goods
column7: but the producer price index for non-food consumer goods was still increasing. Still
column8: the fast decline observed in pressures upstream in the production chain were expected to lead to lower retail prices
column9: as had been the case in the United States.

column1: Mr Lane reported that
column2: in the latest round of the ECB’s Corporate Telephone Survey
column3: firms had stated that input cost pressures had been easing
column4: reflecting declines in energy costs as well as other input costs
column5: and they were expecting input costs to continue to decline.

column3: inflation in owner-occupied housing costs had started to ease in the third quarter of 2022
column4: reflecting the acquisition component. Residential property price inflation in the euro area had eased substantially in the third quarter of 2022
column5: falling to 6.8%
column6: from 9.2% in the second quarter.

column1: Measured wage growth was strengthening
column2: as compensation for past high inflation was becoming the main theme in wage negotiations
column3: but wage developments so far were broadly in line with the December 2022 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area. The ECB wage tracker
column4: which had improved its representativeness with the inclusion of data for France
column5: indicated that new contracts signed during 2022 and coming into effect in 2023 implied ongoing wage increases of around 5%. Similarly
column6: according to the January wage expectations from the Corporate Telephone Survey
column7: firms expected average wage growth of around 5% for 2023

column2: with a more marked correction for 2023 and 2024. In the other direction

column4: longer-term expectations had been revised marginally down to 2.1%
column5: whereas those from the ECB Survey of Monetary Analysts were unchanged at 2%. Finally
column6: the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey for December 2022 indicated a levelling-off of median inflation perceptions and one-year ahead inflation expectations
column7: but continued to point to three-year ahead inflation remaining at around 3%.

column1: Overall
column2: the favourable supply-side developments
column3: if these persisted
column4: should help dampen inflation
column5: including through the impact of lower energy prices on the cost structures of energy-intensive sectors in the goods and services categories and on the real wage gap. At the same time
column6: the improvement in the terms of trade constituted a positive income and wealth shock that would also support demand.

column1: The inflation outlook remained highly uncertain
column2: although compared with the Governing Council’s expectations in December
column3: the risks to the inflation outlook had become more balanced
column4: especially in the near term. On the upside
column5: existing pipeline pressures could still send retail prices higher in the near term. Moreover
column6: a stronger than expected economic rebound in China could give a fresh boost to commodity prices and foreign demand. Domestic factors
column7: such as inflation expectations persistently above the ECB’s target or higher than anticipated wage rises
column8: could drive inflation higher
column9: also over the medium term. On the downside
column10: the recent fall in energy prices
column11: if it persisted
column12: might slow inflation more rapidly than expected. This downward pressure in the energy component could then also translate into weaker dynamics for underlying inflation. A further weakening of demand would also contribute to lower price pressures than currently anticipated
column13: especially over the medium term. The net impact of the reopening of China’s economy on euro area inflation dynamics over the coming months was uncertain. While a strong rebound in Chinese production could further ease supply bottlenecks and increase competition in the global goods market
column14: thus constituting a disinflationary impulse for the world economy
column15: a recovery in Chinese demand could also add to inflationary pressures
column16: especially through higher demand for commodities.

column1: Turning to financial and monetary developments
column2: bank funding costs continued to reflect the transmission of monetary policy. Euro area bank bond yields had increased somewhat further since the December Governing Council meeting
column3: reflecting the movements in the key ECB interest rates and in market rates. Deposit rates had also increased further
column4: rising more strongly for firms than for households since May 2022.

column1: The spread between M3 savings deposits and overnight deposits had continued to widen
column2: broadly in line with past rate hiking periods. Over time
column3: this would likely lead to a considerable downward adjustment to the currently still high share of overnight deposit holdings
column4: as currently there was an incentive to minimise deposit holdings in current accounts. Moreover
column5: as the ECB’s targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTROs) were being repaid
column6: banks needed some longer-term deposits to meet various regulatory ratios. Thus
column7: there was an expectation that this portfolio switch would continue.

column1: The increase in policy rates continued to be passed through to firms. The cost of debt financing had risen substantially since September 2022 and the strong increase in bank lending rates had led to a considerably narrower spread between the cost of market-based debt financing and the cost of bank borrowing at the end of 2022
column2: compared with its September level.

column1: The current pace of monetary policy tightening was faster than in previous rate hiking cycles
column2: reflecting the greater frequency and size of policy rate hikes. However
column3: as this represented a reversal of previous loosening and was a necessary normalisation to address high inflation
column4: it was not viewed as a severe squeeze by the banks or their customers.

column1: The transmission of monetary policy was also reflected in developments in bank lending conditions
column2: as reported by banks in the latest bank lending survey. Banks continued to report a substantial net tightening of their credit standards on loans to firms and on loans to households for house purchase in the fourth quarter of 2022. Mr Lane noted that
column3: since the survey was meant to assess the change in credit standards and not their level
column4: it was legitimate to ask whether banks were tightening or just reversing a very accommodative set of credit standards. Still
column5: as the tightening continued
column6: at some point the trend would move beyond normalisation.

column1: Demand for bank loans to non-financial corporations had also declined in the final quarter of 2022. This was driven mainly by rising interest rates
column2: in line with the increase in bank lending rates for firms. The bank lending survey revealed that the decline in demand for loans stemmed
column3: in particular
column4: from the commercial real estate
column5: residential real estate and construction sectors
column6: the most interest rate-sensitive sectors. In addition
column7: loan demand was being dampened by lower financing needs for fixed investment and a moderation in firms’ financing needs for working capital. The bank lending survey reported a steep drop in demand for housing loans
column8: which was unprecedented in the history of the survey. The main drivers of this fall were rising interest rates
column9: deteriorating prospects for housing markets and low consumer confidence.

column1: Debt financing flows for firms had declined in November and December
column2: owing to net redemptions in bank borrowing. There was therefore evidence of some deleveraging by firms at the end of 2022. Household borrowing dynamics had also weakened
column3: driven mainly by developments in housing loans. The moderating trend in mortgage borrowing reflected tighter credit standards
column4: rising lending rates and decreasing loan demand.

column1: Finally
column2: on monetary developments
column3: Mr Lane reported that the deceleration in loan creation was reflected in a decline in money growth. The moderation in broad money (M3) growth was driven mainly by outflows from narrow money (M1)
column4: the growth of which had fallen markedly. Persistently low remuneration of overnight deposits meant that the opportunity costs of holding M1 instruments had risen significantly. Deposit flows continued to reflect the shifts towards time deposits and to M3 instruments offering a remuneration closely linked to market rates.

column1: Monetary policy considerations and policy options
Against this background
column2: Mr Lane proposed raising the three key ECB interest rates by 50 basis points and communicating that the Governing Council expected to raise them further. The Governing Council should stay the course in raising interest rates significantly at a steady pace and in keeping them at levels that were sufficiently restrictive to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2% medium-term target. Accordingly
column3: in view of the underlying inflation pressures
column4: Mr Lane proposed communicating the intention to raise interest rates by another 50 basis points at the next monetary policy meeting in March and to then evaluate the subsequent path of monetary policy. Signalling a 50 basis point step for the March meeting acknowledged that
column5: in a very wide range of scenarios
column6: the Governing Council saw that a further step of this size remained necessary to bring the key ECB interest rates to levels that would ensure a return of inflation to target in a timely manner. That said
column7: looking beyond the immediate term
column8: the monetary policy meeting in March would provide a waypoint at which to evaluate the subsequent path of monetary policy
column9: including on the basis of a new set of staff macroeconomic projections that would then be available. The Governing Council would in this way ensure that its future policy rate decisions continued to be data-dependent and followed a meeting-by-meeting approach.

column1: Regarding the parameters that would govern the measured and predictable reduction of the asset purchase programme (APP) portfolio that had been decided in December
column2: it was important that the process remained transparent
column3: simple to understand and as neutral as possible vis-à-vis the pricing of the classes of securities held in the portfolio. To this end
column4: Mr Lane proposed that the partial reinvestments be conducted broadly in line with current practice. Without prejudice to the objective of price stability
column5: the Governing Council should also support the gradual decarbonisation of the Eurosystem’s corporate bond holdings
column6: in line with the goals of the Paris Agreement.

column1: As regards the pandemic emergency purchase programme (PEPP)
column2: the signalling power of the framework for PEPP reinvestment flexibility was still supporting the monetary policy transmission mechanism. It was therefore proposed
column3: in the spirit of prudence
column4: to continue to allow flexibility in PEPP reinvestments as an effective first line of defence against remaining fragmentation risks.

column1: Ms Schnabel then detailed the proposal for the modalities to be followed in reducing the APP holdings
column2: following the Governing Council’s decision at its December monetary policy meeting to reduce the APP portfolio by €15 billion per month on average from the beginning of March until the end of the second quarter of 2023. During the partial reinvestment phase
column3: reinvestment amounts were expected to be relatively small. Any changes to the modalities would therefore have a very limited impact on the composition of the APP portfolio. This argued for keeping the modalities for the period of partial reinvestments simple
column4: reflecting as much as possible the practice applied for full reinvestment. This approach would also preserve consistency with the overall monetary policy stance and market functioning
column5: and should facilitate the Eurosystem’s public communication.

column1: 2. Governing Council’s discussion and monetary policy decisions
Economic
column2: monetary and financial analyses

column1: As regards the external environment
column2: members took note of the assessment provided by Mr Lane that subdued global economic activity and high levels of geopolitical uncertainty
column3: especially owing to Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine and its people
column4: continued to act as headwinds to euro area growth. Subdued global activity would weigh on global trade and euro area foreign demand
column5: despite improvements in global supply chains. In their discussion
column6: members argued that
column7: on the one hand
column8: the reopening of the Chinese economy should lead to fewer bottlenecks in global supply chains and thus support global activity. This would also imply stronger foreign demand for the euro area. On the other hand
column9: the reopening of its economy would increase China’s appetite for commodities
column10: including natural gas
column11: and would make China a strong competitor of Europe for supplies of liquified natural gas. This would put upward pressure on European gas prices and act as a headwind to Europe’s recovery. Pressure on prices of other raw materials
column12: such as metals
column13: owing to increased demand from China
column14: was already visible. Which of the various forces at play would eventually prevail was not clear
column15: creating considerable uncertainty for the euro area outlook.

column1: Members highlighted that energy commodity prices had come down significantly
column2: in some cases returning to levels prevailing before the start of Russia’s war in Ukraine. This implied that the euro area’s import bill for fossil fuels would be reduced considerably. At the same time
column3: it was mentioned that there was still considerable scepticism in energy markets about whether the current lower energy prices would persist. Part of the decline in prices seemed to be driven by the current mild winter weather
column4: which would not necessarily be repeated next winter. It was widely stressed that the euro area continued to be confronted by an exceptionally high degree of global uncertainty
column5: owing to both economic and geopolitical factors.

column1: With regard to economic activity
column2: despite the challenging external environment
column3: members concurred with Mr Lane that the euro area was likely to avoid a recession. Together with high inflation and tighter financing conditions
column4: global headwinds were dampening spending and production
column5: especially in the manufacturing sector. However
column6: in addition to easing supply bottlenecks and more secure gas supplies
column7: firms were still working through large order backlogs and confidence was improving. Moreover
column8: output in the services sector had been holding up
column9: supported by the continuing effects of the reopening of the economy and stronger demand for leisure activities. Rising wages and the recent decline in energy price inflation were also set to ease the loss of purchasing power that many people had experienced owing to high inflation. This
column10: in turn
column11: would support consumption. Overall
column12: the economy had proved more resilient than expected and should recover over the coming quarters. The unemployment rate had remained at a historical low of 6.6% in December 2022. However
column13: the rate at which jobs were being created was seen as potentially slowing
column14: with unemployment rising over the coming quarters.

column1: Members commented on the surprising resilience of economic activity to date. The release of Eurostat’s preliminary flash estimate for GDP growth in the fourth quarter of 2022 had surprised on the upside
column2: which was regarded as good news
column3: even if the figure had most likely been pushed up by volatile transactions in Irish intellectual property products. In combination with recent levels of inflation
column4: which had been lower than expected
column5: this stronger activity was seen as indicative of a partial reversal of the negative supply shocks that had shaped developments in the euro area economy over the past year. As a result
column6: the euro area economy was now in a better situation than expected in December
column7: and it was argued that recent developments were in line with a “soft landing” (with the economy slowing but avoiding a recession). In such circumstances
column8: the Governing Council might be able to bring down inflation without overly large sacrifices in terms of economic activity. However
column9: it was also maintained that
column10: despite the better than expected economic news
column11: the underlying economic situation had not fundamentally changed since the December meeting.

column1: Members concurred that government support measures to shield the economy from the impact of high energy prices should be temporary
column2: targeted and tailored to preserving incentives to consume less energy. In particular
column3: as the energy crisis became less acute
column4: it was important to start rolling these measures back promptly in line with the fall in energy prices and in a concerted manner. Any such measures falling short of these principles were likely to drive up medium-term inflationary pressures
column5: which would call for a stronger monetary policy response. Moreover
column6: in line with the EU’s economic governance framework
column7: fiscal policies should be oriented towards making the economy more productive and gradually bringing down high public debt. Policies to enhance the euro area’s supply capacity
column8: especially in the energy sector
column9: could help reduce price pressures in the medium term. To that end
column10: governments should swiftly implement their investment and structural reform plans under the Next Generation EU programme. The reform of the EU’s economic governance framework should be concluded rapidly.

column1: Against this background
column2: members assessed risks to the economic growth outlook as having become more balanced. Russia’s war in Ukraine continued to be a significant downside risk to the economy and could again push up the costs of energy and food. There could also be an additional drag on euro area growth if the world economy weakened more sharply than expected. Moreover
column3: the recovery would face obstacles if the pandemic were to re-intensify and cause renewed supply disruptions. However
column4: the energy shock could fade away faster than anticipated and euro area companies could adapt more quickly to the challenging international environment. This would support higher growth than currently expected.

column1: With regard to price developments
column2: members concurred with the assessment presented by Mr Lane in his introduction. Price pressures remained strong
column3: partly because high energy costs were spreading throughout the economy. HICP inflation excluding energy and food
column4: as a measure of core inflation
column5: remained at 5.2% in January. Other indicators of underlying inflation were also still high. Although supply bottlenecks were gradually easing
column6: their delayed effects were still pushing up goods price inflation. The same was true for the lifting of pandemic-related restrictions: while weakening
column7: the effect of pent-up demand was still driving up prices
column8: especially in the services sector.

column1: Government measures to compensate households for high energy prices were
column2: by contrast
column3: dampening inflation in 2023. However
column4: the scale of some of these measures depended on the evolution of energy prices and therefore their overall contribution to inflation was particularly uncertain
column5: since they were expected to raise inflation once they expired. Market-based indicators suggested that energy prices were seen as being significantly lower over the current and coming years than had been expected at the time of the Governing Council’s December meeting. At the same time
column6: wages were growing faster
column7: supported by robust labour markets. However
column8: recent data on wage dynamics had been in line with the December Eurosystem staff projections. Most measures of longer-term inflation expectations stood at around 2% but warranted continued monitoring.

column1: Members concurred with the view that
column2: although the rate of headline inflation had slowed since October
column3: inflation was still far too high. While the good news ought to be welcome
column4: it was argued that the December assessment of the inflation outlook had not fundamentally changed. Core inflation was still at levels foreseen in December. Therefore
column5: it was much too early to declare victory.

column1: Attention was drawn to the fact that the inflation figures for the euro area’s largest economy had not been available in time to be included in Eurostat’s flash release for January. It was suggested that
column2: in all likelihood
column3: the final release would turn out to be somewhat higher for the euro area. In this context
column4: it was underlined that core inflation had surprised slightly on the upside and remained unchanged from December
column5: which was seen as the reason for the very muted market reaction to the lower than expected headline inflation figure for January. Since core inflation was often regarded as the “attractor” to which headline inflation would revert over the medium term
column6: the latest inflation figures were not necessarily a welcome development overall. However
column7: caution was expressed against focusing too much on measures of core inflation. Indeed
column8: some elements of core inflation could move quite quickly
column9: as seen from the experience in the United States and in line with the latest developments in euro area pipeline pressures. However
column10: that would not necessarily imply that the more persistent elements of inflation
column11: such as those related to wages
column12: would turn around. It was recalled that the ECB monitored a wide array of measures of underlying inflation and undertook a detailed analysis of all components of headline inflation
column13: rather than looking exclusively at particular measures of core inflation excluding several volatile items. Finally
column14: it was mentioned that January inflation developments in Croatia
column15: which had just joined the euro area
column16: had been quite stable overall
column17: compared with December. This suggested that the upward impact on prices from the cash changeover had been rather limited so far
column18: contrary to the expectations of some people.

column1: As regards developments in core inflation
column2: it was stressed that the pass-through of lower energy prices to this measure was a key factor in the assessment of the lag with which the rate of core inflation would show convincing signs of a deceleration. In this context
column3: members debated the extent to which lower energy prices would lead to a moderation in underlying price pressures. This would depend on whether the pass-through from declining energy prices to other components of inflation was symmetric to that observed when energy prices increased.

column1: On the one hand
column2: there were a number of reasons to believe that offsetting factors might lead to a slower pass-through of the disinflationary impulse than had been observed over the recent inflationary phase. In particular
column3: the pass-through of earlier higher wholesale energy prices to retail prices took time and was still ongoing. Demand pressures had increased and wage pressures were rising on the back of wage negotiations that were being increasingly influenced by the high rates of current or past inflation and continued labour scarcity. In addition
column4: the longer duration of wage contracts
column5: rising minimum wages and staggered wage-setting could lead to a longer persistence of wage growth. In this respect
column6: it was underlined that inflation pressures had been broadening for some time
column7: so the driving force behind the inflation process was no longer a pure supply-side inflation shock. While the rise in inflation had started with a supply shock
column8: it had turned into more of a demand-side type of inflation
column9: making inflation more persistent. Moreover
column10: there was evidence that the effect of an increase in energy prices on both GDP and inflation was very different from the effect of a decrease in energy prices
column11: partly owing to downward price and wage rigidities. Recent evidence for the euro area showed that there was significant asymmetry
column12: so the strong and fast pass-through observed as energy prices rose could not be expected to simply reverse swiftly as prices declined.

column1: On the other hand
column2: it was argued that the decline in energy prices could well be transmitted more quickly to items of core inflation
column3: in line with how the inflationary shocks had filtered through to this measure in recent quarters as prices rose. This suggested that core inflation might over time decline faster than envisaged in the December projections. In any case
column4: it was noted that it was too early to observe such a rapid pass-through
column5: as non-energy industrial goods inflation was still increasing
column6: suggesting that the upside pressures from past higher energy prices were still present. Staggered price adjustment implied that households and firms might face higher energy prices only after some time had elapsed
column7: so while energy commodity prices were falling
column8: households and firms would still see some of the pass-through from the previous increase in energy prices. At the same time
column9: it had to be acknowledged that the rate of industrial producer price inflation
column10: excluding energy
column11: had significantly decelerated
column12: which was an important indication that lower energy prices would at some point translate into lower core inflation. In this context
column13: it was also argued that in the three-month-on-three-month changes in the HICP excluding energy and food – the core “momentum” – there were already initial signs that underlying inflation would start to decline in annual growth rates
column14: despite the fact that core inflation naturally responded with a lag to changes in energy prices.

column1: Members considered the implications of the reopening of China’s economy for inflation developments in the euro area. In this context
column2: the remark was made that the reopening of a major global net-exporting economy
column3: such as China
column4: should on balance be expected to have a dampening impact on global price pressures
column5: even if Chinese aggregate demand increased. Moreover
column6: Chinese exporters could also be expected to lower their prices so as to regain some of the market share they had lost during the periods of lockdown
column7: thus spurring price competition worldwide. However
column8: upward pressures on inflation could be expected from an increase in Chinese demand
column9: especially for commodities.

column1: There was still considerable uncertainty about the dampening impact of tighter monetary policy on inflation. The current inflation dynamics most likely did not yet reflect recent monetary policy tightening. In fact
column2: it was argued on the basis of recent survey evidence that current financing conditions were hardly restrictive enough to dampen demand sufficiently to bring inflation back to the ECB’s target in a timely manner. This suggested that the contribution of monetary policy to disinflation had been limited so far
column3: except indirectly through the appreciation of the euro and through the housing market channel in a number of euro area economies. With regard to exchange rates
column4: it was noted that the recent appreciation of the euro implied lower inflationary pressures for the euro area in the period ahead.

column1: Members recalled that wage pressures were key in understanding the risks of second-round effects on inflation and in determining more persistent developments in underlying price pressures. Until a few months ago wage growth had remained moderate
column2: but now there was a clear acceleration
column3: which had to be taken into account in the outlook for core inflation. It was also highlighted that
column4: despite the slowdown in economic activity
column5: the labour market remained exceptionally tight. This meant that price pressures acting on labour-intensive services were unlikely to abate soon. The wage trackers were showing very strong wage increases under newly concluded contracts
column6: which
column7: in a context of the long durations of wage contracts and centralised wage bargaining
column8: might lead to more persistent wage growth. However
column9: it was also noted that wage growth for the pool of job movers should naturally be expected to be much higher than wage growth for job stayers
column10: as the former were expected to account for the bulk of productivity growth. Following the pandemic
column11: the economy was going through a period of intensified job churning
column12: so it was natural that labour productivity and wage growth were accelerating. But this would not necessarily imply an increase in price pressures. At the same time
column13: it was highlighted that the observed strong increase in minimum wages would add to existing wage pressures. There was evidence that
column14: over time
column15: increases in minimum wages could feed into wage increases further up the wage scale. Therefore
column16: while there was wide agreement that there were no signs of a wage-price spiral
column17: it was argued that current wage growth was clearly not consistent with a 2% inflation target
column18: even when taking into account trend improvements in productivity.

column1: In this context
column2: it was reiterated that wages were a lagging indicator
column3: so only the most recent phase of wage growth should be seen as fully reflecting past price increases. In some sectors and some countries
column4: wages were expected to rise by more than 10%. However
column5: it was also observed that there was a lot of heterogeneity across sectors and countries. Moreover
column6: while wage negotiations were still ongoing
column7: wage claims were hardly reliable early indicators for the final wage agreements
column8: which more often than not tended to be more moderate. It was observed that some catch-up effect from the loss of purchasing power accumulated over the past few years would unavoidably exert upward pressure on wage growth
column9: in line with the December staff projections. At the same time
column10: as energy prices had started to decline again
column11: the loss in real income was now lower than previously expected. This could imply that the push to recover purchasing power via higher wages would also diminish
column12: while leading to stronger than expected aggregate demand. It was underlined that
column13: so far
column14: the association of fast-rising prices with lagging wages had implied a large shift in income from labour to capital. Developments in unit profit growth remained very strong
column15: which suggested that the pass-through of higher costs to higher selling prices remained robust. It was therefore widely stressed that developments in profits and mark-up warranted constant monitoring and further analysis on an equal footing with developments in wages.

column1: Members agreed that fiscal policies continued to play a crucial role in determining the degree of persistence of medium-term inflation. Several members were of the view that fiscal policy was working against monetary policy efforts to restore price stability. At the same time
column2: some upward effects on inflation could be expected from the positive demand impact of fiscal policy – especially through the component of fiscal policy aimed at protecting consumers from a loss of purchasing power. Moreover
column3: governments could be expected to refrain from providing additional support if there was a diminished need for it

This is really the best guidance that we can provide and it is 1) the assessment of the inflation outlook in light of the incoming economic and financial data
column3: 2) the dynamics of underlying inflation
column4: and 3) the strength of our monetary policy transmission. So
column5: that's brand new. These three components
column6: we never discussed them
column7: we never let them out and they are clearly identified as the three elements that will be taken into account to determine our reaction function going forward.

column1: Second point: if our baseline was to persist when the uncertainty reduces
column2: we know that we have a lot more ground to cover. But it's a big caveat. If our baseline was to persist. As you know
column3: the projections that were determined by staff – are based on data and assessment of the situation with a cut-off date. That cut-off date was 15 February for the international outlook and technical assumptions and 1 March for the euro area macroeconomic projections. Now
column4: since 1 March a lot obviously has developed and the projections that we have do not incorporate any of the most recent developments and certainly not the impact of the most recent financial tensions that we have observed on the markets.

column1: So
column2: there is a level of uncertainty that has been completely elevated as a result of that
column3: and that is the reason why we reinforced the principle of data dependency that we have indicated in the past with a clear map of the reaction function that we will have in the future. So

column5: which is assessment of the inflation outlook in light of the incoming economic and financial data
column6: it is not possible to determine at this point in time what the path will be going forward. But we know that it will be data dependent and we know that if the baseline as we have it was confirmed and was to persist
column7: we would have more ground to cover.

column1: On your second point
column2: I will again read for you one more time what is in the second paragraph this time of our monetary policy statement

column4: we did increase the capital ratio

column1: Added to which: if it was needed

column1: Well
column2: let me be pretty clear on that point as well: I believe that there is no trade-off between price stability and financial stability. I think that if anything

column2: 15-16 March 2023|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel distinguished two periods when reporting on financial market developments since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 1-2 February 2023.
In the first period
column2: stretching until the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) in the United States
column3: mounting signs of more persistent pressures on core inflation in the euro area – i.e. inflation in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) excluding the food and energy components – had led investors to reassess their views on the likely future path of inflation and interest rates
column4: and they were pricing in a higher-for-longer inflation and rate environment. Expectations regarding the level of the “terminal rate” (the peak rate) in the ECB’s ongoing rate hiking cycle had reached a level of 4.2% in the week prior to the Governing Council’s meeting on 15-16 March
column5: while the expected date of the first rate cut had been pushed out to the third quarter of 2024. Yet
column6: despite this sharp upward revision to the expected policy rate path
column7: market-based indicators of longer-term inflation expectations had continued to point to elevated concerns that inflation would remain above the ECB’s target of 2%.

column1: The second period had started when these market developments had been abruptly halted by the collapse of SVB. Interest rate expectations had been revised downwards sharply
column2: but they had partially reversed this decline on 14 March 2023 before dropping again on the morning of 15 March. Financial market indicators at the close of the markets on 14 March 2023 had not shown signs that the US banking sector turbulence would cause a systemic crisis in the United States or the euro area. However
column3: the moves in these indicators had reversed again on the morning of 15 March
column4: in turbulent market conditions. It would not be possible to get a clearer picture of the most recent change in market perceptions until the dust from the market turbulence had settled.

column1: Amid this market volatility
column2: three observations stood out. First
column3: broad stock indices had remained much more resilient than bank stocks
column4: as the share prices of non-financial corporations had been affected only moderately. Second
column5: spillovers from the United States to the euro area had been contained. Third
column6: bank share prices in the euro area remained well in positive territory relative to their lows in mid-2022
column7: owing to the strong and sustained rally since then on the back of improving earnings expectations.

column1: While stock prices of major global banks had fallen sharply across Europe and the United States
column2: spreads on credit default swaps had increased only moderately for euro area banks. Liquidity conditions also remained solid. The FRA-OIS spread – i.e. the difference between the rate charged on interbank unsecured deposits and the overnight index swap (OIS) rate – had increased significantly in the euro area but had remained near its long-term average level. Moreover
column3: the cost of offshore US dollar funding had increased substantially
column4: although this increase had been partially reversed subsequently. As regards volatility
column5: fixed income markets had reacted much more strongly to the SVB event than equity markets. Overall
column6: these developments suggested that
column7: if there was no intensification of the stress in the banking sector
column8: the inflation outlook would soon come to the fore again in the minds of market participants.

column1: Before the banking sector turbulence had started in the United States
column2: global macroeconomic upside surprises had dominated financial market developments across major economies. Positive data on economic activity had been accompanied by upward surprises for headline inflation and
column3: especially
column4: core inflation in the euro area. This growth and inflation mix had led to a repricing by markets of the inflation outlook for the euro area over the medium term
column5: as market participants perceived the factors driving inflation pressures to have shifted from external supply to internal demand or
column6: put differently
column7: from headline to core inflation. Investors were now pricing in a substantially more sluggish return of inflation to 2%
column8: despite lower natural gas prices.

column1: Expectations of more persistent core inflation had led to a significant reappraisal of policy rate expectations in the euro area. The United States had seen a similarly strong repricing of the forward curve
column2: underlining the perceived close synchronicity in the global economic activity and inflation cycle. These developments had been reversed after the unfolding of the events related to SVB. column1: De Guindos: Turning to your second question
column2: I think that we should start with a consideration: if you look at the characteristics of the US banks that are running into difficulties
column3: I think that there are some common features. The first one is that they are medium-sized
column4: regional
column5: they share very concrete and very idiosyncratic business models
column6: and they are quite open to interest rate risks – they are vulnerable to an increase in yields. And I think that this model
column7: this situation is not extrapolatable to the European banking industry. I will not repeat what we have said many times – that European banks are resilient [because of] their levels of capital
column8: levels of liquidity and quality of the liquid assets – but I think that simultaneously
column9: we have to remember that an increase in interest rates
column10: in yields
column11: is positive for the European banks because the increase in margins outweighs the potential losses that this increase in yields could cause in fixed-income portfolios. But I think that it is quite clear that there is no space for complacency. One of the things that we – all of us – have been surprised about is how rapidly a bank run can take place and how rapidly a bank can be emptied. And I think that this is the combination of new factors. The first one is digital banking and the second one is social networks. The combination of both have even led to a new situation. I think that as supervisors and regulators we have to bear in mind this new framework because we believe that this is going to be key in the near future.

column1: My first question is about whether anyone at the meeting insisted on a larger rate hike or on a clearer commitment to more hikes. You just hinted at that by talking about “ground to cover” but it wasn’t quite as explicit as it was back in the winter when you were talking about “steady pace” and “several rate hikes”.
My second question is about something you just said
column2: which is again that you had “more ground to cover”. Would you say that we are still in the middle of the journey or towards the end
column3: in the home stretch?

column1: I’m tempted to remind you of the Emerson quote
column2: “it’s not so much the destination that matters but the journey”
column3: and we are on a journey and we are not pausing. Under the present circumstances and based on what we have
column4: which is the baseline of March
column5: we know that we have more ground to cover. There is a clear reference in the second paragraph of the Monetary Policy Statement [in which] we explicitly refer to that by saying that our future decisions will ensure that the policy rates will be brought to levels sufficiently restrictive to achieve a timely return of inflation to our 2% medium term target and will be kept at those levels for as long as necessary. We covered a lot of ground in the last nine months [prior to today’s meeting]
column6: moving from minus 50 basis points to plus 300 basis points. We are continuing this hiking process. As I said
column7: this is a journey. We have not arrived yet.

column1: As to the exact amount
column2: by how much we increase rates
column3: as I said in my introduction in the response to the first questions
column4: there were a variety of views. Some governors suggested that maybe 50 [basis points] was appropriate
column5: others believed that 25 was appropriate. I didn’t hear anybody suggest that zero would be appropriate
column6: which confirms to you that this is a hiking journey that we are on and it will continue to be so. But at the end of the deliberations and having had a chance to confront our views and answer the questions and really put everything in perspective

column1: I would like to invite you to elaborate a little bit more on your definition of “sufficiently restrictive”. The IMF had a view the other day
column2: seeing the terminal rate at 3.75%. A lot of economists believe that as well. Would that be something – given the inflation outlook we have at the moment – that would be in the ballpark of “sufficiently restrictive”?

column1: The other question I have is that at the last meeting you had a little bit of a debate about over-tightening and having to reverse course. I’m wondering whether that discussion continued this time and whether you would actually be worried that such a scenario might be interpreted as a policy mistake.

I don’t have a magic number of what constitutes “sufficiently restrictive”. I think that the honest answer is that we will know what that is when we get there and we are in the process of moving into that direction. I think what’s important is to understand what it means to have restrictive rates and to be in restrictive territory. I think the best example is to see whether the rate decisions that we make
column2: the rate increases that we decide
column3: are actually having an impact on the economic actors. And when we look at the Bank Lending Survey or when we look at the interest rates and the pace at which they have increased over the last few months
column4: it is obviously the fact that interest rate decisions that we made and the interest rates level we are on are having an effect. Is it a sufficient effect yet? We don’t know because we are not seeing the transmission at this point in time into what I call the second leg of the economy
column5: which is the real activity
column6: which then has an impact on prices and then reduces inflation. The full cycle we are not seeing yet. We are seeing inflation coming down
column7: don’t get me wrong
column8: because headline is coming down as a result of energy prices having come down significantly
column9: as a result of the easing of bottlenecks. But we are not yet seeing the complete impact that we desire in order to arrive at the 2% medium term that constitutes our target. We are very attentive
column10: we look at that
column11: as you know it’s one of the three components that we look at
column12: the inflation outlook. Is it restrictive? No question about it. Is it sufficiently restrictive? Not yet.

column1: I have two questions. The first one is on the decision to accelerate the pace of shrinking the bond portfolio of the ECB. Does that mean
column2: now that you’re stopping all reinvestments in the APP
column3: that you plan to reduce the APP to zero eventually?

Number one
column2: we made the decision but the decision specifically says “we expect”. So we expect to let the APP run down as time goes by. In answer to your question about whether we go to zero: if we do
column3: then it’s going to take [at least] the next 15 years
column4: so I don’t think I’ll be around for that
column5: I know I won’t
column6: and I’m not sure that you will be around either. But the ultimate perspective is that one
column7: as we consider things today. We’ve decided to expect the effectiveness of the decision as of July
column8: saving a little bit of optionality just in case
column9: simply because we have seen that the partial reinvestment that has been effective since March has actually run very smoothly and has been well-absorbed by markets. We don’t see any point in not accelerating the move because there are valid reasons for [doing] that: it lowers the amount of excess liquidity
column10: complements our policy rate
column11: reduces the side effect of a large balance sheet – all of that completely justifies the fact that the APP is let to run down gradually over the course of time
column12: which will be an average of 25 billion per month that will not be reinvested
column13: roughly. But as I said
column14: running the whole APP programme to zero will take [longer than] 12-15 years
column15: given the maturities we have.

column1: I would just reserve one thing
column2: because we discussed it during the Governing Council and it’s not reflected in the Monetary Policy Statement. As you know
column3: we have adopted a tilting approach to our reinvestment policy of the APP and in particular for the corporate bonds
column4: which are the prime targets of that tilting
column5: in order to privilege those corporates that have a good environmental footprint
column6: that have a transition plan and that disclose all the appropriate information about their plans. Of course if we go to full run-down
column7: that tilting process is not going to be applicable because there will be nothing to tilt it off
column8: there will be no basis for that. The jury is out as to how we can continue to deliver on our Paris agreement compliant investment and reinvestment programme without the reinvestment phase and how we address that
column9: which is something that we agreed we would take into account and consider to see how we respond to that.

column1: Was it a deal? No. There was a general view that that was the right move
column2: completely sensible
column3: legitimate at this point in time given the market absorption. Some might have preferred to wait until the June meeting to announce it

column1: About the last banking lending survey

What are the indicators that you’re looking at? Would you say that there is a banking crisis? What’s your view of what’s happening there in the banking system?

We know of one and only one target and this is our medium-term target of 2%. That’s what is riveting our attention. But of course the Bank Lending Survey that we receive on a quarterly basis informs us about the tightening of credit to the economy

column3: intelligence
column4: anticipation of the credit tightening now and the credit tightening going forward. It’s also illustrative of the demand and that’s an interesting point because in the Bank Lending Survey
column5: the demand from corporates is really
column6: really down. So that’s a learning we take

column8: because
column9: when asked
column10: the corporates – and we had a corporate survey conducted – say “it’s the interest rates
column11: it’s not that we don’t want to invest but the interest rates are pretty high”. And that [brings us back to the question of] restrictive territory or not: yes

column1: On Credit Suisse
column2: number one
column3: it was addressed very swiftly. The Swiss authorities maybe did not have many choices and it was very specific and probably a long-lasting issue that was lingering and had been lingering for a long time. I certainly would not draw the conclusion that the merger between UBS and Credit Suisse to be decided is an indication that there is a financial crisis

I think that we also learnt the value of having rules and the ability we had to come out very quickly on the pecking order of creditors actually mattered a lot and I think we can also take a bit of learning from that. When creditors and investors know exactly who is going to bear the brunt of outstanding liabilities in a situation of insolvency

column6: I’m glad we did.

column3: for instance equity prices
column4: bank bond spreads
column5: the evolution of deposits. We have not seen the kind of situations that happened in other jurisdictions. We had an increase in tensions after the events in the US with Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse. Afterwards

column7: clearly
column8: now the conclusion is that the European banking industry has been clearly outperforming the American one in terms of the tension [reflected] in these kinds of indicators and potential stress in financial markets.

column4: the findings that we have
column5: the data that we can analyse today

column11: it is not time-dependent

column12: it’s the target that we have
column13: that we’ve agreed in our strategy review. It happens to be what matters to people. People see all prices increasing and we are working for the people of Europe. Core
column14: easy to communicate but maybe not as informative as we want it to be

column17: inflation.

column1: Madame Lagarde. I’m sure many people will be interested to know whether the worst of inflation is over for food. Do you have that impression?
Thank you for that question because it is food prices that are hurting most
column2: particularly the most vulnerable people. We know that because in the basket of consumption the most vulnerable spend a lot more on food than those who are well-off. So we pay special attention of course to food and the increase in prices. We have seen it go down
column3: if you compare March and April numbers it is going down
column4: but we have to be extremely attentive because there are multiple factors that apply to food prices
column5: that apply to processed food prices. I think we have also flagged the fact that profits last year and particularly in 2022 have contributed to inflation. This year
column7: what we have seen of 2023
column8: we see more wage increases contributing to inflation. We would hope that through a good social contract
column9: these drivers of inflation do not activate each other in what I have called in other places a tit-for-tat – I want more wages
column10: I’m not going to give up on profits – and you are then at risk of something that is much more difficult and would lead us to have to take more active measures in monetary policy. So
column11: I wish I could tell you “of course it will continue to go down” but I’m observing that it has gone down. There are other factors that will come into play
column12: you know
column13: clearly climate change is something that will have an impact probably on a sectoral basis
column14: probably in relation to certain food items. What happens in Ukraine is also going to bring another uncertainty in the background of cereal price in particular
column15: but commodity prices have gone down
column16: that is a fact. So hopefully it will channel to the ultimate consumer.

column5: from New Zealand

column7: all the way to the Fed and others. And it’s obvious that the US economy
column8: in whichever way it evolves
column9: has spillover effects around the world given its size
column10: the depth of its financial markets. But you know we have a target
column11: we have a journey
column12: we know as of today that we have more ground to cover and whatever the decision of the Fed is in the next few weeks
column13: months
column14: we are going to be riveted to our objective and will of course take into account variables. You know the currency for instance has an impact

column1: As to the actual tightening impact that the APP run-off has
column2: I don’t want to commit a number

column2: Lithuania
column3: Spain that struggle with the much higher interest rates and have had to cut down on their spending

column3: what can you say to them about the future
column4: when can we see the policy rates going down
column5: and maybe affecting also the 12 month Euribor? Thank you.

column1: So
column2: of course we are aware of these households that have contracted loans with floating rates
column3: variable rates
column4: whatever you call it
column5: and from Finland to Portugal
column6: from some of the Baltic countries to Spain

Some countries are taking particular steps and measures and some financial institutions are also looking at offering moratoria or delays. I think that the best we can do is to really tame inflation in a timely manner
column9: meaning as fast as we can

Thank you for giving us that angle from the East. You know I would hope that

column3: we can
column4: one

column1: 2023.06.01 13:30:00|Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday
column2: 3-4 May 2023|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel noted that since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting
column2: the market narrative had shifted back from financial stability concerns to inflation concerns and to potential effects on the economy from the turbulence in the banking sector. Markets seemed so far to have digested the bank failures well
column3: especially in the euro area. Measures of systemic stress
column4: volatility and market liquidity had returned to close to their levels before the failure of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB). Risk assets in the euro area had not only largely recovered the losses experienced following the SVB failure
column5: but in some cases had even rallied to new multi-year highs. Sovereign bond spreads had also shown remarkable resilience. Yet investors had significantly scaled back expectations of ECB monetary policy tightening. While the sharp downward shift in expectations for monetary policy rates at the height of the banking tensions had been partially reversed
column6: the peak rate expected for the deposit facility remained around 50 basis points below levels priced in before the failure of SVB. Three potential factors could explain this repricing: receding inflation risks
column7: heightened recession fears in the face of tighter financial conditions
column8: or financial stability concerns. However
column9: none of these explanations was fully borne out by financial market data.

column1: On the basis of market pricing
column2: current risks of systemic stress seemed contained. Implied volatility in US bond markets had retreated to its 2022 average from very high levels in mid-March
column3: while stock market implied volatility in the United States had recently fallen to its lowest level since November 2021. Similarly
column4: liquidity conditions in euro area sovereign bond markets had normalised.

column1: The turbulence had left a lasting mark on bank stock indices
column2: which remained below the levels observed before SVB’s failure. However
column3: euro area bank stocks currently stood above their level at the start of 2023
column4: and spillovers from the financial sector to the non-financial corporate sector had been limited. Prices for risk assets had generally been less adversely affected in the euro area than in the United States.

column1: The general resilience of financial markets also extended to sovereign bonds. Sovereign spreads had widened only slightly after the SVB failure
column2: had normalised quickly after the banking tensions had subsided and had since remained close to their pre-SVB levels. This resilience had not been challenged by evolving market expectations for the reduction of the asset purchase programme (APP) portfolio. Both the start of quantitative tightening and expectations of a full roll-off had been absorbed smoothly by the market.

column1: Despite fading concerns about market turbulence
column2: investors had
column3: in response to the banking tensions
column4: significantly scaled back expectations for future ECB interest rate hikes.

column1: A first possible explanation for the pronounced repricing of expectations for ECB interest rates could be receding concerns about inflation risks in the euro area. The decline in inflation-linked swap (ILS) forward rates
column2: which had started at the beginning of March
column3: had continued with the onset of the banking turbulence
column4: in line with an initially disinflationary effect from the turbulence. At the same time
column5: market participants did not seem to see the risks to the longer-term inflation outlook as having been alleviated by the banking tensions. The five-year forward ILS rate five years ahead had remained stubbornly above 2.4% since the Governing Council’s March monetary policy meeting. Investors continued to consider a scenario where inflation remained above target over the longer term significantly more probable than a scenario where it dropped below 2%.

column1: An alternative explanation for the repricing of monetary policy expectations was the perception that tighter financial conditions made a recession more likely
column2: implying less need for further rate hikes. However
column3: most common financial conditions indices for the euro area had remained broadly unchanged since the collapse of SVB
column4: even though bank lending rates had been increasing. There was also little indication in financial markets that the banking sector stress had affected economic growth. Investors were currently pricing in only marginally higher tail risks to the economic outlook for the euro area compared with the pre-SVB period.

column1: The evolution of the exchange rate provided further insights into the expected impact of the banking sector turbulence on the economy. Since the start of the banking tensions the euro had appreciated discernibly against the US dollar
column2: in line with the narrowing of the two-year interest rate differential between the euro area and the United States. Monetary policy convergence between the ECB and the Federal Reserve System seemed to have been a key driver of the euro’s appreciation. The scaling back of rate hike expectations had been greater in the United States than in the euro area. Positive economic data surprises in the euro area had also supported the euro
column3: whereas rising downside risks to the US growth outlook had put pressure on the dollar. All in all
column4: euro-dollar exchange rate developments were consistent with a more muted impact of the banking tensions on the economic outlook in the euro area than in the United States.

column1: A third possible explanation for the repricing of interest rate expectations was related to financial stability concerns. With net outflows of deposits from euro area banks
column2: market-based funding was becoming more important. However
column3: short-term funding conditions in the interbank market had returned to pre-SVB conditions. The increase in credit and liquidity risk premia in money markets in mid-March had proved to be only temporary. Similarly
column4: the effect on longer-term market funding conditions had been limited
column5: and asset swap spreads of bank bonds had also almost returned to pre-SVB levels. At the same time
column6: banks’ increasing use of longer-term bond market funding as an alternative to deposit funding tended to increase their average funding costs. Finally
column7: the vulnerability of banks to rising interest rates depended not only on funding considerations but also on the assets side of their balance sheets. Overall
column8: short-run risks to euro area banks from higher interest rates appeared to be contained.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Mr Lane went through the latest economic
column2: monetary and financial developments in the global economy and the euro area since the Governing Council’s last monetary policy meeting.

column1: Global economic activity had been stronger than expected in early 2023. The global composite output Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) had risen further in March and reached 51.8 in the first quarter
column2: up from 48.4 in the last quarter of 2022. At the same time
column3: PMI data signalled a divergence between services
column4: which continued to expand
