Does it mean that the 3.75% terminal rate that was generally expected – at least until recently – isn't going to be enough? Then secondly: you've alluded to the strength of the labour market and the impact that wages are having on inflation. Do you think you can achieve the 2% inflation target with unemployment remaining as low as it is now? Or does it have to go up?
So
column2: your first question referred to the core inflation revision. We revised actually all three. We revised 2023 and 2024 and ultimately to 2.3% [in 2025] which moved by 0.1 from the previous projections [of 2.2%]. I think on the basis of that you can easily conclude that we are not satisfied with the results of that inflation outlook – which is only one of the three components that we look at. That is the reason why we are making the monetary policy decision that we make today
column3: and why we are thinking that
column4: unless there was a material change to the baseline
column5: we would again hike interest rates in July. I don't want to comment about the terminal rate. This is what markets are considering. The terminal rate is something that we will know when we get there because it is not what is driving our analysis and our deliberations. What is driving it is the ultimate destination
column6: which is the 2% inflation. That's what we want and there are lots of components that come in to help us arrive at the 2% target.

column1: We spent a lot of time on the labour market. We spent a lot of time because it is becoming one of the major components of the drivers of inflation. It was energy for a long time. To oversimplify: energy played a significant role
column2: then food kicked in
column3: and energy is now fading
column4: has moved now in May and is in slightly negative territory. But labour
column5: and wages in particular
column6: is playing a significant role as a driver of inflation. It's quite extraordinary because there have been more people employed
column7: the average hours have been up
column8: wages are increasing – we had 5.2% growth for the first quarter in the compensation per employee –
column9: and the output is where it is: stagnant. So
column10: there is an issue of unit labour cost –in other words
column11: productivity – which clearly has an impact on inflation as well. We will continue to really monitor and dissect as well as we can this entire enigma of the labour market – which is
column12: as I said
column13: playing a critical role.

column1: It's especially important because many services which are playing a large part in our economy are labour-intensive
column2: and wages in that respect play a key role. That is partly
column3: by the way
column4: the reason why we have – I was going to say upgraded
column5: but it's not upgraded–
column6: but why we have increased our projection for core inflation in both 2023 and 2024.

column1: My first question: I was a bit surprised by how strong this revision of the core inflation projection was. Could you elaborate a bit on the reason? Is that all due to wages
column2: wage expectations
column3: or are there other reasons behind that? My second question is about the decision today. Was it unanimous? Could you maybe give us a bit of a flavour about the discussion?

column1: On the first one
column2: our revision to core inflation – I've started answering already in the previous question–
column3: a lot of it is attributable to the unit labour cost. That's a large chunk of the revision. The rest is what you have in the monetary policy statement
column4: which is past upward surprises. So
column5: it's a different starting point
column6: which is informed by data that came in after the last projection that we made in March. The latest data that we had in terms of inflation was from January. Now
column7: things obviously changed between those January data and the May data that we have incorporated because we cut off on the 23 May[

column1: ]. I think that's a small part of it. The large part of it is the unit labour cost.
You asked me about the decision and the atmosphere. I have to tell you that it was quite a harmonious discussion and a very good and thorough economic discussion. As I said
column2: we went really deep into the analysis of the labour market and tried to really understand the forces behind inflation to better fight it. It was a very
column3: very broad consensus. By the way
column4: I just want to remind that it was a twofold decision. It was
column5: number one
column6: the 25 basis points but it was also the decision
column7: or the confirmation
column8: that we would stop any reinvestment under the APP.

column1: What does the ECB know about lag effects? What takes longer to transmit into the economy? What are you looking at more closely? The second question
column2: about your targets. According to projections you do not expect to reach the inflation target in the next three years. Some economists suggest that this target is no longer valid
column3: that 3% will be the new 2%. What do you have to say about that?

column1: We have a target. We have agreed on the target. We are in the middle of that fight against inflation and this is what we know. We're going to get to that 2% and we're going to reduce it to 2%. What happens next is another story
column2: but we want to be at target and we want to be confident that it remains at target. So
column3: the two elements are going to really drive our monetary policy going forward.

column1: On the lag time: we know that there is lag time
column2: that the decisions that we have made in the last soon-to-be-a-year – which are monumental
column3: by all accounts
column4: both in terms of speed
column5: in terms of height
column6: volume of hikes
column7: if you will
column8: and we are seeing some effects. We are seeing it in market rates. We are seeing it in banking
column9: financing. We are seeing it in credit
column10: both in volumes and in rates. There is some lag time – not that much by textbook standards
column11: which will typically say that it's anywhere between 18 and 24 months
column12: maybe a bit more. But because it is so unprecedented and such an exceptional situation
column13: we really have to monitor that very carefully. Whether it is going to be faster
column14: whether it is going to be a bit more slow because there has been variation in the terms of loans
column15: for instance
column16: to both corporates and mortgages and therefore the transmission is not operating as smoothly as it would if everything was at floating rates. All of that we are looking at extremely carefully to measure the transmission and see how fast it moves. Suffice to say that we are seeing it already. Do we see all of it? Obviously
column17: no. We want to see it all the way down to inflation.

column1: Two questions from me. Firstly
column2: the Bank of Canada recently restarted its rate hikes
column3: saying that the reason for this was that it thought the neutral rate had risen from its previous expectations. Do you think similarly? Is that part of the reason that you're continuing to raise rates and signal more rate rises are ahead? The second question is about whether the ECB could consider skipping rate rises
column4: certain meetings
column5: perhaps going to only changing policy when you're issuing forecasts – similarly to the Fed's pause or skip yesterday.

column1: It's difficult to say whether we're in the same position as the Bank of Canada because we did not pause. So
column2: in a way we don't have to ask ourselves whether we are at neutral rate or not. We believe that we have ground to cover. So
column3: we are not where we want to be if we want to reach our target. In terms of having to pause or having to skip: as I said
column4: number one
column5: we have not discussed it at all and we have not begun thinking about it because we have work to do.

column1: I have two questions. The first question is: today you confirmed
column2: repeated
column3: that rates will be kept at the restricted levels for as long as necessary. Because inflation will be above 2% in 2025
column4: we can expect restrictive rates for long. How is the Governing Council concerned that you're going far and you
column5: at the same time
column6: would like to avoid unnecessarily harming economic activity? How far do you look at growth weakening in response to your policies? Then a second question regards this June. That is a historical month for the ECB; the €477 billion repayment of TLTROs is seen as the biggest daily reduction of the ECB balance sheet. On the top this June is also the last month of APP reinvestments. So
column7: what is the impact of these two unprecedented events in the ECB on tightening of financing and monetary conditions?

column1: I thought you were going to say that it’s an important month because we are celebrating our 25th anniversary – which was also the date when the ECB was opened first on the ground here in Frankfurt. As I said
column2: the objective that we have is very clear. The destination we know. The journey to get there is not over and we have ground to cover. So
column3: we will be as restrictive as long as needed in order to make sure that we reach that destination. Under the current parameters
column4: 2.2% in 2025 is not satisfactory and it’s not timely – which is why we are making the decisions that we are making today
column5: and later on. At the end of June banks will reimburse €477 billion that they had borrowed under TLTRO
column6: which was this very special facility that we had put in place to help the financing of the economy at the time of the pandemic.

column1: Those loans were granted for periods of three years and there were various operations in the course of the pandemic. The repayment which is coming due now
column2: is known and has been known for a long time. Actually it was so well-known that it should have been a lot higher than that but we took measures in order to avoid that we had this sort of cliff effect of a massive reimbursement which would have exceeded €1 trillion. But banks know about it
column3: they have known about it. They have done their funding plans in order to respond to the situation. In any event
column4: we have the normal facilities available
column5: whether it's MRO or LTRO if that was ever needed
column6: just in case.

column1: The APP reinvestment will be completed at the end of June
column2: and we will let run-off take place as of July. We have experienced that partial reinvestment now for a few months because it was decided back in March. It has been well-absorbed by markets. We have not observed any disruption. Given the amounts that we are talking about
column3: we have reasons to believe that it should be absorbed also in a smooth manner. But
column4: of course
column5: we will be very attentive. We will look at this process. We will
column6: as I said
column7: always have the means to take action and to use all the tools that we have available if it was needed.

column1: You've touched on the problem of the wage increases. At your speech at the European Parliament
column2: you touched on the problem of corporate profits. If you take these both together
column3: how confident are you that the relevant parties actually start to be more moderate on this
column4: in particular as both of them start to criticise that interest rates are already too high? The second question: I'm also a bit puzzled about the real severity and persistency of this core inflation. May I ask you as well
column5: please
column6: to elaborate a little bit more where the Governing Council sees the reason for this really strong persistence?

column1: The labour market situation and the employment situation is the good news in Europe
column2: and we have never seen the unemployment rate be so low. Actually in our forecast we see the unemployment rate go from this 6.5% that we have now
column3: to 6.3%. We see the level of unemployment continuing to decline. We also see wages continuing to increase in the future. Now
column4: you really asked me specifically the question of whether corporations and labour – and I'm using that term in a generic
column5: comprehensive way – will find the terms under which they don't contribute to fuelling even more inflation that would call on us to take harder monetary policy measures. This is the assumption that we make. I think economically it is justifiable
column6: it is rational
column7: but of course humans are humans. It's going to be for the parties around the table to actually determine what they do going forward in terms of allocating profits and organising these social relationships. What they can be certain of in their discussion is that the European Central Bank will take all necessary measures to return inflation to 2%. That
column8: they can count on
column9: and we are confident that we will get there so I hope it helps in their deliberation going forward.

column1: The persistency of inflation
column2: as I said
column3: has a lot to do with this unit labour cost that I have mentioned earlier on. This is really the strong – I don't want to use sticky component
column4: because it is going to be persistent
column5: and we know it. Numbers will continue to be high in the months to come
column6: by the way
column7: because we believe that services are going to continue to grow strongly. Labour-intensive services will. Contact-intensive services will continue to grow strongly. We're heading into the summer: all the summer activities
column8: whether it's transportation
column9: whether it's hospitality
column10: whether it's vacation
column11: all of that is going to go well. So
column12: that persistence is to be expected in the short run. There will be remaining persistency going through into 2024. It declines in 2025 and we have not revised upwards significantly for 2025 because we believe that other elements will kick in
column13: which will reduce inflation numbers – unless risks were to materialise.

column1: But under the baseline
column2: the indirect effect of energy costs will continue to fade. You can still find them in prices
column3: but it is going to gradually fade out. The same goes for food. We expect the persistence of inflation to gradually fade away. As much as it persists
column4: we will persist.

column1: You have delivered quite a strong message about wages
column2: and I'm a little bit scared. Has the risk of an inflation spiral increased since March? The second question about the projections: if 2025 is not acceptable
column3: do we need to see 2% inflation in 2024 for the ECB to consider that the objective will be achieved in a timely manner? Or what is exactly a timely manner?

column1: Well
column2: first of all on wages: we are not seeing second round effects. We're not seeing this wage price spiral. The only thing that I'm trying to say here is that we have to avoid what I have called the tit-for-tat where
column3: in response to inflation
column4: both corporates and labour want to receive full compensation – which obviously would possibly lead to that second-round effect that I was alluding to. Obviously
column5: the sooner the better in terms of when do we bring inflation back to 2%? We have to be also realistic
column6: and we have to be measured in the response that we give
column7: but very determined in the delivery of those measures
column8: and persistent.

column1: You said that wages are having a huge impact on inflation on one side
column2: and on the other side you say that there is no wage price spiral. So
column3: it's not really clear to understand. Can you maybe give us an explanation on how you can come to this conclusion?

column1: We just all wish that everything was clear and simple
column2: wouldn't we? What I said – and thank you very much for your question – is that unit labour cost
column3: which is slightly different from wages
column4: negotiated wages
column5: however you want to measure it– is having an impact
column6: or it is rather causing the revision of core inflation projection. That's what I'm saying. You can certainly have that projection and at the same time acknowledge that today we are not seeing any spiralling of wages and prices that would cause this second-round effect that we would be very concerned about.

column1: You said that the financial markets are not feeling the impact of the balance sheet reduction. Do you expect to
column2: from July onwards
column3: have room to reduce it further?

column1: Well
column2: two things. The TLTRO reimbursement that is falling due at the end of June
column3: which was anticipated
column4: known by all parties involved
column5: is taking place at the end of June. It will
column6: as a result
column7: reduce the balance sheet of the ECB by €477 billion. The second part of the decision that we made today was to stop reinvesting redemptions under APP
column8: and let APP move into a run-off mode. That's all we decided. That means that
column9: for instance
column10: the PEPP continues as it was indicated in the only part of forward guidance that we still have in our monetary policy
column11: which is until 2024 we continue the reinvestment and we apply flexibility if
column12: and where
column13: it is needed. There is no plan to change that."|https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/press_conference/monetary-policy-statement/2023/html/ecb.is230615~3de9d68335.en.html

column1: 2023.07.13 13:30:00|Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday
column2: 14-15 June 2023|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel noted that
column2: since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 3-4 May 2023
column3: the narrative in financial markets had shifted from global tail risks – emanating from the banking sector tensions and the US debt ceiling debate – towards concerns about a deterioration in the euro area macroeconomic outlook and more persistent core inflation pressures globally.

column1: Global market conditions had further normalised as tail risks to the economy had subsided. Volatility in financial markets had decreased notably across market segments and countries
column2: suggesting that risks of systemic stress were currently contained. Stock market implied volatility in the United States
column3: as measured by the VIX volatility index
column4: had declined to its lowest level since the beginning of 2020.

column1: Market conditions had also normalised across market segments in the euro area. Banks had restarted primary market issuance activity not only for covered bonds and senior bonds
column2: but more recently also for subordinated bonds. Moreover
column3: banks’ asset swap spreads of subordinated and senior bonds had decreased substantially
column4: but remained slightly above the levels seen before the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB). Spreads of non-financial corporate bonds had remained broadly stable and stood below the average levels recorded in 2022.

column1: Developments in sovereign bond markets had been even more benign. Sovereign spreads relative to overnight index swap (OIS) rates had decreased during the market turmoil in March and had continued to narrow since then. Both the start of partial reinvestments and the expected end of reinvestments under the asset purchase programme (APP) had been absorbed smoothly by the market. Nevertheless
column2: sovereign spreads had remained sensitive to fundamentals
column3: as illustrated by the response to recent shifts in rating outlooks.

column1: Negative macroeconomic data surprises had sparked investor concerns about a deterioration in the economic outlook. However
column2: developments in equity markets argued against the hypothesis that markets were pricing in a severe economic downturn. Equity indices for euro area banks and non-financial corporations had seen only small changes. Moreover
column3: defensive equity sectors
column4: i.e. stocks which tend to be more stable during periods of expected economic weakness
column5: had underperformed sectors more sensitive to the business cycle.

column1: Developments in long-term risk-free bond yields had also provided little indication that negative data surprises had left a significant mark on the economic growth outlook. A decomposition of long-term yields into real rates and the inflation component in the euro area showed that real rates were slightly up since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 3-4 May 2023
column2: and only marginally down since the collapse of SVB.

column1: In the United States
column2: real interest rates had continued to recover strongly from the banking sector turmoil. Markets were no longer pricing in the banking sector stress driving a significant wedge between the growth outlook in the euro area and the United States. This was also evident in the gap between ten-year real rates
column3: which had widened again and was now as large as in early March. The divergence in risk-free rates in the euro area vis-à-vis the United States had also been reflected in the EUR/USD exchange rate. The euro had depreciated by around 3% since the previous monetary policy meeting
column4: closely tracking movements in interest rate differentials.

column1: Regarding the evolution of interest rate expectations
column2: the front end of the euro short-term rate (€STR) forward curve had remained broadly unchanged. The forward curve was pricing in two more 25 basis point rate hikes – one at the present meeting and another in July – and a 20% probability of an additional 25 basis point hike afterwards
column3: implying a peak deposit facility rate slightly above the level that had been expected at the time of the previous monetary policy meeting. The inversion of the forward curve had moderated. By contrast
column4: the US federal funds futures curve had shifted upwards markedly since the previous monetary policy meeting.

column1: Uncertainty about the future path of monetary policy in the euro area had declined substantially since the collapse of SVB. Volatility in expected euro area short-term interest rates had reached its lowest level since May 2022
column2: before the start of the ECB’s rate hiking cycle
column3: reflecting the increasing convergence of monetary policy expectations among market participants.

column1: The reduction in uncertainty about the ECB’s medium-term policy rate path seemed somewhat at odds with market participants’ inflation expectations. Inflation-linked swap forward rates had continued to gradually increase from their mid-March lows. Remarkably
column2: this repricing had come despite the weaker macroeconomic data as well as softer than expected inflation data releases and falling commodity prices. The increase in inflation-linked swap rates could partly be attributed to rising inflation risk premia
column3: also reflecting the fact that many commodity prices appeared to be subject to pronounced upside risks for which investors demanded compensation. Such risks also related to food prices
column4: which were exposed to upside risks posed by Russia’s war in Ukraine as well as to a rising probability of more frequent extreme weather events occurring this year as a result of El Niño. The second factor driving up inflation compensation was the increase in expected core inflation rates.

column1: Market-based measures of longer-term inflation compensation in the euro area had trended upwards since the summer of 2022
column2: amid some volatility. The persistent upward trend of these measures was unique among major currency areas. Option prices also pointed to rising upside risks to inflation. Such elevated and rising market-based inflation expectations over the medium and long run indicated that investors may have some doubts as to whether the currently priced-in ECB policy rate path was sufficient to rein in inflation in a timely manner. Real one-year OIS rates one year ahead were currently 45 basis points below their level before the SVB collapse and were expected to remain at around 0.25% or lower over the coming years.

column1: Ms Schnabel then turned to the market impact of some of the ECB’s recent policy decisions. As announced in February
column2: the ceiling for the remuneration of government deposits held with the Eurosystem and for the rate on deposits of non-euro area residents held under the Eurosystem reserve management services framework had been set at a spread of 20 basis points below the euro short-term rate (€STR) from 1 May 2023. Overall
column3: the new level of remuneration for these deposits had achieved the desired effects. Nevertheless
column4: developments would be closely monitored to assess whether the pricing had been adequately calibrated.

column1: Turning to the implications of the upcoming large repayments due under the targeted longer-term refinancing operation (TLTRO) in June
column2: banks were expected to predominantly draw on their excess liquidity holdings as well as on market funding. Recourse to the ECB’s regular refinancing operations – the main refinancing operations and three-month longer-term refinancing operations – would be a natural choice for banks that required other funding sources.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Starting with the outlook for the global economy
column2: Mr Lane recalled that
column3: after a rebound in the first quarter of the year
column4: global economic growth had decelerated
column5: especially in advanced economies
column6: and was heavily skewed towards the services sector. The gap between the global output Purchasing Managers’ Indices for the services and manufacturing sectors had reached a historical high. The euro had depreciated both against the US dollar and in effective terms since the last monetary policy meeting. Oil futures had remained broadly stable and natural gas futures prices were lower than at the time of the May Governing Council meeting. Non-energy commodity prices had declined
column7: with both food and metal prices falling compared with the last meeting.

column1: The euro area economy had stagnated in recent months: contracting public and private consumption and a negative contribution from inventories had only partly been offset by expanding net trade and investment. Business investment had held up in the first quarter of 2023
column2: thanks to the easing of supply bottlenecks
column3: as car production in particular had resumed. At the same time
column4: survey data pointed to only a modest recovery in the second quarter of the year.

column1: Developments had diverged sharply across sectors also in the euro area. Hard data and surveys indicated very weak activity in the manufacturing sector amid feeble demand and the running down of order backlogs. By contrast
column2: the services sector remained resilient
column3: still benefiting from the stimulus provided to contact-intensive services by the reopening of the economy. However
column4: historical patterns suggested that the weakness in manufacturing could spill over to the services sector in the months ahead. One possible reason for expecting a lagged slowdown in services related to the fact that monetary policy had been shown to have a more powerful and faster effect on manufacturing than on services.

column1: The contractionary impact of monetary policy was gradually reaching the components of aggregate demand that were typically more sensitive to interest rate changes
column2: namely housing and business investment
column3: as well as durable goods consumption. Expectations of higher mortgage rates weighed heavily on the perceived attractiveness of housing as an investment
column4: while short-term indicators suggested a weakening in business investment owing to tighter financing conditions and falling orders. Consumers were also less inclined to purchase big-ticket items
column5: and survey-based evidence suggested that a rising share of households with variable rate mortgages expected to have difficulties in making their mortgage payments on time. At the same time
column6: private consumption was still expected to pick up
column7: driven by remaining pent-up demand for contact-intensive services following the pandemic and by rising incomes as a result of nominal wage increases and rising employment. Looking ahead
column8: a modest increase in exports was also expected.

column1: The June Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area had revised the outlook for GDP growth downwards slightly for 2023 and 2024
column2: while leaving it unchanged for 2025. Average annual real GDP growth was expected to slow to 0.9% in 2023 (from 3.5% in 2022)
column3: before rebounding to 1.5% in 2024 and 1.6% in 2025.

column1: Output was expected to increase over the projection horizon. On the supply side
column2: favourable developments included the ongoing expansion in productive capacity after the pandemic
column3: the easing of supply bottlenecks and the expansion in labour supply (including through immigration). Demand was expected to increase owing to rising domestic incomes
column4: underpinned by a robust labour market; the improvement in the terms of trade and the associated decline in uncertainty; and the recovery in foreign demand. At the same time
column5: the scale of the recovery in demand would be constrained by the ECB’s policy tightening. Together with a gradual withdrawal of fiscal support
column6: tighter financing conditions would restrict economic activity in the medium term.

column1: Downside risks to economic growth included Russia’s war against Ukraine and an increase in broader geopolitical tensions
column2: which could fragment global trade and thus weigh on the euro area economy. Growth could also be slower if the ECB’s monetary policy was transmitted more forcefully than expected. Renewed financial market tensions could lead to even tighter financing conditions than anticipated and could weaken confidence. Moreover
column3: weaker growth in the world economy could further dampen economic activity in the euro area. However
column4: growth could be higher than expected if the strong labour market and receding uncertainty meant that people and businesses became more confident and spent more.

column1: The labour market remained strong. The unemployment rate had stood at its historical low of 6.5% in April. Employment continued to benefit from a strong increase in the labour force
column2: while demand for labour remained at high levels
column3: including as a result of labour hoarding. At the same time
column4: average hours worked per person employed was still somewhat below pre-pandemic levels. Wage pressures continued to strengthen
column5: adding to underlying inflation pressures. Nevertheless
column6: recent wage increases were broadly in line with the March staff projections and therefore had not led to a reassessment of the wage pressures for 2023 in the June projections. At the same time
column7: in some sectors profit levels placed employers in a favourable position to absorb wage increases even as the scope for price increases declined.

column1: There had been large increases in unit profits between the first quarter of 2022 and the fourth quarter of 2022 across all sectors
column2: ranging from around 15% in contact-intensive services to around 23% in agriculture. In the first quarter of 2023
column3: by contrast
column4: some divergence had started to emerge across sectors. While the energy
column5: utility and construction sectors had seen another strong increase in unit profits
column6: the manufacturing sector and contact-intensive services sectors had seen declining unit profits. This implied that the sizeable wage increases had not been passed on to customers in the first quarter. This early evidence of lower unit profits in both manufacturing and contact-intensive services was consistent with the baseline assumption of declining unit profits in the June projections.

column1: Headline inflation as measured by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) had declined to 6.1% in May
column2: from 7.0% in April. Following an uptick in April
column3: energy inflation had resumed the downward trend seen since last autumn. Food inflation was likely to have peaked in March and stood at 12.5% in May. HICP inflation excluding energy and food (HICPX
column4: or core inflation) had also declined for a second consecutive month
column5: reaching 5.3% in May. In terms of pipeline pressures for food and goods inflation
column6: there was an ongoing improvement at earlier stages of the production process. This improvement was expected to translate into a reduction in pressures from input costs over the rest of the year.

column1: A number of indicators of underlying inflation – notably trimmed measures
column2: exclusion-based measures and model-based indicators
column3: such as the Persistent and Common Component of Inflation (PCCI) – showed signs of softening. The “Supercore” indicator and wage-sensitive components of the HICPX were levelling off
column4: while domestic inflation was still continuing to increase
column5: reflecting continued strong wage growth and demand for contact-intensive services. This configuration suggested that the external drivers of underlying inflation (rising energy costs and supply bottlenecks) were easing
column6: but rising wages and ongoing effects from the reopening of the economy were still putting upward pressure on the domestic component of underlying inflation.

column1: The different dynamics of goods inflation compared with services inflation
column2: which were related to differences in the tradability and labour content of the different inflation components
column3: implied that it was important to look separately at underlying measures of these two components of the HICP. For goods inflation
column4: the Supercore and PCCI measures had both been declining
column5: with the PCCI having been on a downward path since the end of 2022. The significant downward adjustment of the PCCI indicator largely reflected the decline in energy prices
column6: since a large share of goods production was energy-intensive. Momentum in goods inflation was also on a downward path. By contrast
column7: for services inflation the underlying measures and the momentum did not yet point to any visible decline. While the PCCI indicator for services had stabilised
column8: the Supercore measure was still on an upward trend. Services inflation had declined marginally in May; however
column9: these data were in part affected by a new
column10: cheaper monthly ticket for public transport in Germany.

column1: Turning to inflation expectations
column2: respondents in the Survey of Monetary Analysts had kept their expectations for 2025 and 2026 unchanged. The Consumer Expectations Survey showed that consumer inflation perceptions and expectations had both decreased significantly in April and May after the temporary increase in March.

column1: The June staff projections saw headline HICP inflation slightly above the path envisaged in previous exercises. Headline inflation was expected to decrease from 8.4% in 2022 to an average of 5.4% in 2023
column2: 3.0% in 2024 and 2.2% in 2025. The downward impact from lower energy price assumptions was more than offset by upward revisions in food inflation and core inflation. Underlying price pressures remained strong. Staff had revised up their projections for core inflation
column3: especially for this year and next year
column4: owing to past upward surprises and the implications of the robust labour market for the speed of disinflation. The staff projections now saw core inflation averaging 5.1% in 2023
column5: before declining to averages of 3.0% in 2024 and 2.3% in 2025.

column1: Russia’s war against Ukraine remained a significant upside risk to the inflation outlook

column3: because it is a matter that we have reviewed
column4: that staff are doing a lot of work on and that we have discussed. It is the role of wage growth and the role of profit margins as two key drivers of inflation
column5: which are gradually eliminating the external causes that were prevalent before. The wage increases are definitely playing an increasing role as a driver of inflation and so have profit margins. On the profit margins front
column6: we are seeing a slight decline in the first quarter of 2023 and as you may remember
column7: our projection is also predicated on the fact that profit margins are wide enough to accommodate the squeeze that will be needed in order to allow for wage increases. But if we look at inflation expectations
column8: if we look at how wages and profit margins are evolving
column9: we are not seeing a second-round effect and for the moment at least
column10: nothing suggests the risk of strengthening any second-round effects. But we are really monitoring that very carefully because
column11: as you know
column12: service inflation is the sort of hard nut to crack in terms of inflation
column13: given that on goods it’s going down
column14: energy is coming out and it’s negative. Clearly
column15: we are focusing on services that are labour-intensive and that are also not as sensitive to interest rates. But we are looking at that very carefully and will continue to look at that extremely carefully.

column1: Regarding the September meeting and the possibility of hiking or pausing
column2: as of today
column3: does the burden of the proof fall on an improvement of the inflation outlook
column4: or will it be enough if the situation does not worsen? And a second question if I may: Spanish headline inflation is now in line with the mandate and the labour market is as hot as it has been for more than a decade. Is it something you would like to see for the full eurozone or is it necessary for the unemployment rate to go up for the ECB to stop hiking?

column1: Do you mind me asking you to repeat what you said about the unemployment rate in Spain.
It’s at the lowest point for more than a decade.
Including for young people?
Yes
column2: I was just saying that would you like to see that for the whole euro zone? I mean inflation going to 2% and unemployment being low. Or is it just not possible and the labour market has to cool down?

column1: I’ll start with that one
column2: your question about Spain
column3: because it demonstrates the beauty of Europe and the heterogeneity that we have among the 20 countries that are members of the euro area. Obviously
column4: the numbers that we see now for Spain
column5: with inflation trending towards 2% and hopefully sustainably so
column6: plus unemployment numbers that are as low as they have ever been
column7: is a good set of numbers for the country and for the economy at large. It is not the same for all Member States and there are Member States where inflation is still very high and has been high and is expected to remain high for longer. So we have to be very attentive to the aggregate numbers. Those are the ones that are driving our inflation outlook
column8: helping us determine our policy. But we also have to look at each Member State and the characteristics of each Member State. We shall see. Data will actually inform us better. But the hope that we have is that inflation will come down to 2% in the medium term. That is our primary mandate. As you know
column9: we don’t have a dual mandate
column10: unlike the Fed.

column1: That’s what going to drive our determination. If we can do that with unemployment at the lowest level and staying there
column2: that could be very good. It’s funny because you ask the question of a lawyer. The issue of the burden of proof is very often a lawyer’s issue. I think the burden of proof is going to be on the data. Because we are determined to bring inflation back to target
column3: but we are also going to be in the hands of data and the assessment of data. So the burden of proof is going to be on data.

column1: Two questions for you. First of all
column2: how much do you think tighter monetary policy is contributing to the weakness in the euro zone economy that you identified? And secondly
column3: what would it take in terms of reduction in your growth forecast and a reduction in your inflation forecast in September for you to pause interest rate rises?

column1: What we are working on and what staff is trying to be as detail-specific and conclusive about is the impact of our monetary policy on inflation. So this is really what is the focus and what is driving us. What impact our interest rate hikes have produced
column2: produce
column3: and will produce on inflation. And obviously
column4: the exercise of producing the inflation outlook that will be conducted in September by ECB staff will be very informative for the Governing Council to determine how much has been transmitted and what is expected to continue to be transmitted. As I said earlier on
column5: in the financing leg
column6: a lot has been transmitted. A lot. We know that. In the economy at large
column7: not as much yet. And your second question is totally hypothetical
column8: and I understand why you would want me to answer that question. But there are so many data and so much to take on in terms of the projection that will be produced in September
column9: that I cannot answer your question in advance. We will really have to see.

column1: You are suggesting a possible pause in rates in the near future. Does this mean that during this period of possible pause
column2: we could see an acceleration of the QT. And then it would be like a trade-off among doves and hawks at the Governing Council?

column1: Our key tool
column2: our key instrument in the current circumstances
column3: given the level of inflation that we have at the moment
column4: is interest rates. So there will be no trade-off between either interest rates or QT. Interest rates are the main tool and the most efficient one. So it is the one that we will be using. There is the possibility of a hike
column5: there is the possibility of a pause. It’s a decisive maybe. But don’t expect me to go one way or the other. As I said
column6: the burden of proof is going to be the data and the ultimate point that we are determined to reach is the 2% inflation.

column1: You’ve mentioned that several economic indicators recently have been weaker than expected and there are some economists warning already that the ECB is overdoing it with rate hikes
column2: and they think that more patience would be necessary. So what’s your response to that? And my second question. Climate activists criticize that the green bond purchases by the ECB under the new scoring system have largely stopped. Have you perhaps promised too much in terms of what the ECB can contribute to climate protection?

column1: So we would be doing too much and promising too much. Look
column2: doing too much is certainly not something that we are considering. What we are focusing on is the inflation numbers. We are committed to delivering 2% headline
column3: medium term
column4: on a sustainable basis
column5: in a timely manner. This is our commitment. This is the drive of the Governing Council. When I look at headline numbers
column6: when I look at core inflation numbers
column7: when I look at all the many measures of underlying inflation
column8: trying to really isolate the most robust element
column9: and removing the most volatile part of it
column10: we are seeing inflation that is still too high and that we project to remain too high for too long. So we have to do what we have to do
column11: which is currently to hike. We know that we are getting closer
column12: but we also know the options that are on the table: to continue to hike or to hold. And we also know that it will vary meeting by meeting because we want to be determined by the data and the analysis
column13: and the assessment we make of the data. It’s not surprising that it is transmitting to the financing channel. It is not surprising that there is less investment in housing. It is not surprising that there is less investment altogether. This is the intended impact of the monetary policy stance that we have determined. And this is precisely what will return inflation to target.

column1: On the other point: have we promised too much? We have promised in our strategy review and subsequent decision
column2: we have promised to be Paris Agreement-aligned. And obviously
column3: as noted by all of you and as noticed by Greenpeace as well
column4: we stopped any asset purchases under the Asset Purchase Programme
column5: because we are no longer reinvesting. So as a result of that under the CSPP
column6: we are not reinvesting. We are letting that portfolio into run-off mode. What we have decided is that we will stick to our commitment to be Paris Agreement-aligned
column7: and we will in the course of 2023 elaborate the means and the ways by which we will be Paris-aligned. I just want to remind you
column8: and this is not just to distract me for a second from the fight against inflation
column9: but I just want to call your attention to the massive amount of work that is being done in the supervision arm of the ECB in order to really raise the level of awareness and the level of concern by banks and through banks by their clients. This is really beginning to work.

column1: You say that the burden of proof is in the data for future decisions. What data is it that gives you more confidence that you may be able to pause and what data would you be looking at especially over the next months
column2: that would stop those rate hikes? Is it core inflation
column3: is it more that you are looking at the downturn in the euro zone economy and concerns about that? And my second question is about the US and the comparison with the euro zone. The US has raised rates significantly more than the ECB for a similar core inflation rate
column4: or even the euro zone core inflation rate is slightly higher. The IMF
column5: your former employer
column6: said this week that the ECB might have more ground to cover
column7: do you agree? Do you think that there is a suggestion that there might be more work to do in raising rates?

column1: What data will be important? All data. And obviously we will be looking at all inflation data
column2: starting with headline
column3: we will have two readings before our September monetary policy Governing Council. We will look at core inflation
column4: but we will go deeper into underlying inflation numbers to really appreciate and understand what is moving and what is steadily
column5: sustainably moving. We know that some indicators are showing
column6: particularly in goods
column7: it’s pretty obvious
column8: you look at producer prices
column9: it’s pretty obvious. But when you start looking into services in particular
column10: you have to really dissect those that are energy intensive
column11: those that are interest sensitive
column12: what share of labour there is in various segments of services. So we have to look into all that to understand whether the action that we have determined in the last year-and-a-half now
column13: is really having a long-standing impact that will take inflation back to 2%. Don’t forget also that we will be looking at the inflation outlook that will be produced by the ECB
column14: which will give us again the expected path of inflation
column15: and the readings for 2024 and 2025 will obviously be very informative for us. We will look at labour numbers
column16: we will look at investment numbers
column17: we will look at just every single parameter of the whole economy of the euro area that we can look at in order to inform ourselves. I know it would be helpful for those who are using the same models
column18: that are playing the same exercise
column19: to understand from us that there is one particular specific indicator
column20: one particular set of data that prevails over the others. No
column21: it is not the case. We are looking at all of it and expectations are part of the picture as well.

column1: The institution that I used to lead
column2: the IMF
column3: has updated its real April numbers and I don’t think that any of its terribly talented staff would argue with me that inflation in the United States and inflation in Europe are two different beasts
column4: that are fueled by different drivers and in a context that is vastly different
column5: both in terms of fiscal
column6: in terms of labour market
column7: in terms of energy and that certainly has something to do with explaining why figures are where they are. You know that better than anyone else
column8: the Fed started a little bit earlier than the ECB and started from a base that was not negative interest rates either. You asked
column9: do we have more ground to cover. At this point in time
column10: I wouldn’t say so because as I said
column11: the data we just discussed
column12: and the assessment of data
column13: will actually tell us whether and how much ground we have to cover in September and at subsequent meetings. And as I said in the early part of this press conference
column14: it may vary from one month to the other.

column1: I have two questions. One is on this message that you are conveying of the next meeting
column2: that it could be a hike or a pause.

column1: The next meetings.
And so compared to what we had up to now
column2: that is a 25 basis points hike
column3: coming to the next meeting
column4: well
column5: do you have a message to the European citizens that in the fight against inflation
column6: you are getting closer to break the back of inflation? There is some good news in this announcement or these comments that you are making. And then the second question for me is on your assessment of the ECB euro area bank lending survey because it had some data on demand that was
column7: I think
column8: never seen in the past 20 years and so whether it was discussed at the Governing Council and it had an impact also on today’s decision?

column1: Yes
column2: we are making progress. And I think the good news for European compatriots is that inflation is declining. You know we had a reading of 10.6% in October
column3: we are now at 5.5%. But is that enough? Is that good as a result? Not quite. We have a target which is medium term 2% sustainable and we want to get there. But I’m sure that people when they do their shopping
column4: when they fill up their tank
column5: when they pay the gas bill
column6: they see that the increase is not quite the same as six
column7: seven months ago. Are we satisfied? Are we claiming victory? No
column8: we want to go to the end of the game. The bank lending survey
column9: yes
column10: we looked at it carefully
column11: it was debated with governors. And if you look at the monetary policy statement in the last paragraph that we have
column12: it’s very significantly described. The annual growth rate of lending continued to decrease in June falling to 3% for firms and 1.7% for households
column13: with annualised growth rate of 0%
column14: completely flat
column15: and -0.2% in the second quarter
column16: respectively. So not only are we seeing it very mildly grow year on year
column17: but we are seeing a decline in the last quarter and the same holds for both corporates and households. So yes
column18: of course
column19: this is one of the elements of transmission that we have seen discussed and the fall in demand is also obvious
column20: particularly on the part of corporates. A bit less so for households
column21: but on the part of corporates
column22: absolutely
column23: absolutely yes."|https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/press_conference/monetary-policy-statement/2023/html/ecb.is230727~e0a11feb2e.en.html

column1: 2023.08.31 13:30:00|Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday
column2: 14-15 June 2023|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel noted that
column2: since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 3-4 May 2023
column3: the narrative in financial markets had shifted from global tail risks – emanating from the banking sector tensions and the US debt ceiling debate – towards concerns about a deterioration in the euro area macroeconomic outlook and more persistent core inflation pressures globally.

column1: Global market conditions had further normalised as tail risks to the economy had subsided. Volatility in financial markets had decreased notably across market segments and countries
column2: suggesting that risks of systemic stress were currently contained. Stock market implied volatility in the United States
column3: as measured by the VIX volatility index
column4: had declined to its lowest level since the beginning of 2020.

column1: Market conditions had also normalised across market segments in the euro area. Banks had restarted primary market issuance activity not only for covered bonds and senior bonds
column2: but more recently also for subordinated bonds. Moreover
column3: banks’ asset swap spreads of subordinated and senior bonds had decreased substantially
column4: but remained slightly above the levels seen before the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB). Spreads of non-financial corporate bonds had remained broadly stable and stood below the average levels recorded in 2022.

column1: Developments in sovereign bond markets had been even more benign. Sovereign spreads relative to overnight index swap (OIS) rates had decreased during the market turmoil in March and had continued to narrow since then. Both the start of partial reinvestments and the expected end of reinvestments under the asset purchase programme (APP) had been absorbed smoothly by the market. Nevertheless
column2: sovereign spreads had remained sensitive to fundamentals
column3: as illustrated by the response to recent shifts in rating outlooks.

column1: Negative macroeconomic data surprises had sparked investor concerns about a deterioration in the economic outlook. However
column2: developments in equity markets argued against the hypothesis that markets were pricing in a severe economic downturn. Equity indices for euro area banks and non-financial corporations had seen only small changes. Moreover
column3: defensive equity sectors
column4: i.e. stocks which tend to be more stable during periods of expected economic weakness
column5: had underperformed sectors more sensitive to the business cycle.

column1: Developments in long-term risk-free bond yields had also provided little indication that negative data surprises had left a significant mark on the economic growth outlook. A decomposition of long-term yields into real rates and the inflation component in the euro area showed that real rates were slightly up since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 3-4 May 2023
column2: and only marginally down since the collapse of SVB.

column1: In the United States
column2: real interest rates had continued to recover strongly from the banking sector turmoil. Markets were no longer pricing in the banking sector stress driving a significant wedge between the growth outlook in the euro area and the United States. This was also evident in the gap between ten-year real rates
column3: which had widened again and was now as large as in early March. The divergence in risk-free rates in the euro area vis-à-vis the United States had also been reflected in the EUR/USD exchange rate. The euro had depreciated by around 3% since the previous monetary policy meeting
column4: closely tracking movements in interest rate differentials.

column1: Regarding the evolution of interest rate expectations
column2: the front end of the euro short-term rate (€STR) forward curve had remained broadly unchanged. The forward curve was pricing in two more 25 basis point rate hikes – one at the present meeting and another in July – and a 20% probability of an additional 25 basis point hike afterwards
column3: implying a peak deposit facility rate slightly above the level that had been expected at the time of the previous monetary policy meeting. The inversion of the forward curve had moderated. By contrast
column4: the US federal funds futures curve had shifted upwards markedly since the previous monetary policy meeting.

column1: Uncertainty about the future path of monetary policy in the euro area had declined substantially since the collapse of SVB. Volatility in expected euro area short-term interest rates had reached its lowest level since May 2022
column2: before the start of the ECB’s rate hiking cycle
column3: reflecting the increasing convergence of monetary policy expectations among market participants.

column1: The reduction in uncertainty about the ECB’s medium-term policy rate path seemed somewhat at odds with market participants’ inflation expectations. Inflation-linked swap forward rates had continued to gradually increase from their mid-March lows. Remarkably
column2: this repricing had come despite the weaker macroeconomic data as well as softer than expected inflation data releases and falling commodity prices. The increase in inflation-linked swap rates could partly be attributed to rising inflation risk premia
column3: also reflecting the fact that many commodity prices appeared to be subject to pronounced upside risks for which investors demanded compensation. Such risks also related to food prices
column4: which were exposed to upside risks posed by Russia’s war in Ukraine as well as to a rising probability of more frequent extreme weather events occurring this year as a result of El Niño. The second factor driving up inflation compensation was the increase in expected core inflation rates.

column1: Market-based measures of longer-term inflation compensation in the euro area had trended upwards since the summer of 2022
column2: amid some volatility. The persistent upward trend of these measures was unique among major currency areas. Option prices also pointed to rising upside risks to inflation. Such elevated and rising market-based inflation expectations over the medium and long run indicated that investors may have some doubts as to whether the currently priced-in ECB policy rate path was sufficient to rein in inflation in a timely manner. Real one-year OIS rates one year ahead were currently 45 basis points below their level before the SVB collapse and were expected to remain at around 0.25% or lower over the coming years.

column1: Ms Schnabel then turned to the market impact of some of the ECB’s recent policy decisions. As announced in February
column2: the ceiling for the remuneration of government deposits held with the Eurosystem and for the rate on deposits of non-euro area residents held under the Eurosystem reserve management services framework had been set at a spread of 20 basis points below the euro short-term rate (€STR) from 1 May 2023. Overall
column3: the new level of remuneration for these deposits had achieved the desired effects. Nevertheless
column4: developments would be closely monitored to assess whether the pricing had been adequately calibrated.

column1: Turning to the implications of the upcoming large repayments due under the targeted longer-term refinancing operation (TLTRO) in June
column2: banks were expected to predominantly draw on their excess liquidity holdings as well as on market funding. Recourse to the ECB’s regular refinancing operations – the main refinancing operations and three-month longer-term refinancing operations – would be a natural choice for banks that required other funding sources.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Starting with the outlook for the global economy
column2: Mr Lane recalled that
column3: after a rebound in the first quarter of the year
column4: global economic growth had decelerated
column5: especially in advanced economies
column6: and was heavily skewed towards the services sector. The gap between the global output Purchasing Managers’ Indices for the services and manufacturing sectors had reached a historical high. The euro had depreciated both against the US dollar and in effective terms since the last monetary policy meeting. Oil futures had remained broadly stable and natural gas futures prices were lower than at the time of the May Governing Council meeting. Non-energy commodity prices had declined
column7: with both food and metal prices falling compared with the last meeting.

column1: The euro area economy had stagnated in recent months: contracting public and private consumption and a negative contribution from inventories had only partly been offset by expanding net trade and investment. Business investment had held up in the first quarter of 2023
column2: thanks to the easing of supply bottlenecks
column3: as car production in particular had resumed. At the same time
column4: survey data pointed to only a modest recovery in the second quarter of the year.

column1: Developments had diverged sharply across sectors also in the euro area. Hard data and surveys indicated very weak activity in the manufacturing sector amid feeble demand and the running down of order backlogs. By contrast
column2: the services sector remained resilient
column3: still benefiting from the stimulus provided to contact-intensive services by the reopening of the economy. However
column4: historical patterns suggested that the weakness in manufacturing could spill over to the services sector in the months ahead. One possible reason for expecting a lagged slowdown in services related to the fact that monetary policy had been shown to have a more powerful and faster effect on manufacturing than on services.

column1: The contractionary impact of monetary policy was gradually reaching the components of aggregate demand that were typically more sensitive to interest rate changes
column2: namely housing and business investment
column3: as well as durable goods consumption. Expectations of higher mortgage rates weighed heavily on the perceived attractiveness of housing as an investment
column4: while short-term indicators suggested a weakening in business investment owing to tighter financing conditions and falling orders. Consumers were also less inclined to purchase big-ticket items
column5: and survey-based evidence suggested that a rising share of households with variable rate mortgages expected to have difficulties in making their mortgage payments on time. At the same time
column6: private consumption was still expected to pick up
column7: driven by remaining pent-up demand for contact-intensive services following the pandemic and by rising incomes as a result of nominal wage increases and rising employment. Looking ahead
column8: a modest increase in exports was also expected.

column1: The June Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area had revised the outlook for GDP growth downwards slightly for 2023 and 2024
column2: while leaving it unchanged for 2025. Average annual real GDP growth was expected to slow to 0.9% in 2023 (from 3.5% in 2022)
column3: before rebounding to 1.5% in 2024 and 1.6% in 2025.

column1: Output was expected to increase over the projection horizon. On the supply side
column2: favourable developments included the ongoing expansion in productive capacity after the pandemic
column3: the easing of supply bottlenecks and the expansion in labour supply (including through immigration). Demand was expected to increase owing to rising domestic incomes
column4: underpinned by a robust labour market; the improvement in the terms of trade and the associated decline in uncertainty; and the recovery in foreign demand. At the same time
column5: the scale of the recovery in demand would be constrained by the ECB’s policy tightening. Together with a gradual withdrawal of fiscal support
column6: tighter financing conditions would restrict economic activity in the medium term.

column1: Downside risks to economic growth included Russia’s war against Ukraine and an increase in broader geopolitical tensions
column2: which could fragment global trade and thus weigh on the euro area economy. Growth could also be slower if the ECB’s monetary policy was transmitted more forcefully than expected. Renewed financial market tensions could lead to even tighter financing conditions than anticipated and could weaken confidence. Moreover
column3: weaker growth in the world economy could further dampen economic activity in the euro area. However
column4: growth could be higher than expected if the strong labour market and receding uncertainty meant that people and businesses became more confident and spent more.

column1: The labour market remained strong. The unemployment rate had stood at its historical low of 6.5% in April. Employment continued to benefit from a strong increase in the labour force
column2: while demand for labour remained at high levels
column3: including as a result of labour hoarding. At the same time
column4: average hours worked per person employed was still somewhat below pre-pandemic levels. Wage pressures continued to strengthen
column5: adding to underlying inflation pressures. Nevertheless
column6: recent wage increases were broadly in line with the March staff projections and therefore had not led to a reassessment of the wage pressures for 2023 in the June projections. At the same time
column7: in some sectors profit levels placed employers in a favourable position to absorb wage increases even as the scope for price increases declined.

column1: There had been large increases in unit profits between the first quarter of 2022 and the fourth quarter of 2022 across all sectors
column2: ranging from around 15% in contact-intensive services to around 23% in agriculture. In the first quarter of 2023
column3: by contrast
column4: some divergence had started to emerge across sectors. While the energy
column5: utility and construction sectors had seen another strong increase in unit profits
column6: the manufacturing sector and contact-intensive services sectors had seen declining unit profits. This implied that the sizeable wage increases had not been passed on to customers in the first quarter. This early evidence of lower unit profits in both manufacturing and contact-intensive services was consistent with the baseline assumption of declining unit profits in the June projections.

column1: Headline inflation as measured by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) had declined to 6.1% in May
column2: from 7.0% in April. Following an uptick in April
column3: energy inflation had resumed the downward trend seen since last autumn. Food inflation was likely to have peaked in March and stood at 12.5% in May. HICP inflation excluding energy and food (HICPX
column4: or core inflation) had also declined for a second consecutive month
column5: reaching 5.3% in May. In terms of pipeline pressures for food and goods inflation
column6: there was an ongoing improvement at earlier stages of the production process. This improvement was expected to translate into a reduction in pressures from input costs over the rest of the year.

column1: A number of indicators of underlying inflation – notably trimmed measures
column2: exclusion-based measures and model-based indicators
column3: such as the Persistent and Common Component of Inflation (PCCI) – showed signs of softening. The “Supercore” indicator and wage-sensitive components of the HICPX were levelling off
column4: while domestic inflation was still continuing to increase
column5: reflecting continued strong wage growth and demand for contact-intensive services. This configuration suggested that the external drivers of underlying inflation (rising energy costs and supply bottlenecks) were easing
column6: but rising wages and ongoing effects from the reopening of the economy were still putting upward pressure on the domestic component of underlying inflation.

column1: The different dynamics of goods inflation compared with services inflation
column2: which were related to differences in the tradability and labour content of the different inflation components
column3: implied that it was important to look separately at underlying measures of these two components of the HICP. For goods inflation
column4: the Supercore and PCCI measures had both been declining
column5: with the PCCI having been on a downward path since the end of 2022. The significant downward adjustment of the PCCI indicator largely reflected the decline in energy prices
column6: since a large share of goods production was energy-intensive. Momentum in goods inflation was also on a downward path. By contrast
column7: for services inflation the underlying measures and the momentum did not yet point to any visible decline. While the PCCI indicator for services had stabilised
column8: the Supercore measure was still on an upward trend. Services inflation had declined marginally in May; however
column9: these data were in part affected by a new
column10: cheaper monthly ticket for public transport in Germany.

column1: Turning to inflation expectations
column2: respondents in the Survey of Monetary Analysts had kept their expectations for 2025 and 2026 unchanged. The Consumer Expectations Survey showed that consumer inflation perceptions and expectations had both decreased significantly in April and May after the temporary increase in March.

column1: The June staff projections saw headline HICP inflation slightly above the path envisaged in previous exercises. Headline inflation was expected to decrease from 8.4% in 2022 to an average of 5.4% in 2023
column2: 3.0% in 2024 and 2.2% in 2025. The downward impact from lower energy price assumptions was more than offset by upward revisions in food inflation and core inflation. Underlying price pressures remained strong. Staff had revised up their projections for core inflation
column3: especially for this year and next year
column4: owing to past upward surprises and the implications of the robust labour market for the speed of disinflation. The staff projections now saw core inflation averaging 5.1% in 2023
column5: before declining to averages of 3.0% in 2024 and 2.3% in 2025.

column1: Russia’s war against Ukraine remained a significant upside risk to the inflation outlook
column2: as it could push energy and food costs up again. A lasting rise in inflation expectations above the ECB’s inflation target of 2%
column3: or higher than anticipated increases in wages or profit margins
column4: could also drive inflation higher
column5: including over the medium term. Recent wage agreements in a number of countries had added to the upside risks to inflation. By contrast
column6: renewed financial market tensions could bring inflation down faster than projected. Weaker demand
column7: for example owing to a stronger transmission of monetary policy
column8: would also lead to lower price pressures
column9: especially over the medium term. Moreover
column10: inflation would come down faster if declining energy prices and lower food price increases were to pass through to the prices of other goods and services more quickly than was currently anticipated.

column1: Tighter monetary policy continued to be transmitted to bank funding costs. Together with increases in spreads on subordinated bank bonds and on hybrid instruments
column2: and the increased cost of equity for banks
column3: the impact of monetary policy tightening on the risk-free yield curve continued to drive up lending rates for firms and households. The cost of borrowing for firms had increased to 4.4% in April and mortgage rates had risen to 3.4%. Average monthly flows of lending to firms had been negative since November last year
column4: and lending had also contracted slightly in April. Small and newer firms
column5: which tended to be more dependent on bank credit
column6: faced particularly steep increases in their borrowing rates and weak loan flows. Overall
column7: the recent contraction in credit had exceeded the scale indicated by historical patterns.

column1: The short-term dynamics of monetary aggregates had weakened further since the start of the year. The three-month annualised growth rate of M3 had been negative since the start of the year
