column4: the non-bank part of the financial system. I think that in terms of financial stability
column5: we have identified many more vulnerabilities now. That is the focus of our attention now in terms of financial stability.

column1: Firstly
column2: what do you say to people who might accuse you of making a likely recession worse and adding to the woes of the eurozone economy? The second question is whether the expectations that national central banks and the ECB are likely to make sizable losses in coming years. Is that having any impact on your discussions? Is that something that is having an impact on your decisions at the ECB?

column1: I will dispose of the second question first because I think it is going to be a fast response to the point about whether the likelihood or possibility of national central banks or the ECB to make a loss impacts on the decision-making process and our decision. The answer to that is no. This is because
column2: and it also addresses the first questions
column3: the objective that we have and the mandate that we were given is price stability. It is not to make profit. It is to procure price stability within the euro area. And I would observe that the fight that we are leading against inflation – we are not the only ones – is making progress and what we are doing today is trying to reinforce that progress. Back in October we were at 10.6%. We are down to 5.3% now
column4: so it's been divided by two. Is it satisfactory? No
column5: because our projection expects it to still remain too high and for too long. But inflation has declined and we want it to continue to decline and to reinforce that process. And we are doing that
column6: not because we want to force a recession but because we want price stability to be there for people who are taking the brunt of inflation and high prices
column7: and predominantly for those who are not the most privileged people.

column1: My question is If the data dependency and held for long are at odds with each other
column2: and if this can be contradictory and if you are prepared to cut rates if growth slows further. In other words
column3: if it is sufficiently restrictive
column4: could that sentence imply a cut?

column1: This [rate cut] is not even a word that we have pronounced. Yes
column2: the data dependency applies to both the determination of the sufficiently restrictive level as well as the length of time where it has to stay at that level. So we don't see any contradiction in having the two components in the same sentence. One will drive the other
column3: actually. I think I addressed the other one.

column1: How much are the problems in the real estate market affecting the ECB?
That is certainly an area
column2: whether you're looking at residential real-estate
column3: which affects
column4: obviously
column5: at the end of the day households and people
column6: or whether you look at commercial real-estate.This is a sector that is clearly responding very much to the current circumstances. The level of interest rates and the financing tightening that we are conducting to bring inflation down is one of the factors that caused this overall real-estate sector to be in a difficult situation at the moment. We are not oblivious to it. We know it. As I said earlier on
column7: we're not driven to sustain and support a particular sector. We are driven by the imperative of delivering on our mandate
column8: which is price stability. And we want to do that timely.

column1: Can I ask for your assessment on the pace and the strength of the transmission of monetary policy? You noted the fastest contraction in household loans. Do you feel that monetary policy is transmitting as quickly as you would like
column2: too quickly
column3: too strongly or slow enough? And then in the past
column4: you've talked a lot about the ability for wages to keep rising as long as companies absorb those labour costs in their profits. Are you starting to see that to be possible. Or is there a risk of either wages diminishing or profits returning to where they were?

column1: On the transmission channel
column2: there is evidence that the current hiking cycle is transmitting to financing conditions faster than previous ones. You will remember that we use three criteria
column3: three elements in our assessment. One is the inflation outlook
column4: the second one is underlying inflation and the third one is the strength of monetary policy transmission. On the third one
column5: I think we all shared the same view in the room earlier today
column6: that this channel of transmission is strong and stronger than we have seen in previous cycles. So when you look at how fast it transmits to various rates
column7: whether it is overnight or whether it is longer term
column8: it's extremely rapid. It is reflected in the lending rates for corporates
column9: in the lending rates for households
column10: which I think are mentioned as 3.8 in the monetary policy statement. There is a transmission and it is having a constraining impact that is visible when you look at M3
column11: when you look at the volume of loans and when you look at the interest rates. So it is clearly a fact that transmission is effective and more so than in the past.

column1: With regard to the second question: one of the bright spots that we have in terms of activity in the euro area is the labour market. The labour market is still going strongly
column2: the employees’ wages are growing
column3: the employee remuneration is still increasing at 5.5% and the participation has increased by 0.2%. We are beginning to see some signs of weakening in the volume of hires and notably in some sectors
column4: particularly in the services sector that is related to manufacturing. We are beginning to see some signs. But overall
column5: when I look at my numbers today it’s employee remuneration: plus 5.5%; employee participation in the economy: 0.2% plus; and the lowest unemployment rates we have ever had. We are looking very
column6: very carefully at that
column7: because it is having a serious impact on inflation
column8: particularly inflation in the service sector
column9: which is typically much more labour intensive.

column1: Now what are we seeing in in terms of profit? When we look at profit unit cost and its growth
column2: it is still growing. But that growth is
column3: for the first time
column4: having an inflection downwards. So that would comfort the assumption that we have made throughout – we made that at the June projection and we are making it yet again – it comforts the projection that gradually profits will squeeze in order to allow for the wage increases. We are beginning to see it. This is the first time. So we want to be confident that that is a lasting component. It should normally be so because as demand is dampened
column5: this should normally be the reaction in the corporate world.

column1: I would like to come back to the housing market. You mentioned that interest rate hikes have dampened the housing market. But how much of a drag on overall growth is it? How much of a systemic risk is it? Could you please elaborate on how you reached this conclusion of doing a hike today
column2: despite the risk. How do you reach this decision on “yes
column3: a hike is needed after all”?

column1: I will take you through the reasoning that we adopted. We had indicated and we are bound by that intellectual reasoning that we would approach the assessment using three key criteria – inflation outlook
column2: underlying inflation
column3: strength of the transmission of monetary policy. As I said earlier on regarding the third criterion
column4: there is no question in anybody's mind around the Governing Council table
column5: if you want to propel yourself into that room. There was shared analysis of that
column6: with little variations on the margin. On the first item
column7: which is the inflation outlook
column8: we looked at the projections that were given to us by ECB staff. We looked at experts’ reading and analytical work. When you look at the projections
column9: and notwithstanding the GDP revision
column10: we have a revision upward of headline inflation in both 2023 and 2024 and a 0.1 revision downward for 2025
column11: which is hallowed with uncertainty. Because the further out you go into the projection
column12: the less certain it is. On the core inflation which we look at as well – not the only one
column13: but we also look at core inflation – core inflation is maintained in 2023 and revised by 0.1 in 2024 and 2025. But overall
column14: we are not at target in 2025 on headline inflation and we are almost on target on core and we only hit around 2% in the fourth quarter of 2025. So when we look at that
column15: we ask ourselves “how does the inflation outlook compare with our commitments and our target? Not there yet”.

column1: And as I said
column2: it's the key sentence in that monetary policy statement
column3: under current assessment with this decision of a 25 basis point hike
column4: we believe that we are making a substantial contribution etc. etc. So those are the elements that we take into account. The real purpose of what we're doing here is not to be found in that sentence. It’s somewhere else in the beginning of the document that you have where we say “in order to reinforce progress towards our target
column5: the Governing Council today decided to raise the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points”.

column1: We want to reinforce progress. We want to be as timely as is possible and by doing that we support our projections with a higher degree of confidence and I think it will reinforce progress towards target. So we’re determined to get there to that 2% and we see that as the best way to accelerate the process. And by the way: it also reinforces the anchoring of inflation expectations which are broadly at 2%
column2: but which warrant monitoring.

column1: De Guindos: As regards the question how much of a drag the property market is for the financial system
column2: I will follow what the President has indicated before. I think that we have two different situations. In the case of the residential market
column3: what we have started to see is that there is a slowdown in the evolution of prices in residential property
column4: whereas in the case of commercial property
column5: commercial real-estate
column6: the situation is different because we identified a decline in prices even before the tightening cycle of monetary policy. This was related to the situation of COVID
column7: teleworking and these kinds of things. We have made a lot of analysis about the potential impact that the commercial property might have in the financial system and we have identified some channels
column8: some links between commercial property
column9: commercial real-estate
column10: and mutual funds that could reinforce the comment that I have made before about non-banks as a potential source of vulnerability for the financial system. This is the element that we are trying to analyse. There are real-estate funds
column11: property funds
column12: that have a lot of investments and a lot of great exposure to the commercial property. This is something that we have to look at and monitor very closely.

column1: Given the sharp downward revision to GDP in 2024
column2: which you have already explained
column3: can you give us a sense of how concerned the Governing Council is about the chance of a recession? And especially in places and countries like Italy where most
column4: if not all
column5: the economic activity depends on banks?

column1: Well
column2: I think it's in all countries that economic activity depends on financing. So in Europe it's largely banks
column3: but it's not something that is peculiar to Italy. Banks in Europe play a critical role in financing the economic activity both for corporates and for households. We are going through a phase of very sluggish growth. We move from -0.1 to revised 0.1 to revised 0.1 and we see also very weak signs whether you look at PMI
column4: or the gap between manufacturing and services that is now being reduced. We are clearly in a period of slow and sluggish growth. But as I said
column5: the revision that we're making for the next year
column6: where we're moving from 1.5% to 1% of growth
column7: is for three quarters attributable to the sluggish growth that we are going through at the moment. So the difficult times are now and the recovery that we had anticipated is pushed out into 2024. And when you look at the September projection that we have on a quarter-by-quarter basis
column8: it is the same as the one that we had in June
column9: which shows that we are confident that growth will pick up in 2024. Now
column10: of course
column11: we need to succeed
column12: we need to bring inflation down and wages have to be sustained and labour has to hold. Those are some of the assumptions that we make in that respect.

column1: President Lagarde
column2: you alluded to the risk of food inflation peaking up because of adverse weather conditions related to climate change. I know this happened in 2022 already. Have you got concrete indications that this is happening again and could this impact the inflation number? And related to that
column3: my second question
column4: has the ECB made any progress in thinking about how to make its operations aligned with the Paris Agreement in times of monetary tightening?

column1: On the first one
column2: as I said
column3: the food inflation has come down but it is still at 10% at the moment. So it is still hard for people because food is obviously a component of the basket which matters a lot and which matters more for those who earn less. We know that for a fact. So we hope that food will continue to go down but it's one of the components that is still very high. I would maybe enlarge your question to the price of commodities in general because we are seeing movements
column4: whether it is on grains
column5: and obviously the Black Sea Agreement denunciation by Russia is flying in the face of stability
column6: if anything. But whether it's grain
column7: oil
column8: gas
column9: we're looking at all those components very
column10: very carefully because some of them are volatile
column11: some of them are on their way up and they will have consequences on prices. I think we will have to assess on a projection-by-projection basis to really appreciate what impact it has in view of activity around the world as well. We had a good scenario analysis produced by staff about China and the role that China’s growth or deceleration of growth would have on our own GDP and our inflation. That
column12: combined with the price of oil is obviously something that we need to be attentive to.

column1: On the compliance with the Paris agreement
column2: as you know
column3: because of the tilting programme that we’ve put in place since last October
column4: that we have improved and modified. We can tell you very seriously that until the end of 2023
column5: we are Paris-compliant. But I can also tell you that we need to look at other measures and more measures in order to make sure going forward that we will remain Paris-compliant. given the fact that we have gradually phased out any reinvestment under the APP and under the PEPP
column6: the volume of corporate bonds is extremely limited. So we will be looking at that and there will be work done by staff to propose options in order to remain Paris compliant."|https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/press_conference/monetary-policy-statement/2023/html/ecb.is230914~686786984a.en.html

column1: 2023.10.12 13:30:00|Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday
column2: 13-14 September 2023|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel noted that
column2: since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 26-27 July 2023
column3: investors’ growth outlook for the euro area and for the United States had continued to diverge
column4: widening the gap in both nominal and real yields between the two economies and driving the euro lower against the dollar. Despite the expected deceleration in the euro area’s growth momentum
column5: market expectations for inflation in the medium and longer term had edged up further. Torn between the perception of a weakening euro area economy and stubborn inflation
column6: expectations for the peak deposit facility rate and the shape of the forward rate curve had remained broadly unchanged.

column1: Long-term sovereign yields had risen across major advanced economies
column2: but the increase had been more muted in economies where there had been negative macroeconomic surprises
column3: such as in the euro area. Regarding the impact of these developments on exchange rate markets
column4: the euro had depreciated markedly against the US dollar but only slightly in nominal effective terms
column5: on account of the widespread weakness of other currencies.

column1: A decomposition of nominal one-year yields in the euro area and the United States into real rates and the inflation component showed that the difference in the macroeconomic outlook had been reflected in a stark divergence of real rates across the two economies. Investors priced future one-year euro area real rates lower over the next four years
column2: while the strength of the US economy had pushed investor expectations of future one-year US real rates significantly higher. At the same time
column3: despite the weakening cyclical outlook
column4: euro investors had increased the inflation compensation they demanded over the near and medium-term horizons.

column1: Rising inflation-linked swap (ILS) rates partly reflected an upward revision of investors’ core inflation expectations. Market-implied pricing of euro area genuine synthetic core inflation expectations – that is synthetic core expectations adjusted for risk premia – suggested that market participants had revised up their core inflation expectations from May 2023. Market-based measures of longer-term headline inflation compensation in the euro area had also continued to edge higher. While the continued rise in inflation risk premia accounted for most of the increase in inflation compensation
column2: genuine long-term inflation expectations had also shown a small uptick.

column1: With weakening domestic economic activity and sticky inflation
column2: monetary policy rate expectations in the euro area had remained by and large unchanged since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. Respondents to the ECB Survey of Monetary Analysts continued to expect a peak deposit facility rate of 4%
column3: to be reached only in October 2023. For September 2023
column4: respondents were almost evenly split
column5: with a slight majority of 53% expecting a pause and 47% expecting another interest rate hike.

column1: The overall amount of rate-cutting priced in from the peak over the course of 2024 was only slightly higher than that expected at the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. The weakening economic developments had hence not prompted investors to expect a quicker reversal of monetary policy. Instead
column2: investors remained positioned for policy rates to stay at peak levels for an extended period of time. In other words
column3: the shape of the forward curve suggested market participants did not seem to expect a severe recession
column4: which was consistent with the resilience of most risk assets during the current tightening cycle. Sovereign bond spreads had largely withstood the downward revision of the near-term growth momentum and had widened only slightly since the previous meeting. Greek sovereign bonds had outperformed on the back of expected and materialising rating upgrades. Corporate bond spreads had also ticked up but remained below 2022 levels.

column1: In contrast
column2: euro area equity prices had generally declined since the Governing Council’s July meeting
column3: driven
column4: to a significant degree
column5: by a decompression of risk premia over recent weeks. Still
column6: stock prices had been very resilient since the beginning of the tightening cycle
column7: with diverging drivers for non-financial and financial firms. While the shares of non-financial corporations had benefited mostly from a compression of risk premia consistent with improving investor risk sentiment
column8: as well as from dividend pay-outs and share buybacks
column9: their longer-term earnings expectations and higher interest rates had had a dampening effect. For financial firms
column10: stock prices had benefited from higher earnings expectations
column11: as well as from strong dividend pay-outs and share buybacks.

column1: The general resilience of risk assets had been supported by the gradual decline in volatility
column2: on the back of perceptions that the global tightening cycle might be nearing its end. A second explanation for the resilience of risk assets could be that markets were pricing in an increasing probability that the pass-through from tighter financial conditions to growth could be nearing its peak. Financial conditions had tightened sharply in 2022 but had since tightened only moderately. Considering standard lags in the transmission of financial conditions to economic activity
column3: this would suggest that the drag on growth from the tighter conditions was currently likely to be large but could start receding relatively soon. A third explanation of the resilience in risk assets was related to the less pronounced tightening of long-term rates. Nominal longer-term yields had hovered around 3% since October 2022
column4: suggesting that there had been hardly any tightening impulse from the longer end of the curve for almost a year
column5: with term premia remaining compressed. Euro area real rates had also remained by and large unchanged since December 2022 and stood visibly below the peak reached in October 2022.

column1: Developments in commodity markets since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting illustrated the upside risks to inflation. Oil prices
column2: at USD 91 per barrel
column3: had reached their highest level in ten months after OPEC+ producers agreed to extend their supply cuts for the rest of the year. European gas prices had also increased markedly since the July meeting and had shown increased sensitivity to supply outages. Finally
column4: upside risks to inflation could also emanate from food prices
column5: which could react with a lag to this year’s extreme weather events caused by climate change and amplified by El Niño.

column1: In money markets
column2: non-monetary policy deposits had continued to decline since the 26-27 July meeting. Secured money market rates had been broadly unchanged amid limited volatility
column3: suggesting that there was no downward pressure in repo markets from scarcity concerns. Three-month asset swap spreads had narrowed notably since May 2023
column4: as collateral scarcity concerns had receded amid increasing sovereign debt issuance and more balanced positioning. The unsecured money market had also been broadly stable after the change to the remuneration of minimum reserves.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Mr Lane then went through the latest economic
column2: monetary and financial developments in the global economy and the euro area. The present meeting offered the opportunity to take stock of what had been learnt over the summer. Starting with the international environment
column3: global growth had been supported by services during spring 2023. Its momentum had then started to soften in the second quarter
column4: owing to a growth slowdown in both China
column5: which had slipped back after its post-pandemic reopening
column6: and Japan. Global economic activity had slowed further in the third quarter
column7: but this did not result in a huge slump. It had rather fallen back towards its long-term average. However
column8: the importance of global activity for the euro area was primarily through trade
column9: and global trade in goods had seen a protracted period of decline owing to the ongoing rotation from goods to services
column10: which were less trade-intensive.

column1: Turning to the euro area economic outlook
column2: Mr Lane recalled that in August the flash estimate for annual Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) inflation had remained unchanged at its July level of 5.3%. The decline in inflation had been interrupted owing to the recent jump in energy prices
column3: as the annual inflation rate for energy had risen to -3.3% in August from -6.1% in July. The upward shift in energy price expectations would affect the dynamics of headline inflation in the coming months. Food price inflation had come down from its peak of 15.5% in March but had still been almost 10% in August.

column1: Annual inflation excluding energy and food had fallen to 5.3% in August from 5.5% in July. The non-energy industrial goods inflation rate had declined to 4.8%
column2: since past energy price surges were receding and supply bottlenecks were being resolved. Services inflation had edged down to 5.5% but remained elevated in August
column3: owing to still strong dynamics in tourist-related services and wage pressures.

column1: Overall
column2: the moderation in core inflation was in line with a continued softening in underlying inflation
column3: which reflected the fading impact of previous supply side shocks
column4: a fall in demand-supply mismatches and the gradual pass-through of energy price disinflation. In the coming months
column5: the sharp price increases recorded in the autumn of 2022 would drop out of the yearly rates
column6: thus pulling inflation down.

column1: The momentum of HICP inflation
column2: measured as the annualised rate of the three-month-over-three-month change in the HICP
column3: had been around 3% in August 2023. In other words
column4: the 5.3% outcome was largely the legacy of carry-over effects. This 3% momentum had been helped by still negative momentum for energy inflation. For food inflation
column5: the momentum had been 4%
column6: significantly lower than the annual rate of inflation of around 10%. For the core components
column7: it was possible to observe a significant drop in the momentum of goods inflation during 2023 but a much smaller decline in the momentum of services inflation.

column1: Most indicators of underlying inflation continued to fall
column2: reflecting the fading impact of previous shocks and supply bottlenecks. “Decontaminated” measures
column3: i.e. measures of underlying inflation corrected for past supply shocks
column4: also showed a further
column5: small decline in recent months. While
column6: overall
column7: not all the measures of underlying inflation showed a further
column8: substantial downward adjustment
column9: those that were the best predictors of future inflation were at the lower range of all the measures and continued to decline considerably
column10: with the exception of domestic inflation.

column1: The analysis of pipeline pressures showed a continued downward adjustment upstream in the production chain for both food and goods inflation. It remained the case that the reduction in consumer food inflation had been minor compared with the evolution of the producer price index. The downward pressures from producer prices were expected to start kicking in more substantially as of autumn. However
column2: climate change events and the succession of natural disasters were increasing the risks of price increases in food commodities
column3: feeding into risks of higher food inflation.

column1: For goods
column2: the significant downward correction in pipeline pressures
column3: in particular in import prices for intermediate and non-food consumer goods
column4: was also expected to exert further downward pressure on HICP goods inflation in the coming months.

column1: Services inflation had remained persistently high
column2: largely reflecting the effects of past energy shocks and the post-pandemic reopening. Inflation in the contact-intensive and energy-sensitive categories was still making the largest contribution to total services inflation and had not yet shown signs of a turnaround
column3: with annual price changes remaining around 8%. By contrast
column4: inflation in the non-contact-intensive services categories was significantly lower.

column1: In line with projections from previous rounds
column2: wage pressures had remained elevated in the second quarter of the year. With some decline in the accumulated real wage loss and lower inflation
column3: wage growth should decelerate over time. Mr Lane noted that there was a seasonal pattern in wages
column4: as most contracts were renewed at the start of the year. In other words
column5: the compensation per employee data for the first quarter of 2024 would give an important signal as to whether or not the euro area was on a disinflationary wage path. Until then
column6: it was likely that any additional data would provide little information on the expected path of wages
column7: with uncertainty expected to remain large for some time.

column1: The contribution of unit profits to annual inflation
column2: as defined by the GDP deflator
column3: in the first half of 2023
column4: had moderated relative to its contribution in 2022
column5: suggesting that the rising wage pressures were starting to be absorbed by firms. Most measures of longer-term inflation expectations currently stood at around 2%
column6: although some indicators had increased and needed to be monitored closely.

column1: The September ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area saw headline inflation higher than previously expected for 2023 and 2024
column2: driven by higher energy prices
column3: but lower for 2025 owing to the appreciation of the euro
column4: tighter financing conditions and greater economic slack. Headline inflation was expected to decrease from 8.4% in 2022 to an average of 5.6% for 2023
column5: 3.2% for 2024 and 2.1% for 2025. At the same time
column6: staff had revised down their projections for inflation excluding energy and food for 2024 and 2025
column7: in line with the weaker growth prospects and the appreciation of the euro over the last year. They now saw it reaching 5.1% in 2023
column8: before falling to 2.9% in 2024 and 2.2% in 2025. After the cut-off date
column9: part of the appreciation of the euro embedded in the September projections had reversed. However
column10: the past appreciation was still feeding through into the euro area economy owing to its lagged impact.

column1: Focusing on the fourth-quarter-over-fourth-quarter percentage changes
column2: which allowed the impact of carry-over effects to be cleaned from the data
column3: it was possible to see that the HICP was only revised upwards in the fourth quarter of 2023. HICP inflation was projected to be 0.4 percentage points higher in the fourth quarter of 2023 than in the fourth quarter of 2024
column4: and no extra inflation momentum was expected in 2024.

column1: Upside risks to inflation included potential renewed upward pressures on the costs of energy and food. Adverse weather conditions
column2: and the unfolding climate crisis more broadly
column3: could push food prices up by more than expected. A lasting rise in inflation expectations above the 2% target
column4: or higher than anticipated increases in wages or profit margins
column5: could also drive inflation higher
column6: including over the medium term. By contrast
column7: weaker demand – for example owing to a stronger transmission of monetary policy or a worsening of the economic environment outside the euro area – would lead to lower price pressures
column8: especially over the medium term.

column1: Euro area economic growth had broadly stagnated over the first half of 2023
column2: while the composite output Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) had fallen in August – at the fastest rate in nearly three years – to a level of 46.7. Manufacturing output was set to remain weak in view of the further moderation in export demand and tight financing conditions
column3: while the past support from order backlogs was declining. Services had so far contributed positively to growth owing to higher demand in contact-intensive categories
column4: but there had been clear signs of a slowdown since June. The worsening of survey indicators had led to a reassessment of the GDP outlook for the second half of 2023. According to the September staff projections
column5: real GDP was expected to stagnate in the third quarter of 2023 and to increase by 0.1% in the fourth quarter.

column1: As regards domestic demand
column2: private consumption had stagnated
column3: while housing investment had contracted in the second quarter
column4: having been on a declining path for most of the past year. Residential building permits
column5: a leading indicator of housing investment
column6: had also fallen in the second quarter and firms’ assessment of their order books had become more downbeat for the third quarter
column7: pointing to a further contraction in housing investment in the period ahead. Higher interest rates had already had a visible impact on this demand component. Business investment growth excluding volatile Irish intellectual property products had moderated significantly in the second quarter
column8: and survey indicators from the European Commission and the PMI for capital goods output were indicating a decline in the second half of the year.

column1: In the near term
column2: private consumption was expected to remain weak
column3: while housing investment and business investment were expected to decline
column4: driven in part by the monetary policy tightening. Over time
column5: economic momentum was expected to pick up
column6: as real incomes were expected to rise
column7: supported by falling inflation
column8: rising wages and a strong labour market
column9: and this would underpin consumer spending. However
column10: activity levels would be dampened as the monetary policy tightening and adverse credit supply conditions increasingly fed through to the real economy. The expected gradual withdrawal of fiscal support was also likely to weigh on economic growth in the coming quarters.

column1: The labour market had so far remained resilient in the face of the slowing economy but showed signs of losing momentum. The unemployment rate had stayed at its historical low of 6.4% in July. While employment had grown by 0.2% in the second quarter
column2: the latest survey data suggested that it had come close to stalling. The strong demand for labour had also started to moderate
column3: with indicators of job vacancy rates edging down over recent months. The growth of the labour force
column4: which had been the main source of employment growth
column5: had slowed in the past few months. Owing to the weaker economic activity
column6: the September projections embedded a lower increase in employment and an increase in unemployment over the projection horizon
column7: which had still been expected to decline further in the June projections. Recent PMI indicators confirmed the slowing of momentum in employment growth
column8: which was particularly notable in the services sectors.

column1: Turning to the fiscal outlook
column2: the September projections incorporated relatively limited changes
column3: with fiscal projections highly uncertain as governments had yet to decide on budgets for next year. Still
column4: on the basis of governments’ intentions
column5: the fiscal projections implied a significant improvement from 2023 to 2024 in the cyclically adjusted primary balance.

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel started her presentation by noting that the market’s immediate response to the dramatic geopolitical upheaval in the Middle East
column2: following the terrorist attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023
column3: had so far been contained. Bolstered by continued robust economic growth in the United States
column4: the surge in global long-term bond yields that started over the summer had continued in recent weeks
column5: as investors were increasingly internalising the prospect of interest rates staying high for longer. At the same time
column6: expectations for the future path of short-term interest rates had remained broadly unchanged.

column1: Long-term sovereign bond yields had risen globally. Yields on both sides of the Atlantic were now approaching levels seen from 2005 to 2007 during the last monetary policy tightening cycle. The differential between US and euro area ten-year interest rates had fallen back to the levels observed when the ECB started increasing its key policy rates in July 2022. On aggregate
column2: the recent rise in sovereign bond yields in the euro area had been predominantly driven by an increase in the risk-free rates. However
column3: the rise in yields had not been uniform across euro area countries. Idiosyncratic factors had likely contributed to these developments
column4: and there had been no signs of market fragmentation.

column1: The question arose as to why long-term risk-free rates had risen so sharply at a time when most central banks were nearing the end of the tightening cycle. A decomposition of the increase into real rates and the inflation component showed that the higher ten-year overnight index swap (OIS) rate since the beginning of September 2023 had entirely reflected a rise in the real interest rate. Furthermore
column2: a substantial change could be seen in the term premium
column3: which had increased by around 25 basis points since early September. ECB staff analysis suggested that the repricing of term premia was likely to have largely emanated from the United States as a result of policy and macro spillovers.

column1: Looking at the evolution of the ten-year term premia for the United States and the euro area since the last tightening cycle that started in 2005
column2: the US term premium had remained exceptionally compressed. From a historical perspective
column3: this was exceptional for periods in which interest rates were above the effective lower bound. In the euro area
column4: the term premium had been rising continuously and persistently for over a year. This rise in risk compensation had been broadly expected
column5: as uncertainty about the inflation and policy outlook had increased. However
column6: in the euro area too
column7: the term premium remained visibly below the levels observed during the previous tightening cycle.

column1: The timing of the rise in the global term premium could be explained by the coincidence of three broad factors. The first factor was that many investors had become convinced earlier this year that a global recession was imminent and that central banks worldwide would have to cut interest rates substantially in 2024. Policy expectations had changed substantially since then
column2: however. Investors currently expected cumulative rate cuts of around 60 to 70 basis points in 2024 in the euro area
column3: down from 100 basis points in May. In the latest ECB Survey of Monetary Analysts
column4: median expectations regarding the timing of the first 25 basis point cut had been pushed out to September 2024
column5: from June 2024 previously. At present
column6: investors appeared less certain that the fight against inflation could be rapidly won. This was a global phenomenon extending to many advanced economies. It raised uncertainty about the entire future path of short-term interest rates
column7: resulting in a higher term premium.

column1: Monetary policy considerations and policy options

The risks to economic growth remain tilted to the downside. Growth could be lower if the effects of monetary policy turn out stronger than expected. A weaker world economy or a further slowdown in global trade would also weigh on euro area growth. Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine and the tragic conflict in the Middle East are key sources of geopolitical risk. This may result in firms and households becoming less confident about the future and global trade being disrupted. Growth could be higher if rising real incomes mean spending increases by more than anticipated
column2: or if the world economy grows more strongly than expected.

column1: Upside risks to inflation include the heightened geopolitical tensions
column2: especially in the Middle East
column3: which could push energy prices and freight costs higher in the near term and hamper global trade. Inflation could also turn out higher than anticipated if wages increase by more than expected or profit margins prove more resilient. By contrast
column4: inflation may surprise on the downside if monetary policy dampens demand by more than expected
column5: or if the economic environment in the rest of the world worsens unexpectedly. Moreover
column6: inflation could decline more quickly in the near term if energy prices evolve in line with the recent downward shift in market expectations of the future path for oil and gas prices.

column1: Financial and monetary conditions

Market interest rates have moved broadly sideways since our last meeting. Our restrictive monetary policy continues to transmit strongly into broader financing conditions. Lending rates on business loans declined slightly
column2: to 5.2 per cent in November
column3: while mortgage rates increased further to 4.0 per cent.

column1: High borrowing rates
column2: with the associated cutbacks in investment plans and house purchases
column3: led to a further drop in credit demand in the fourth quarter
column4: as reported in our latest bank lending survey. While the tightening of credit standards for loans to firms and households moderated
column5: they remained tight
column6: with banks concerned about the risks faced by their customers.

column1: Against this background
column2: credit dynamics have improved somewhat but overall remain weak. Loans to firms stagnated in November compared with a year earlier – after contracting in October – as the monthly flow of short-term loans rebounded. Loans to households grew at a subdued annual rate of 0.5 per cent.

column1: Conclusion

The Governing Council today decided to keep the three key ECB interest rates unchanged. We are determined to ensure that inflation returns to our two per cent medium-term target in a timely manner. Based on our current assessment
column2: we consider that the key ECB interest rates are at levels that
column3: maintained for a sufficiently long duration
column4: will make a substantial contribution to this goal. Our future decisions will ensure that our policy rates will be set at sufficiently restrictive levels for as long as necessary. We will continue to follow a data-dependent approach to determining the appropriate level and duration of restriction.

column1: In any case
column2: we stand ready to adjust all of our instruments within our mandate to ensure that inflation returns to our medium-term target and to preserve the smooth functioning of monetary policy transmission.

column1: We are now ready to take your questions.
Last week in Davos

column4: Bloomberg

column3: in dispatching of containers
column4: which was really a very sizeable disruption in the whole logistics chain. But we are observing very carefully because we are seeing what you are all observing

column6: delivery delays are increasing and
column7: while we all know that there is more shipping capacity than there was in 2020 and 2021

column9: I think most observers agree to say that it has a moderate impact. The percentage of the water transport costs is a little north of 1.5% of total input costs. But we are being very careful and looking attentively to the developments

column11: the OECD
column12: or other commentators
column13: if the conflict in that region was to develop further

column1: I have a question because you are always referring to wage data. There’s loads of wage data around. What are you actually really looking at

column15: wages

column1: As I said

column1: 2024.02.22 13:30:00|Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday
column2: 24-25 January 2024|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel noted that
column2: since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 13-14 December 2023
column3: the rapid easing of financial conditions observed after the 25-26 October meeting had levelled off and been pared back slightly.

column1: Financial conditions had eased sharply in November and December
column2: as the narrative in financial markets had shifted from “high for longer” to swift disinflation and imminent monetary policy easing. After the Governing Council’s 13-14 December meeting
column3: financial conditions had continued to ease until late December but had tightened slightly thereafter. This followed ECB communication that had countered the aggressive market pricing of a rate-cutting cycle starting as early as March 2024.

column1: While the probability of a 25 basis point cut in April still stood at around 60%
column2: a first cut was now fully priced in only for June. Expected cumulative rate cuts by the end of the year had declined slightly since the December meeting
column3: to around 130 basis points. Policy rate expectations in US forward markets had also been scaled back
column4: although to a slightly lesser extent. US interest rate markets were positioned for an initial 25 basis point cut in May
column5: with a 40% probability of a March cut. Moreover
column6: investors expected almost the same magnitude of cumulative cuts as in the euro area in the course of 2024
column7: anticipating a globally synchronised normalisation cycle.

column1: However
column2: the uncertainty around this policy path was high
column3: as reflected in the persistent volatility in bond markets. The easing of global financial conditions in November and December 2023 had gone hand-in-hand with lower volatility in risk asset markets. Implied volatility in euro area equity markets had dropped to its lowest level since the onset of the coronavirus pandemic in February 2020
column4: despite significant geopolitical tensions and risks of protracted economic weakness. Yet
column5: lower implied volatility in risk asset markets was not accompanied by meaningfully lower implied volatility in bond markets
column6: which had decoupled from equity market volatility.

column1: There were two potential sources of heightened monetary policy uncertainty. The first was the timing and pace of the policy adjustment
column2: while the second was the extent of the required policy adjustment. Respondents to the January 2024 ECB Survey of Monetary Analysts (SMA) had raised their expectations for the pace of rate cuts over the year but remained more cautious than financial market pricing. While markets foresaw a cumulative easing of around 130 basis points
column3: SMA respondents expected total cuts of 100 basis points by the end of the year. Differences in the outlook for inflation could explain the discrepancy between market pricing and analysts’ expectations for the future path of monetary policy. Investors trading in financial markets were discernibly more optimistic about the inflation outlook than the median SMA respondent. Another explanation could be different speeds in adjusting to new information. During the interest rate tightening cycle in 2022 and 2023
column4: rate markets had consistently led survey expectations
column5: often by several months.

column1: The second source of uncertainty about the medium-term policy rate path concerned the extent of adjustment required to return to a neutral policy rate and the uncertainty surrounding estimates of such a rate. SMA participants had raised
column2: noticeably
column3: their median longer-run expectations for policy rates compared with levels during the period before the start of the ECB’s hiking path.

column1: The expected reversal of the 2023 tightening was also visible in longer tenors of the yield curve. The euro area ten-year real overnight index swap (OIS) rate remained close to early 2023 levels and slightly below its September 2023 level
column2: when the ECB had last hiked interest rates. The corresponding nominal OIS interest rate had even fallen below early 2023 levels. In the United States
column3: the ten-year real OIS interest rate had fallen to a similar degree since late October but remained above early 2023 levels. The reappraisal of the monetary policy outlook had been the dominant driver of the decline in bond yields since the Governing Council’s October monetary policy meeting
column4: along with news on the growth outlook and fiscal developments.

column1: The rescaling of the earlier aggressive market pricing had also affected risk asset markets. Yet
column2: euro area equity markets remained broadly unchanged since the December meeting. A longer perspective
column3: since the start of 2023
column4: revealed that developments in equity markets
column5: as in other risk asset markets
column6: had been robust
column7: providing an easing impulse to financial conditions. The somewhat stronger repricing of monetary policy expectations in the euro area than in the United States had been reflected in a slight appreciation of the euro

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel noted that
column2: since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 24-25 January 2024
column3: monetary policy expectations had retracted further from the early and large interest rate cuts initially foreseen at the turn of the year.

column1: More favourable news on the global economy and less favourable news on inflation had both been key factors in shaping financial market developments. In the case of the first factor
column2: macroeconomic data surprises had moved into positive territory in the euro area
column3: the United States and China for the first time since May 2023. As a result
column4: investors attached a discernibly lower probability to the scenario of a hard landing for the global economy.

column1: The second factor related to a reassessment of the medium-term inflation outlook. Higher than expected inflation releases in the euro area and the United States
column2: especially for core inflation
column3: had dented investors’ hopes of rapid and smooth disinflation. Looking at the path of headline and core inflation in the euro area (as measured
column4: respectively
column5: by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices – HICP – and the overall index excluding energy and food) over 2024
column6: inflation-linked bond markets were pricing in somewhat higher headline inflation rates throughout the year
column7: compared with expectations at the time of the Governing Council’s monetary policy meeting in January.

column1: In response to investors’ expectations of lower downside tail risks to economic activity and a slightly bumpier path of disinflation
column2: rate markets had priced in a substantially shallower easing cycle in the euro area
column3: with expected cumulative interest rate cuts by the end of 2024 having declined notably from around 160 basis points in late December to around 90 basis points at present. After the latest repricing
column4: the gap between expectations in interest rate markets and those reported by market analysts had largely disappeared.

column1: In the United States
column2: strong labour market data
column3: higher than expected inflation figures and more cautious communication by the Federal Reserve System had triggered an even greater repricing of policy rate expectations. As a result
column4: overnight index swap (OIS) forward curves were also pricing in a substantially shallower easing cycle in the United States.

column1: A key explanatory factor for expectations of a synchronised monetary policy easing cycle across advanced economies was the common component in global inflation. Markets anticipated that the disinflationary momentum would continue unfolding synchronously over the coming year. Spillovers from the United States were another factor explaining the close co-movement of monetary policy expectations across jurisdictions. US data releases continued to exert a significant influence on yields in other advanced economies.
A decomposition of euro area and US OIS rates across different maturities into inflation compensation and real rates showed that
column2: in the euro area
column3: inflation compensation had increased notably across the curve. At the same time
column4: real rates had declined
column5: in particular at the longer end
column6: implying a mild loosening of financing conditions through risk-free rates. In the United States
column7: the rise in inflation compensation was slightly less pronounced
column8: with real rates remaining firm across the curve.

column1: The widening yield differential had been mirrored by a slight depreciation in the euro’s exchange rate against the US dollar. In nominal effective terms
column2: the euro had remained broadly unchanged
column3: while the US dollar had appreciated.

column1: Despite the repricing of the near-term inflation outlook
column2: risks to the longer-term inflation outlook had not materially changed since January 2024
column3: as the five-year forward inflation-linked swap (ILS) rate five years ahead had remained broadly unchanged. Compared with the close-to-peak levels at the September 2023 Governing Council meeting
column4: ILS forward rates had come down materially

column6: the five-year forward ILS rate five years ahead still stood markedly above its historical mean. Consistent with ILS rates
column7: euro area option prices also indicated that risks of high inflation had come down but remained somewhat elevated compared with historical averages.

column3: including China
column4: had followed a bullish trend since the Governing Council’s January meeting.

column3: with the differential between Italian and German ten-year government bond yields at its smallest since March 2022. Investors appeared to remain keen on locking in attractive returns amid expectations that the peak of the tightening cycle had been reached. Bid-to-cover ratios continued their gradual upward trend
column4: pointing to strong demand for bonds despite record high sovereign issuance for the year to date.

column4: but these had not had broader repercussions for financial intermediaries and markets. Moreover

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Starting with the global outlook
column2: Mr Lane noted that global economic activity was still subdued but there were some signs of improvement. Trade momentum in goods and services was expected to strengthen in the first quarter of the year. The March ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area foresaw a significant pick-up in euro area foreign demand
column3: in line with previous exercises. Euro area foreign demand was projected to grow by 2.4% in 2024
column5: reflecting expectations of a normalisation in demand for goods
column6: which would benefit European producers. As for commodities
column7: since the last meeting oil prices had increased
column8: while gas prices had declined further. International metal prices had also declined
column9: although food prices had edged up.

column1: Turning to the euro area
column2: Mr Lane recalled that
column3: according to the recent Eurostat flash release
column4: euro area headline inflation had declined to 2.6% in February from 2.8% in January. While energy inflation had become less negative
column5: partly owing to the withdrawal of some fiscal support
column6: food inflation had fallen strongly to 4.0% in February from 5.6% in January. This reflected an easing in both processed and unprocessed food inflation. Core inflation had decreased to 3.1% in February from 3.3% in January. Over the same period

column8: supporting the view that high wage growth was playing an important role in elevated services inflation.

column2: as the impact of past adverse supply shocks continued to fade
column3: lower energy prices reduced cost pressures and tighter monetary policy weighed on demand. At the lower end of the range
column4: the indicator of the Persistent and Common Component of Inflation had been close to 2% since November. However
column5: the annual growth rate of the indicator of domestic inflation was unchanged at 4.5%. Domestic price pressures as measured by growth in the GDP deflator were still high
column6: although the deflator was projected to continue to decrease gradually. Profit growth offered a first buffer against high labour cost pressures and would recover thereafter.

column1: According to the March ECB staff projections
column2: growth in compensation per employee was estimated to have slowed to 4.8% in the fourth quarter of 2023

column4: the forthcoming release of euro area data on 8 March for the growth in compensation per employee in the fourth quarter of 2023 was expected to turn out slightly lower than projected. column3: headline inflation was expected to decline to the ECB’s target as labour cost dynamics moderated and past energy shocks
column4: supply bottlenecks and pandemic reopening effects dissipated. Headline inflation was projected to average 2.3% in 2024
column5: 2.0% in 2025 and 1.9% in 2026. Relative to the December projections
column6: headline inflation had been revised down by 0.4 percentage points for 2024 and 0.1 percentage points for 2025

column9: 0.2 percentage points for next year and 0.1 percentage points for 2026.

column6: demand for euro area exports should improve as global demand rebounded and price competitiveness pressures eased.

column3: with goods consumption playing a key role. This was

column7: especially

column4: employers were announcing fewer job vacancies and fewer firms were reporting that their production was being limited by labour shortages.

column1: Financial market developments
