We will continue to follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate level and duration of restriction. In particular
column4: our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of the inflation outlook in light of the incoming economic and financial data
column5: the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

column1: In any case
column2: we stand ready to adjust all of our instruments within our mandate to ensure that inflation returns to our medium-term target and to preserve the smooth functioning of monetary policy transmission.

column1: We are now ready to take your questions.

My first question would be on the next steps. It sounds like you expect to reach a 2% target maybe sooner than predicted in September. Does the decision to cut today really represent a shift of gear? Do you expect a cut at every meeting for the next few meetings now to be the most likely scenario? And the second question would be on the US election. You mentioned trade tensions as a risk
column2: but can you elaborate how you think a return of Donald Trump to the White House and his plan to impose tariffs will alter the outlook for growth and inflation in the euro area?

column1: We decided to cut all our rates by 25 basis points because we believe that the disinflationary process is well on track and all the information that we received in the last five weeks since our last monetary policy decision was heading in the same direction – lower! Whether you looked at inflation numbers
column2: headline core
column3: whether you looked at PMI numbers
column4: all categories
column5: composite manufacturing
column6: services
column7: employment – are heading downwards as well. If we look at all the surveys that are in the works at the moment
column8: of which the specific numbers and data will be available soon
column9: it is the same story. Whether it is the corporate telephone survey or other surveys that we have available
column10: it’s all heading in the same direction – downwards! That really confirmed for us the confidence that we have that the disinflationary process is well on track. That is what has caused us to make the decision to cut our three rates by 25 basis points. We have also reiterated that we will continue to be data dependent and honestly
column11: this decision is a case in point of us being data dependent. We have all the available data all heading in the same direction
column12: the largest countries all also moving in negative territories in PMI numbers. Those are really strong elements – and because of their synchronisation and the similar direction – we have to take into account those data and make the decision that we have made. We are going to continue doing exactly the same thing. It’s clear that between this meeting and the next meeting we have in December
column13: we will be receiving more data – some of it soft
column14: some of it hard – and more readings. All of that will help us decide
column15: as I have said
column16: “meeting by meeting
column17: ” what monetary policy stance we should decide at that time. I think there were no variations in that respect from the decision that we made in the past
column18: in terms of methodology. It’s the same steer
column19: the same stance
column20: the three-pronged approach and the meeting-by-meeting data dependency
column21: no predetermined path. On the other point you raised: Trade is obviously an important element and as part of the drivers of activity going forward
column22: we obviously have consumption and investment
column23: but we also have trade. Any restriction
column24: any uncertainty
column25: any obstacles to trade matter for an economy like the European economy
column26: which is very open. Trade within itself
column27: of course
column28: but trade also with the rest of the world. Any hardening of the barriers
column29: the tariffs
column30: the additional obstacles to that possibility to trade with the rest of the world is obviously a downside.

column1: My first question would be on the economic outlook. You were now referring to and pointing out that the economy doesn’t really look great and all signs point towards more downspin. Why didn’t you go for a 50 basis point cut? Is that something you have discussed or whether this is on the table for the next ones? And have you been discussing the topic of the possibility that inflation could also undershoot
column2: if you keep your policy stance restrictive? Thank you.

column1: It is a fact that the economic activity has come in
column2: on the basis of the elements that we have and the indicators that are available
column3: a bit below what we had anticipated. But this is not a projection exercise. We are in between two projection exercises
column4: and clearly December will be another opportunity for us to run all the data and all the information through our models and to apply the three-pronged approach to our stance. What was on the table and what was debated and proposed by our Chief Economist Philip Lane was a 25 basis point cut. End of the story. We had discussions and debates and rationales and narratives
column5: and all of that is part of the debate and the legitimate discussions that we have within the Governing Council. But at the end of the day
column6: there was a unanimous decision to cut rates by 25 basis points. It may have been the Slovenian great atmosphere that precipitated this more than consensus. There was a unanimous decision to cut by 25 basis points and we thought that it was the appropriate decision to make in view of the moment
column7: in view of the indicators that we have and our assessment of this disinflationary process that is really under way and well on track. On the risk of undershooting or overshooting
column8: we can debate ad nauseam on this particular matter and you will find views on both sides of the equation. What is clear to all is that we still have risks on both sides of our forecast
column9: upside and downside
column10: probably a bit more on one than the other
column11: probably more downside risk than upside risk. But I’m talking here about our forecast for inflation and that’s what we are looking at.

column1: Inflation is expected to reach target in the course of next year instead of at the end. Will we reach the neutral rate earlier than before? Will you recalibrate monetary policy and cuts to come? The second question is whether the German economy is the main reason for the shift since September
column2: when today’s cut was unlikely
column3: or at least is it a good reason?

column1: First of all
column2: we don’t recalibrate
column3: we calibrate
column4: and this is really the process through which we go. As laborious as it is
column5: we believe in our three-pronged approach. I won’t bore you with the repetition of it all
column6: but it is inflation outlook
column7: underlying inflation and transmission. And we calibrate our monetary policy on the basis of all the data that are available and applying that three-pronged approach. It’s obvious that the state of the economy and the activity has a bearing on inflation. And to that extent
column8: of course
column9: we take that into account in order to assess inflation and its return in a timely manner to our target. But that’s the extent of our consideration: the bearing of activity on inflation. Because our job is price stability and our mission is to return inflation back to the 2% target in the medium term.

column1: You said earlier we will have more data in December
column2: not much more
column3: but more data
column4: and if they all point in the same direction as you outlined earlier as well
column5: you will just have opened the door widely for a new rate cut in December if I interpret you well? You mentioned tensions in the Middle East that could feed inflation through energy prices. What about domestic stimulus in China
column6: which is huge and could also revive pressures on energy prices through domestic demand and then feed inflation? Is it something that you will combine with those Middle East tensions and look very carefully at in the next months?

column1: It is a fact that at each projection exercise
column2: we receive more data and in particular more updated projections of course
column3: and typically
column4: given that between now and the December meeting there will be more than six weeks
column5: we will also receive more data. As I said
column6: I did not open the door to anything. I repeated that at each and every meeting we will look at the data. Hence we will be data dependent
column7: not data point dependent
column8: nor anything else. Data dependent – all of it. We will determine what is the best rate
column9: what is the best speed
column10: how far and how deep we have to go in order to return inflation to its 2% medium-term target. This is what we will do in December
column11: and I would not give any other commitment
column12: nor make any other statement in that respect. As I said in the monetary policy statement that I read earlier on
column13: we are not pre-committing. Again
column14: I think that the decision that we’re making today is a perfect example of how we can be data dependent. You refer to two areas of big concern. One coupled with obviously a major conflict and horrifying one that is taking place in the Middle East. We of course are concerned beyond the humanitarian approach
column15: beyond the conflict aspects. We are looking at the economic consequences and we are looking in particular at the impact that this conflict could have on trade
column16: because that part of the world is very much open to trade and the passing of ships of all sorts. We are also very attentive to the price of oil that can be impacted
column17: and this oil price is a good segue into your question about China. What will happen in China
column18: what kind of stimulus will be activated
column19: with all full details as is expected at some stage
column20: will also be an indication of the demand addressed by China to the oil market and the impact that it will have on the price of such a commodity. We are looking at all those components and obviously focusing on the economic consequences and the impact that they could have on inflation
column21: and obviously activity to the extent that it impacts inflation.

column1: The first question is about economic growth. Is a soft landing still your main scenario
column2: and am I correct to see that perhaps your attention has shifted slightly from inflation concerns to growth concerns? The second question is about a line in the statement which says the rate is still restrictive. But I’m curious. We thought restrictive is this unobservable concept because we don’t know where the neutral rate is. Perhaps you maybe started having a discussion in the Governing Council on where does restrictive stop? I’m curious if you have any thoughts about where does restriction end and where does accommodation begin?

column1: On the issue of economic growth
column2: are we still on a soft landing expectation? The answer is: on the basis of the information that we have
column3: we certainly do not see a recession. The euro area
column4: on the basis of what we have
column5: is not heading for a recession
column6: and we are still looking at that soft landing that you have just mentioned. You asked me whether we are more concerned about growth than we are about inflation. I would say that we are concerned about growth to the extent that it has an impact on inflation
column7: and we have to be particularly attentive to both because of the impact that it has on inflation
column8: which is our main focus and our key objective
column9: as you know. So there is
column10: and you pointed to it
column11: that sentence which is sort of the magic language. And I’m sure that you will be very attentive if and when that magic language changes a bit. We still say that “we will keep policy rates sufficiently restrictive for as long as necessary to achieve this aim”
column12: which refers to the previous sentence
column13: which is that “we are determined to ensure that inflation returns to our 2% medium-term target in a timely manner”. So there is no question in our mind that we are currently restrictive
column14: hence that sentence. There is also no question in our mind that we are not yet at this 2% medium-term target in a timely manner
column15: and this has to be sustainable. So even if it could well be as markets anticipate
column16: but they are not always right
column17: that the time at which we reach that 2% sustainably has advanced a bit
column18: it is not yet now. And we will have to wait further in order to make sure that we are at that 2% sustainable medium-term target.

column1: In the introductory statement you refer to this updated assessment of your inflation outlook. Does this refer to the September staff forecast
column2: or has this changed since September within the Governing Council? And if so
column3: could you give us a little bit more colour on what the actual change in the inflation outlook has been that you’re referring to? And my second question is also again on the theme of undershooting the 2% target. Even the September forecast projected the 1.9% inflationary rate for 2026
column4: I think from the second or third quarter onwards. Has this been changed
column5: and to which degree do you think it already shows that monetary policy is too tight?

column1: If anything
column2: I would say that what the numbers are showing at the moment is that our monetary policy is working. And the fact that we’ve managed to bring inflation down as we have so far
column3: not to a complete victory
column4: but to have brought it down so much is an indication that our monetary policy is actually working. It’s not the only thing that is operating in that respect
column5: but it is certainly part of the elements to explain that we have moved from very high inflation numbers to much lower [inflation] and hopefully soon to target on a sustainable basis. Our assessment of inflation as we stand now is really based on all the numbers that are available
column6: and that leads us to assess and take a view on inflation now and the potential impact going forward. But that will be done in a strict
column7: rigorous
column8: published way when we have our December projection exercise. And you will be obviously not privy because it will be public
column9: but you will be on the receiving end of this very clear updating. But in the meantime
column10: we are not blind to what happens. And when we receive inflation by way of HICP at 1.7%
column11: when we see core at 2.7%
column12: when we see services moving down to 3.9% and when we look at the three-month-over-three-month services moving significantly from August to September
column13: all of that put together leads us to believe that inflation is definitely on that disinflationary track that I was referring to earlier. On the forecast
column14: again we had a forecast in September. Between September and December
column15: a lot of data
column16: a lot of numbers
column17: a lot of indicators and a lot of surveys will come into play and will be integrated in the work that we do. And we will have a forecast that will be
column18: by the way
column19: extended to 2027 because the December forecast always takes one further year into account. And we shall see. We shall see whether there is a move and in which direction in terms of inflation and in terms of activity. But in between projection exercises
column20: as I said as a case in point
column21: that data matters. We look at everything that we have available
column22: and if it is appropriate to take us closer to this timely reaching of our target of 2% medium-term symmetric
column23: we make the decision
column24: as we have today.

column1: Are you in the ECB somehow surprised by such a rapid drop in inflation
column2: enabling you to perform an actual rate cut which wasn’t fully expected or priced in in September?

column1: That’s a really good question actually. What is a little bit irritating sometimes is the lapse of time between meetings. And on this occasion there were only five weeks. But in those five weeks we received quite a lot of information
column2: some of it by way of hard numbers and readings that were actually updated downwards a little bit today
column3: and some of it by way of PMIs
column4: which are a bit softer than hard data
column5: but all synchronised and moving in the same direction. So were we surprised? I’m not sure that we had anticipated that 1.7% [inflation]
column6: nor did anyone else for that matter. Because if I look at analysts and if I look at those whose job it is to project and to forecast
column7: or markets
column8: I think we were all a little bit surprised by the acceleration that is being demonstrated by that number. But it’s certainly raised our confidence that the disinflationary process is well on track. But having said that
column9: we are data dependent. And that’s the beauty of the English language: data are either singular or plural
column10: but it’s the same word. We are not data point dependent. So it’s not because HICP came out at 1.7% or core at 2.7% that we made that decision. We need an array of information and data. And
column11: by the way
column12: we also know for instance
column13: based on the work that has been done and that was already mentioned during the previous press conference in September
column14: on the basis of projections
column15: that the next three months will not have this linear low and below-target inflation number. We know that it will be higher than that because of obvious base effects that we know of already. And we shouldn’t be surprised by that
column16: and we should not be jumping to any kind of conclusions either.

column1: My first question relates to your statement some months ago when you promised the population in the eurozone to break the neck of inflation. If you look at some of the points which you mentioned
column2: like the fact that inflation is going to rise again
column3: and if you look at the service sector
column4: at food prices and all the effects which really concern normal people
column5: would you say that the neck is broken or not? And the second question relates to your interesting speech you held to the Governing Council last night
column6: in which you described the admirable economic development of our host country here. Could you perhaps briefly summarise again what we actually could learn in other countries from this interesting path here in Slovenia?

column1: Thank you for bringing Slovenia back into the picture
column2: because there is a lot to be learned from Slovenia. Have we broken the neck of inflation? Not yet. Are we in the process of breaking that neck? Yes. I was in the market in Ljubljana a couple of days ago to check on prices
column3: because I come to Ljubljana on a regular basis if I can. Food prices are still growing at 2.4% on average in the euro area. And this is not the 2% that we want. We are clearly still above target
column4: and it’s one area
column5: together with energy prices
column6: to which consumers are highly sensitive
column7: which has a bearing on what they do
column8: whether they consume
column9: whether they save
column10: which matters a lot. So we are extremely attentive. We know that food prices in particular are very sensitive
column11: and we know that we are not at target yet on that front. But are we breaking the neck of it? Yes
column12: I think so. It’s not broken completely yet
column13: but we’re getting there. On your second question
column14: I think that the key messages that I wanted to make yesterday
column15: using the beautiful example of Slovenia
column16: is that in times of uncertainty
column17: you have two options. You can either resign yourself and suffer
column18: or you can get a grip of yourself and take uncertainty as an opportunity
column19: which is exactly what Slovenia did when it became independent
column20: when it fought inflation and when it really bounced back in terms of its economy. The second lesson
column21: which is interesting and which I mentioned yesterday as well
column22: is that when there is that expansion and when there is prosperity
column23: it needs to be widely shared. And that is particularly the case in times of the risk of a digital divide. I think it’s a very good case in point where digitalisation has been widely spread and where the Gini coefficient of Slovenia is in the top two of all the OECD countries. So I think the lessons we can learn is that when it’s hard
column24: we have to get a grip of ourselves. We have to push for reform. We have to continue to integrate and innovate. And from our perspective as a central bank
column25: if anything
column26: it should push us in the direction of the capital markets union
column27: of the banking union and making sure that capital flows can actually fuel innovation in Europe.

column1: How important was it for the decision and the debate that even with the new rate cut
column2: financial conditions will remain restrictive? And do recent macroeconomic surprises grant a downward revision on growth in December?

column1: October is not December. I cannot tell you today what our December outlook will be and what the projections will say. I think we have to be nimble. We have to be attentive to the data that we get and work on the basis of that. On the issue of being restrictive
column2: I made the point that we are restrictive at the moment
column3: at the current rate. Even with the 25 basis point cut
column4: we will continue to be restrictive. And we believe that it is necessary and would have to continue to be so until we are confident that we are reaching the 2% target in the medium term. That will come in due course
column5: but we’re not there yet.

column1: You’ve mentioned you do not foresee a recession for the euro area
column2: but at least from Germany we are getting some worrying data. Is there still a chance that this may turn
column3: so that we might see a recession in the euro area?

column1: Even with one of the Member States
column2: however large it is
column3: facing difficult circumstances on the basis of what they themselves are producing
column4: it does not necessarily imply that the whole of the euro area is going to be affected in the same way. And based on the information that we have at the moment
column5: we do not
column6: we do not see a recession in the euro area. Of course
column7: we have to be attentive to particular sectors of the economy. And as we stand here in Slovenia
column8: which is a country that participates in the supply chain of the automotive sector in particular
column9: of course many countries will be paying attention to these sectoral developments. But to your specific question of whether we see a recession
column10: the answer is no.

column1: You talk about fiscal consolidation and how governments must steadily reduce deficits and public debt. The IMF said the same thing just a few days ago. What are the market risks in the event of a failure to consolidate? And my second question is about bank consolidation. There’s a huge debate in the eurozone. Do you see bank consolidation as an opportunity for the area to compete more in the global market?
On fiscal consolidation
column2: we now have a fiscal governance framework that identifies the right equilibrium and balance between fiscal consolidation that is needed in many countries and the necessary investment in growth-enhancing reforms. And I think it is that balancing act which is the virtue and the value of this revised governance framework for fiscal purposes. It’s associated with a timeframe of four or seven years depending on the level and degree of reforms that the Member States will propose and will implement. So if those rail guards are followed and observed by Member States
column3: we believe that it’s the right environment within which to develop activity. And for our part
column4: while the fiscal authorities will do what they have to do in fiscal terms and while the authorities will do what they have to do in structural reforms
column5: we will do our part by maintaining price stability. But of course we are interested in what they do
column6: because everyone has to play their part.

column1: On your bank consolidation question
column2: I have said this last time around
column3: our view is that for bank mergers
column4: to the extent that they strengthen the banking system and on the basis of the cost-benefit analysis that the shareholders and the stakeholders conduct
column5: which is not to say that we are directly involved other than through the supervision authorities that we apply to the requests and applications that are filed with us
column6: it is for them to decide how to progress those projects. And I’m not referring to any particular project
column7: as you know."|https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/press_conference/monetary-policy-statement/2024/html/ecb.is241017~59ad385bab.en.html

column1: 2024.11.14 13:30:00|Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Ljubljana on Wednesday and Thursday
column2: 16-17 October 2024|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel noted that since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 11-12 September 2024
column2: policy rate expectations had shifted back and forth. Incoming data had made it challenging for market participants to price in the speed and extent of both disinflation and the monetary policy easing cycle. The key drivers of financial market developments since the September meeting had been a sluggish euro area economy
column3: a robust US economy and rising and volatile commodity prices.

column1: The combination of weaker euro area macroeconomic data and higher commodity prices had affected the market’s view of the inflation outlook and the perceived balance of risks to inflation. Inflation fixings (swap contracts linked to monthly releases of the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices excluding tobacco) had recently shifted upwards significantly
column2: reversing part of the decline seen following the Governing Council’s July meeting
column3: when energy prices had dropped notably. These swings in investors’ view of the inflation outlook illustrated the significant impact of energy prices on inflation expectations. At the same time
column4: market-based indicators of risks to inflation based on option pricing remained tilted to the downside over the near and medium term
column5: although they had become more balanced recently
column6: while risks to the longer-term inflation outlook had become tilted to the upside again.

column1: Incoming data for the euro area had also had a significant impact on monetary policy expectations. Market participants currently expected front-loaded rate cuts
column2: with a 25 basis point rate cut at the current meeting and another cut in December 2024 fully priced in. But they also expected a more contained rate-cutting cycle overall
column3: with lower total cuts from March 2025 onward and a higher terminal rate compared with expectations in September 2024. Participants in the Survey of Monetary Analysts (SMA) held broadly similar views on the near-term outlook for interest rates to those of markets
column4: with some deviations as of the second half of 2025.

column1: The reappraisal of the expected policy rate path had been much more pronounced in the United States
column2: where market participants had notably revised up their expectations regarding the terminal policy rate. Expectations regarding the ECB’s terminal rate had also been pulled higher
column3: albeit by less than in the United States
column4: reflecting the weaker incoming macroeconomic data for the euro area. This had increased the divergence between the two terminal rates. At the same time
column5: the uncertainty in rate markets
column6: as measured by the dispersion of analysts’ forecasts for three-month forward interest rates one year ahead
column7: had remained higher than the historical average in both the euro area and the United States
column8: indicating that uncertainty around the policy rate path remained material.

column1: The decomposition of changes in the risk-free rate curve in the euro area and the United States into inflation compensation and real rates showed that nominal rates had increased for medium and longer-term maturities in both currency areas. However
column2: the rise had been much more pronounced in the United States
column3: on the back of a stronger increase in both inflation compensation and real rates. In the euro area
column4: the repricing of the inflation outlook had put upward pressure on risk-free rates
column5: with inflation compensation rising significantly across maturities. By contrast
column6: euro area real interest rates had declined across maturities
column7: with the most pronounced drop at the short end of the curve
column8: implying a further loosening of financing conditions. Almost the entire euro area real rate curve was currently close to neutral territory.

column1: Bond investors at present expected a soft landing in the euro area with the policy rate moving back to a broadly neutral level. This view was supported by recent equity market developments
column2: as major equity market indices had risen significantly in September and October. Developments in corporate bond markets also suggested that investors had shrugged off the weakening of the euro area economy. Corporate bond spreads had declined across the board
column3: with the sharpest decline observed for high-yield non-financial corporate bonds. This was partly supported by a benign outlook for default rates in the corporate sector. Sovereign spreads relative to the German Bund
column4: other than for French bonds
column5: had declined over the inter-meeting period.

column1: All in all
column2: there had been a broad-based and pronounced easing of financial conditions since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. This was driven by lower short-end real rates
column3: higher equity prices and the weakening of the euro by 1% against the US dollar
column4: in line with developments in the two-year yield differential between the euro area and the United States.

column1: Regarding recent dynamics in money market rates
column2: the pass-through of changes in policy rates to money market rates had been effective. At the same time
column3: the gradual upward drift in repo rates relative to the deposit facility rate over the past few months had brought secured rates into the close vicinity of the deposit facility rate
column4: which had not happened since 2020. By contrast
column5: the spread between the unsecured euro short-term rate (€STR) and the deposit facility rate had remained broadly stable.

column1: Several factors could explain the counterintuitive situation of borrowing cash being cheaper in the unsecured market than in the secured market. The dominant factor appeared to have been the significant improvement in collateral availability
column2: partly as a consequence of the reduction in the Eurosystem’s market footprint. In contrast
column3: there had been little evidence so far of upward pressure on repo rates stemming from liquidity shortages. In addition
column4: factors related to regulation and market microstructure had limited the ability of cash lenders to arbitrage between secured and unsecured markets
column5: with only a few lenders active across both markets.

column1: Since the narrowing of the spread between the rate on the main refinancing operations and the deposit facility rate to 15 basis points as of 18 September 2024 there had been only limited recourse to the Eurosystem’s standard refinancing operations
column2: as market-based funding had remained attractive.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Starting with inflation in the euro area
column2: Mr Lane recalled that headline inflation had been 1.8% in September according to the Eurostat flash estimate (subsequently revised down to 1.7% in the final release
column3: which became available on 17 October)
column4: substantially lower than in August and below the path foreseen in the September ECB staff macroeconomic projections. The downside surprise largely reflected a drop in energy inflation
column5: but core inflation had also played a role. This
column6: in turn
column7: was due to downside surprises in goods inflation and – to a lesser degree – services inflation. With respect to underlying inflation
column8: the exclusion-based indicators that were already available for September had moved down. Meanwhile
column9: the underlying inflation indicators available up to August had eased or were stable. The Persistent and Common Component of Inflation (PCCI) remained at the bottom of the range
column10: at 2.0%. The higher levels of some of the other measures reflected their more backward-looking nature at a time when the propagation of past shocks was still ongoing. The domestic inflation indicator
column11: in particular
column12: remained high at 4.4%
column13: as it mainly covered services items. However
column14: taken together
column15: the month-on-month seasonally adjusted services inflation rates for August and September were closer to the long-term average
column16: suggesting a moderation in inflation dynamics compared with earlier in the year.

column1: Services inflation remained high but was expected to decelerate. This prediction was supported for example by the PCCI for the services component. Services PCCI had stood at around 2.4% since the start of the year – reflecting that a significant part of services inflation
column2: at around 4%
column3: was due to backward-looking elements and one-off factors. For example
column4: large increases in insurance fees at the start of 2024 had continued to push up the annual services inflation rate
column5: but would lead to negative base effects at the start of 2025. Historically
column6: such increases had not been signals for future inflation in the services segment. This implied that services inflation should over time converge to the level of services PCCI
column7: as those one-off factors dropped out of the data.

column1: The incoming data and signals for wage growth in 2025 were either in line with or below the September projections. Forward-looking wage trackers were broadly in line with the September projections and pointed to an easing of wage growth in 2025. Survey indicators also suggested a marked deceleration in wage growth in the coming year.
After the recent downside surprises to inflation
column2: the December Eurosystem staff projections would allow a comprehensive assessment of the inflation outlook. Headline inflation was expected to rise again later in 2024
column3: before declining to target in the course of 2025
column4: earlier than had been foreseen before. The latest expert surveys indicated inflation rates for 2024 and 2025 that were below the September projections baseline. The inflation expectations of euro area firms and consumers had also declined across all horizons.

column1: Turning to the external environment

column1: 2025.01.16 13:30:00|Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday
column2: 11-12 December 2024|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel noted that
column2: since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 16-17 October 2024
column3: the narrative in financial markets had shifted as a result of rising trade and economic policy uncertainty. Investors had increasingly focused on the divergence in growth prospects between the euro area and the United States. This had manifested itself in a divergence of bond yield and equity price developments between the euro area and the United States
column4: as well as a pronounced weakening of the euro against the US dollar. While the euro area near-term inflation outlook embedded in market pricing had shifted upwards
column5: inflation compensation had declined over longer horizons. This had led investors to expect a frontloading of ECB rate cuts and a lower terminal rate. Owing to these expectations regarding the rate-cutting cycle
column6: combined with the weakening of the euro exchange rate against the US dollar and still benign risk asset price constellations
column7: financial conditions had loosened further.

column1: Two key factors had shaped euro area financial market developments in the inter-meeting period: the US presidential election and the surge in policy uncertainty in the two largest euro area economies. However
column2: so far the rise in macroeconomic uncertainty had not translated into higher financial market volatility. On the contrary
column3: market volatility had decreased since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. But even in an environment of generally benign financial market conditions
column4: higher economic and political uncertainty could have implications for economic sentiment
column5: with knock-on effects on asset prices. A case in point was the weak euro area Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) in November 2024. Initially
column6: after the Governing Council’s October monetary policy meeting
column7: macroeconomic data had surprised consistently to the upside
column8: both in the United States and in the euro area. However
column9: the November euro area PMI – produced after the US presidential election in November – had disappointed
column10: pulling the Citigroup Economic Surprise Index back into negative territory. Meanwhile
column11: the equivalent index for the United States had remained firmly in positive territory.

column1: Rising uncertainty and diverging macroeconomic data had been reflected in a sharp divergence in monetary policy expectations. In the euro area
column2: the overnight index swap (OIS) forward curve had shifted lower compared with the expectations prevailing at the time of the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. Markets currently expected a further frontloading of rate cuts and the expected terminal rate had moved lower
column4: compared with 1.84% at the time of the October meeting. Participants in the December round of the ECB Survey of Monetary Analysts (SMA) also anticipated that rate cuts would be brought forward
column5: but they had not lowered their expectations for the terminal rate relative to the October round of the survey.

column1: In contrast
column2: the US fed funds futures curve had moved in the opposite direction
column3: as investors had scaled back expectations of further rate cuts by the Federal Reserve System. Whereas for most of 2024 global investors had been expecting a broadly synchronised easing cycle across economies
column4: the picture had changed markedly
column5: bringing the differential between the expected terminal rates of the ECB and the Federal Reserve System to almost 200 basis points.

column1: The divergence in risk-free rates between the euro area and the United States was visible across maturities. A breakdown of euro area and US OIS rates into changes in inflation compensation and real rates showed that the main driver had been a divergence in real rates.

The perception of heightened downside risks to economic growth had not exerted downward pressure on near-term inflation expectations as reflected in inflation fixings (swap contracts linked to specific monthly releases in euro area year-on-year HICP inflation excluding tobacco). The latest inflation fixings had shifted upwards significantly
column2: reversing part of the previous decline
column3: and were currently close to 2% – converging with the inflation trajectory implicit in the December Eurosystem staff projections. Over the longer term
column4: five-year forward inflation compensation five years ahead had continued its decline and currently stood at 2%. According to evidence from option prices
column5: the risks to inflation were broadly balanced.

column1: Turning to foreign exchange market developments
column2: the main driver of the EUR/USD exchange rate had been the sharp divergence in interest rates. The reappraisal of expectations regarding the ECB’s monetary policy had led to lower risk-free OIS rates
column3: which in turn had been transmitted to euro area sovereign bond markets. Sovereign bond yields had declined across euro area jurisdictions since the Governing Council’s October meeting. At the same time several euro area sovereigns had seen increased spreads between their bond yields and OIS rates. This mainly reflected the reduced scarcity of sovereign bonds
column4: driven by the reduction of the Eurosystem’s monetary policy bond holdings as well as prospects of increased net issuance.

column1: The structural factors influencing asset swap spreads had also recently shaped dynamics in the repo market. As the Eurosystem balance sheet was being reduced and excess liquidity was declining
column2: the repo market was shifting towards a regime of collateral abundance: a trend expected to persist into 2025. Rising collateral availability had contributed to the convergence of repo rates toward the deposit facility rate (DFR) across jurisdictions.

column1: Market perceptions of diverging growth trajectories had also been reflected in equity markets. While US stocks had rallied to new historical highs
column2: euro area equity prices had temporarily dropped back to near early 2024 levels before gradually recovering from early December onwards. The better performance of US equity markets had been driven
column3: in particular
column4: by those sectors expected to benefit most from the incoming US Administration. Higher risk premia in the euro area
column5: coupled with a further fall in risk premia in the United States
column6: had contributed to a historically large valuation gap between the US and euro area equity markets.

column1: Recent financial market developments had had implications for overall financial conditions. Taking a longer-term perspective
column2: financial conditions had eased significantly since the Governing Council’s last interest rate hike in September 2023 and currently stood close to the accommodative levels seen in early 2019. In particular
column3: euro area real risk-free interest rates had declined further markedly across all maturities. Overall
column4: recent developments had accelerated the easing of euro area financial conditions
column5: while inflation expectations had firmed up around the ECB’s inflation target of 2%.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Starting with inflation in the euro area
column2: Mr Lane recalled that headline inflation had been 2.3% in November according to Eurostat’s flash estimate
column3: 0.3 percentage points higher than in October. The increase had been expected and primarily reflected developments in energy inflation
column4: which had moved up from -4.6% in October to -1.9% in November
column5: owing mainly to base effects. Food inflation had edged down to 2.8% in November
column6: from 2.9% in October. Core inflation (excluding energy and food) had been unchanged at 2.7%.

column1: Indicators of underlying inflation ranged between 2% and 2.8% when excluding the measure of domestic inflation. The indicators of underlying inflation with the highest predictive power for headline inflation were suggesting a sustained return of inflation to target. In particular
column2: the Persistent and Common Component of Inflation (PCCI) remained at around 2.0%. The domestic inflation indicator
column3: which closely tracked services inflation
column4: had again eased somewhat. But at 4.2% in October
column5: it had remained high
column6: reflecting strong wage pressures and the fact that prices of some services had still been adjusting to the past inflation surge.

column1: At the same time the incoming information pointed to a moderation in services inflation dynamics
column2: which should support an easing of domestic inflation. The three-month-on-three-month seasonally adjusted services inflation rate had fallen to 2.6% in November
column3: from 3.4% in October
column4: indicating a further softening in momentum. Meanwhile
column5: the sizeable gap between services inflation and its medium-term underlying trend – captured by the PCCI for services
column6: which stood at 2.5% – suggested there should be further downward adjustment in services inflation in the coming months. The gap suggested that idiosyncratic and non-persistent factors were contributing to the current high level of services inflation. The last step towards achieving the inflation target would be a moderation in services inflation
column7: which was projected to decrease noticeably in the first half of 2025.

column1: The incoming wage data broadly confirmed the previous assessment of elevated but easing wage pressures. The growth rate of compensation per employee had moderated to 4.4% in the third quarter from 4.7% in the second quarter
column2: 0.1 percentage points below the December projection. The growth rate of unit labour costs had eased to 4.3% from 5.2%. Profit margins continued to buffer the impact of elevated labour costs on inflation: annual growth in unit profits had remained negative in the third quarter. Forward-looking wage trackers continued to point to a material easing of wage growth in 2025.

column1: Headline inflation was expected to fluctuate around its current levels in the near term
column2: as previous sharp falls in energy prices continued to drop out of the annual rates. It was then expected to settle sustainably at around the 2% medium-term target in the course of 2025. Easing labour cost pressures and the ongoing impact on consumer prices of the ECB’s past monetary policy tightening should help this process.

column1: According to the latest Eurosystem staff projections
column2: headline inflation was expected to average 2.4% in 2024
column3: 2.1% in 2025 and 1.9% in 2026. It was then projected to increase to 2.1% in 2027 as a result of the expansion of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS). The projections continued to foresee a rapid decline in core inflation
column4: from 2.9% in 2024 to 2.3% in 2025 and then 1.9% in 2026 and 2027. Compared with the September round
column5: the projections had been revised down by 0.1 percentage points for headline inflation in 2024 and 2025
column6: and by the same amount for core inflation in 2026. The latest inflation expectations from the ECB’s Survey of Monetary Analysts (SMA) were broadly in line with the December staff projections for headline inflation. Market-based indicators of inflation compensation were also consistent with a timely return of inflation to target
column7: while also showing a marked reduction in inflation risk premia for medium and longer-term maturities. This could suggest that markets had revised down the risk of future adverse supply shocks and revised up the risk of future adverse demand shocks.

column1: Turning to the global environment
column2: global growth momentum remained strong but was vulnerable to trade policy uncertainty. The global composite PMI excluding the euro area had increased further in November
column3: to 53.2 from 52.8 in October
column4: owing to improvements in both the services and the manufacturing sector. Anticipation of higher tariffs could support goods trade in the near term by leading to a further frontloading of imports
column5: but implementation of such policies would ultimately weigh on trade. In the December Eurosystem staff projections global real GDP was expected to grow by 3.4% in 2024 and 3.5% in 2025
column6: slowing to 3.3% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027
column7: with the outlook being largely unchanged from the September ECB staff projections.

column1: Since the October Governing Council meeting
column2: the euro had depreciated by 1.2% in nominal effective terms and by 3.0% against the US dollar. Oil prices had seen considerable volatility
column3: with the forward curve fluctuating. But overall the curve was lower than that embedded in the ECB staff September projections and displayed a slightly negative profile over the coming years. Gas prices had increased quite substantially
column4: although these had been very low at the start of the year and remained well below the peaks of 2022. Furthermore
column5: the gas futures curve was downward sloping – partly due to expanded global supply capacity only becoming available in the future
column6: rather than immediately. Food commodity prices had also been quite volatile
column7: increasing by approximately 40% since the start of the year.

column1: The euro area economy had grown by 0.4% in the third quarter
column2: exceeding the September ECB staff projection. Excluding Irish data
column3: the economy had grown by 0.3%. Growth had been driven mainly by an increase in consumption
column4: partly reflecting one-off factors that had boosted tourism over the summer
column5: and by firms building up inventories. These factors had outweighed a negative net contribution from trade. Overall
column6: private domestic demand had remained subdued
column7: as investment had contracted when excluding the contribution of the Irish data to the euro area aggregate. On the production side
column8: growth had been driven by services. The interest-sensitive manufacturing sector had continued to contract
column9: owing to competitiveness losses
column10: still-high energy prices in relative terms
column11: rising uncertainty
column12: high regulatory costs and the lagged effects of previous monetary policy tightening.

column1: The incoming information suggested a slowdown in the near term. The euro area composite output PMI had declined from 50.0 in October to 48.3 in November. The deterioration in the PMI continued to be broad-based across countries and sub-indices. The manufacturing PMI output index had fallen to 45.1 in November from 45.8 in October. The forward-looking PMI for new manufacturing orders had also fallen
column2: pointing to a weak short-term outlook for industry. The PMI for services activity had fallen into contractionary territory for the first time since January
column3: declining to 49.5 in November from 51.6 in October. Business and consumer confidence remained subdued in an environment of high uncertainty
column4: which was leading to strong household savings and to firms holding back investment. Monthly indicators suggested a deceleration in private consumption growth and a continued contraction in both housing and business investment. The export sector also appeared to have weakened further.

column1: The labour market remained resilient. Employment had grown by 0.2% in the third quarter
column2: again surprising to the upside
column3: and the unemployment rate had remained at its historical low of 6.3% in October. However
column4: the demand for labour continued to soften. The job vacancy rate had declined to 2.5% in the third quarter
column5: 0.8 percentage points below its peak
column6: and surveys also pointed to fewer jobs being created in the fourth quarter.

column1: Regarding fiscal policies
column2: there had already been a significant correction in the euro area budget balance after the pandemic. The further reduction of national deficits
column3: as foreseen in the projections
column4: reflected countries’ fiscal and structural plans under the reformed EU economic governance framework. These plans needed to actually be delivered.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: conditions were in place for growth to strengthen over the projection horizon. According to the staff assessment
column3: while structural factors had weighed on the euro area economy and especially the manufacturing sector
column4: the weak productivity growth since 2022 also included a significant cyclical component. This component had largely been driven by the past tightening of monetary policy and weak external demand. Domestic demand should benefit from rising real wages
column5: the gradual fading of the effects of restrictive monetary policy
column6: and the ongoing recovery in the global economy. Although fiscal policies were set to remain on a consolidation path overall
column7: Next Generation EU funds would still support investment in the next two years. On the external side
column8: euro area export growth was expected to benefit from strengthening foreign demand. At the same time trade uncertainty had increased materially
column9: and the effects of a potential increase in tariffs on the euro area economy would depend on the extent
column10: timing and magnitude of tariff and non-tariff measures
column11: as well as on the responses of the EU and other jurisdictions.

column1: According to the December Eurosystem staff projections
column2: real GDP growth was expected to average 0.7% in 2024
column4: 1.4% in 2026 and 1.3% in 2027. Compared with the September projections
column5: it had been revised down by 0.1 percentage points for 2024
column6: 0.2 percentage points for 2025 and 0.1 percentage points for 2026. The latest SMA indicated a lower growth profile than the staff projections for 2025

column1: Market interest rates in the euro area had declined further since the Governing Council’s October meeting
column2: reflecting the perceived worsening of the economic outlook. Regarding monetary and financial analysis
column3: a degree of normalisation had been observed in monetary dynamics. The annual growth rate of M3 had risen to 3.4% in October
column4: up from 2.9% in August. Growth in the narrow monetary aggregate M1 had also continued to recover and its annual growth rate had turned positive for the first time since December 2022
column5: standing at 0.2% in October. So far
column6: the current monetary dynamics had to a large extent been driven by sizeable net monetary inflows from the rest of the world.

column1: The ECB’s past interest rate cuts were gradually making it less expensive for firms and households to borrow. The average interest rate on new loans to firms had been 4.7% in October
column2: more than half a percentage point below its peak a year earlier. The cost to firms of issuing market-based debt had fallen by more than a percentage point since its peak. The average rate on new mortgages had also come down
column3: to 3.6% in October
column4: around half a percentage point below its peak in 2023.

column1: But financing conditions remained restrictive. The cost of new credit for firms was elevated from a historical perspective
column2: particularly in real terms
column3: and the cumulative tightening of credit standards since the beginning of the hiking cycle remained substantial overall. The average rate on the outstanding stock of mortgages was set to rise as fixed-rate loans were repriced at higher levels.

column1: Bank lending to firms had only gradually picked up
column2: from low levels
column3: with the annual rate of increase rising to 1.2% in October. The annual growth rate of debt securities issued by firms
column4: net of redemptions
column5: had stood at 3.1% in October
column6: remaining within the narrow range observed over recent months. Mortgage lending had continued to rise gradually
column7: with an annual growth rate of 0.8% in October.

column1: Monetary policy considerations and policy options
In summary
column2: the incoming information and the latest staff projections indicated that the disinflation process remained well on track. While domestic inflation was still high
column3: it was likely to come down as services inflation dynamics moderated and labour cost pressures eased. Recent cuts in the key ECB interest rates were also gradually being transmitted to funding costs
column4: but financing conditions remained restrictive along the entire transmission chain
column5: from the DFR to the rates that financial intermediaries charged to households and firms. Staff now expected a slower economic recovery than in the September projections
column6: marking another downward adjustment in the growth outlook relative to recent projection rounds. Although growth had picked up in the third quarter of this year
column7: survey indicators suggested it had slowed in the current quarter.

column1: Under the December baseline projections
column2: lower policy rates and a further easing of financing conditions were prerequisites for inflation to stabilise sustainably at the 2% target. Mr Lane therefore proposed that the three key ECB interest rates be lowered by 25 basis points. In particular
column3: a decision to lower the DFR – the rate through which the Governing Council steered the monetary policy stance – was justified by the updated assessment of the inflation outlook
column4: the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission.

column1: In the current environment of high uncertainty
column2: it was prudent to maintain agility by following a meeting-by-meeting approach and not pre-commit to any particular rate path. In terms of risk management
column3: in the event of upside shocks to the inflation outlook and/or to economic momentum
column4: monetary easing would be able to proceed more slowly than the path embedded in the December projections. Equally
column5: in the event of downside shocks to the inflation outlook and/or to economic momentum
column6: it would be able to proceed more quickly.

column1: While policy was still restrictive and weighing on demand
column2: the disinflation process was sufficiently advanced for the emphasis in communication to be adjusted
column3: from expressing determination to ensure that inflation would “return to the target” to pledging that it should “stabilise sustainably at the target”. This alternative expression better described the Governing Council’s primary task on an ongoing basis. In connection with this
column4: the intention to keep policy rates sufficiently restrictive should be replaced with a more two-sided pledge to adopt the appropriate stance to stabilise inflation sustainably at target. At the same time
column5: Mr Lane proposed preserving continuity in the other key communication elements – including the commitment to a meeting-by-meeting
column6: data-dependent approach to setting rates
column7: supported by the three-pronged reaction function – and refraining from any pre-commitment on the speed and scale of monetary easing at future meetings.

column1: Finally
column2: in line with the Governing Council’s monetary policy strategy
column3: a regular assessment of the links between monetary policy and financial stability had been carried out. It indicated that euro area banks remained resilient and there were few signs of financial market stress or a build-up of financial sector vulnerabilities. Financial stability risks nonetheless remained elevated. Macroprudential policy remained the first line of defence against the build-up of financial vulnerabilities
column4: enhancing resilience and preserving macroprudential space.

column1: 2. Governing Council’s discussion and monetary policy decisions
Economic
column2: monetary and financial analyses

column1: As regards the external environment
column2: members took note of the assessment provided by Mr Lane. Global activity had developed better than expected and the December staff projections saw global growth remaining solid overall. Both the United States and China were projected to grow more strongly than in the September projections
column3: although their growth rates were likely to ease slightly over the projection horizon. Euro area foreign demand was seen to have recovered in 2024 and was expected to grow in line with global activity over the rest of the projection horizon. The dominant risk was related to increased fragmentation and to trade protectionism
column4: notably in the United States. This could dampen trade and economic activity while also pushing up consumer prices in the United States – and globally in the event of retaliation. This risk notwithstanding
column5: global activity was likely to have remained robust in the second half of 2024. Resilient trade growth in the third quarter likely reflected frontloading of goods imports amid uncertainty surrounding the trade policies of the incoming US Administration. Container freight rates for shipments from Asia to Europe and the United States had increased over the summer but had fallen back in the autumn. In the United States
column6: economic activity had been strong in the third quarter and was expected to remain strong. Real GDP growth in 2025 had been revised up in the December projections
column7: while uncertainty around the baseline projection had declined. In China
column8: activity had been strengthening
column9: which was supported by developments in consumption. The housing market had been the main weak spot and was likely to remain a drag on growth for the foreseeable future. The euro had depreciated in nominal effective terms since the last Governing Council meeting. And while oil prices had remained broadly stable and metal prices had declined
column10: gas and food commodity prices had increased. There had been a broad-based appreciation of the US dollar after the US elections

column3: lower demand for euro area exports as a result of higher tariffs and a re-routing of exports into the euro area from countries with overcapacity would put downward pressure on inflation. Geopolitical tensions create two-sided inflation risks as regards energy markets
column4: consumer confidence and business investment. Extreme weather events
column5: and the unfolding climate crisis more broadly
column6: could drive up food prices by more than expected. Inflation could turn out higher if wages or profits increase by more than expected. A boost in defence and infrastructure spending could also raise inflation through its effect on aggregate demand. But inflation might surprise on the downside if monetary policy dampens demand by more than expected.

column1: Financial and monetary conditions

Market interest rates in the euro area decreased after our January meeting but have risen over recent days in response to a revised outlook for fiscal policy. Our interest rate cuts are gradually making it less expensive for firms and households to borrow and loan growth is picking up. At the same time
column2: a headwind to the easing of financing conditions comes from past interest rate hikes still transmitting to the stock of credit
column3: and lending remains subdued overall.

column1: The average interest rate on new loans to firms declined to 4.2 per cent in January
column2: from 4.4 per cent in December. By contrast
column3: firms’ cost of issuing market-based debt rose to 3.7 per cent
column4: 0.2 percentage points above its December level. Over the same period
column5: the average interest rate on new mortgages declined to 3.3 per cent
column6: from 3.4 per cent.

column1: Growth in bank lending to firms rose to 2.0 per cent in January
column2: up from 1.7 per cent in December
column3: on the back of a moderate monthly flow of new loans. Growth in debt securities issued by firms rose to 3.4 per cent in annual terms. Mortgage lending continued to rise gradually but remained muted overall
column4: with an annual growth rate of 1.3 per cent.

column1: Conclusion
The Governing Council today decided to lower the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. In particular
column2: the decision to lower the deposit facility rate – the rate through which we steer the monetary policy stance – is based on our updated assessment of the inflation outlook
column3: the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. We are determined to ensure that inflation stabilises sustainably at our two per cent medium-term target. Especially in current conditions of rising uncertainty
column4: we will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance. In particular
column5: our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of the inflation outlook in light of the incoming economic and financial data
column6: the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

column1: In any case
column2: we stand ready to adjust all of our instruments within our mandate to ensure that inflation stabilises sustainably at our medium-term target and to preserve the smooth functioning of monetary policy transmission.

column1: We are now ready to take your questions.

So in other words

column1: So you asked me the second question

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel started her presentation by noting that
column2: since the Governing Council's previous monetary policy meeting on 29-30 January 2025
column3: euro area and US markets had moved in opposite directions in a highly volatile political environment. In the euro area
column4: markets had focused on the near-term macroeconomic backdrop
column5: with incoming data in the euro area surprising on the upside. Lower energy prices responding in part to the prospect of a ceasefire in Ukraine
column6: looser fiscal policy due to increased defence spending and a potential relaxation of Germany’s fiscal rules had supported investor sentiment. This contrasted with developments in the United States
column7: where market participants’ assessment of the new US Administration’s policy decisions had turned more negative amid fears of tariffs driving prices up and dampening consumer and business sentiment.

column1: A puzzling feature of recent market developments had been the dichotomy between measures of policy uncertainty and financial market volatility. Global economic policy uncertainty had shot up in the final quarter of 2024 and had reached a new all-time high
column2: surpassing the peak seen at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. By contrast
column3: volatility in euro area and US equity markets had remained muted
column4: despite having broadly traced dynamics in economic policy uncertainty over the past 15 years. Only more recently
column5: with the prospect of tariffs becoming more concrete
column6: had stock market volatility started to pick up from low levels.

column1: Risk sentiment in the euro area remained strong and close to all-time highs
column2: outpacing the United States
column3: which had declined significantly since the Governing Council's January monetary policy meeting. This mirrored the divergence of macroeconomic developments. The Citigroup Economic Surprise Index for the euro area had turned positive in February 2025
column4: reaching its highest level since April 2024. This was in contrast to developments in the United States
column5: where economic surprises had been negative recently.

column1: The divergence in investor appetite was most evident in stock markets. The euro area stock market continued to outperform its US counterpart
column2: posting the strongest year-to-date performance relative to the US index in almost a decade. Stock market developments were aligned with analysts’ earnings expectations
column3: which had been raised for European firms since the start of 2025. Meanwhile
column4: US earnings estimates had been revised down continuously for the past eleven weeks.

column1: Part of the recent outperformance of euro area equities stemmed from a catch-up in valuations given that euro area equities had performed less strongly than US stocks in 2024. Moreover
column2: in spite of looming tariffs
column3: the euro area equity market was benefiting from potential growth tailwinds
column4: including a possible ceasefire in Ukraine
column5: the greater prospect of a stable German government following the country’s parliamentary elections and the likelihood of increased defence spending in the euro area. The share prices of tariff-sensitive companies had been significantly underperforming their respective benchmarks in both currency areas
column6: but tariff-sensitive stocks in the United States had fared substantially worse.

column1: Market pricing also indicated a growing divergence in inflation prospects between the euro area and the United States. In the euro area
column2: the market’s view of a gradual disinflation towards the ECB’s 2% target remained intact. One-year forward inflation compensation one year ahead stood at around 2%
column3: while the one-year forward inflation-linked swap rate one year ahead continued to stand somewhat below 2%. However
column4: inflation compensation had moved up across maturities on 5 March 2025. In the United States
column5: one-year forward inflation compensation one year ahead had increased significantly
column6: likely driven in part by bond traders pricing in the inflationary effects of tariffs on US consumer prices. Indicators of the balance of risks for inflation suggested that financial market participants continued to see inflation risks in the euro area as broadly balanced across maturities.

column1: Changing growth and inflation prospects had also been reflected in monetary policy expectations for the euro area. On the back of slightly lower inflation compensation due to lower energy prices
column2: expectations for ECB monetary policy had edged down. A 25 basis point cut was fully priced in for the current Governing Council monetary policy meeting
column3: while markets saw a further rate cut at the following meeting as uncertain. Most recently
column4: at the time of the meeting
column5: rate investors no longer expected three more 25 basis point cuts in the deposit facility rate in 2025. Participants in the Survey of Monetary Analysts
column6: finalised in the last week of February
column7: had continued to expect a slightly faster easing cycle.

column1: Turning to euro area market interest rates
column2: the rise in nominal ten-year overnight index swap (OIS) rates since the 11-12 December 2024 Governing Council meeting had largely been driven by improving euro area macroeconomic data
column3: while the impact of US factors had been small overall. Looking back
column4: euro area ten-year nominal and real OIS rates had overall been remarkably stable since their massive repricing in 2022
column5: when the ECB had embarked on the hiking cycle. A key driver of persistently higher long-term rates had been the market’s reassessment of the real short-term rate that was expected to prevail in the future. The expected real one-year forward rate four years ahead had surged in 2022 as investors adjusted their expectations away from a “low-for-long” interest rate environment
column6: suggesting that higher real rates were expected to be the new normal.

column1: The strong risk sentiment had also been transmitted to euro area sovereign bond spreads relative to yields on German government bonds
column2: which remained at contained levels. Relative to OIS rates

column1: Conclusion
The Governing Council today decided to lower the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. In particular
column2: the decision to lower the deposit facility rate – the rate through which we steer the monetary policy stance – is based on our updated assessment of the inflation outlook
column3: the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. We are determined to ensure that inflation stabilises sustainably at our two per cent medium-term target. Especially in current conditions of exceptional uncertainty
column4: we will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance. In particular
column5: our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of the inflation outlook in light of the incoming economic and financial data
column6: the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

column1: In any case

column2: 16-17 April 2025|"1. Review of financial
column3: economic and monetary developments and policy options

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel recalled that President Trump’s announcement on 2 April 2025 of unexpectedly high tariffs had sparked a sharp sell-off in global equity markets and in US bond markets
column2: leading to a surge in financial market volatility. The severity of the tariffs and the manner in which they had been introduced had led to a breakdown of standard cross-market correlations
column3: with a sell-off of US equities occurring at the same time as a sell-off of Treasuries in the context of a marked depreciation of the US dollar against major currencies.

column1: Movements in euro area risk-free rates reflected the opposing impacts of the historic German fiscal package and the global trade conflict. At the long end of the yield curve
column2: the expected positive growth impulse from fiscal policy
column3: as well as expectations of tighter monetary policy in the future
column4: had been the dominant factors
column5: pulling up nominal and real interest rates. At the short end of the yield curve
column6: the decline in inflation compensation
column7: driven mainly by falling inflation risk premia
column8: had been larger than the rise in real yields
column9: leading to a decline in nominal rates. These developments reflected both the negative fallout from tariffs and lower commodity prices. Investors expected the ECB to react to the evolving situation by lowering rates more than had previously been anticipated
column10: but to start raising them again in the coming year. Amid the market turbulence
column11: euro area bond markets had continued to function smoothly
column12: and the bond supply had been absorbed well in the context of strong investor demand and well-functioning dealer intermediation. On the back of the sharp correction in stock prices and the marked appreciation of the euro exchange rate
column13: financial conditions in the euro area had tightened
column14: despite lower nominal short-term rates.

column1: Turning to market developments since the previous Governing Council meeting
column2: President Trump’s announcement on 2 April 2025 had led the VIX volatility index to temporarily reach levels not seen since the COVID-19 pandemic. Within a few days the S&P 500 index had dropped by 12%
column3: triggering sharp corrections in stock markets around the world
column4: including in the euro area. Despite a rebound after the pausing of “reciprocal” tariffs on 9 April 2025
column5: the US benchmark equity index had lost 8% in the year to date while euro area stock markets were almost back to the levels seen at the start of the year. Stocks in trade-sensitive US sectors had been hit much harder than other stocks
column6: and they had also dropped by much more than their euro area counterparts.

column1: The market turbulence had spilled over to government bond markets
column2: but the reaction had differed markedly between the euro area and the United States. US government bond yields had risen at the same time as the US equity sell-off
column3: which was highly unusual because Treasury bonds normally benefited from safe-haven flows. US ten-year asset swap spreads had likewise risen sharply
column4: which was also unusual. Meanwhile
column5: Bund yields had declined and the spread between the Bund and overnight index swap (OIS) rates had narrowed substantially as German government bonds had continued to perform their role as a safe-haven asset.

column1: The risk-off sentiment had also affected the dynamics of the US dollar exchange rate
column2: but this too had reacted differently from what would normally have been expected. In January 2025 the EUR/USD exchange rate had hit a low of 1.02
column3: but the euro’s downward trend had been reversed around the time of the announcement in early March 2025 of the reform of the German debt brake
column4: with a positive growth narrative for Europe emerging in light of higher defence and infrastructure spending. The euro exchange rate had received a second major boost after the 2 April tariff announcement in the United States. This strong upward move had not been driven
column5: as was usually the case
column6: by changes in the yield differential
column7: which had moved in the opposite direction
column8: but by US dollar weakness as investors had revised down their US growth expectations. Over recent weeks the US dollar had thus not benefited from the widespread risk-off mood.

column1: Recent developments had been reflected in global portfolio flows. The March 2025 round of the Bank of America Fund Manager Survey had recorded the strongest shift out of US equities on record
column2: with 45% of managers reporting that they had reduced their positions. At the same time
column3: a significant share of fund managers had reported that they had changed their positioning in favour of euro area equities. This marked a significant shift of perspectives away from US exceptionalism towards Europe being seen as the bright spot among major economies
column4: given the expected fiscal boost in Germany and the pick-up in European defence spending.

column1: Dynamics in risk-free bond markets illustrated the opposing impacts of the German fiscal package and the tariff announcements over recent weeks. In the euro area
column2: the overall increase in longer-term nominal interest rates had been driven by a rise in real rates
column3: indicating that market participants viewed the German fiscal package as fostering long-term growth. Real rates had kept rising during the tariff tensions
column4: as investors had continued to expect
column5: on balance
column6: an improved growth outlook for the euro area. By contrast
column7: inflation compensation had decreased across the yield curve after increasing only briefly in response to the German fiscal package.

column1: Ms Schnabel then turned to the drivers of developments in euro area inflation compensation. On the one hand
column2: bond market investors were pricing in higher inflation compensation owing to the expansionary German fiscal measures to be implemented over the next decade. On the other hand

column1: Financial market developments

Ms Schnabel started her presentation by noting that the narrative in financial markets remained unstable. column3: which had now more than recovered from the shock triggered by the US tariff announcement on 2 April. On the back of these developments

column7: expectations regarding ECB monetary policy had not recovered and remained near the levels seen immediately after 2 April.

column2: reaching levels last seen around the time of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the COVID-19 pandemic shock in 2020. However
column3: compared with these shocks

The first had been the reassessment of the near-term macroeconomic outlook for the euro area since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting.
