column2: when taking into account currency risk-hedging costs
column3: US companies had increasingly turned to euro funding. This underlined the increased attractiveness of the euro.

column1: Financial market developments

column2: interest rate markets in the euro area and the United States had been pulled in different directions
column3: leading to a convergence of policy rate expectations. In the euro area
column4: expectations for interest rates had shifted higher
column5: with reduced uncertainty around the rate outlook
column6: as a consensus had formed that interest rates were currently in a “good place” and close to or at the end of the monetary policy cycle. Markets had fully priced out any rate cut at the current meeting and assigned a significantly lower probability to another 25 basis point rate cut by year-end. The median participant in the ECB Survey of Monetary Analysts anticipated no further rate cuts in 2025
column7: while the median respondent in both the Bloomberg and Reuters surveys did not expect any further rate cut in the current cycle. In the United States
column8: market expectations of a quicker easing cycle had increased after weak labour market data. As a result

column2: which had been interpreted as signalling that no further rate cuts were imminent. Subsequent data releases had confirmed and reinforced this new baseline path. Moreover
column3: uncertainty around the expected rate path had decreased. This stood in contrast to developments in the United States
column4: where option-implied probabilities suggested that US rate uncertainty remained elevated.

column1: The key fundamental driver of the gradual convergence in policy rate expectations had been the narrowing gap in the economic outlook between the euro area and the United States. Consensus Economics growth expectations for the euro area in 2025 were now well above their levels prior to the US tariff announcement on 2 April
column2: and expectations for 2026 had declined only mildly. By contrast
column3: growth expectations for the United States for both 2025 and 2026 had been revised down sharply. Developments in the inflation outlook seemed to be less in line with the converging rate outlook. In the euro area
column4: investors’ inflation expectations had stabilised at around the ECB’s inflation target. By contrast
column5: medium-term inflation compensation in the United States had trended higher after the drop in April
column6: despite the substantial downward revision in US growth expectations over the same period.

column1: Market pricing of looser US monetary policy could be explained by pointing to the fact that
column2: over the past year
column3: US interest rates had become far more sensitive to surprises in US non-farm employment figures than in previous years. Sensitivity to US inflation surprises had
column4: however
column5: fallen to close to zero
column6: indicating that investor focus in the United States had shifted towards real economic data.

column1: In the euro area
column2: medium and longer-term interest rates had remained broadly stable over recent months. In the United States
column3: the slight decline in the ten-year rate since April 2025 had been due to offsetting factors. Investors expected a more accommodative monetary policy stance in the United States
column4: but at the same time demanded higher compensation for the various risks surrounding that scenario

column3: this steepening appeared to be a normalisation after a long period of compressed term premia
column4: as yield curves remained much less steep than before the start of large-scale asset purchases across most major central banks.

column2: the exchange rate had remained broadly constant. The largest part of the appreciation of the euro in 2025 could be explained by relative demand and sentiment. Important drivers of exchange rate developments had been the announcements of tariffs and the subsequent trade agreements. A comparison of bilateral exchange rate movements of a broad set of currencies against the US dollar showed that the initial depreciation of the US dollar against almost all currencies after the April tariff announcement had been followed by an appreciation after the July tariff agreements

column1: Regarding the economic analysis

column9: it was observed that the real effective exchange rate – the main metric used to measure competitiveness – had appreciated by much less than the nominal rate.

Market indicators of expectations for euro area growth continued to suggest a robust economic expansion. Growth expectations for 2025 had been revised up and stood well above their level prior to the initial announcement of higher US tariffs. Growth expectations for 2026 and 2027 were close to pre-tariff expectations and were near to the level of potential growth. Market indicators of medium-term inflation expectations were close to 2%. column6: in combination with increased hedging of US dollar exposures

column2: the exchange rate had decoupled further from interest rate differentials. In other words

column3: with the second following the US tariff announcement in April 2025. The German fiscal package had increased confidence in the euro area
column4: as it would allow for more public investment
column5: supporting potential output growth. In a similar vein

column4: and therefore warranted close monitoring. In the largest euro area economy

column1: The “second China shock” – referring to the country’s increased global presence in more advanced products and technologies – was also widely highlighted as a major challenge for the euro area economy and its competitiveness. column2: China’s increasing competitiveness was reflected in the scale and scope of its exports to the euro area. column2: low-value imports from China into the United States had dropped significantly. From July 2026
column3: the EU would also impose a duty on small value imports from China
column4: so a similar outcome could be expected in the euro area. Nevertheless
column5: the impact on overall euro area inflation was expected to be negligible. Trade barriers would not
column6: however
column7: protect euro area exporters in third-country markets
column8: where Chinese competition was also fierce. Moreover
column9: competition from other Asian economies could present similar challenges for the euro area. Therefore
column10: it was argued that a durable solution to the euro area’s competitiveness challenges required long-lasting structural reforms to make the economy more productive.

column2: it was noted that there was plenty of existing evidence. Cheaper intermediate and final goods from China – subsidising the euro area via low-cost imports – were invariably found to be good for Europe in most macroeconomic models on account of the support given to real incomes. However
column3: several caveats were raised with respect to the argument that lower import prices would unequivocally raise real incomes and welfare in Europe. First
column4: in the event of abnormally low pricing and certain key European sectors such as the steel industry disappearing
column5: lower import prices in the short term would lead to more market power for Chinese companies and could ultimately result in higher import prices for Europe. The impact of the earlier China shock on US manufacturing

column1: Financial market developments

Ms Schnabel started her presentation by noting that the period after the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 4-5 February 2026 could be divided into two distinct phases. In the first phase
column2: up to the start of the war in the Middle East
column3: the low-volatility and strong risk appetite environment had remained in place. In the second phase
column4: when energy prices had surged in response to the war
column5: volatility had increased in equity markets and especially in bond markets
column6: and there had been sell-offs in both risk asset markets and bond markets.

column1: Brent crude oil prices had surged above USD 100 per barrel to levels last seen after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Natural gas prices had also increased substantially
column2: but had remained well below their 2022 levels. At the same time
column3: the Brent crude oil futures curve had shown historically high backwardation – a strong negative slope – suggesting that traders were expecting the spike in oil prices to be reversed quickly. However
column4: over time traders had pared back expectations of a swift reversal of the spike in energy prices. Since the beginning of the war
column5: the Brent crude oil futures curve had gradually shifted upwards and stood visibly above the curve that had prevailed shortly after it started.

column1: Comparing market reactions in the first week of the war with past geopolitical shocks accompanied by energy price increases showed that the reactions of euro area equity prices
column2: the EUR/USD exchange rate and financial market volatility had been at the upper end of the historical ranges. Interest rate markets had reacted more strongly than suggested by historical regularities. The increase in near-term inflation compensation had been at the upper end of the range seen with previous shocks
column3: and was only comparable to the sharp increase after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Most notably
column4: in previous episodes
column5: risk-free overnight index swap (OIS) rates and policy expectations had tended to decline in response to energy price shocks
column6: as investors had seemingly priced in the negative impact on economic growth as dominating the inflationary impulse. This time around
column7: markets were pricing in the view that the inflationary effects of the war dominated
column8: requiring a tightening of monetary policy.

column1: The energy supply shock had had a large impact on near-term inflation compensation in the euro area. Inflation fixings (excluding tobacco) for 2026 had increased sharply and inflation-linked swap forward rates stood above 2% across horizons. Longer-term inflation compensation had remained broadly stable
column2: however
column3: reflecting market participants’ assessment of the credibility of monetary policy. The shifts had been driven in broadly equal parts by higher genuine inflation expectations and by higher inflation risk premia
column4: as investors expected higher inflation but also demanded compensation for higher inflation uncertainty in a geopolitically fragmented world. Based on evidence from option prices
column5: the balance of risks to the outlook for inflation over the two-year horizon and the five-year horizon had also shifted up sharply and was currently tilted to the upside
column6: especially over shorter horizons. By contrast
column7: risks over the longer term had remained broadly balanced.

column1: Shifts in inflation compensation
column2: rather than in real rates
column3: had dominated developments in euro area risk-free rate markets. Nominal rates in both the euro area and the United States had moved up significantly. The reassessment of inflation prospects had been substantially more pronounced in the euro area across horizons. At the same time
column4: euro area two-year real rates had declined
column5: reflecting a downward revision to economic growth
column6: whereas US two-year real rates had remained broadly stable. Long-term real rates had increased in the United States but had remained stable in the euro area. Both in the euro area and in the United States
column7: the rise in longer-term nominal rates had been driven by higher short-term rate expectations
column8: indicating expectations of tighter monetary policy
column9: and a higher term premium
column10: reflecting greater uncertainty about the impact of the war on the longer-term outlook for the economy and for inflation.

column1: Following the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting the OIS forward curve had edged lower
column2: pricing in a roughly one-third probability of a 25 basis point rate cut by the end of 2026. This trend had reversed sharply following the start of the war. According to the latest curve
column3: investors were pricing in rate hikes of about 40 basis points by the end of 2026
column4: with some volatility regarding the exact number. Moreover
column5: there had been a sharp rise in uncertainty surrounding the path of the ECB’s monetary policy in response to the energy price shock
column6: after rate uncertainty had hovered around multi-year lows ahead of the war. By contrast
column7: in the Survey of Monetary Analysts
column8: as well as in the subsequent Bloomberg and Reuters surveys
column9: participants had reported that they anticipated that policy rates would remain at their current levels throughout 2026 and 2027. In the United States
column10: markets had revised their monetary policy expectations to a similar degree
column11: despite the US economy being more shielded from the energy shock.

column1: The degree to which asset prices had been affected across countries and sectors depended on their exposure to the energy price shock. The euro area’s terms of trade had deteriorated markedly since the start of the war
column2: reflecting its position as a net energy importer. The exposure to the energy shock was affecting exchange rate dynamics. The EUR/USD exchange rate had closely tracked changes in European energy prices over recent weeks
column3: with the euro depreciating markedly against the US dollar. The euro had
column4: however
column5: held up slightly better than the euro area’s large net energy import position would have suggested. Nevertheless
column6: near-term risks to the EUR/USD exchange rate remained tilted to the downside
column7: while medium-term risks remained broadly balanced
column8: suggesting that markets perceived the terms-of-trade shock to be short-lived.

column1: Risk appetite had deteriorated since the start of the war. The decline had been somewhat more pronounced in the euro area than in the United States
column2: which was consistent with the greater energy dependence of the euro area. That said
column3: the deterioration had remained contained overall. By way of comparison
column4: in response to the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the April 2025 tariff shock
column5: risk sentiment had deteriorated much more sharply. The dominant driver of the correction in equity prices since the outbreak of the war in the Middle East had been the rise in risk-free rates. Higher risk premia and somewhat weaker long-term earnings expectations had contributed only to a limited extent. The sharpest correction had been seen for euro area financial stocks
column6: which had underperformed after having significantly overperformed in 2025.

column1: One reason for the underperformance of financial stocks had been their exposure to private markets
column2: which had come under increased scrutiny over past months. Euro area private markets remained small compared with the US market
column3: but they too had grown at double-digit rates since 2010
column4: across both private equity and private credit. One major concern about private markets was their opacity. Recent concerns had focused on the sizeable and growing exposures of private funds to the technology and software sectors. The escalation of geopolitical tensions had added to the concerns about private markets. Tighter financing conditions and weaker growth would exert pressure on highly leveraged firms
column5: reinforcing downside risks in this segment. Several large funds had experienced an increase in the volume of redemption requests and had applied – often contractually stipulated – withdrawal restrictions.

column1: Credit spreads in fixed income markets had also come under some upward pressure. Euro area sovereign bond spreads over OIS rates had widened
column2: with the exception of German bond spreads. Markets judged that the conflict in the Middle East would have some impact on growth and fiscal balances
column3: and this was contributing to a rise in risk premia. Overall
column4: the widening of spreads had remained contained
column5: including in corporate bond markets. This was consistent with the modest tightening seen in financial conditions so far. The ECB’s Macro-Finance Financial Conditions Index (“Macro-Finance FCI”) had tightened on the back of lower risk asset prices and higher long-term interest rates. However
column6: so far it had remained in the range observed since the summer of 2025.

column1: Finally
column2: money markets had hardly been affected by recent events. Demand in the Eurosystem’s standard refinancing operations had been low and stable over the past year as excess liquidity had remained abundant. However
column3: there were encouraging signs that banks were increasingly making sure that they were ready to borrow in these operations
column4: as the number of banks participating in operations had been rising steadily
column5: even if the amounts involved remained small.

column1: The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Mr Lane then went through the latest economic
column2: monetary and financial developments in the global economy and the euro area.

column1: Prior to the onset of the war in the Middle East
column2: the incoming information had appeared to broadly confirm the December projections baseline. The war had made the outlook significantly more uncertain
column3: with upside risks to inflation and downside risks to output.

column2: headline inflation had increased to 1.9% in February
column3: from 1.7% in January. Energy inflation had risen to -3.1%
column4: from -4.0% in January
column5: while non-energy inflation had risen to 2.4% from 2.3%. Food inflation had edged down to 2.5%
column6: from 2.6% in January

column10: from 3.2%
column11: partly reflecting the temporary impact of the Winter Olympics on services inflation in Italy. Indicators of underlying inflation had changed little over recent months and
column12: before the onset of the war

column1: Wage growth had continued to decelerate
column2: with the growth rate of compensation per employee slowing more than expected in the fourth quarter
column4: from 4.0% in the third quarter of 2025. This was due to a marked compression in wage drift. Negotiated wage growth had increased to 3.0% in annual terms in the fourth quarter
column5: from 1.9% in the third quarter
column6: driven by fading base effects related to previous one-off payments. Forward-looking indicators
column7: such as the ECB wage tracker and surveys on wage expectations
column8: had suggested that labour costs would ease further in the course of 2026. But close monitoring of wages and underlying inflation dynamics would be important
column9: as the energy shock – especially if it turned out to be strong and persistent – had the potential to trigger material indirect and second-round effects.

column1: The war in the Middle East would have a marked impact on near-term inflation through higher energy prices. Crude oil and gas prices had risen sharply since the end of February amid significant disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on energy infrastructure in the Gulf region. Oil prices had risen by 47%
column2: to slightly above USD 100 per barrel
column3: since the previous Governing Council meeting
column4: amid considerable volatility. This oil price reaction had been significant but not unprecedented. Oil futures curves had shifted upwards but indicated that investors expected oil prices to fall again over the coming year. European gas prices had risen by 52% since the previous monetary policy meeting and the gas futures curve had shifted upwards
column5: especially at shorter horizons. The increase in gas prices had been compounded by the current low levels of gas inventories in Europe
column6: which left prices vulnerable to supply disruptions. As with oil futures
column7: gas futures displayed a steep downward-tilting slope. The medium-term implications of the war would depend both on the intensity and duration of the energy shock (connected to the intensity and duration of the conflict) and on the strength and breadth of the propagation of the energy shock to the economy and inflation.

column1: In the baseline of the March ECB staff projections
column2: which exceptionally incorporated information up to 11 March
column3: a later cut-off date than usual
column4: headline inflation was seen to average 2.6% in 2026
column5: 2.0% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028. Relative to the December projections
column6: it had been revised up by 0.7 percentage points for 2026
column7: 0.2 percentage points for 2027 and 0.1 percentage points for 2028. The upward revision for 2026 reflected the marked increase in energy prices. Beyond the near term

Inflation was projected to edge up in 2028 as this base effect faded and the Emissions Trading System 2 was due to be implemented. Inflation excluding energy was seen to average 2.3% in 2026
column9: 2.4% in 2027 and 2.2% in 2028. Core inflation was projected to average 2.3% in 2026
column10: 2.2% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028. It had been revised up by 0.1 percentage points for 2026
column11: 0.3 percentage points for 2027 and 0.1 percentage points for 2028.

column1: Both market-based and survey-based measures of inflation expectations recorded after the onset of the war had moved up significantly over shorter horizons but pointed to a stabilisation at the 2% target in the medium term. The inflation expectation component derived from market-based inflation compensation measures stood on average at 2.9% for 2026
column2: 2.2% for 2027 and 2.0% for 2028. The profile of a short-lived jump in inflation followed by stabilisation at the target was consistent with the latest round of the ECB Survey of Monetary Analysts
column3: conducted during the first week of the war
column4: and with the most recent Reuters survey
column5: carried out during the second week of the war. In terms of the balance of risks to the inflation outlook

column1: The global economy had been resilient so far
column2: but the war in the Middle East created headwinds and the external environment also remained challenging owing to volatile global trade policies. Global GDP growth excluding the euro area had been 0.8% in the fourth quarter of 2025
column3: while global imports had grown by 0.6%. The global growth outlook had remained broadly unchanged in the March projections relative to the previous projection exercise. The carry-over from stronger than expected data releases for 2025 had been offset by downward revisions due to the adverse impact of the war in the Middle East. The euro exchange rate had weakened by 2.9% against the US dollar since the last Governing Council meeting
column4: as the war had triggered a deterioration in global risk sentiment and an adverse energy terms-of-trade shock for the euro area. Against the currencies of the euro area’s major trading partners
column5: the euro had weakened by a more modest 1.4%.

column1: The euro area economy had grown by 0.2% in the fourth quarter of 2025
column2: which was in line with the December staff projections
column3: and by 0.4% when excluding volatile Irish data. Growth had been driven by stronger domestic demand and had been underpinned mainly by services. Rising real incomes had supported private consumption
column4: which had expanded by 0.4% in quarterly terms in the fourth quarter. Construction and housing renovation had strengthened. Non-construction investment had grown by 0.4% – excluding volatile Irish data – supported by investment in intangibles such as research and development
column5: software and databases. Surveys conducted before the war also pointed to resilient activity at the start of the year. However
column6: declines in the euro area Sentix Economic Index and the German ZEW Indicator of Economic Sentiment – both published after the war had started – suggested that the conflict was already weighing on sentiment.

column1: The unemployment rate had remained close to its historical low in January
column2: at 6.1%. Employment growth had been unchanged at 0.2%
column3: quarter on quarter
column4: in the fourth quarter of 2025
column5: supported by an expanding labour force. However
column6: labour demand had continued to soften. The job vacancy rate published by Eurostat had stood at 2.2% in the fourth quarter
column7: while job postings from Indeed pointed to a moderation in demand in February relative to the end of 2025. Meanwhile
column8: the share of firms in the European Commission’s business survey citing labour as a factor limiting production had declined for both manufacturing and services.

column1: With respect to fiscal policies
column2: the euro area fiscal stance was projected to have loosened slightly in 2025 and to continue loosening in 2026
column3: after which it was expected to tighten somewhat over 2027-28. Compared with the December staff projections
column4: the March projections for the fiscal stance were broadly unchanged overall. These projections had followed the usual convention of only including fiscal measures that had already been legislated
column5: or had been announced and were highly likely to be legislated
column6: whereas possible future measures by governments to contain the economic impact from the crisis had not been included.

column1: Looking ahead
column2: the war in the Middle East was clouding the growth outlook by disrupting commodity markets and weighing on real incomes and confidence
column3: which was likely to dampen private consumption and investment dynamics. The economy was now expected to expand at a slower pace in the short term than previously envisaged. The March baseline projections saw growth at 0.9% in 2026
column4: 1.3% in 2027 and 1.4% in 2028. Relative to the December projections
column5: growth had been revised down by 0.3 percentage points for 2026 and 0.1 percentage points for 2027
column6: while it was unchanged for 2028. Private consumption was expected to remain the main driver of growth over the medium term. Investment should also continue to grow
column7: with governments spending more on defence and infrastructure
column8: and firms increasingly investing in new digital technologies.

column1: The war in the Middle East was a major risk event. In line with the Governing Council’s monetary policy strategy commitment to incorporate risks and uncertainty into its decision-making
column2: staff had assessed how the war could affect growth and inflation under some alternative illustrative scenarios. The scenario analysis suggested that a prolonged disruption in the supply of oil and gas would result in inflation being above
column3: and growth being below
column4: the baseline projections in 2026 and 2027. The implications for medium-term inflation depended on the magnitude of indirect and second-round effects of a stronger and more persistent energy shock. Under the severe scenario
column5: medium-term inflation would be markedly above the target in the absence of policy action beyond that embedded in the baseline. By contrast
column6: if the war-related disruptions to commodity markets were to end earlier than assumed and second-round effects remained contained
column7: inflation would be lower and growth higher than in the baseline in 2026 and 2027.

column1: The war in the Middle East had had a pronounced impact on global financial markets. Overall financial conditions had tightened since the Governing Council’s last meeting. Stock markets had fallen and market interest rates in the euro area
column2: especially short-term rates
column3: had risen notably.

column2: reporting lags meant that the available data did not yet offer insights into the impact of the war. In January bank lending rates for firms and the cost of issuing market-based debt had both remained at 3.6%
column3: while the average interest rate on new mortgages had edged up to 3.4% after remaining broadly stable at 3.3% for a year. Bank lending to firms had grown by 2.8% on a yearly basis in January
column4: down from 3.0% in December. However
column5: this had been offset by stronger issuance of corporate bonds
column6: with the annual growth rate rising to 4.0%
column7: from 3.5% in December. Mortgage lending had grown by 3.0%
column8: unchanged from December. The upcoming bank lending survey for the euro area and the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises would offer valuable information on the impact of the war on financing and credit conditions.

column1: Monetary policy considerations and policy options
Based on the incoming information and the March 2026 staff projections (including the scenario analyses and the risk assessment)
column2: as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of transmission

column1: Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel started her presentation by noting that since the Governing Council's previous monetary policy meeting on 18-19 March 2026
column2: movements in euro area financial markets had continued to be driven by developments in the Middle East and their impact on energy prices. Amid elevated volatility
column3: markets continued to expect the oil price shock to be persistent. Although upside risks had moderated
column4: oil was priced significantly higher
column5: over an extended period of time
column6: than it had been before the start of the war in the Middle East. As a result
column7: markets continued to price in a notable and sustained inflationary impact. Inflation fixings had increased further for both 2026 and 2027. This suggested that investors anticipated some indirect or second-round effects extending beyond the first year of the conflict
column8: before inflation was expected to return to the target of 2% in 2028. At the same time
column9: markets continued to expect the economy to be relatively resilient. Prices of risk assets
column10: including equities
column11: as well as sovereign and corporate bond spreads
column12: and the exchange rate of the euro had moved back towards the levels observed prior to the conflict. Earnings expectations had been revised up since the beginning of the war
column13: which was consistent with the view that the impact on economic growth would be short-lived. At the same time
column14: there had been negative surprises in macroeconomic data for the euro area. Therefore
column15: buoyant risk asset markets
column16: which were hovering near all-time highs
column17: might indicate some investor complacency given the size and persistence of the energy price shock. With inflation still perceived as the dominant risk
column18: investors were pricing in cumulative policy rate hikes by the ECB of 73 basis points in 2026. Overall
column19: financial conditions had eased since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting
column20: driven mainly by strong risk asset markets
column21: but they remained somewhat tighter than before the war.

column1: Energy prices were unchanged from the levels prevailing at the time of the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting
column2: but remained subject to heightened volatility. Oil prices had been strongly affected by the changing probabilities of a potential reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. The Brent crude oil futures curve had retreated from the peak level reached in late March 2026
column3: but still stood at about the level observed at the time of the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. Moreover
column4: the curve remained materially above the pre-war level over the next two years
column5: suggesting that market participants assessed the energy price shock to be not only large but also highly persistent.

column1: Energy price developments had been the dominant driver of movements across euro area financial markets. Expectations of persistently higher energy prices had been reflected in inflation compensation
column2: which had increased sharply in response to the energy shock
column3: and higher short and longer-term interest rates. By contrast
column4: riskier market segments had shown less persistent reactions.

column1: A key factor underlying the divergence between the responses of interest rate markets and segments for riskier asset classes was the assessment by investors of the relative impact of the energy shock on inflation and growth. Inflation expectations reported by Consensus Economics had shifted higher for the euro area for both 2026 and 2027
column2: and for the United States they had shifted higher for 2026. By contrast
column3: there had been a more modest adjustment in growth expectations. Both euro area and US growth projections had edged down
column4: while not pointing to a pronounced slowdown. However
column5: recent incoming data had been more favourable in the United States than in the euro area
column6: which was consistent with the different impact of the terms-of-trade shock across the two economies.

column1: Regarding the market’s view of the inflation outlook for the euro area
column2: at the time of the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting
column3: inflation fixings for 2026 and 2027 had already shifted up sharply compared with before the start of the war in the Middle East. The latest fixings had edged up further for 2026
column4: trading at levels of up to 3.6%. For 2027
column5: inflation fixings were even more clearly above their March 2026 levels. This suggested that investors were expecting more persistent inflationary pressures
column6: reflecting some indirect or second-round effects. The balance of risks to inflation over the next two years and also over the next five years remained clearly tilted to the upside
column7: while longer-term risks had started to point more to the upside
column8: but inflation expectations continued to be well anchored.

column1: The shifts in inflation compensation had dominated developments in euro area risk-free rates across all maturities. Since the start of the war in the Middle East
column2: euro area overnight index swap rates had moved up significantly
column3: with the reassessment of inflation prospects pushing rates higher across the curve and leading to a flattening of the nominal yield curve. By contrast
column4: the real overnight index swap curve had steepened
column5: with real rates declining markedly at the front end of the curve relative to pre-war levels and contributing to a loosening of financial conditions.

column1: After the previous monetary policy meeting on 18-19 March
column2: markets had priced in a further tightening of monetary policy. Rate market investors were now fully pricing in one 25 basis point policy rate hike by June 2026
column3: two by September and a 92% probability of a third by December. At the time of the previous meeting
column4: participants in the Survey of Monetary Analysts had expected the ECB to look through the energy supply shock
column5: but their responses had now become more aligned with market pricing and the median expectation was for two hikes in 2026. In the United States
column6: market-based measures of policy rate expectations had remained broadly unchanged since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting.

column1: The EUR/USD exchange rate had rebounded to close to pre-war levels since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. The euro had initially depreciated markedly
column2: both in bilateral and nominal effective terms
column3: as the terms-of-trade shock had been expected to weigh on the currencies of net energy importers. However
column4: it had almost fully recovered its losses over recent weeks. Improved global risk sentiment and expectations of tighter ECB monetary policy relative to US policy had contributed to the euro’s recovery.

column1: Investor optimism regarding the impact on economic growth was most visible in equity markets
column2: which appeared to be largely looking through the energy price shock. The benchmark stock index for the euro area had initially corrected significantly in response to the war
column3: but since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting it had partly recovered its losses. In the United States
column4: benchmark stock indices had even surpassed pre-war levels and risen towards new all-time highs
column5: supported by renewed optimism about the potential impact of artificial intelligence. Model-based analysis showed that the dominant driver of the initial decline in euro area equity prices had been the rise in risk-free rates. Since the Governing Council’s meeting on 18-19 March
column6: higher longer-term earnings expectations had pushed up euro area equity markets
column7: while higher risk premia had pulled in the opposite direction. Looking at the entire period since the start of the war
column8: earnings expectations had been revised up overall
column9: indicating that analysts did not expect the war to have a lasting impact on corporate profits.

column2: euro area sovereign bond spreads had also narrowed from the peaks recorded in the second half of March. The dispersion of euro area sovereign spreads had remained contained over the entire period since the start of the war. This appeared to reflect not only market perceptions that the real economic fallout from the energy shock would be limited
column3: but also expectations of a prudent fiscal response
column4: as measures taken to shield households and firms from higher energy prices remained limited so far. Another factor supporting euro area government bond markets had been increased inflows of global funds into European sovereign bonds
column5: which pointed to continued confidence in European sovereign debt. In corporate bond markets
column6: pricing had also remained benign. Spreads of high-yield euro area corporate bonds had temporarily widened at the onset of the war
column7: but the increase had remained contained. Overall
column8: financial conditions for the euro area had initially tightened in response to the war

column1: Ms Schnabel concluded by summarising how the rise of tokenised financial markets might affect market functioning and monetary policy implementation. Tokenised finance had expanded rapidly over recent years and was concentrated in three segments: stablecoins
column2: decentralised finance and tokenised traditional assets
column3: with stablecoins dominating. Broader adoption of tokenised finance would take time
column4: as it was being held back by regulatory and structural barriers. From a central bank perspective
column5: the fragmentation of liquidity remained a key concern in relation to tokenised financial markets. On the positive side
column6: tokenisation was expected to give rise to significant efficiency gains
column7: for example by reducing the cost of bond issuance and post-trade processing and by mitigating settlement risk through near-instantaneous settlement of transactions. Given the fast evolution of tokenisation
column8: it was important to foster these developments through the Eurosystem’s own innovation activities
column9: especially in the context of the ongoing Pontes and Appia projects.

column3: pushing up inflation and weighing on economic sentiment. The implications of the war for medium-term inflation and economic activity would depend on the intensity and duration of the energy price shock and the scale of its indirect and second-round effects.
